article:
The gang murder and the women who went to the White House looking for answers

Robert McCartney's sisters from left, Catherine, Donna, Paula, Claire and Gemma with his partner Bridgeen Hagans (seated, centre) have long campaigned for justice over his murder

It is a Sunday night in the pub.

There is football on the TV and people packed around the bar - then suddenly, violence erupts.

Bottles are smashed and broken glass is slashed across the throat of one of the biggest men in the bar.

The melee spills out into the street, where the injured man says out loud the name of the man he believes attacked him.

There is, he says later, an immediate reaction with hostile men in the crowd around him saying: "You're getting it, you're getting it."

A knife flashes and two friends are left bleeding heavily on the pavement.

One of them is dying.

Robert McCartney, an engaged father-of-two, took no part in the violence, according to the few available accounts of what happened that night in January 2005.

But the 33-year-old ended up losing his life, and no one has ever been held to account for his murder – an outcome that reverberated across the world and is now the subject of a documentary series, Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice.

Robert McCartney was engaged when he was killed in January 2005

The failure to secure convictions can be linked to the organisation which exercised power over many of those present.

Even while Robert McCartney was being treated by paramedics on the street, his killers' tracks were being covered.

Back in Magennis's bar, right behind the Royal Courts of Justice in central Belfast, the pub's CCTV tape was snatched and the bar was cleaned with bleach.

"It wasn't their first rodeo," said David Lowans, a former Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) detective who worked on the case.

"They were experienced in clearing themselves forensically."

The bar was a popular venue in central Belfast, which backed on to a series of smaller streets

The series, made by BBC Northern Ireland in association with Irish broadcaster RTÉ, obtained crime scene video and photos showing the aftermath of the incident.

The clean-up wasn't complete and police were able to find some blood stains in parts of the bar.

But substantial evidence seemed to have gone.

The knife used in the murder was never found and reportedly destroyed.

Crucially, witnesses appear to have been silenced .

"Out of the 70 people who were in the bar, we got no information from anybody to say the detail of what happened," said Lowans.

"We either got: 'I was in the toilet' or 'I didn't see anything', which is unbelievable.

"Whenever this altercation took place there were lots of people there."

David Lowans was a PSNI detective for more than 15 years

In the days after the murder, Robert's five grieving sisters and his devastated fiancée, Bridgeen Hagans, had even less information about the murder than the police.

"We were still completely in the dark as to what had happened," said his sister Paula McCartney.

"Didn't know where it had happened, how it had happened, who'd done it. Nothing."

But they soon began to hear rumours.

"It was just people coming in and telling what they'd heard in the street and 'such and such was in the bar that night'," said another sister, Catherine McCartney.

"All the talk about who'd done it, who was involved."

The information they were receiving explained why some witnesses weren't talking.

The killers were said to be members of the Provisional IRA.

Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice: Part 1 - An Innocent Man

25 October 2026

Stabbed on the street, Robert McCartney dies hours later. Evidence has vanished. Witnesses are frightened, and the police aren’t the only organisation trying to talk to them.

The IRA had waged a campaign of violence for 30 years.

In 2005, as Northern Ireland's peace process was being cemented, the group was observing a ceasefire.

It issued a statement denying involvement in McCartney's murder, but that didn't convince witnesses who feared deadly consequences if they named IRA members to the police.

Robert McCartney and another man were attacked in Market Street after leaving the bar

"I've been about these areas enough to know how dangerous this organisation can be when they want to be," said Ed Gowdy.

He was McCartney's friend and one of the witnesses telling his story on television for the first time.

"I do know exactly the treatment informers get throughout the years.

"If I tell what happened, am I an informer?

"My mate's dead, heartbreaking. But I had to survive what had happened here."

Gowdy was one of several witnesses who were then questioned by the IRA, conducting its own secret investigation running parallel to police inquiries.

Another witness, who was also interrogated by the IRA, gives for the first time on TV a personal account of what happened in the bar.

The McCartney sisters, meanwhile, found themselves fronting a campaign for justice that increasingly drew attention to the case.

All five sisters were interviewed for the series.

"It was my brother, and I just felt the world needs to know... what has happened to him," said Paula.

Catherine (left) and Paula McCartney, speaking at a press conference in Belfast in January 2006

"I think [it was] the way we came across on TV, down to earth, working-class women, standing up for justice," said Gemma McCartney, the eldest sister.

"And doing something, breaking away from the old custom of not reporting these things to the police."

Their campaign produced some extraordinary results, forcing the IRA to acknowledge several of its members were involved in the murder – though it said the killing was not done on behalf of the IRA.

The IRA said three members were expelled from the organisation. It even claimed it offered to kill them – although the McCartney sisters say that offer was never made.

(L-R) Bridgeen Hagans, the partner of Robert McCartney, walks with his sisters; Donna, Paula, Claire, Gemma, and Catherine outside the White House

The sisters' campaign caught the attention of America's then Special Envoy to Northern Ireland, Mitchell Reiss.

He recognised an opportunity to put pressure on the IRA to make moves that would complete the peace process.

"Our feeling was that if the McCartney family was willing, and it didn't seem exploitative, that they would be a very attractive poster for the criminality, the vigilantism, the injustice, the rough justice that was taking place across republican communities by the IRA," he said.

Just two months after Robert McCartney's murder, the sisters and his fiancée Bridgeen were invited to the White House for St Patrick's Day, where they met the then President George W Bush.

President Bush said he hoped the campaign would bring peace to Northern Ireland

Northern Ireland politicians were kept out of the event, an exclusion that was widely interpreted as being aimed mainly at the IRA's allies in Sinn Féin.

Mitchell Reiss tells the documentary series that advances which followed in the peace process – including the IRA's announcement of an end to its armed campaign – were "a direct consequence" of the McCartneys' campaign.

In a statement, then Sinn Féin president Gerry Adams credits negotiations and amendments to policing and justice arrangements as key drivers in completing the peace process.

Mitchell Reiss served as US special envoy to Northern Ireland from 2003 to 2007

In the aftermath of those advances, the intense attention on the McCartney sisters' campaign began to fade.

But, as the documentary shows, their pursuit of justice was not over.

In 2008, three men were brought to trial and acquitted.

Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice uses original court material to bring two key witnesses and the McCartney sisters back over the dramatic evidence from that trial.

All episodes of Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice will be available on the BBC iPlayer on Sunday 25 October.

The series will begin on BBC One Northern Ireland that evening at 22.30 GMT.

article:
Pupils pen special song to give classmates a voice

Gemma she said that she wanted people to be more aware that not everyone communicates the same way

It is a special song for young people who struggle to speak.

Many pupils at Mitchell House Special School in east Belfast are non-verbal but that does not mean they cannot communicate.

And to get that message across they have written and recorded a song called My Voice.

It aims to educate people about alternative communication like Makaton, eye gaze and electronic devices and those who use them.

The lyrics and music to My Voice were written by the "Moon" Class in Mitchell House School, made up of pupils from 11 to 13 years-old.

"Sometimes my voice is confident, sometimes my voice is calm, sometimes I use my talker, to tell you who I am," one of the verses goes.

Katie-Louise said the class are celebrating how they all communicate differently

Gemma,12, was one of those behind the song and she said that she wanted people to be more aware that not everyone communicates the same way.

"The meaning of the song is that we wanted to tell you that no matter how you use your voice, it's still important and that's really the school motto that we wanted to embody," she said.

"And it's really important to me personally being friends with a lot of people who are non-verbal that people understand that they're not actually non-verbal.

"It's people who don't understand them that think they're non-verbal."

Caelainn is the school's deputy head pupil

Katie-Louise, 11, used an electronic communication device to take part.

"We're celebrating how we all communicate differently," she told BBC News NI.

"This month we wrote a song with our teacher Miss Ryan to show how we all communicate differently and that our voices matter."

Matthew operates an electronic communication device with his eyes

The school's deputy head pupil Matthew uses eye gaze to communicate with his friend, the head pupil Caelainn.

Eye gaze lets people operate a computer or tablet to communicate using their eye movement, or communicate with the use of cards as visual cues.

"Matthew usually uses cards for yes or no questions," Caelainn said.

But Matthew also operates an electronic communication device with his eyes.

"So if Matthew looks whatever way it picks up on his eye," Caelainn explained.

"It's been a privilege to be here for 16 years, it's been amazing and all the kids are amazing, they're so friendly, they're so respectful to people and they're good with other people's needs."

Principal of Mitchell House Miriam Donnan said that they were proud to share the different ways their pupils communicated

Due to its work, Mitchell House has been accredited as a Communication Friendly Setting by Elklan, a UK-wide organisation supporting children's speech, language and communication.

It is one of only two schools in Northern Ireland to achieve the accreditation for its work using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC).

Principal Miriam Donnan said that they were proud to share the different ways their pupils communicated.

"We want to tell the world that communication is not just about speech," she said.

"We work really closely with our speech and language therapy department here in school to really promote lots of different ways of communicating and we wanted to celebrate that and share that with everybody.

"So the class themselves came up with the idea for the song and the words are all their own that they came up with their teacher Miss Ryan and it's really a lovely celebration of everybody's voice matters."

And Gemma wants everyone to know that sometimes a little patience and consideration might be required.

"It's really important that people understand that you have to take time and be patient to understand how other people communicate," she said.

article:
Monk on Caldey Island gave naked photos of himself to visitors

Brother Titus denies sexually assaulting a visitor, who says he also gave her naked photos of himself

A woman has spoken out for the first time about an alleged sexual assault by a monk who lived on a private island off the coast of west Wales.

Brother Titus Keet, 78, has also been accused of sexually harassing and sexually assaulting a former Caldey Island employee as well as giving women naked photos of himself.

He denied the allegations saying "a woman who feels rejected can become very vicious" and said the pictures were not sexual, but he would reflect on his behaviour.

The claims, revealed in a new BBC podcast Dark Island , were investigated by Dyfed-Powys Police but there was no further action.

Caldey Island is off the coast of Tenby, Pembrokeshire, and is owned by a group of Cistercian monks.

Single mum Natalie Roberts was a regular visitor from the early 2000s and would spend holidays there with her two sons.

She told the Dark Island podcast that Keet would give her photos of himself posing naked on beaches on Caldey, often accompanied by a poem.

He shared photos with other women too.

In Detail: Dark Island

An island of dreams for some, a place to hide for others. Investigative journalist India Pollock uncovers the disturbing secrets beneath the tranquil image of Caldey Island.

In 2016, Natalie went for a walk from Caldey to nearby St Margaret's Island with her sons and a friend.

She did not know Keet would be there.

The walk is quite dangerous and you have to scramble across slippery rocks to get from one island to the other.

Natalie claims it was then, when Keet was walking behind her, he repeatedly sexually assaulted her over her clothes.

She said she was horrified, adding: "I was so angry because I knew this was an absolute violation.

"You know, this wasn't spiritual. This was his opportunity just to do that."

Brother Titus Keet would take naked photos of himself at different places around Caldey Island

She said she was stunned but did not say anything to Keet because she thought he would deny it and she might be asked to leave the island.

Natalie said: "I think the worst thing it did, if I'm completely honest, it took away my whole spiritual belief in Catholicism."

But Keet claimed she turned "wickedly against him" after he rejected her attempts to seduce him.

It is also claimed Keet made several unwelcome sexual advances towards an employee of the abbey.

Allegedly, he touched her breasts and bottom, commented on her body and referred to her genitals, despite being asked not to.

Other allegations included making sexualised comments while showing nude photos of himself and pictures of naked women.

It is claimed Keet was confronted at the time but said UK law did not apply to him as he was a Dutch citizen, that he could do as he liked as he was on a private island and allegedly, he called the employee "too sensitive".

He is also accused of saying the woman was lucky to receive sexual attention from him and "women welcomed male attention".

It is also claimed the monk told her she would lose her job if she complained.

Keet said the allegations were false and quoted The Bible in his statement to the podcast: "To all who are pure themselves, everything is pure; but to those who have been corrupted and lack faith, nothing can be pure [Letter to Titus 1,15]."

He said the employee had made up the allegations in the hope the monastery would pay her money and that she was paid to "keep quiet".

"If it was not so sad, it would be laughable, how she could make up so many allegations spread out over three years, in which we had co-operated so pleasantly together. Very sad," he added.

Brother Titus Keet would write letters or poems to accompany his naked photographs

In response to the allegation from Natalie, he said: "This is a classic example of a woman who felt frustrated in her advances, disappointed in her expectations, feeling rejected and then turns against the other in a very vicious way."

Natalie denied that claim and said he was in a position of "significant power" and she was in a position of vulnerability.

She added he used victim-blaming language and had attempted to discredit her.

The abbot of Caldey Abbey, Father Jan Rossey, said they referred complaints in line with their safeguarding procedures.

He said in 2024, Keet was "required to leave" Caldey Island and will not be allowed back.

This was years after the employee made a complaint of sexual assault.

Keet has moved to another monastery.

About 50,000 day trippers catch the boat from the popular seaside resort of Tenby to visit Caldey island every year.

It is owned by the order of monks that live there, and is only 1.5 miles (2.4km) long and a mile (1.6km) wide.

Visitors who stay overnight can do so in the guesthouse or other properties the monks own.

There are also about 30 lay people who live there.

Caldey Abbey has been home to Cistercian monks since a group moved from Scourmont Abbey in Belgium in 1929

Caldey Island was once known for being "crime free", but in 2017, six women settled a civil claim against the abbey .

They had been sexually abused as children by the monk Thaddeus Kotik .

The former abbot Robert O'Brien knew about the abuse but did not report it.

An independent review, published in 2024, found that victims were treated in a heartless, hostile and cruel way.

It said frequent allegations of abuse were made, but not followed up on or reported to police, and the lack of challenge had enabled Kotik to abuse children over four decades "in plain sight".

Other offenders have also stayed on the island, including a man who was wanted by police and lived under an alias for seven years before being jailed for 30 months for possessing child abuse images.

The abuse by Kotik was investigated by the police in 2014 and 2017, but officers concluded there was little they could do as he died in 1992.

However, a former head of crime for the force has called for a renewed investigation into the abuse by Kotik, which could also look at how three other offenders - Paul Ashton, John Cronin and John Shannon - came to stay on the island.

Steve Wilkins, who led the operation behind the conviction of serial killer John Cooper, said: "Was the magnet that drew them there that they could go and hide in plain sight?

"They could continue their offending with little chance of it being reported to the authorities."

Dyfed-Powys Police said it had followed all appropriate lines of enquiry and there were no ongoing investigations.

Rossey apologised and acknowledged child abuse was previously ignored.

He said it was deeply concerning people felt unable to speak up or feared exclusion if they raised concerns.

He said things had changed on the island, that new safeguarding measures had been introduced including a committee with police, council staff and a survivor of abuse.

People who live and work on the island must now have criminal record checks, original ID and have interviews with the abbot and island manager.

He said the abbey was committed to openness, listening to those harmed and learning from past failures.

He said all recommendations from an independent review into abuse on the island had been implemented.

Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy

Green leader Zack Polanski has faced criticism over his response to the Zionism motion

Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.

The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.

Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.

But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.

The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.

These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.

The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.

In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.

In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.

But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.

In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.

Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.

The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.

Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.

Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.

Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.

The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.

The "Zionism is racism" motion was passed by members of the Green Party of England and Wales at its annual conference in Brighton last month.

The policy motion adopted by members said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.

It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.

Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.

Labour councillors require the approval of the party's NEC before entering into local tie-ups.

According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power-sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.

By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.

"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic."

Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water

This video can not be played

'Be prepared': PM Andy Burnham suggests stocking up on basic food items

The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.

With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."

At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box , external would include a bottle of wine.

She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."

Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.

"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."

Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit.

The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates.

The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents.

Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis.

He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time".

He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet."

Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time".

She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things.

"Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming."

'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber-security scramble

This video can not be played

How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?

Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".

Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks".

Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse.

"It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd.

He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites.

"The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said.

"Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem."

PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites.

But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline.

Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems.

In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP.

"Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said.

He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action.

Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts.

"Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said.

"But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene."

The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it.

Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday.

"It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said.

The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks.

But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real.

"We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card.

He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating.

"This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said.

He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose.

As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help.

One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it.

In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks.

It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon.

AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades.

The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking.

But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it.

"We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool.

He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose.

Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m

John Healey becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to cut red tape for businesses ahead of his first Budget

The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m.

Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.

The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs.

In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses.

"Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said.

Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses.

He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs.

The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said.

Ministers have claimed this will save almost £800m in administrative and tariff costs.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North.

Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses.

"If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said.

The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform.

Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the employment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency".

"John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said.

article:
How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race

A student at a rally for President Lula da Silva

In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.

Like many of Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.

"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.

"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

Tairine says high prices are a problem for her

"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.

One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.

Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.

Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.

Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.

For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.

But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments.

"There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.

Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father and Brazil's president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil.

But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."

Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the UN's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" in which people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.

Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.

But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending.

"Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.

In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.

In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people.

"A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."

Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.

The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.

Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.

Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected

In Maré, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.

This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in Maré, Vitoria, earns less than £300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off per week, and providing essential medicines for free.

She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.

She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.

Another resident, Andreza Dionísio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."

Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo

Increasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.

Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.

Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.

Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine".

'An IRA boss wanted me dead - my best mate was killed beside me'

Robert McCartney and Brendan Devine had been friends for more than 15 years

The survivor of a notorious knife murder that got the attention of the White House has told his story on television for the first time.

Brendan Devine's throat was slashed and he suffered a severe stab wound to the abdomen in a 2005 attack involving members of the Provisional IRA.

His friend Robert McCartney was killed. In the fallout McCartney's sisters and fiancée mounted a campaign for justice that won support from US President George W Bush and the European Parliament.

But the crime remains unsolved – and in a new BBC documentary series Devine tells of his guilt over the way the attack unfolded, and for the failure to catch the killers.

Brendan Devine was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder after his friend was killed

"I don't feel guilty for the actual happening but I do worry that my big mouth could have inflamed the situation, and got Bert killed," he said.

"It's terrible. To have to live with that and to think that you could be a reason for the death of your mate.

"That kills me."

The two men were stabbed near Market Street in Belfast city centre, after leaving Magennis's bar on 31 January 2005.

A former detective who worked on the case tells the documentary Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice that 33-year-old Robert McCartney was "as innocent as they come".

Devine had been attacked with bottles and had his throat cut inside the bar, after an argument about an alleged rude gesture.

Despite as many as 70 people being in the pub at the time, no witnesses came forward to identify the attackers.

Robert McCartney, a father of two, was planning to marry his partner Bridgeen Hagans

Pub CCTV was taken and destroyed and some forensic evidence appears to have been wiped away when the bar was cleaned with bleach.

The IRA initially denied involvement, but later issued a statement which said three of its members were involved, including two "high-ranking volunteers".

It said it had expelled them.

The murder came at a crucial time in the peace process in Northern Ireland.

The IRA was observing a ceasefire but had been accused of carrying out a series of high profile robberies, including the theft of £26.5m from the Northern Bank in Belfast.

McCartney's family launched a campaign to bring his attackers to justice.

The murder drew political attention from as far as the United States, where the sisters were invited to meet President George W Bush in Washington DC.

McCartney died after being beaten and stabbed outside the pub in Belfast city centre in January 2005

Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice tells the story of the murder and the McCartney family's campaign – revealing that Devine believes they were stabbed because he named IRA leader Gerard "Jock" Davison outside the bar.

"I says 'who's Jock Davison? Did he do this to my throat?' And as soon as I said that name, four or five guys were in front of me, and they started shouting, `you're getting it, you're getting it, you're getting it'.

"I do and have struggled with guilt of slabbering outside the bar, of shouting at Jock Davison, of inflaming an already hostile situation," he said.

Devine says intimidation and rumours surrounding the murder led to intense stress which impacted his mental health at the time.

"I had loads of death threats and it was a wee bit daunting trying to juggle all this.

"So you're hearing all this, and then even top republicans were saying to me, 'you open your mouth about anything', more or less, 'you're in trouble'."

25 October 2026

Stabbed on the street, Robert McCartney dies hours later. Evidence has vanished. Witnesses are frightened, and the police aren’t the only organisation trying to talk to them.

Davison, who was reported to be one of the most senior IRA figures in Belfast , was killed in a gun attack in Belfast in 2015.

Devine also tells the documentary series about being questioned by the IRA as they conducted a secret investigation parallel to the police inquiry.

He later testified at the 2008 trial of three men who faced charges in connection with the attack.

All three were acquitted.

Police photographs released to the BBC show suspected blood stains marked for forensic examination.

Devine told the trial that he met the IRA four times after the stabbings.

He said he only cooperated fully with the police after being given clearance by the IRA to do so.

In the witness box he also changed his account of what had happened on the night, but denied claims that was to "dovetail" with the account of another witness.

In the documentary - made by BBC Northern Ireland in association with RTÉ - Devine says he regrets that his evidence was not more helpful in establishing who carried out the attack.

"Am I going to be held responsible for not getting justice?" he asked.

"How am I going to get a result with the whole shenanigans of it?

"The whole lot. It was just a stressful time."

Parents call for tougher measures in schools to tackle allergies

Stephanie Kerr is one of a number of parents calling for new mandatory measures

For Stephanie Kerr's five-year-old son Caolán many foods come with a serious risk.

"Caolán's allergic to milk, egg, wheat, oat, cumin, tuna, strawberry," she said.

"We have a running joke that it would be quicker listing what he's not allergic to so that's just some of them."

Kerr is one of a number of parents calling for new mandatory measures in schools to keep pupils like Caolán safe.

In England, Benedict's law came into force in September, requiring all schools to follow strengthened allergy guidelines including training for staff and storing equipment like life-saving allergy pens.

It was named after Benedict Blythe, who died aged five after accidental exposure to cow's milk protein while at Barnack Primary School, near Peterborough, in December 2021.

The Education Minister, Paul Givan, has committed to a consultation on a similar change in Northern Ireland to introduce stronger allergy guidance for Northern Ireland schools.

At present though, the onus is mainly on parents and individual schools to ensure safety measures for pupils are in place.

Stephanie Kerr was one of several parents and experts in Regent House School in Newtownards on Friday training teachers about safety for pupils with severe allergies.

And that meant confronting some fears.

"I find it difficult as well sometimes talking about the reactions that Caolán has had in the past and what could potentially happen in the future," she said.

But she was not alone.

Niamh Kennedy's three children have allergies

Niamh Kennedy has three children who have food allergies and she is the chair of Food Allergy NI, the voluntary group who organised the training.

"Our eldest is the most severe. He's had anaphylaxis in the past," she said.

"We're very reliant here at the moment on goodwill, individual school policies and individual awareness so it's very much left to up to the school to initiate and to design what works for them.

"But the problem with that is that there's huge variation."

She estimates that about two children in every class could have a food allergy and said that, aside from school canteens and packed lunches, risks could lurk in expected places.

"One of the things that we experience as a campaigning group is that most people understand that food allergies need to be considered at mealtimes, but it can be the other moments in the day that can sort of be underestimated," she said.

"Things like making cakes or buns or using crafts.

"There can be quite a lot of allergens in some of the craft materials, there can be allergens in simple things like hand soaps.

"This is a potentially life-threatening medical condition."

Tracey Dunn said some of the most common foods that can trigger anaphylaxis are milk, fish and eggs

That point was reinforced by Tracey Dunn, from the Allergy UK incorporating Anaphylaxis UK organisation, who also spoke to teachers at Regent House School.

"Anaphylaxis is the most serious form of an allergic reaction that can be fatal," she said.

"During anaphylaxis the airways are closing and blood pressure is dropping and that leads a person to have symptoms where they are unable to breathe or have noisy breathing or they develop a persistent cough where their voice changes.

"But they can also have, related to the blood pressure, circulatory difficulties where they feel cold, pale clammy or they may feel faint, dizzy."

While most people may be aware of nut allergies or the risk of shock from insect stings, other common foods can also pose a risk to some people.

"Some of the most common foods that can trigger anaphylaxis are things like milk and fish and eggs," Dunn said.

The consultation on changes to how pupils with severe allergies are supported in schools in Northern Ireland is due to take place before the end of 2026.

Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron homes

More than 200 families have been displaced, Palestinian officials say

The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.

Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.

The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.

Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.

He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.

Wreckage was seen around the site of Friday's shooting following demolitions by Israeli forces

Bulldozers began demolitions on Friday afternoon

Photos of one of the suspected gunmen in Friday's attack were shared by AFP news agency

1 of 3

It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.

Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.

Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.

Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene.

"We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said.

He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.

In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.

In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.

Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.

Speaking to journalists, Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test

Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test

Giving the north of England a crack at hosting the globe's biggest sports event might seem about as Brand Burnham as it gets.

Seven million pounds of taxpayers' cash is a teeny drop in the context of the overall Budget, to pay for the government to take a closer look at possible plans. But the idea is sure to get tongues wagging - and headline writers scribbling.

A "Northern Games" in 2040 or beyond just might create a massive sense of national feel-good, jobs and development, as the Olympics in east London did more than a decade ago.

But it's a promise of a possibility at least a decade away. And what could be more in tune with the Manchester-loving prime minister and his proud Yorkshireman chancellor than a sporting plan fixed firmly on the top geographical chunk of the country?

Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget

It's Brand Burnham alright, popular with most of the Labour backbenches, just add the Twiglets and the pint in the stands.

The prime minister and his team are proud of a distinct feature of their government so far, focusing on small things that might make a big difference: fines for blaring out music on your phone on the bus, cracking down on "rip-off" parking charges, investing a small amount of cash in a big ambition for a sporting event in future.

It's what some ministers call "the politics of trying" – putting time and effort into ideas that you don't pretend are revolutionary, but give direction, and a sense of sympathy to the public.

It's an echo, deliberate or not, of another Labour Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, who sent memos to his cabinet in 1974 demanding "little things that mean a lot".

He ended up with a list of plans including nationalising small breweries to stop them being gulped up by big firms (paging Andy Burnham), freezing phone installation charges for pensioners, and plans for empty office blocks.

But the next few days could bring an end to that "politics of trying" phase, with one senior official describing the coming Budget as "the first proper moment for the government, which will then be in the pipeline for the 10-year plan, then a very difficult spending review".

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

An influential Labour MP told me: "The Budget has to be the beginning of the future story."

A fancy way of saying, beyond the short-term announcements and clear long-term aspirations, what is this government actually going to do?

"Steady as she goes," is what one well-connected senior MP predicts, and how expectations of the Budget are being managed across Westminster. They tell me: "Not doing a lot might be more reassuring to people than promising the earth with whose money?"

The boss of one well-known high street business told me they are even hoping there won't be any big bazookas. "Just do no harm," they implored the Chancellor John Healey.

"The hole is too big that they are trying to fill, so my view is don't try and do anything big to help because you don't have the money, but don't do anything to harm us either."

After all, the chancellor is bound by Labour's manifesto promises not to fiddle with the main taxes – income tax, VAT, National Insurance for workers. And you don't need me to remind you that public spending, borrowing and tax are all at historic highs.

Chuck in prices jacking up again because of war in the Middle East and there isn't much money to spray around. In fact, some big cuts to public spending are already pencilled in for the later years of this parliament.

The chancellor and prime minister face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending

But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions.

And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again.

John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'."

Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly.

One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy.

They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day."

Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party.

MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs.

One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see backbenchers.

It's paying off in the mood among MPs. One told me: "You're not feeling like the only way you can ever have a chat with a minister is by arranging an appointment for three months down the line – the soft touches really matter."

Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October

A party that feels the boss has their back is more likely to be receptive to hard decisions, that's simple psychology, and guess what? Politicians are humans too.

But the equilibrium is fragile. One source involved in the Budget prep told me the government "is like a seesaw".

"It's John and James on the right (Healey and Purnell, Burnham's chief of staff), Lou (Haigh) on the left, and Andy balancing it in the middle," adding that "Andy is not as on the left as many of his supporters want to believe".

That balance could be more strained in the coming weeks as choices over immigration and welfare reform loom after the Budget. And how the numbers stack up on Wednesday matters intensely too.

The Labour left will be looking keenly to see if people who are really struggling financially receive meaningful support.

Those on the right will be scouring the statement for measures that display a tight control on spending and help businesses grow. Even small moves could upset the seesaw.

One former minister doubts there will be anything major enough to upset the delicate balance, not because of an abundance of caution but they suggest, "John has been struggling a bit - he hasn't gone into this with a philosophical direction".

There is also a risk that by deferring big decisions until the Spending Review next year - which sets out longer-term spending than an annual budget - it looks like the government is just putting off the hard stuff.

Another acknowledges the danger of looking like it's a budget on the never-never, delaying decisions on "welfare, defence and social care – Andy goes in with political stock quite high – he needs to spend it on difficult stuff and there isn't much sign of it yet".

In an interview with The Times, Andy Haldane, a former chief economist at the Bank of England and an ally of Burnham, said he feared the government would deliver a "mañana budget" that deferred difficult decisions on public spending and "doesn't speak to the urgency of now".

With friends like these…

The former mayor of Greater Manchester became the UK's fourth prime minister in five years and the seventh since 2016

It's a good bet that the opposition parties will pile in on this angle, accusing Healey and Burnham of ignoring the long-term pressures next week. One prominent opposition politician said: "This Budget can only be postponing, you have to assume that's cynical because you are going to have an early election, or you are storing up a car crash for next year (the Spending Review)."

Downing Street sources counter that argument with Burnham's decision to unpick the expensive triple lock to pay, at least in part, for future social care. Or his bolder approach to potentially ask to re-enter the EU, or certainly pursue much closer ties.

And remember that list of small things that could make a big difference? They have made political decisions that the polls suggest voters have noticed.

Even some of Burnham's backers admit quietly that he is aware his first job in office was clear: to show action, to cheer up his party, and that seems to have had a positive effect in the polls.

His long-term view of the UK he wants is well known – with devolution, a national care service, and greater public involvement in the economy.

But the middle bit?

One official says: "Unless the prime minister has said something quite specific about something everyone is scrambling around trying to work out what he wants to do."

Another well-connected source says: "The challenge has always been with this project, how do people feel in the medium term – it's huge."

​​Burnham and his chancellor's start in office has been broadly successful if you look at the polling, or read the mood inside the Labour party.

Their dreams of future glories, long-term plans and policies, and gold medals on UK soil could point ahead to many years time.

But neither deal with the issues that need to be confronted in the middle.

The chancellor was working late in his Downing Street flat last night, finishing off his plans after having fish pie for tea, conscious his first Budget starts the between times - and they're almost here.

UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says

The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.

There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.

But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaí (Irish police) have said.

Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month .

A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.

On Saturday, gardaí said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.

A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.

The rise of new black spaces in music

African diaspora is finding new audiences in a city celebrated for its musical heritage

A new sound is taking Bristol's dancefloors by storm.

Driven by rolling log drums, syncopated rhythms and infectious melodies, amapiano and other electronic sounds from across the African diaspora are finding new audiences in a city celebrated for its musical heritage.

Behind these parties is a new generation of black promoters passionate about creating spaces where black people can hear their music, celebrate their cultures and feel like they belong.

But for some, building these spaces has also meant confronting the familiar challenge of finding spaces where black music and the communities around it are welcomed and not feared.

Unkle Mykel started hosting events to connect to different cultures

Bristol-based promoter Unkle Mykel's journey into events began in his own back garden after he moved to Bristol in 2017.

What started as garden barbecues gradually grew into a way of bringing people together, particularly members of Bristol's black, Asian and minority ethnic communities.

"It's about celebrating our cultures, bringing people into that fold and connecting," says the 32-year-old, who hosts Bristol Barbecue Family and The Aux Social.

Originally from Kenya, Mykel moved to the UK in 2005. Since then, he has witnessed changes in the visibility of African music.

"There was no Afrobeats on the airwaves," he laughs, recalling his early years in the country, when he says Caribbean reggae, dancehall and soca were more prominent in the musical landscape he encountered.

Now, he sees the growing popularity of genres such as amapiano - a popular South African house music subgenre - as an opportunity to broaden the scene.

"We don't need to pretend to be nobody else, we're just us. It just took a while to get there."

DJ and promoter Khiah Lou runs amapiano event called Khaya Nights

For 30-year-old DJ and promoter Khiah Lou, representation, she says, is central to her work.

Last year she launched Khaya Nights, an event dedicated to amapiano and other African Caribbean electronic dance music.

Having performed internationally, she had seen how other cities had developed a wider range of events celebrating these sounds. Bristol, she felt, was lagging behind.

Rather than wait for the scene to develop, Khiah decided to help build it herself.

"If we don't do it, who else is going to do it?" she says.

"Young black people are starting to make a way for themselves because I don't think we have a choice."

Khiah says these nights provide a place where people can connect with their identities and see their cultures reflected in the city around them.

"At first it seems like it's just a party, but it's so much more than that," she says.

"It's really important for your own self-identity. If your community doesn't have events, where do you feel you can go?"

"At first it seems like just a party, but it's so much more than that,' says Khiah

Tazmin Samuels, who DJs as Azumei, shares those concerns about representation.

As part of Rushtown, a black-led music collective, Tazmin wants to champion sounds and subcultures from across Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean.

"My main motivation for getting together with people and starting Rushtown came from seeing the lack of representation of black music that black people are currently listening to within the city," says Tazmin.

She sees encouraging signs, with more black music-focused brands emerging in Bristol. But she believes the wider music industry has yet to recognise the value of what these promoters are building.

Tazmin says the wider music industry must recognise the value of black promoters

But creating these spaces is not always straightforward.

Khiah says she has struggled to find venues willing to host nights aimed at black audiences. Although she considers Bristol an inclusive city, her experience as a promoter has revealed a different side of its nightlife.

"I've had some venue owners straight up tell me they're worried about having a black event," she says.

"I feel like black crowds are kind of met with fear, and that's really disheartening."

Mykel describes similar tensions, saying that some venues are enthusiastic about hosting his events, only to face objections from people in the surrounding community.

The Bamboo Club opened in 1966 as a social hub for Bristol's Caribbean community

The young promoters' experiences echo a much longer history of black Bristolians having to create their own spaces for music and social life.

Many black people were turned away from existing clubs and bars in Bristol during the 1960s, which led to the creation of "blues parties", un-licensed house parties where people danced to genres such as ska, reggae and rocksteady.

In 1966, Tony Bullimore and his Jamaican-born wife Lalel, opened the Bamboo Club, which served as a cultural lifeline for the city's Caribbean community.

Glen Crooks, 70, who used to perform at the Bamboo Club when he was younger, remembers "sneaking in" with his friends when they were young.

"It was the only place that we could have," he recalls.

"Especially all the Caribbean people could go and really have a good time."

Rushtown aims to champion a variety of music genres from the African diaspora

Marti Burgess, who has been a co-owner of the nightclub Lakota since 1994, says although attitudes have changed over the years, some prejudices remain.

"There is a long history of treating a predominantly black audience as a concern, rather than recognising the audience, creativity and business that a promoter is bringing," she says.

"They should not have to keep proving that black audiences are welcome or commercially worthwhile."

Growing up, Marti was surrounded by music. Her parents went to the blues clubs and attended the Bamboo Club when it hosted artists such as Bob Marley, Desmond Dekker and Johnny Nash.

"It was through listening to the adults' conversations that I came to understand how much those spaces had grown out of exclusion from mainstream venues," she says.

"Creating somewhere of their own was both a necessity and a source of joy."

Lakota has expanded its programme to include genres including amapiano and Afrobeats

" St Pauls Carnival was hugely important for those of us growing up in the 1970s and 80s, and for our developing identities as Black British people."

Lakota is predominantly known to be a bass music venue, but over the years it has broadened its programme to include Afrobeats and amapiano events.

"Latino Fest this summer opened our eyes further to the audiences and musical communities we could welcome," says Marti.

"We want people across the different genres of black music to see Lakota as a venue that is open to them, where they can bring their music and their audiences."
