How a California mansion filled with surrogate children became a 'House of Horrors'

Silvia Zhang (left) and Guojun Xuan were charged with conspiracy to commit child abuse.

In May 2025, a two-month-old baby named Walter was taken to hospital in the affluent Californian suburb of Arcadia, with a head injury. A woman who claimed to be his mother said the baby had accidentally fallen from bed per police report. But something did not seem right to the doctor, who said Walter's condition felt more similar to injuries sustained during a car accident or from being shaken.

Suspecting child abuse, police searched the stately mansion where Walter lived and briefly detained his parents, Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39. Prosecutors said what they found "could only be described as a house of horrors"- a camera-laced labyrinth with 14 surrogate children aged between six months and three, who they say faced beatings on a daily basis.

The address of the mansion, the authorities later discovered, was also registered to a surrogacy agency run by the couple and used by them to recruit multiple surrogates.

In October this year, the couple was arrested again and charged with conspiracy to commit child abuse. They deny the charges and remain in custody. The bond is set at $20m (£15m) each. If convicted, Xuan faces up to 17 years and four months in prison, while Zhang could face up to 11 years and eight months.

The couple moved into the Arcadia mansion in April 2021. Online listings show that the 10,000 sq ft (929 sq m) mansion sold for $3.3m (£2.48m) that same year. It features nine bedrooms, 11 bathrooms, and a heated pool.

This wealthy suburb on the east side of Los Angeles has been dubbed the "Chinese Beverly Hills" by local media. Almost 60% of its population was recorded as Asian in the most recent US Census and predominantly Chinese. Household incomes there are well above those of most US families.

Xuan and Zhang's 10,000-sq-ft mansion in the affluent suburb of Arcadia, California had motion-activated cameras installed throughout, prosecutors say.

"This house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredibly young children that had been brought to this house through this surrogacy process," LA County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said at a press conference in October following the charges.

Thirty-two cameras were set up in the mansion, according to the complaint. Young children often spent hours sitting by the desks, footage showed. One room had no camera, but other cameras captured video of nannies carrying these children into that room, and children could then be heard screaming from inside.

Prosecutors claimed that baby Walter's injuries were caused by one of the nannies, Chunmei Li, and have charged her with child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Li remains on the run and has not been arrested.

The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News, BBC's news partner in the US, reported.

Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.

"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.

The United States has become one of the world's leading destinations for surrogacy, which is when a woman carries someone else's child to term. A 2024 study of US surrogacy data found that nearly one-third of intended parents between 2014 and 2020 came from outside the country. China, where surrogacy is banned, was the single largest source of international clients, accounting for roughly 42% of foreign intended parents.

The United States offers assisted reproductive technological services that many people from China cannot easily access at home. Single women and LGBTQ individuals often face barriers to IVF and egg freezing. There are also couples who were limited by China's decades-long One-Child Policy and, by the time it ended in 2016, were physically challenged to carry a baby themselves, prompting some to turn to surrogacy abroad.

To surrogates who carried babies for Xuan and Zhang, their request to have a surrogate baby did not raise much suspicion at first, court documents reveal. Several surrogates were hired through an agency named "Mark Surrogacy". While an agency is often seen as an independent third party, Mark Surrogacy, it turns out, was run by the couple - a fact that was not always disclosed, according to two lawsuits filed against the couple by some of their surrogates.

Silvia Zhang was named the manager for Mark Surrogacy in a corporate registration record, and their Arcadia mansion is listed as the company's address in that same document. During the hearing on 16 October, Deputy District Attorney MacKenzie Cameron Teymouri also told the judge that there is not a single other-intended parent that was ever matched with a surrogate through the surrogacy agency that Xuan and Zhang ran out of their home.

One of the surrogates, Tronderrica James, sued the couple in 2025 for damages including fraud and intentional misrepresentation. She alleged that Zhang did not disclose her ties with Mark Surrogacy during the initial stage, and that she would not have proceeded had she known the true nature of the arrangement. James did not respond to the BBC's request for interview.

The defendants later filed a motion to dismiss the case, arguing the woman had no sufficient basis for a lawsuit. The case is still pending.

Another five women, Stacy Raelyn King, Evelyn Senolos Areja, Kayla Elliott, Hallie Hernandez, and Vanity McGoveran, alleged similar experiences in a separate lawsuit filed in August against Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang. The suit alleged Zhang failed to disclose her and Xuan's connections to the agency, and also the actual number of children they have had.

"Each Plaintiff was led to believe she was the only woman carrying for the couple, and that she was helping a family conceive a single, cherished child," their complaint alleged.

The couple had also used another outside surrogacy agency - California-based Babytree Surrogacy. Patrick Yu, Babytree's founder, told the BBC they were approached by Xuan in 2018.

Yu told the BBC that he was told by Xuan that he wanted to have a big family. They helped Xuan match with several women who delivered at least four babies.

"When we saw the news reports that he was under investigation, that was when I first realised he had so many children. We immediately stopped working with him," said Yu.

One of the women he helped matched in 2024, however, was already pregnant when news about Walter's injuries broke out in May last year. The authorities had placed their 21 children under protective custody while police investigated alleged child abuse.

Yu told the BBC he arranged a meeting for the couple and the then-newly pregnant surrogate. He described that the couple sounded very confident, reassuring the surrogate mother that they treat the children well. The woman decided to continue the journey and gave birth to a baby in early 2026.

There is no legal limit to the number of surrogacies an intended parent can request, neither is there any requirement to disclose such information, according to Dr Liang Yu, Vice Chair of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine's Chinese Special Interest Group and Program Director of Reproductive Clinical Science at Old Dominion University.

Liang said that certain banks or agencies might have their own requirements, but it was not required by law. And a couple might also work with several different agencies at the same time without fully disclosing all of their information to each agency.

"This creates a grey area in the law and in industry regulations."

Liang added that within that grey area she has seen many examples involving wealthy clients, not just Chinese ones. But because of privacy protections and confidentiality agreements signed with doctors and fertility clinics, most are not known to the public.

"In other words, this kind of behaviour (like Xuan) is not unprecedented."

The BBC approached the lawyers representing Xuan and Zhang about the allegations. Mitchell Krems - who represents both - did not respond. Matt Koohanim, who represents Zhang, said the case would be addressed through appropriate legal channels.

At a hearing on October 16th, Teymouri told the judge that their financial net worth substantially exceeded $100m (£75m) in 2025.

Teymouri added that found three passports for Xuan were found - Mexican, Chinese, and one from the US.

Xuan was born in Zhejiang in eastern China in 1959 according to local Chinese media. At the age of 18, he started as an accountant in a state-owned grocery company in Urumqi. He became a deputy of the People's Congress in Urumqi in 1997, and later, a deputy for Xinjiang Autonomous Region in 2008 - a position at the provincial legislative body similar to a state representative.

His involvement in public life did not stop after he moved to the US. He became the president of 'US Xinjiang Chamber of Commerce' and vice president of "China America Federation", showing up at public events as early as 2019.

In one photograph seen by the BBC, Xuan was holding hands with former Arcadia mayor, Eileen Wang, at an event in 2022. During Wang's mayoral election campaign that year, Xuan donated $4,900 through a company under his name. Wang resigned as the mayor of Arcadia in May this year after the US Department of Justice charged her with acting as an illegal agent of China. She pleaded guilty to the felony count.

There is less known about Zhang, who worked as a real estate agent. Xuan and Zhang were never married. Zhang was married to another man whom she divorced in 2022, according to court documents.

At a hearing earlier this month, Teymouri told the judge that there are 26 children involved with this family.

Zhang kept a spreadsheet of a total of 21 children as of May 2025, according to the complaint. They have been removed to state custody. Five more were born since then, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported in January 2026.

One child born to a surrogate is still living with her surrogate mother in Virginia. Melissa Epps, a surrogate hired by the couple, was pregnant when she learned about the investigation last year and decided to keep the child.

The couple filed a lawsuit against Epps for breaching their surrogacy contract, demanding the return of the baby girl, in addition to a million dollars from Epps. Epps had no lawyers at first and had to represent herself in court, until Pamela DeCamp, attorney of the Virginia Legal Aid Society, took her case.

Epps declined an interview with the BBC. In a statement given to the BBC, her lawyer DeCamp said they were "very thankful for the efforts of the Los Angeles, California District Attorney to obtain justice for the young children".

Their case will continue until next March. The baby girl is under social service custody but currently living with Epps. She recently celebrated her first birthday.

"She remains safe and happy in Virginia. And we are confident she will continue to do so," said DeCamp.

Sharon Osbourne: 'I visit Ozzy's grave every day'

Sharon Osbourne spoke to BBC News as the family prepares to release a film about Ozzy's final concert with Black Sabbath

It's been 15 months since Ozzy Osbourne died, at the age of 76, at his home in Buckinghamshire.

Although he had suffered from health problems for years, including Parkinson's disease and a fractured vertebra, his death was a shock.

Less than three weeks beforehand, he had been on stage in Birmingham, playing a triumphant farewell concert.

After the show, he was on a high.

"He was just so, so happy," recalls his wife Sharon.

"He was online, going through the reviews and saying, 'There's something terribly wrong', and I'm like, 'Why?'

"He goes, 'I didn't get slagged by anybody. Why are people being nice to me?'

"And I'm like, 'Because they like you'."

On the morning he died, Ozzy had woken up early and gone downstairs for his usual morning workout. Shortly afterwards, he had a heart attack. An air ambulance was called and paramedics tried to save him. But it was too late.

"I was asleep," says Sharon.

"We'd spoken in the night. Ozzy had woken in the night and he asked me to kiss him twice, and I did.

"And then he said, 'Hold me, hold me tight,' and I did.

"And then the next thing I know, it's early in the morning, and someone comes rushing into the room saying, 'Come down now'.

"I ran down, and that was it."

Sharon and Ozzy Osbourne, pictured in 2017 after renewing their wedding vows

The grief, she says, will never leave.

"You've lost the love of your life, so you don't just wake up and go, 'I'm fine now. I'm cured'.

"You never get over it. But you learn to live with it, and that's what I'm trying to do. So you either sit in a room and don't come out, or you accept it, befriend it, and that's it."

The affection among Ozzy's fans was apparent before the singer's funeral. Thousands of people lined the streets of Birmingham, laying floral tributes and singing Black Sabbath songs as Ozzy's body was transported through his home city in a hearse topped by a purple floral tribute in the shape of a cross.

Sharon says he would have been mystified by the outpouring of love.

"He'd have been like, 'What's the matter with you guys? Go home!'" she says.

But for the family, the public response was a huge source of comfort.

Daughter Kelly said last year: "I never could have imagined it to be as helpful as it has been to know that we're not alone in our grief and our sadness, and that the rest of the world loved him as much as we did."

Sharon says the fans' cards and messages were all collected, sorted and photographed; while the flowers were composted for the family garden, where Ozzy is buried.

"There was no way I could put Ozzy in a public graveyard," she says.

"I've seen what happens to other people in the public eye. There's no peace because people want to come and they want to pay their respects. That's an ongoing thing, and I wanted Ozzy to rest and just be."

Does she visit him often?

"Of course, every day. I can see him from my window."

She still talks to him regularly, she says. Asked what she discusses, she puts a finger to her lips and gives a gentle "shh".

Ozzy's family - including children Jack and Kelly - stopped to read the tributes during his funeral procession last July

Ozzy and Sharon's relationship spanned more than 50 years.

They met in 1970 and married in 1982. Their time together could be turbulent - he was arrested for attempting to murder her in 1989 (she dropped the charges), and they split briefly in 2016 amid rumours of infidelity - but the couple maintained that they were soulmates.

"It was an unusual relationship because we had such highs and such terrible lows," she admits. But at the end of his life, "he knew" how much he was loved.

You can see proof of that love - from his family, his fans and his bandmates – in a new documentary about his final gig at Birmingham's Villa Park last year, when he reunited with heavy rock legends Black Sabbath.

Titled Back To The Beginning, it features more than 25 of the songs played at that star-studded concert, including Ozzy's solo set and Sabbath's entire performance.

In backstage footage, fellow A-list performers discuss the star's influence in awestruck tones.

"If there was no Sabbath, there's no Metallica," says the band's frontman James Hetfield. "It's as simple as that."

Yungblud, whose version of Changes was one of the concert's emotional high points, talks about how, as a kid who didn't fit in, Ozzy changed his life.

"The fact he was celebrated for his madness and his individuality gave me hope."

This video can not be played

Watch: Black Sabbath blast out Iron Man at final gig

Sharon says the concert was Ozzy's final wish: the one thing that would make him happy after years of deteriorating health.

But it almost never happened.

Six months before the show, Ozzy fell and fractured his vertebrae. In recovery, he caught pneumonia three times. After surgery on his back, he caught sepsis and nearly died.

Two weeks before the show, doctors urged him to call it off.

"They came to see us at the house and they said, 'You can't do this. We're advising you not to do this. Your heart's too weak'," Sharon recalls.

But the singer was determined to see it through. In the film, it's hard to believe he's so ill. Although he performs seated on a throne, his eyes are full of life and his voice is powerful. As he looks out at the crowd, he seems elated.

Backstage, Sharon admits, "the whole family was terrified". But something changed when Ozzy entered the stadium.

"He was sat in his dressing room, watching everybody on a screen performing, and he was like, 'I just can't believe they're all here'.

"It's amazing what support and love and determination can do for you, because [before the show] he was somebody that couldn't breathe. He had a lung condition. He had a heart condition. He had terrible, terrible agony from his spine. He had blood clots and he had Parkinson's.

"Some days just to even talk was an effort, let alone sing. And I don't know how he did it, but he did it.

"And you saw it in his eyes, in his face. It just made him feel like he was alive again."

Ozzy is survived by Sharon, their three children (left-right: Kelly, Aimee and Jack) and three children from his previous marriage

The effect was so galvanising that, when he came off stage, Ozzy declared he wanted to go on tour.

"He was raring to go," Sharon laughs. "He was like, 'I can do this, and the fans don't mind if I'm sat down'."

It's an incredible and rare thing, I suggest, to be able to grant your partner their last wish.

Ozzy may have suffered immense pain in his final years, but he was able to say goodbye in style.

"To quote one of his songs, he was flying high again," Sharon says.

"He was just floating for those last 17 days. It was great. It was joyous."

Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing

Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.

Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.

Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.

The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.

"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.

Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".

He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party

Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year

A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.

The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.

The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.

The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.

They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.

There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.

The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.

Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.

The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.

Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.

This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.

Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.

This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.

Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.

"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".

The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.

The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.

This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

Is 'ferritin face' a real thing - and can you really spot low iron from looks?

Lucy says she noticed changes in her skin and hair (left photo) alongside symptoms including fatigue and hair loss when her ferritin levels were low. Lighting and shadows also play a part

"Do you have ferritin face?" a young woman asks on TikTok, pointing to dark circles, washed-out skin and brittle hair, alongside before-and-after style photographs. The content creator puts these features down to her iron levels.

It is one of a growing number of videos and posts on TikTok and Instagram claiming that low ferritin - a protein which stores iron in the body - can leave visible clues on your face.

Users list pale or grey-looking skin, dark under-eye circles, dry or cracked lips, hair shedding and weak nails, while others share portraits claiming stark visual differences.

The phrase "ferritin face" has spread widely across social media, with videos attracting millions of views.

But doctors say appearance alone cannot diagnose iron deficiency.

"Ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis," said GP Dr Aziza Sesay, who is based in the West Midlands. "However, it may be a clue to tell us that something is going on."

Pale skin, hair shedding or brittle nails can accompany low iron, but can also be signs of other conditions, she told BBC News.

Your ferritin levels show how good your body's iron stores are, while haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells which carries oxygen. When haemoglobin is low, the blood cannot carry as much oxygen - a condition known as anaemia.

But iron stores can become depleted before that happens, meaning someone can be iron-deficient and have symptoms without being anaemic.

This video can not be played

Can you tell your ferritin levels from your face?

"You've got no stored iron but you're maintaining your haemoglobin. That's the big disconnect," said consultant haematologist Dr Drew Provan.

Dr Sue Pavord, also a consultant haematologist, said iron deficiency is common and often under-diagnosed in women.

UK guidelines from the British Society of Gastroenterology say ferritin below 15 micrograms per litre indicates absent iron stores, while below 30 generally indicates low iron stores.

Social media users have shared posts and videos claiming that low ferritin can cause visible changes to the face

Lucy M, 32, who posts about hair loss as @marvluceskin on Instagram and TikTok, said "ferritin face" seemed to describe changes she had noticed in herself.

In 2021 she developed heart palpitations, fatigue and hair loss. After being told her blood tests were normal and being diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, a later test showed her ferritin was 12 micrograms per litre.

Lucy said she looked "grey" and her hair had become dull and brittle.

She shared photographs with the BBC from when her ferritin was low, compared to when it had recovered, and said the difference between how she felt and looked was "night and day".

Videos about "ferritin face" often encourage viewers to look for a combination of physical signs - from dark circles and pale skin to dry lips, thinning hair and brittle nails - and compare them with their own appearance.

"You're not ugly, your ferritin is low", one creator says, pointing to the camera.

Provan said it was "impossible" to determine someone's ferritin levels from how their face looks.

People who are significantly anaemic may look pale, he explained, while fatigue can contribute to dark circles, but these visual signs are "subjective and unreliable".

In people with darker skin, changes in skin colour may be less obvious, Sesay added, meaning someone looking specifically for the signs described online could miss iron deficiency.

Doctors say appearance alone cannot tell you whether your ferritin is low, and that iron deficiency should be confirmed with a blood test

For doctors, symptoms and how someone feels are more useful than appearance.

Blood tests matter not only to confirm iron deficiency, Provan and Sesay said, but to establish the cause and guide treatment.

Both said treatment should also address the cause. Heavy periods, low dietary iron, gastrointestinal blood loss and problems absorbing iron through the gut can all play a role.

Iron deficiency is commonly treated with oral iron. Pavord said iron tablets are best taken on an empty stomach, ideally first thing in the morning, and advised avoiding tea or coffee around the time they are taken because they can inhibit iron absorption.

Iron can also be obtained naturally from foods including meat, beans, lentils, leafy green vegetables and fortified cereals.

Taking iron supplements without a diagnosis can be harmful, while self-treating could delay the investigation of an underlying problem.

Lucy said social media has nevertheless helped women take symptoms more seriously, and has given some the confidence to ask questions when something feels wrong.

"There are so many women saying, 'Oh my gosh, this is me," she said, adding that she is not a doctor and presents her content as her own experience.

For her, doing so has been empowering - giving women information with which to advocate for themselves.

Sesay called social media a "double-edged sword" - it can encourage people to seek help, but can also lead them to incorrectly diagnose themselves from a short video.

For Lucy, the useful part is not diagnosing yourself from your appearance, but knowing when something doesn't feel right, and when to ask questions.

Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement

This video can not be played

Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeat

Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.

Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.

The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.

"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.

The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.

Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.

Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost

The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."

He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".

There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."

How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić

During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.

Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous".

"We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.

An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at Slavija square in Belgrade

Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.

The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told BBC Serbian.

The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.

"This is not an ordinary election victory, this is an avalanche that has wiped out an authoritarian regime and entire political scene," said Nebojša Vladisavljević, professor of political science at the University of Belgrade.

There were now two big political groups in Serbia, and the Student List had "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years, he told BBC Serbian.

The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.

Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.

Vučić, who backed Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Vučić's contribution to relations with Russia and hoped "the new political force" in Belgrade would understand that co-operation with Moscow was in Serbia's interests: "But, as you know, it takes two to tango."

His defeat was welcomed by Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, who said he was delighted to hear from the Student List's leaders "how much strength our victory in April had given them". Magyar's party ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán rule, while Vučić's SNS party had been in power since 2012.

Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on Sunday

European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said "a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together".

Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.

This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.

In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.

The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.

Attention will now turn to who will lead the Student List as prime minister. Presidential elections are due to take place in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić currently filling the role in a caretaker capacity.

Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on Wednesday

Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.

He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.

Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.

That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.

When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.

Rosebank is the UK's largest untapped oil field

A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband.

At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse.

A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions.

Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones.

But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear.

What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible.

It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement.

Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field .

She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

Campaigners have called for the Rosebank plans to be rejected

Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics.

But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in.

Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank.

Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course.

Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it."

Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it.

Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday.

Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear.

Michael Marra will be meeting both the chancellor and the energy secretary

"I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me.

"We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in.

"You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland."

He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living.

That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly.

On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go.

But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality.

Ireland prop Furlong cited over alleged groin grab

Tadhg Furlong has been included in Ireland's squad for November's Nations Championship fixtures

Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday.

Munster back row Gavin Coombes raised the allegation against an unnamed Leinster player with match referee Andrew Brace in the closing stages of the first half at the Aviva Stadium, but television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find any video evidence at the time.

However, three-time British and Irish Lions tourist Furlong has now been cited over an act of foul play under Law 9.27, which says a "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals".

A statement from the URC said "arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course".

If found guilty of the offence, the 33-year-old would be in danger of missing Ireland's Nations Championship matches with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in Dublin, as well as the finals weekend in London.

In October 2025, South Africa front-rower Jan-Hendrik Wessels received a nine-match suspension for grabbing Josh Murphy's genitals in the Bulls' URC win over Connacht.

For that incident, Wessels was handed a 12-week suspension - the shortest ban under World Rugby rules for such an offence - that was reduced by three weeks due to his "good conduct prior to and at the hearing and good record".

If similar action was taken against Furlong, he would potentially miss Leinster's Investec Champions Cup Pool match with Sale, as well as the festive inter-provincial derbies with Ulster and Munster.

Speaking after the 24-18 defeat at the Aviva Stadium , Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said he would "back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that".

Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said he did not see the incident, which occurred in the 37th minute when Munster were leading, but acknowledged it was a "serious matter".

article:
Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global

Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global

In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.

By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.

Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.

A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.

For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.

The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.

And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.

The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.

He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.

His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.

US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.

"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.

Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.

The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.

How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić

Although it was a students' movement that won Serbia's election, no student has been elected

Theirs is a movement born from tragedy that began with students blockading streets and turned into almost daily protests and a national movement against corruption and government negligence.

In just under two years the students have succeeded in tearing up 14 years of political dominance under Aleksandar Vučić, who has seen support for his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) ebb away and ultimately fail in what became a referendum on the future of Serbia.

From Belgrade to Novi Sad and Niš, the mood was euphoric as supporters gathered in town centres or in front of Student List headquarters. In a post on social media, the students declared "Serbia is free".

Most symbolic of all was the demise of so-called Ćaciland, a pro-Vučić tent camp set up 18 months ago at Pioneers Park in central Belgrade in front of the Serbian parliament. Metal fences were torn down amid shouts of "Vučić is leaving".

They have no obvious leaders and have no grounding in politics, and yet the "Student List-Students Win" movement attracted anti-government voters across Serbian society.

They fielded candidates for all 250 parliamentary seats, and yet no students were among them.

As he joined the students marching towards Belgrade last week, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."

"We offer our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time," he told the BBC.

It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.

The tragedy was seen as emblematic of widespread corruption. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.

"When the canopy collapsed that served as the last straw," says Helena Ivanov of the think tank the Henry Jackson Society.

It was an emotional moment that triggered a spark and a national campaign of marches and events, she said, that captured the hearts and minds of Serbians in a way no opposition party had been able to do.

Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement

Aleksandar Vučić conceded victory, but said the students' movement would fail

What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.

Vučić's SNS was clearly shaken and by January 2025 his prime minister had resigned "to defuse tensions". In March 2025 Belgrade saw Serbia's biggest ever anti-government protest and as the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.

By the time Vučić had announced snap elections last month, they were ready. "They have been able to take that emotional momentum into a proper organisation and have people learn how to protect fairness at polling stations," Helena Ivanov explained.

"The message was clear: the rule of law and not ruled by the law," said Gordana Delić, head of the Balkans programme at the German Marshall Fund of the US, who said Sunday's vote was in effect a referendum.

Initially Vučić sought to praise the protesters as "well-intentioned", but ahead of the elections he accused them of trying to "bring down" Serbia. Even after conceding victory on Sunday night he made the unfounded allegation that they had the support of unnamed "European countries and the American deep state".

Ilija Srdanović topped the Student List's candidates but is not seen as a likely prime minister

One thing is clear, it will not be the students, as they were not standing for election. That was a calculated decision as the electorate would probably not have voted for a list of candidates with little life experience.

Although their top candidate was Ilija Srdanović, a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, he is not really seen as a likely prime minister.

Few candidates stand out as potential leaders.

According to a final projection by independent polling groups CeSID and Ipsos, 141 people on the list have won seats in parliament. They include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga (24th on the list), renowned actor Tihomir Stanić (8th), opera singer Nikola Mikić (46th), former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić (27th), and a rather large number of professors.

Šoškić's name has been mentioned in connection with the top post. He has spoken out about reforms he would make to the economy, and he has been widely criticised in pro-government media.

The elected MPs will have the task of fulfilling what is in effect a manifesto.

In the words of the students themselves, they were looking for people who could enter institutions "do their jobs responsibly and not forget why they are there".

Under an 11-point programme, , external the student movement wants to:

Eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it

Purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime

Reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control

Stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises

Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.

Although they have not been elected, it is the students who have made the promises to the Serbian people and they will come under pressure to follow through on their manifesto.

The ordinary Serbian citizens they chose to represent their movement have "been entrusted with transferring part of the struggle we have been waging on the streets for the past year into the institutions", the students say.

In his speech on Sunday evening, Vučić told party supporters that the students had destroyed two years of life in Serbia and they would be defeated "faster than they think".

Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up

Mbappe scores twice to give Real Madrid El Clasico victory

Jose Mourinho has done it again.

The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe's late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, as he maintained his midas touch over their bitter rivals.

Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture.

Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona puts him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003).

It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions

And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe's double in Real's 2-1 win ended Barcelona's nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou.

A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals.

"In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga," Mourinho said.

"We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit," he said. "It's a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win.

"The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that's why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week."

The Portuguese has now won six and lost six El Clasicos across his two stints as manager.

He said: "I've learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play.

"In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack.

"We've beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don't go over the moon after this win."

Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he did not want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks.

"We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat.

"In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side.

"I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change."

Real Madrid have now won five consecutive games in all competitions

article:
On frontline at hospital denying online claims it is 'dangerous' and 'dreadful'

This video can not be played

'We're very busy' - inside Wales' newest hospital

It is the £350m "super hospital" that has been slammed as "dangerous" and a "disgrace" on social media.

At just six years old, the Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran has already come under fire for long delays, overcrowding, staff shortages and the quality of its care.

But senior staff insist it's one of the safest in Wales on patient safety and survival rates.

BBC Wales spent the day on the frontline at the hospital as 999 calls came in.

The Grange has arguably the best view of any hospital in Wales

The PA announcement in A&E is clear, somebody's life is in danger and they'll soon be arriving by ambulance.

But all eight beds at the Emergency Department's (ED) resuscitation unit, where the sickest patients go, are already full.

Staff have to decide quickly which patient to move.

But two similar "crash calls" have already come in by ambulance, as well as someone who walked into an already-full reception having a suspected heart attack.

Overall there are more than 90 patients in the department with the longest wait about 18 hours.

Medical staff in resus swarm a patient supported by an Air Ambulance crew

"We're currently over capacity," says Dr Zoe Morgan-Pittard, who is so busy that she's placed stickers on her arms to remind her who she's been assessing.

"We've had to move three patients already who probably aren't well enough.

"But the sickest patients have to take priority, we're having to make fluid decisions.

"We're putting patients in any extra space we can find... but there's a lot of block and very little flow.

"Everybody is working hard, but unfortunately the hospital isn't big enough."

Margaret Giles slipped while helping her granddaughter, whose husband had suffered a serious medical emergency

One of those extra spaces is located behind some cubicles at the back of A&E.

Margaret Giles, 84, from nearby Croesyceiliog, has spent the past nine hours on a trolley after slipping and injuring her hip.

"It's not satisfactory, but needs must," she says.

But Alan, Margaret's husband, is angry.

"I went to see the lady at the desk [during the night] because she wanted to go to the toilet... and [the lady] said, 'can't she walk to the toilet?' I said 'no, it's a suspected broken hip'."

There is relief when X-rays show Margaret's hip isn't broken, and soon she'll be able to go home.

Staff tell us there are strict criteria, meaning only the least sick patients can be kept in these open spaces, but it's an experience both Margaret and Alan don't want to repeat.

"We've never been in here before," Alan gestures, "it's the first time for me, and hope it's the last.

"I don't think it's the staff, it's the system."

Margaret Giles spent the night in a corridor with her husband Alan by her side

One reason people are treated in open spaces is to free up ambulances arriving outside. We counted at least eight waiting outside during our visit.

But, previously, crews could expect to spend an entire 12-hour shift waiting to hand over patients. Now, the target is to release them within 45 minutes.

On the day of our visit, because of the pressures, 33% of the ambulances were released within 45 minutes, but it was 67% for the previous 30 days - a huge improvement compared to before.

"We've seen a vast improvement," Darren Panniers of the Welsh Ambulance Service says.

"We are responding to patients quicker in the community, particularly around calls which involve stroke and heart attacks."

Ambulances could be seen queuing outside the hospital's A&E but handover times have improved

But the efforts to release ambulances also involves improving the flow of patients through and out of the entire hospital.

Surgical teams now go to A&E to spot the patients they can treat more quickly, while urgent patients needing same-day care can go to different departments.

But, for years, the biggest logjam has been delays in releasing patients who have completed treatment.

So, the Grange has built a portable cabin with 10 beds and 15 chairs where patients can prepare to go home or move to another hospital and staff can wash, feed and care for them, as if on a ward.

The Transfer Lounge hosts patients waiting to go home or those who need ongoing care in the community or other hospital settings

They also liaise with families and social services to try to speed up discharge.

"It allows us to free up beds quickly and it's somewhere quieter more comfortable for patients to wait," senior nurse Sian Williams tells us.

"I always say even one bed makes all the difference to the ambulances outside."

Yet, despite these and other efforts, the Grange, since it opened early because of Covid in September 2020, has been under intense scrutiny .

It was based on a model where lots of specialist care including intensive, surgery and A&E were centralised from existing hospitals in Newport and Abergavenny.

The assumption was that community services would be strong enough to take up the slack.

Chief operating officer Leanne Watkins says it's her "firm belief" centralising services in the Grange was right

One of the health board's top bosses, chief operating officer Leanne Watkins, says: "Bringing our teams together, for example, in paediatrics and obs and gynae, we had very fragile services spread across the system, and when you think of the risk that are contained in maternity services, for example, in paediatrics, that's enormous.

"So, I think we would have really struggled without [the Grange].

"I think we could have benefited from some additional beds."

Despite this, the health board remains in level four measures, the second highest level of Welsh government oversight, because of worries linked to urgent and emergency care.

And social media posts go further, dubbing the Grange as "dangerous", "awful" and "a disgrace".

"I don't believe that [those criticisms] are fair," Watkins says.

"We have amongst the best mortality rates in Wales, and, in fact, for some procedures, things like fractured neck or femur (hip) and emergency surgery, we rate right up there with the best in the UK.

"If you're unwell, critically unwell, it is a great place to be."

She said the criticisms were driven by a small number of complaints, and has reduced public confidence.

"For our staff, it is devastating to read what's been said.

"We know we need to do better, we know delays are unacceptable, but the teams work incredibly hard, and I'm for one proud of them.

"It absolutely is a safe hospital."

By late afternoon, the A&E waiting room has fewer patients waiting to be seen

The health board's own data suggests death rates at the hospital are lower than in similar hospitals in Wales, taking into account the nature of the population and the severity of cases.

Figures also suggest the proportion of patients who die in the Grange's emergency department remains below the Welsh average and has shown sustained improvement.

"I just encourage people to look at the facts. I know sometimes it's really hard, especially on social media that people can get messages that can make them feel low in confidence [but] please come and talk to us," Dr Seema Srivastava says.

"It makes me sad," deputy head of nursing Lorna Lear says.

"Obviously, sometimes there are instances where the care is less than what we expect.

"But we always listen to the feedback... and we always want to improve our services and give our patients the best possible care."

"So when we do see those negative headlines, it can be quite upsetting."

"If you have been waiting excessive hours to be seen, you're going to be frustrated and that's okay. It's understandable," consultant and director of urgent care Owain Chandler adds.

A&E nurse Sam Taylor-Harley has to be aware of every patient coming and going

After a seven-hour tour of the hospital, we're back at A&E where staff have seen 274 patients during the course of the day.

The nurse in charge, Sam Taylor-Harley, says: "We've had some more heart attacks, myocardial infarctions, we've had a couple of trauma calls, we've had a couple of admissions to the ITU upstairs, and we've also had some infection prevention control issues coming in as well."

Air ambulance teams escort a patient involved in a serious incident through the emergency department

As we prepare to leave the hospital, a patient with life-threatening wounds is flown in by air ambulance.

More than a dozen staff from across the hospital are ready and waiting.

If you're as seriously ill as this, you'll never have to wait to be seen, but that means less serious cases are likely to wait even longer.

The Welsh government said NHS staff were "working incredibly hard" to give patients compassionate care, and early plans are in place to help with a challenging winter.

Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days

There are several issues on the horizon for the prime minister

This feels like the week where the rubber hits the road for the prime minister's new government.

It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet.

Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.

Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.

You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week.

There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.

But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.

Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.

Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.

You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.

In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.

Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.

Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.

On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.

Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that , instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.

Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.

While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise.

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

Some Labour MPs representing seats in the north of England and Midlands, which backed Brexit, are privately nervous about anything coming across as too enthusiastic an embrace of Brussels. A nod to that scepticism appeared to come publicly from Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood who noted that a call for an honest discussion is "not the same as settled policy".

She added: "The prime minister has also observed that there were very significant issues with freedom of movement when we were within the EU. An honest debate means actually being honest about all of the aspects of that debate and not cherry-picking."

Next month, there will be a UK-EU Summit in Brussels, which was due to happen in the summer but was postponed when Sir Keir Starmer resigned.

We can expect both sides to talk up tweaks to the current deal and the government to also, in time, set out options for what the long term relationship might look like.

On the detail, there are divisions from the cabinet and down. The key thing will be what the party decides to include or not in its next general election manifesto.

Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.

The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

But what about the Rosebank field , 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?

Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.

It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it.

His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."

Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw.

Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels?

Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.

Expected before long, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn's review into young people and work – and with it a set of suggestions to try to cut the number of young people not in work, education or training and, in time, to try to cut the benefits bill too.

Plenty of Labour MPs acknowledge these are nettles that need grabbing, but how many may flinch when presented with the sharper edges of what might be proposed?

Meanwhile, we await where the government eventually ends up on how long migrants should have to wait to claim permanent residence in the UK .

And then, beyond what is set out in the Budget, how ministers will find the money to spend 3% of national income on defence by the end of the decade – and with what trade offs to make that happen.

There will be plenty to observe in the second 100 days of Burnham's government and beyond.
