Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent

The Amos Channel sits between Rothschild Island (bottom centre) and Alexander Island, which is the larger landmass to the right

Part of Antarctica has been named after former BBC science correspondent Jonathan Amos.

A stretch of water between Rothschild Island and Alexander Island in the west of the White Continent is now called the Amos Channel.

Amos was given the honour for his "exceptional and influential role in bringing Antarctic research to the forefront of public understanding" during his 38-year career at BBC News, the naming committee said.

The channel is a new feature in Antarctica that appeared when a chunk of ice that connected Rothschild and Alexander Islands disintegrated.

Jonathan Amos reported on science at the BBC for many years

The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs , the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship , the Endurance.

"It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said.

Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent.

"I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit.

"Antarctica is the front line of the biggest news story on planet Earth - climate change," he added.

The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.

The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.

"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."

Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.

"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile

This video can not be played

Watch: Supporters fill streets of Caracas to welcome María Corina Machado

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.

"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.

In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro.

The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.

Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.

She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.

She was photographed smiling as she leaned out of the sunroof of a car as she entered Caracas late on Sunday night.

"Night of reunion in our Caracas. For the reunion of each family, for the Freedom of each political prisoner, for the Freedom of Venezuela," she wrote on X.

Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil."

"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said.

He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".

An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied.

It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held . Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.

A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote.

Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize.

In the 2024 election, Machado's ally, Edmundo González ran in her place against Maduro.

The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.

The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.

Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty.

A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future".

"We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe".

"I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said.

In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump . The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks.

"The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X.

He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy."

article:
India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted

Satish Acharya is among Indian cartoonists whose work has been restricted by Meta recently

For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.

The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.

Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.

The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.

Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.

Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.

The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.

The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.

"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."

He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.

In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.

The message on Satish Acharya's profile when it was last blocked between 20-22 October

Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.

Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.

The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged minister s to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.

At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.

The Indian Express reported , external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.

The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.

Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.

The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.

Earlier this week, several media outlets reported , external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".

The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.

RK Laxman is among the most recognisable political cartoonists in India

Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.

Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman 's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.

But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".

In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trived i was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.

Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.

Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra , known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.

For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.

"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.

"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.

Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.

"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.

Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.

One of Manjul's cartoons which criticised the controversial voter roll revision that has resulted in the removal of 130 million names from the electoral rolls

Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.

"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.

But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.

No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.

"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.

"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.

Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.

Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.

Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.

When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.

Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".

"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.

Spook-tacular Derry Halloween festival turns 40

Now billed as Europe's biggest Halloween, the Derry festival kicks off on Wednesday

Tens of thousands of people are expected in Londonderry this week as the city celebrates the 40th anniversary of its Halloween festival.

From humble beginnings in the mid 1980s, the festival is - according to the organisers Derry City and Strabane District Council - Europe's largest Halloween festival.

Mayor of Derry Grace Uí Niallais said the festival, which begins on Wednesday, has grown to become "one of Ireland's most famous cultural events".

This year the city celebrates four decades of the festival with events inspired by folklore, mythology and the traditions of Samhain , the ancient festival in which Halloween's roots lie.

Whether you're visiting for the first time or coming back once again to Derry for Halloween, here's what you need to know.

This video can not be played

Thousands watched last year's fireworks display over the river Foyle

The Carnival Parade takes place on 31 October and is due to begin at 19:00 GMT.

It is expected to feature more than 600 community performers, with floats, music and street theatre forming part of the procession.

It starts on Strand Road, making its way to Harbour Square roundabout, then along the Foyle Embankment and back along Queen's Quay.

The Fireworks Finale will light up the skies over the Foyle at 20:15.

The festival's closing parade and firework display draws thousands of people into the city centre each year

The festival programme extends well beyond the parade and fireworks, with events taking place in the city over five days.

Aerial performances above the Diamond, giant installations around Guildhall Square and characters inspired by local folklore feature across the city centre.

Live music, family activities and street entertainment are planned at venues and public spaces throughout the city, alongside a full programme of daytime and evening events.

One of the festival's best-known attractions is the Awakening the Walled City Trail, which runs over the festival's first three nights.

Derry Halloween attracts visitors from across the island of Ireland, the UK and beyond

The trail takes visitors through part of the city's historic walls, bringing together aerial performances, music, fire displays and visual installations.

Festival manager Aisling McCallion said this year's event would be "bigger and more ambitious than ever".

Several new performances and installations have been commissioned to mark the festival's 40th anniversary.

The Awakening the Walled City Trail is among the festival's centrepieces

Among this year's highlights are:

Descent, a visual installation designed to transform the city walls into a portal between worlds

Samhain Sisters, a specially commissioned 40th anniversary production by In Your Space Circus

Through the Veil, an aerial performance above the Diamond

New installations and performances created by local artists and creative organisations

The trail runs from 18:00 to 21:00 on 28, 29 and 30 October.

A ticketing system is in use for part of this year's festival

Most events are free and do not require advance booking.

For the first time, however, visitors will need tickets for the section of the Awakening the Walled City Trail taking place on the city's historic walls.

The ticketing system has been introduced to help manage visitor numbers and improve safety.

Tens of thousands of tickets were booked within days of release .

A further 2,500 tickets for each evening will be released at midday on 28, 29 and 30 October through the Millennium Forum box office and website.

Music features prominently throughout the festival, with local artists performing on the Samhain Sounds Stage in Guildhall Square and Waterloo Place.

A programme of After Dark events will take place at venues including the Guildhall, the Tower Museum and the Centre for Contemporary Art, extending the celebrations into the evening.

Guildhall Square will host a Halloween food market, while bars, cultural venues and public spaces across the city will stage live entertainment.

The closing night parade is known to encourage the best of fancy dress

The festival includes a range of events and facilities for visitors with special educational needs and disabilities.

SEN-Sational Derry Halloween sessions at the Guildhall will include sensory play, storytelling, music and interactive activities, while several productions will offer relaxed performances with reduced noise, softer lighting and smaller audiences.

Dedicated quiet spaces, accessible parade viewing areas, accessible toilets and safety wristbands will also be available.

Organisers said more than 100,000 people celebrated Halloween in Derry last year

Temporary road closures and traffic diversions will be in place across the city centre throughout the celebrations.

From 28 to 30 October, Upper Magazine Street and Palace Street and Society Street will close from 06:00.

Bank Place, Lower Magazine Street, Shipquay Street, Butcher Street, Ferryquay Street and Bishop Street Within, Fountain Street, Artillery Street will close between 14:00 and 22:00.

Further closures will affect Foyle Street, New Market Street and Market Street from 16:00 to 22:00.

The annual city centre parade begins at 19:00 on Saturday

On 31 October, additional restrictions will be introduced to accommodate the parade and fireworks.

Queen's Quay will close from 16:00 to 22:00 and the Peace Bridge is also due to close temporarily from about 19:00.

Foyle Street Car Park and Queen's Quay Car Park are also to close on 31 October.

Accessible parking will be available at Strand Road, Victoria Market and St Columb's Park and additional parking will be provided at Ulster University on Halloween night.

Visitors are being advised to plan ahead and use public transport where possible.

The Halloween Hay Trail takes in nine communities in and around Strabane

There is plenty happening beyond Derry city centre.

Across the Strabane district, people can explore pumpkin patches, haunted attractions and the Halloween Hay Trail.

Events are planned for Artigarvan, Castlederg, Newtownstewart and Strabane.

On Saturday night, Strabane will host trick-or-treat trails, live performances and interactive activities before a fireworks display at the Melvin Sports Complex.

A special mural to celebrate four decades of the festival has been unveiled in the city

The festival is now promoted across the UK, North America, Europe and Australia, while international broadcasters and media organisations regularly feature Derry Halloween.

In 2015, a USA Today readers' poll named Derry the world's best Halloween destination, while the New York Times later included it in a list of leading spooky-season travel destinations.

About a quarter of the 120,000 people expected to attend the event are travelling from outside Northern Ireland.

You can follow all the sights and sounds of the spectacular parade and see the dazzling firework finale on our dedicated live page on Halloween night.

On Friday, BBC Radio Foyle's The Mark Patterson Show will be broadcasting live from Guildhall Square, soaking up the Halloween atmosphere.

On the same night, True North: Derry: A City Spellbound will air on BBC One at 22:40.

On 31 October, Eve Blair hosts a Halloween Your Place and Mine on BBC Radio Ulster , while on the same day there will be two collections of short stories on BBC iPlayer from 06:00 - Haleve and Bogle Cove - each featuring four short spooky tales.

Leicester's ABC tribute win & Morgan heroics - Prem analysis

There were only 21 tries across five games in the Prem this weekend

For all the free-flowing, high-scoring rugby in the Prem so far this season, this weekend was something of a throwback.

There were only 21 tries across the five games, whereas a fortnight ago there were 18 tries in the Northampton against Bath game alone.

But, despite the abominable weather altering the whole complexion of round four, there was no shortage of drama.

In the East Midlands derby on Saturday, Leicester Tigers produced a second-half performance that was as vintage Leicester Tigers as you could possibly get: a brutal set-piece and forward display that shook the old foundations of the Crumbie Stand and would have made the ABC Club proud.

In front of a febrile sell-out crowd, the game was played on the edge - a major scuffle breaking out on the stroke of half-time with England team-mates Henry Pollock and Ollie Chessum in the thick of it.

But tensions will have eased quickly. Thirteen of those involved in the derby met up for dinner in the England camp on Sunday.

"This fixture always has some heat behind it, and we know it means a lot to each other and to the fans," Leicester and England scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet explained to BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We just try and put all our heart on to the pitch. Sometimes it boils over into a little scuffle, but we will go and have a beer with them now. That's what rugby is about. You play fierce with each other and then enjoy each other's company.

"We always end up laughing about it. Being in England camp with them almost makes the fixture mean a bit more, because you always want one over them."

Northampton are the champions and still the team to beat. However, that's twice in six months they've been handed a lesson by the Tigers at Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

Saints fans will be comforted by the fact the title is decided in the warm early summer months of May and June, but boss Phil Dowson will still want his side to be as effective in the wet as they are in the dry.

England’s World Cup thinking and the rotation gamble

Are Gloucester now officially the real deal?

While the opening-round win at Exeter, the humiliation of Harlequins and the Champions Cup draw with the mighty Bordeaux were all impressive, the Friday night vanquishing of bitter rivals Bath was even better from the Cherry and Whites.

Tough up front and lively out wide, Gloucester have been a pleasure to watch this campaign, with centre Will Joseph rewarded with an England recall and the Wales talisman Jac Morgan the signing of the season so far.

It was as good a win, performance and atmosphere as Gloucester have had at Kingsholm in years.

"If you don't believe after these two weeks how good we could be then I don't know what you can do to get any more belief," said Glos boss George Skivington.

With Gloucester's defence inspired in the face of a Bath first-half onslaught, it was a great example of how a game of rugby doesn't need a bucketload of tries to be a captivating contest.

Gloucester are top of the Prem after the opening four games

Speaking of tries, Christian Wade nabbed one more in Newcastle Red Bulls' victory over Sale, drawing him level with Chris Ashton's all-time record of 101 Prem scores.

It has been some journey for Wade to get to this point, with the popular 35-year-old playing for five different teams across three different sports since leaving Wasps at the peak of his powers in 2018.

Meanwhile, things are moving in the right direction for the Red Bulls. Last season Newcastle had to wait until round nine and the new year for the first of their two victories, this time they are up and running by the end of October.

A few weeks back Harlequins looked to be in crisis after a chastening 48-0 defeat at Gloucester. Since that low point, Quins have pushed Sale close, easily beaten French side Vannes and dispatched London rivals Saracens, with Marcus Smith to the fore on his 200th appearance.

Sale on the other hand, have followed up an impressive win at Sarries with a series of poor performances. Next the Sharks go to Bath, who themselves are stuttering after three defeats in a row.

What to make of it all? Just four rounds in, and it's already hard to keep up.

Gloucester are top and Harlequins are bottom. But Gloucester beat Bath, who beat Exeter, who beat Newcastle, who beat Sale, who beat Sarries, who beat Leicester, who beat Northampton, who beat Bath but lost to Bristol, who lost to Sarries, who lost to Quins.

It looks like it will be one of those seasons.

Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street

Andy Burnham has not formed a view on the suitability of Downing Street as a workplace, it is understood

Sir Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of Downing Street because of concerns about its suitability as a workplace, senior figures from his administration have said.

Ministers and officials from successive governments have privately complained that Number 10's rabbit warren-like layout can lead to a lack of collaboration among those working there.

James Lyons, who served as Sir Keir's director of communications, said over the weekend that "moving out was something that was discussed" during his time in post.

Two other senior figures confirmed that discussions were had about moving staff into an open plan space in another government department.

One source said a space inside the Foreign Office building, a short distance from Downing Street, had been identified.

Both stressed that discussions did not go beyond an early phase and it's not known whether Sir Keir himself was consulted.

There's no suggestion that the prime minister would have stopped living in Downing Street if the plan had gone forward.

10 Downing Street is more than 300 years old and is an amalgamation of three houses, which comprises more than 100 rooms.

Downing Street's White Room is one of many in the building

The building was given to Robert Walpole, widely regarded as the UK's first prime minister, by King George II in 1732.

Lord Walker, the boss of supermarket Iceland and a former adviser to Sir Keir, told the Financial Times on Friday that Number 10 was no longer "fit for purpose".

He said: "I think we should turn it into residences, or a museum. It's a national treasure. It's amazing. But it's ridiculous.

"It's just a Stuart-era building, not fit for purpose. It has tiny, tiny meeting rooms, all on different levels. There are hazards."

Lyons, who led Sir Keir's communications operation from October 2024 to September 2025, posted on LinkedIn that "Lord Walker is 100% right".

He added that staff were "deeply envious" of other departments and described Number 10 as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".

Lyons added: "Moving out was something that was discussed when I was in 10 Downing Street."

Downing Street's famous staircase is lined with portraits of former prime ministers. Pictured are former PM David Cameron and British astronaut Major Tim Peake

One source said "there were chats at senior staff level about moving to an open plan office in FCDO" (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office).

They said they didn't believe the idea went far, but said "the reason for discussion was serious" and added that the alternative plan was "about staff being open plan and able to collaborate".

Sir Keir became increasingly frustrated at Whitehall's ability to deliver change during his time as prime minister.

He was accused of picking a fight with civil servants when he said "too many people in Whitehall are comfortable in the tepid bath of managed decline".

Darren Jones, who served as Sir Keir's chief secretary, told MPs last week that he "tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed".

One of Downing Street's ornate rooms was used to stage government press conferences during the early days of the Covid pandemic

He proposed replacing it with a new department that would "abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward".

In his first days after succeeding Sir Keir, Andy Burnham created the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

The move was seen as an attempt to ensure that things happen when metaphorical levers of power are pulled.

It comprises Number 10, Number 10 North and other key parts of the Cabinet Office and is led by the UK's most senior civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo.

The government says the new office will "ensure the centre of government is focused on our top strategic priorities".

Those around Burnham say he is yet to form a view about the adequacy of Number 10 as a workplace.

Correction: This story has been amended to make clear King George II offered Number 10 Downing Street to Robert Walpole in 1732, not King George III as an earlier version stated.

'Safety first' as wedding guests stranded on island after Storm Boelo

Shéa Clarke was among those stranded on Lusty Beg Island due to the storm

Guests attending a wedding on an island in Lower Lough Erne in County Fermanagh ended up stranded after a ferry took on water during Storm Boelo.

At the weekend, the storm brought winds of almost 80mph (129km/h) in some parts of Northern Ireland and caused the cancellation of flights and ferries.

About 12,500 households were left without electricity as a result of the storm, although all have since had power restored, according to Northern Ireland Electricity Networks.

Further strong winds - of up to 65mph (105km/h) - are expected on Monday night, with the Met Office issuing a yellow weather warning for coastal areas in counties Antrim and Down from 18:00 GMT until 03:00 on Tuesday.

This video can not be played

Waves crashed along the pier in Portstewart in County Londonderry during Storm Boelo

Wedding guest Shéa Clarke, who was on Lusty Beg Island, said: "You could see the waves were rough and the wind was going."

A yellow warning for wind along the north coast of counties Antrim and Londonderry takes effect from 03:00 GMT on Tuesday until 21:00 , with gusts of up to 60mph (97km/h) expected.

"Obviously it's too dangerous to cross and the boat can't cross so safety comes first," he added.

Despite the weather, the mood among the wedding guests on the island was good, he said.

"Some people have slept in cars, some people have slept on sofas there's been eight people in one room sleeping on the floor," said Clarke.

"But the spirit has been good the craic is 90... "as long as we don't run out of Guinness or chips."

A boat has since been taking guests off the island.

Olivia Millar was also a guest at the wedding on the island

Olivia Millar, an airline cabin crew worker based in London, was also a guest at the wedding and had planned to be in South Africa on Monday night.

"It hasn't felt like real life but everyone's been amazing and we've just made the most of it," she said.

Michael Cadden, managing director at the Lusty Beg Island Resort and Spa, which hosted the wedding, said the ferocity of the storm was "unlike anything we've experienced on the island before".

"This was a crisis but we've now arranged to transport and are getting all our staff and customers safely home," he said.

Kacper Dymarczyk, a bartender, was locked down with the guests and worked through the storm.

He said there was "no concern" of running out of food or drink as the hotel was "well stocked at all times".

A number of trees fell on roads across Northern Ireland at weekend

Flights were cancelled at airports across the island of Ireland at the weekend including about 40 at Belfast International Airport and about 30 at Dublin Airport.

On Sunday, the Department for Infrastructure (DfI) said about 470 storm-related incidents had been reported, including fallen trees and flooding.

A spokesperson for Northern Ireland's public transport provider Translink said that some bus services were diverted over the weekend due to fallen debris and rail restrictions were put in place in affected areas.

The Foyle Bridge in Londonderry was closed on Saturday due to high winds but reopened again on Sunday evening.

SDLP assembly member Mark H Durkan said he understood the need to close the bridge during the storm but added that its prolonged closure caused major traffic congestion in the city.

Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today , Durkan said redirecting vehicles to the lower deck of the Craigavon Bridge caused a traffic build-up and showed that the city was in desperate need of a third bridge.

"The infrastructural capacity of Derry needs increasing," said Durkan.

"I don't think two vehicular bridges for a city of this size and a population of this city is enough."

article:
Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or

Alexia Putellas won four trophies with Barcelona last season and 38 over the course of 14 years

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.

Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July .

She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022.

The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize.

Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022.

"All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said.

"Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."

She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.

Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or , becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001.

This video can not be played

Putellas wins Ballon d'Or for third time

While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite.

Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues.

Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons.

Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade.

But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself.

In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40).

Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151).

In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana.

Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38).

Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona.

She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou.

With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols.

After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy.

Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012.

Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups.

But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament.

Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung.

After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner.

If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense.

With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught.

She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July.

"I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August.

With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname.

article:
All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics

Dakar was originally due to host the Youth Olympics in 2022 but it was postponed to this year because of the Covid-19 pandemic

On Saturday, 31 October the Olympic rings will be raised for an event hosted on African soil for the first time as Senegal stages the Youth Olympic Games.

The cities of Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly will host 15 days of competition running until 13 November.

About 2,700 athletes are set to compete across 25 sports, with 153 medal events.

There will also be 10 engagement sports held without medals awarded.

Organised by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the event is an elite multi-sport competition for athletes predominantly aged from 15 to 17.

The aim is not only to inspire young people, but also to promote Olympic values and encourage them to see sport as a vehicle for peace and solidarity.

First held in Singapore in 2010, the Youth Olympics contain several elements of the senior Games but add newer sports, mixed-gender events and cultural activities.

Nanjing, China, staged the second edition in 2014 and Argentina's capital Buenos Aires was the venue four years later.

Dakar was due to host in 2022 before the Covid-19 pandemic forced its postponement.

Since its inception, several participants have gone on to top the podium at the Olympic Games.

South African swimmer Chad le Clos and British taekwondo athlete Jade Jones featured at the the inaugural edition in Singapore and two years later became Olympic champions at London 2012.

American sprinter Noah Lyles claimed 200m gold in Nanjing 12 years ago before winning 100m gold at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

Having the Youth Olympics in Senegal is "monumental" for the continent, according to IOC official Christophe Dubi.

"Africa has hosted many international competitions but this is the first time we have anything labelled with the Olympic rings," he told BBC Sport Africa.

Thierno Cisse, deputy chief operating officer of the Local Organising Committee (LOC), says the whole country feels the weight of the moment.

"We know we are going to be ambassadors for Africa," he said.

"It's really important for us to proudly represent the whole continent and show that Africa has high standards."

There is another link to the top of the Olympic movement.

Zimbabwe's Kirsty Coventry, who last year became the first woman and first African to be elected president of the IOC, previously chaired the coordination commission for Dakar 2026.

Youth unemployment remains a pressing issue across much of Africa, the world's youngest continent, including in Senegal.

While some residents remain sceptical, organisers hope these Games can provide both immediate and longer-term benefits through employment, tourism, volunteer programmes and skills development.

More than 400 young Africans have already received training in event operations, logistics, technology, accreditation and venue management.

"The impact will be much wider," Dubi claimed. "It starts with sports and this is where it will permeate across the continent."

Baseball5, a simplified version of the traditional game, is one of three sports making its debut at the Youth Olympics alongside skateboarding and martial art Wushu Taolu

Nineteen of the 25 competition sports, including athletics, swimming and more youth-focused events like breaking and skateboarding, are ones which were held at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

Beach handball, beach wrestling, futsal and rowing coastal beach sprints are also included alongside Baseball5 and Wushu Taolu, which are both making their debut at the Youth Olympics.

Baseball5, an urban, simplified version of traditional baseball requiring no equipment, will kick off competition at Dakar 2026 on Friday, 30 October.

Wushu Taolu is a modern Chinese martial art practiced competitively via choreographed sequences and sparring, while the coastal rowing takes place on the sea, unlike traditional Olympic rowing.

Golf, karate and surfing are among the 10 engagement sports staged to encourage participation among locals.

Climbing, hockey, modern pentathlon, paddlesport (canoe slalom and canoe sprint), shooting, tennis and weightlifting round out the events intended to deliver gender equality across the Youth Olympics for the first time.

Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026

Skateboarding, a medal event at both the Youth Olympics and Olympic Games, has grown in popularity in Senegal since the country's first skate park was opened in the Ngor neighbourhood of Dakar in 2022

Rather than constructing an expensive collection of new venues, organisers have focused on renovating and repurposing existing facilities that can continue serving local communities after the Games.

Dakar hosts athletics, rugby sevens and futsal at the historic Iba Mar Diop complex, while swimming, 3x3 basketball, breaking, skateboarding and Baseball5 will take place at the waterfront Tour de l'Oeuf complex.

Road cycling races will be staged along the Corniche Ouest.

The new city of Diamniadio , being developed south east of Dakar, will serve as the operational heart of the Games.

The Abdoulaye Wade Stadium there will host the opening ceremony and archery competition, with badminton at the Dakar Arena.

The Dakar Expo Centre welcomes gymnastics, fencing, table tennis, judo and Wushu Taolu.

Senegal's Atlantic coastline in Saly provides the backdrop for sailing, triathlon, beach handball and coastal rowing at Saly Plage Ouest.

IOC president Kirsty Coventry (left) joined a group of Senegalese women known as Lingueres to welcome the Olympic flame to Dakar in September

The Games are also designed as a celebration of Senegalese and African culture.

The mascot Ayo, a young lion, was designed by a student while another chose the name from the Yoruba word meaning joy.

The Dakar 2026 medals feature a lion on one side and a baobab tree on the other, with the images intended to represent both Senegal and Africa's heritage, resilience and longevity.

The official song 'Teranga', the Wolof word for hospitality, is performed by Senegalese artist Mamy Mbaye, and the athletes' village programme includes lessons in traditional sabar and djembe drumming and dance.

The Olympic flame was lit in Athens on 10 September and reached Dakar two days later. Since then it has travelled around 3,600km through all 14 regions of Senegal, with about 450 torchbearers over 30 stages.

The tour ends on 30 October at Place de la Nation in Dakar before the flame lights the cauldron at the opening ceremony a day later.

Nigerian wrestling star Blessing Oborududu and Algerian Olympic gymnastics champion Kaylia Nemour are among those who have been recruited to inspire competitors.

Ambassadors for the Games include Senegal football captain Kalidou Koulibaly, Kenyan marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge and social media star Khaby Lame.

Kipchoge has taken on a particularly significant role, mentoring the refugee team making its debut at a Youth Olympics, having been introduced at the senior Games at Rio 2016.

Six young athletes, identified through trials and development programmes in East Africa , will compete in athletics, judo and taekwondo, and receive education and wellbeing support.

The 50,000-capacity Abdoulaye Wade Stadium will stage the opening and closing ceremonies and the archery competition

Neither the LOC nor the IOC could provide a figure on what the Games will cost when asked by the BBC, but Senegal's government committed to spend at least $60m (£44.8m) as part of the host contract.

There are also loans, thought to have increased to around $90m (£67.2m), being spent on long-term sports infrastructure projects.

The Abdoulaye Wade Stadium, which opened in 2022 , cost a reported $270m (£202m).

A post-Games impact report should reveal the ultimate cost, but both the LOC and IOC say the event should be judged by its legacy.

"The Games are opening a whole range of new sports that are not famous here," said Cisse.

"Maybe we'll be able to say in 20 years from now that some champions were discovered."

For Dubi, the ambition is wider than Senegal.

"It's not only about sport. People will be amazed by what they will see."

Meg Hamon says she hopes her story might help others who struggle with excessive drinking and partying

Meg Hamon was struggling with her self-confidence after she began to rely on partying and drinking to get by.

The problems began to develop during the Covid-19 pandemic and then continued until the start of this year when Hamon decided a change was needed as she was going to turn 30, she said.

Since then, she had focused on exercising through activities such as gym workouts and running, as well as going to therapy to improve her wellbeing, she added.

Hamon said: "Exercise has helped me massively with my confidence... If I'm ever feeling low, a good gym session will always help."

Hamon felt her problems had been growing for some time before she decided to take action to make a change in her life.

She said: "I think my lowest was Covid. I think that was like a struggle for everyone and I just had gone through quite a bad breakup.

"I was struggling with that and I just think I'd never really processed my emotion.

"I really neglected myself mentally and physically... but I just never really noticed how unhappy I was until I started to make a change."

Hamon said she had felt the benefits on focusing on her physical and mental wellbeing since making lifestyle changes.

Forty Iranian sailors stranded off Sri Lanka coast rescued

Sri Lanka's foreign ministry says it has coordinated efforts to treat and repatriate 40 Iranian sailors suffering from unspecified medical emergencies in international waters off the island's southeastern coast.

Ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo told BBC Sinhala they received a distress call on Saturday from Iranian ships "regarding an urgent medical need".

The rescue operation was planned by the Iranian Embassy in Colombo, he said.

Iranian ships have been stranded at sea due to a US naval blockade. Sri Lanka stresses it is neutral in the conflict, but has at times offered help to Iranian sailors in what it says is an obligation to international law.

A BBC Sinhala report last month found that there were 21 Iranian vessels located in international waters near Sri Lanka.

The 40 rescued sailors served on different ships - though Sri Lankan authorities do not have information on how many ships they belonged to, Rodrigo said.

The sailors were brought ashore and taken to Colombo for medical treatment before being sent back to Iran by plane on Saturday night, he added.

He said that several agencies were involved in the operation, including local shipping companies.

According to Rodrigo, Sri Lanka was obliged under international law and humanitarian grounds to provide the necessary facilities for medical emergencies.

"This does not mean that we will provide assistance to those ships," he said. "It is generally an internationally accepted tradition to respond to a distress call after receiving it."

"We have dealt with such cases before. This is a normal process that continues to be implemented."

The ongoing conflict in Iran started when the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on the country in February. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.

Attacks by both sides have persisted as negotiations stalled.

Sri Lanka has sought to remain neutral in the conflict, having rejected military access requests from both the US and Iran and urged both parties to prioritise dialogue.

It has also offered assistance to Iranian ships caught in the conflict on what it argues are humanitarian grounds.

In March, Sri Lankan authorities said they responded to a distress call from the Iranian ship the Iris Dena, which had sunk off its coast after a US torpedo attack.

More than 80 crew members were killed in the attack, and injured survivors were taken to a hospital near the Galle Harbour.

The following day, Sri Lankan authorities allowed another Iranian naval vessel to dock at one of its ports, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake saying that they would "never hesitate to protect humanity".

Sri Lankan authorities said earlier this month they had no immediate plans to send aid to 19 Iranian ships near its coasts which had reported shortages of food, water and fuel. The authorities said they had to prioritise national interests, the Associated Press reported.

Doha to Omagh - A 7,160-mile journey for 'my World Cup'

Neil Kilpatrick travelled from Doha in Qatar to help Edendork win their first ever Tyrone SFC title

The round trip journey from Edendork to Healy Park in Omagh is around 60 miles.

But for Neil Kilpatrick, the journey towards helping his club to a first-ever Tyrone Senior Football Championship title was just a little longer.

It's just the 7,160 miles, to be exact, from Doha to Omagh as Kilpatrick made the journey from his teaching job in Qatar to line-out for his beloved Edendork.

It was a journey he had to make twice in less than a week after the first game ended in a draw, which meant a replay and a few hastily arranged long-haul flights.

The former Tyrone underage player landed back in Dublin on Friday morning, before making the quick dash home to get ready for the biggest night in his club's history.

Weather bulletins across the UK and Ireland were dominated by the impending arrival of named storms, so the Edendork defender was just glad to make it back without any hiccups.

It's fair to say that 14,320 miles in less than seven days is the longest commute for anyone bringing the O'Neill Cup home.

"I flew back to Qatar on Monday morning after the drawn game and then I flew back and I landed into Dublin [Friday] at 6am. But it's worth every single bit of it," Kilpatrick told BBC Sport NI.

"I heard rumbles that we might have got diverted to Shannon Airport so I was a wee bit weary, but thankfully I got up the road alright. A few hours' sleep and then I got playing the game here.

"You know you're never going to do anything without a wee bit of extra sacrifice."

When Mr Kilpatrick returns to his classroom in Doha after mid-term, the scale of the achievement back home may be lost on those around him.

So he admits he may have to get creative when explaining the events of his trip back home.

"Well it's funny, it's a Spanish outfit that I'm working for so they haven't got a clue who Edendork are or what Gaelic football is.

"But they don't need to know, I'll tell them that I had a great week.

"It's my World Cup, every bit of it. I'll be able to enjoy myself now and then I'll get back next week, and we'll just reminisce about what's happened."

Neil is the brother of Tyrone star Conn Kilpatrick, so the club's first senior county title was an extra special.

"It's definitely special and I was gutted at the last couple of years that I didn't come home for the championship.

"I was watching it on TV and just to experience this with Conn, and experience this with family, is something that I'll never forget."

He adds that living away from home means he only gets six or seven weeks in the summer back in Tyrone, and winning a title with those he grew up with means "it's probably hard to put into words".

"To many people this probably means nothing, but to the few that are out here on the field and are part of the Edendork community this is everything.

"We'll probably never experience a day like this ever again so you just have got to soak it up and enjoy every single bit of it."

article:
Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US

Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.

Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.

But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.

Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.

He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.

But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.

His signature policy has played out in five key ways.

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.

His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.

When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.

By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.

To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.

"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.

"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."

A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.

Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures , external , about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.

Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.

Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

"Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.

There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.

Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."

Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project , external , a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data , external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll , external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First , external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.

Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms

After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".

Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.

One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.

Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again

Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.

Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.

Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers , mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X , external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business , external , found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.

Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.

The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.

At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

Consultant doctors in England to strike next month

Consultant doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and working conditions.

The walkout will begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only.

This is known as Christmas Day cover and is likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services.

The announcement comes after talks had been taking place with the government over the past month, following the vote in favour of strike action by British Medical Association members in July.

Consultants – the most senior doctors in hospitals – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.

But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account.

The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken.

In a joint statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, said they had tried to negotiate with the government in "good faith", but "time-and-time again ministers have kicked the can down the road".

"Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.

"Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough."

Average earnings for consultants top £150,000 a year.

Basic pay starts at £113,500, with the most experienced getting £150,500.

But many earn tens of thousands in extra payments and awards.

In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who took part voted in favour of strike action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.

The government says this represents only around one in five consultants employed by the NHS in England voting for strike action, as nearly half are not BMA members.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government had been in "constructive discussions" with the BMA so it was "disappointing" the strike dates had been announced.

She said taking strike action would be "irresponsible" and "place the health service under even greater pressure".

The strike announcement comes as consultants and other doctors are taking part in strike action during November in Northern Ireland .

Consultants last took strike action in England in 2023. The long-running dispute involving resident doctors in England came to an end earlier this year after more than three years of on-and-off strike action.

article:
Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas

The pledge was one of Burnham's key early announcements after becoming prime minister in July

Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.

Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.

Ahead of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.

Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough , external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.

The government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will either be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas or will have been offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.

Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.

Burnham told ITV's Good Morning Britain he was confident it could be done, saying: "I have this strong feeling about putting the right standards at the heart of the country again and we can't get to a position where we just become used to walking past people sleeping rough: it's about care for people."

He added: "In the end, actually, it's cheaper to do that than to leave people sleeping rough going in and out of A&E, that's not good for anybody."

As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in in the region by 2020, setting up the Bed Every Night scheme, which now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.

When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.

The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021, but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.

Asked about his previous attempts to end rough sleeping in Manchester during his time as mayor of the region, he said: "I bring the learning from that to this.

"The reason why the figures went back up is because we were the only place that was offering a bed every night, so people came to Greater Manchester knowing that we were providing a higher level of support...I realised that it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping."

The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."

Across England, government figures show the number of people sleeping rough is at its highest level since records began in 2010.

Lam said: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises.

"Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.

"Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."

Burnham unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas

Key takeaways as Andy Burnham becomes PM

Burnham pledges to end rough sleeping in first speech as prime minister

More than 30 organisations have pledged support for Burnham's plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities who attended Monday's summit.

Initial funding has seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks.

The National Housing Federation will now work with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.

However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.

While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.

Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.

The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.

It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.

Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.

article:
Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback

This video can not be played

Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting.

Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy".

Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election.

Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same.

But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed.

Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias.

But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason.

Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to miss out.

The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques – appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race.

The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies - 4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult to challenge.

Lula is making history as the first Brazilian to be elected four times

The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.

But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.

Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989.

Bolsonaro had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable".

As his disconsolate supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate.

"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker told supporters. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."

After pulling off this victory, Lula faces big hurdles: a divided country, an opponent that won't recognise the result, and a hostile Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies.

Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans.

Reacting to the result, US President Donald Trump suggested the election had been stolen.

"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," he told reporters on Monday, without providing evidence or more details. "It looked very bad to me."

Other world leaders from across the political spectrum have congratulated Lula. Mexico's left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum said in a post on X: "The people of Brazil won."

Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, calling for it to be annulled

In a video posted on Instagram later on Monday, Flávio Bolsonaro said police had told him to hand over his passports and had been banned from leaving the country.
