Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.

Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".

But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.

He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."

"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.

"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."

She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

There have been almost no Budget leaks.

The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them. There are codenames. The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media.

Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising.

As a recent former defence secretary, Chancellor John Healey has embraced such strict procedures, and has approached most of his public engagements and interviews with a sturdy refusal to break the Budget omertà, akin to his fellow Yorkshireman Geoffrey Boycott's at times ultra-defensive stance on a cricket pitch.

The economic news has been good - growth has been better than expected and the International Monetary Fund has endorsed the UK for "standing out" among the G7 countries for at least planning to cut borrowing.

John Healey has embraced strict security procedures to keep this year's budget secret

The bond market's reverse beauty contest, in which investors single out the countries they distrust most, has moved on from Britain. Traders I occasionally hear from who were once focused on UK borrowing costs are now more preoccupied with "le spread" - the widening gap between French and German borrowing costs (the former being higher than the latter) - and with America's long-term debt outlook.

And yet there are clouds on the horizon. The inflation rate rose more than forecast to 3.5% in September, and borrowing numbers were also higher than forecast. This means an imminent Bank of England rate rise is very much on the cards, with the resultant rise in mortgage repayments for some.

Credibility with investors requires not just that Budget maths add up on Wednesday, but also belief that growth plans are realistic, and the perception that Downing Street can actually convince MPs to pass its Budget.

The question for John Healey is whether he can deliver a Budget that can sustain the revival in growth and offer the help with the cost of living that his backbenchers demand. At the same time he needs to reassure the markets that his budget will keep a check on borrowing.

"Is it resilient, or is it actually strong?" has been the tone of the debate among economists about the curious case of the UK economy ahead of what is a vital Budget.

The UK is the fastest growing G7 country so far this year, at 0.6% in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2. The widespread assumption of stagnation in the second half is being defied with Q3 heading for 0.6 to 0.8%.

Each quarter has seen growth twice as fast as predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March and independent forecasters. This is the fastest growth in the first eight months of a year since 2017, ignoring the post-lockdown re-opening.

It's more resilient than it was in 2022. Back then, the Ukraine war, massive energy bailouts, and Liz Truss' mini budget all culminated in the UK facing the highest borrowing costs in the G7, in what was derided in financial markets as a "moron premium".

Then last year, with constant policy u-turns, UK borrowing costs rose the most of the G7.

This year the gap has narrowed, as uncertainty about the US and France takes centre stage, but all advanced economies are feeling the heat from the Iran war energy shock.

Inflation has risen, but not just in Britain. The link between gas and electricity prices has weakened, meaning spikes in gas prices have less impact on electricity bills than they used to and helping to keep inflation lower than it otherwise might have been.

The fact that up until now the Iran war has been more of an oil shock than a gas shock (where the UK is more exposed) has been another saving grace. Meanwhile, the significant amount of AI and tech investment in the UK is another boost to the economic numbers.

The net result is that doom-mongering predictions of recession, of being hit worst by the Iran war, and, in some quarters, of imminent national bankruptcy, have been defied.

That economic defiance of the early part of 2026 has persisted in the first three months of the Burnham-Healey tenure in Downing Street, buoyed by a lull in the Iran war and the energy price shock.

Post Liz Truss' mini-budget the UK faced the highest borrowing costs in the G7

Burnham was advised upon entry to Downing Street that if consumers could at least feel more confident, they might save less and spend more and therefore help boost growth.

So far Burnham and Healey appear to be relying on a series of relatively inexpensive "feel-better" policies - such as capped bus fares and a temporary VAT cut on household energy bills - that have improved confidence without significantly increasing spending.

But there isn't a lot of spare money, which limits just how much can be offered for "temporary and targeted" measures. And come January, the clouds on the horizon could be overhead, with typical energy bills predicted to rise by 16%, interest rates potentially up and an enduring fear that the AI bubble could burst.

At a gleaming hi-tech robotics research facility in Coventry last month, John Healey sought to set out the broad contours of his approach to the economy. On a walkabout at the Manufacturing Technology Centre, I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongery.

"I know the global conditions mean that it is hard… we have huge latent potential in this country. Great talent, and deep capital markets.

"The challenge now is to make sure that we balance the books, we manage and control public spending, and the prime minister and I are in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer," he said.

The giant orange robot arms whizzing around were being trained by AI to use lasers to carve the most intricate metal shapes for prototype parts for the jet engines of the future. The Budget manoeuvres required by Healey may require even more precision.

The essential question is whether he has chosen to impress the markets and explain himself to his MPs, or impress his MPs and explain himself to the markets. Judging by my three interviews with him in recent weeks, it is more the former than the latter.

At Labour conference Healey wore the same tie once worn by Gordon Brown

The answer may not be found in his speech at all, but in the borrowing tables that will reveal how much money the government expects to borrow over the coming years, published in the OBR's forecast released - assuming no repeat of last year's disaster - when Healey sits down in the House of Commons around 13.00.

Just after that, as Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is delivering the Opposition's response, the real reaction the chancellor's team will be looking for is whether the markets move, particularly when the Debt Management Office publishes the "gilt remit" - the detail of any changes to its plan to sell UK government bonds to investors.

My sense is that every effort is being made to minimise this number, and help guide down medium and long-term borrowing rates for the government and for mortgages. (It was at this moment in 2022 that markets vomited at the prospect of how much extra they thought the government would need to borrow after Liz Truss' mini budget.)

From Healey's first day in office, the prudence message was practically tattooed to his head. He has spent more time working in the Treasury than any recent chancellor. He spent five years from 2002 to 2007 as a junior minister when Gordon Brown was chancellor - five finance bills, five Budgets, pre-Budget reports and two Spending Reviews.

Healey says he will take on some of the challenges Rachel Reeves found tricky to resolve

For his Labour Party conference speech, Healey sported Brown's old conference tie. But the Treasury he returned to this year is a changed place in important ways. When his predecessor wore the tie, the Treasury was running an annual surplus, not a £120bn deficit adding to a £3 trillion total national debt.

I asked him just afterwards, and just before he was whisked off to a meeting of the government's emergency COBR committee on RAF Fairford, if he was going to have another go at some of the things that proved so difficult for his predecessor, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves.

He replied: "100%. I was very clear to the conference today and the public beyond. There isn't the money that there was in the 1990s. People understand that. The public aren't daft.

"Running through the Budget I deliver must be fiscal discipline and the maintenance of control on the public finances, because otherwise we won't get on top of the debt costs."

One intriguing element of what we may see on Wednesday is that this theoretically more left-leaning Labour government appears to believe they have the political capital to save money on welfare payments.

The aim is to get some of the 1.35 million people currently off work with mental health issues back into jobs.

Some reporting suggests some affected younger people may see benefits payments cut, with the government instead investing more in getting them into jobs and keeping them in them through the offer, for example, of in-work therapy.

Back in Healey's time under Gordon Brown, there was no OBR. Back then it was not unknown for late budget maths problems to be settled with an optimistic tweak of a forecast, a date change to the economic cycle, or choosing a stronger rate of long term growth.

The OBR's verdict is crucial now - to what extent it agrees with projected welfare savings or even the importance it places on stronger GDP figures matters now.

The bigger point here is that the chancellor must be shocked by the contrast between the sheer power of the Brown Treasury to do what it wanted, and the reality of what he currently faces: the constraints of the OBR, manifesto red lines, bond markets, significant debts and an energy shock.

There are reasons to postpone some of the toughest decisions beyond this Budget, such as how to fund desired increases in spending on defence and social care. The economic outlook could improve were the Iran war to settle at some point in the next few months, and after revised statistics the OBR may also have cause to rethink last year's downgrade to long term economic growth.

There is an imaginable pathway to a forecast next year with higher growth, lower inflation and lower debt interest costs, plausibly improving the public finance projections by tens of billions.

This would be a much more agreeable basis upon which to decide the pace of those big ticket spending rises. It also may be a tempting option for anyone thinking about an election. Former Treasury officials lament: "There is always a reason for procrastination."

Expect the Chancellor to laud the resilience and strength of the UK economy and seek to sustain it, and spread growth geographically. His key judgement, however, will be a balance between extra financial and economic support and the peril of still elevated borrowing costs.

He will try to offer breathing space. It may be needed not just for households and families, but for the Exchequer itself.

How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around

Lula's supporters mobilised en masse despite polls pointing to a defeat for the incumbent

A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.

Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.

At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.

Led by Congressman André Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.

Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.

For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

Lula called André Janones "our General" after his major contribution paid off

The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.

Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".

"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.

On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.

In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".

Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.

Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.

Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."

By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.

Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.

"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."

In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.

"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.

She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."

Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.

In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.

"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

Invest NI to open new north west office at Ebrington Plaza

Formed in 2002, Invest NI is the economic development agency for Northern Ireland

Invest NI is to establish its new north west regional office at Ebrington Plaza in Londonderry.

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said it would serve as a base for driving economic development across the region.

Invest NI has been based at Timber Quay in Derry since 2006 but has been seeking a new location following Ulster University's purchase of their building.

The economic development agency hopes to move into the new premises in early 2027 and has agreed a 10-year lease.

The new office will be located at Ebrington Plaza in the Waterside area of the city

Archibald said would strengthen Invest NI's regional presence and improve its accessibility to businesses across the north west.

The minister said she looked forward to the office officially opening as a base to meet local businesses and inward investors.

In a statement, Foyle DUP MLA Julie Middleton said the opening of the office in the Waterside "is a positive development for Londonderry and the wider north west".

Middelton said it "demonstrates a commitment to supporting local businesses, encouraging investment and creating opportunities for economic growth across our region".

"The north west has significant potential, with talented people, innovative businesses and a strong entrepreneurial spirit."

The minister is flanked by Invest NI chief executive Kieran Donoghue and Aeidin McCarter, head of regional business for the north west

Invest NI has previously faced criticism over the level of inward investment in the north west.

An independent review led by Sir Michael Lyons in 2023 found "profound divisions" at the top of Invest NI were having a damaging impact on the organisation.

In 2025, Strabane business leader Kieran Kennedy resigned from the board of Invest NI after alleging discrimination against the north west.

In July 2026, Invest NI gave a presentation to Derry City and Strabane District Council, which provided a breakdown of the organisation's performance across all 11 council areas since 2021.

The figures from 2021–22 to 2025–26 showed a significant disparity between Belfast and Derry City and Strabane.

Belfast recorded 8,733 new jobs, almost half of the 17,932 recorded across Northern Ireland, compared with 1,176 in Derry City and Strabane.

Speaking earlier this year, Aeidin McCarter, who was announced as Invest NI's head of regional business for the north west in May, admitted "mistakes have been made" in the past but regional balance is now "front and centre" for the organisation.

Invest NI chief executive Kieran Donoghue said stimulating further economic development in the north west and across Northern Ireland was a key priority for the agency.

Last year, Invest NI said they supported 263 projects in the north west, which are expected to result in more than £80m of investment and create more than 400 new jobs.

Donoghue said the Ebrington Plaza location would place the agency close to some of its most significant clients in the region while providing access to the wider city.

Aeidin McCarter says the new office will help connect with partners to explore opportunities within the region

Aeidin McCarter, Invest NI's head of regional business for the north west, said the premises would provide a modern and welcoming space for businesses, entrepreneurs, partner organisations and potential investors.

article:
From agriculture to AI-griculture: How tech is changing farming

George McMaster uses technology to help him with work on his farm

George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.

He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.

The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.

For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".

Jack and his father George on their Islandmagee farm

It is just one example of how technology is changing the traditional profession.

George's son Jack, who is taking over the farm, jumped at the chance to get involved with the CattleEye app when a local developer approached him.

He, too, is astonished by the potential.

"There's cows there we would never have thought of as lame when we were just watching them every day, but whenever the camera's watching they're picking them up so much earlier, any emergencies that we have, to check cows before they lose condition and get sick," he said.

"And if cows are in better health, we get more milk and they're happier - happy cows make happy farmers."

AI is helping farmers monitor the health of their herds

Caleb Howard is using technology to manage his 90 Jersey cows on the farm near Coagh in County Tyrone.

They filter in and out of a robotic milking machine when they want to, rather than being herded in at set times.

Like the McMasters, he thinks "everything is going down the robotic route" to improve efficiency.

But historically in a place like rural Tyrone, that has come with its own challenges.

Getting high-speed broadband was a game-changer for him - he has been able to open a farm shop with an electronic payment system.

Caleb Howard is a farmer in County Tyrone

"Ten years ago, in our area, phone signal was rubbish, the broadband wasn't great, it was just like a slightly faster dial-up," he said.

"So now everything is much simpler and much easier-used when you've got a good internet connection."

Project Stratum was set up to deliver high-speed broadband to areas like the one Howard lives in.

Colin Hutchinson from Fibrus, which delivered the project, said it had had a "massive" economic impact.

"Being online and having good broadband access is really crucial now," he said.

"And it's enabling businesses like this to thrive in really rural locations."

A milking machine screen is used on Caleb Howard's farm

Robert Smyth runs a herd of 100 dairy cows in another rural location, near Randalstown in County Antrim.

For four years now, he has used the FarmDrive app to run the business.

"It's so much handier - beforehand you're writing things down, bits of paperwork in the cattle house and writing them down in the office, whereas now you just do it at that time," he said.

"And then whenever you have inspections coming up, all you have to do is go into your compliance section, select reports, and there's your reports for your medicine, for your meal records, for everything.

"The AI really should be looking towards how to manage your farm better and how to reduce your inputs and increase your outputs."

Gareth McDonald developed the FarmDrive app

Developer Gareth McDonald describes FarmDrive as "Facebook for cows". Each animal gets a profile with all her records in one place and a photo can be added.

He comes from a farming background and studied computer science.

Although he is passionate about the technology, he does not believe it will replace humans.

"It's allowing us to work a lot more quickly and efficiently, and on the farming side, it's basically allowing the farmer to see the right information at the right time, where it's kind of that adviser to the farmer," he said.

"We're very much of the opinion we don't want the AI making the decision for the farmer."

Almost a century ago, County Down-born inventor Harry Ferguson transformed the farming industry when he developed the linkage system still used in tractors today.

Former president of the Ulster Farmers' Union Ian Marshall says AI is similarly revolutionary.

While the industry has always relied on data, he believes technology will drive how information is used.

"When we take all the datasets, then I think we can deliver on the three pillars of sustainability - economic, environmental and social," he said.

"So I think that because we've got so much data and so much digitalisation in the industry, that farmers will certainly use this to their advantage and can meet their targets, meet their objectives and meet the obligations whilst delivering good quality, sustainable food."

Watch: How President Lula turned it around to beat Flávio Bolsonaro

Brazil's veteran left-wing president has pulled off a surprise win - but his road to victory was not a smooth one and he faces the most challenging political landscape since first taking office in 2003.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in a bitterly fought campaign by 4.4m votes.

Bolsonaro has told his supporters in Brasilia that he would seek the annulment of the election. But this has not stopped Lula and his supporters from celebrating what they describe as a "historic victory".

It was a dramatic comeback after the former metalworker, who has already served three terms as president, lost the first round of voting.

Many had not thought it possible for him to turn the result around in just three weeks. But Lula's campaign sprang back, driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push.

His election win has bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters have punished incumbents and turned to the right. Across the region, large countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia all now have conservative leaders at their helm.

But his new term, set to begin on 5 January 2027, will start amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.

Live coverage of this story

Lula greets supporters after casting his ballot on Sunday

While Trump did not endorse Lula's rival, Bolsonaro, directly – something he did with the right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections held in Colombia and Honduras – there is little doubt his administration would have preferred to see a conservative at the helm of this country of 213 million people.

The White House regards Latin America as an area of US influence with the Trump administration keen to have leaders in power who support its policies, including on defence, security and trade.

It is also keen to reduce China's influence in the Western Hemisphere.

Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback

Brazil, which is oil-rich and holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only big country in South America not governed by a right-wing leader, with Lula largely seen as China-friendly.

Bolsonaro had promised to align Brazil more closely with Washington while Lula had warned the US not to interfere in the election and insisted that Brazil would "never fit into anyone's backyard".

But while there may be disappointment in the White House, Lula's victory will be welcomed by environmentalists who had feared that a win by Bolsonaro would have given Brazil's influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power.

They had pointed to record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during the presidency of his father, Jair, arguing that under the younger Bolsonaro laxer environmental policies could again lead to destruction in this key ecosystem.

An aerial view from a Greenpeace flyover shows a fire burning in the Amazon rainforest during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30), held near Centro Novo in the state of Maranhao, Brazil, in 2025

While Lula's supporters are ecstatic about his victory, the result shows that the country remains deeply divided, with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro.

In addition to the challenge of uniting such a deeply polarised country, Lula will have to govern alongside the most right-wing Congress in Brazil's democratic era.

Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) was the party that made the biggest gains in the election.

And yet, Lula's Workers' Party managed to organise huge rallies ahead of the run-off, showing the strong grassroots support it commands.

Before the election, Lula had described the poll as "a parting of the waters for Brazil".

He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil's opposing political poles with "a new way of governing", adding in a WhatsApp livestream before the election that "this country will never be the same again".

While he provided little detail as to what the new way of governing would entail, he insisted he would "remain firm in the fight for a more just country, with opportunities for all and policies directed at the needs of the population".

With a largely hostile Congress, this fight just may prove much harder for the veteran leader - who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term - than in his three previous terms in office.

Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.

Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.

The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.

Anthropic also detailed some of the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.

Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.

Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.

Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.

But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.

Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.

Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.

The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.

Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.

"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.

Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.

At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.

Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.

Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.

The leasing of data centres alone is set to cost the company $321.4bn through agreements struck so far this year.

Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.

Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.

Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.

A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10m in the past year.

An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".

The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.

Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.

Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".

The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.

For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.

"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.

That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission."

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.

Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalised therapy.

Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.

"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

What do we still need to know about the Tyne nurdle spill?

The pellets have washed up on several North East beaches

On 19 July about 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles, consisting of hundreds of millions of tiny balls , spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between ships at the Port of Tyne.

It is believed to be the worst recorded incident of its type in Europe.

In the months since, teams of volunteers have joined in efforts to collect the microplastics that continue to wash up on north-east England's coast.

But several questions remain. So what do we know about the spill right now - and what are we still waiting to find out?

What is a nurdle and why do they matter?

Port of Tyne criticised over nurdle spill response

Nurdles clean-up volunteers meet Port of Tyne boss

A wind turbine installation vessel called the Wind Orca collided with a container ship berthed at the Port of Tyne.

A gantry crane on the quayside collapsed and ended up lying across the ship.

Two containers on the BG Orange were full of nurdles. These are pre-production plastic pellets, about the size of a lentil, which are used as the raw material to manufacture nearly all everyday plastic goods.

About 18 tonnes of these pellets spilled into the water because of the crash.

A crane collapsed following the crash

It is not possible to answer this question precisely, according to Dr Matthew Perks at Newcastle University.

But we can make a rough estimate, taking into account the total mass of nurdles that went overboard and the average weight of each nurdle.

Using this average figure, Dr Perks said the team estimated about 768 million nurdles had been spilled.

However, as each nurdle can weigh a slightly different amount, the true number of spilled pellets could range from 639 million to as much as 1.2 billion.

This is still being investigated.

Northumbria Police said it was investigating the collision and so far, no-one has been arrested. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch is also investigating.

The Port of Tyne previously said it, along with others, had asked the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to consider enforcing safer transportation methods for nurdles , something environmental groups have long called for.

By the end of September about 28% of the nurdles had been recovered, according to scientists.

But the Port of Tyne, the Environment Agency and the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) said the numbers of nurdles washing up ashore had already "reduced significantly" by then and numbers were continuing to fall.

They said they believed the full recovery of the 18 tonnes was not achievable. When asked what percentage recovery rate would be considered a success, the bodies said they would measure success via various metrics including shoreline surveys.

The pellets from the spill have been found along the English coast from Northumberland to North Yorkshire.

On Friday the Danish Environment Protection Agency confirmed pellets found on the country's western coast had also likely originated from the Tyne spill.

Dr Perks and his colleagues are monitoring the movement of the nurdles and examining how the pellets may deteriorate in water.

The team's modelling so far suggests about one in eight of the 768 million nurdles remain in the Tyne estuary and high river flows could flush these microplastics downstream in the autumn.

Perks said this was a crucial opportunity to collect the pellets.

The Danish Environment Protection Agency said the pellets along the Wadden Sea coast looked similar to those from the Tyne spill

Nevertheless he said it was unclear how far some of the nurdles could really travel.

"As time goes by, it becomes more difficult to pinpoint the areas where these nurdles are likely to be," he said.

It is also unclear when the nurdles will start breaking down into nanoplastics. "That will change the way they behave," he said.

Long story short – we do not know yet.

Professor Bhavani Narayanaswamy at the Scottish Association for Marine Science said it could be months or years before we understood the full impact of the spill.

She said the nurdles could affect wildlife in various ways, including getting stuck in animal digestive tracts and adsorbing chemicals which then may be toxic to wildlife when ingested.

Prof Narayanaswamy said there was little research on the long-term impact of plastic pollution on animals compared with its immediate effects.

Dan Turner, who coordinates the North East England Beached Bird Survey, said the group had collected several dead birds along the coast which they would be testing for nurdles next month.

"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs," he previously told the BBC .

This video can not be played

Birds have been seen appearing to eat nurdles on a beach in Tynemouth

Recovery is largely being paid for by insurers representing BG Orange, which was carrying the pellets, as well as local councils and the Port of Tyne.

Thousands of volunteers have also been involved in the clean-up.

The Port of Tyne and the local authorities involved have been told to record their costs so they can seek compensation from the insurers of those ultimately found responsible.

The multi-agency group, consisting of the North East MSA, Port of Tyne and the EA, said the nurdle recovery programme was continuing but it had increasingly moved away from "large-scale clean-up activity" towards "targeted recovery and monitoring".

Environmental charity Fidra said it was unclear how long the clean-up would need to continue, considering the fact that nurdles could stay in water for years.

It said a long-term plan was required to tackle the pollution and the plans should be "adequately resourced" with responsibility clearly defined.

Volunteer Lou Shackleton said there was still a core group of individuals who gave up their spare time to monitor and recover nurdles on local beach.

She said the group needed all the help they could get.

"If you're happy to wrap up against the rain and the wind... come and join us," she said.

Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

Even for a veteran politician like Lula, uniting a divided nation will be a challenge

On the face of it, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president.

It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully.

When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century.

Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump.

This video can not be played

Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.

The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.

He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.

Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.

The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.

Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.

He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.

In this picture Lula is seen meeting fellow Polish trade unionist - and subsequently president - Lech Walesa in Rome, Italy, in 1981

In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.

However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.

Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback

Lula faces hostile congress and divided country after Brazil election win

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.

He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.

In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.

Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.

When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.

Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.

His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.

Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.

Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.

The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.

The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump .

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".

In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods , external from Brazil.

The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

Trump and Lula had warm words when they met in Washington earlier this year

Lula has criticised the fact that five countries - the permanent members of the UN Security Council - have the power to veto decisions and argued that this tilted the balance in favour of those who won World War Two, excluding nations representing billions of people like Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan, as well as African countries.

Brazil is an active member of the Brics - a grouping that unites Brazil with Russia, India, China and South Africa.

Lula defends his continued alliances with Russia and China and sees the Brics as an emerging counterweight to the West.

He has defended his choice to continue to purchase Russian oil while Russia wages war in Ukraine.

Two men killed by falling trees as Storm Boelo leaves 90,000 properties without power

Storm Boelo floods town centre of Largs, Scotland

Two men have been killed by falling trees on Sunday as Storm Boelo continues to bring severe weather to the UK.

A man in his 20s was pronounced dead in north London after the car he was driving was hit by a falling tree. It came hours after a 60-year-old man died in Dumfries and Galloway.

The harsh weather battering the UK had left more than 90,000 properties without power as of 19:00 GMT on Sunday, the Energy Networks Association (ENA) said.

Those still without electricity have faced delays as the dangerous conditions were "limiting network engineers' opportunities to safely start the work", the ENA added.

Roads across Scotland have been flooded, including part of the A82 at Dumbuck Quarry in Dumbarton

The Metropolitan Police were called to Dollis Road in Finchley at around 12:40 GMT to reports a tree had fallen onto a moving car, and the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

Chief Inspector Guy Ellwood, from the North West Command Unit, said: "This is a deeply tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the young man who lost his life."

A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said it sent incident response officers, paramedics from its hazardous area response team, and a trauma team from London's Air Ambulance to the scene.

Earlier, Police Scotland said a man died after being hit by a falling tree at Mid Kelton near Castle Douglas. Meanwhile, two women were also taken to hospital after being hit by a another falling tree in Aberfeldy.

During Storm Boelo and the earlier Storm Austen, which hit the UK on Friday, 838,700 properties across the country faced power cuts, according to the ENA.

Wind gusts peaked on Sunday morning at 85mph in Machrihanish, in Argyll and Bute, and 84mph in both Stornoway in the Outer Hebrides, and Capel Curig in north Wales.

An amber wind warning issued by the Met Office was in place until 21:00 on Sunday across Scotland and parts of northern England.

A yellow warning that also covered other areas of the north of England, including Liverpool, Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield and Newcastle-upon-Tyne, as well as parts of the East and West Midlands and North Wales, also expired at 21:00.

The Met Office urged people to "stay indoors as much as possible", adding: "If you do go out, try not to walk, or shelter, close to buildings and trees."

The strongest gusts have continued to spread eastwards across the UK on Sunday.

The sea wall at New Brighton promenade in Merseyside took a battering over the weekend

Four flood warnings have been issued for parts of England and Wales on Sunday, while there are 17 flood warnings in place in Scotland.

High rainfall totals have been recorded in the Scottish Highlands, peaking in Cluanie Inn which received 130mm.

Scottish government ministers and officials gathered on Sunday afternoon to discuss the impact of Storm Boelo.

In a statement, the Scottish government said while conditions may ease later on Sunday, there is potential for adverse weather to return in the coming days.

In Aberfeldy, Perth and Kinross, two women were taken to hospital after being struck by a fallen tree at around 12:50 GMT on Sunday, police said.

A person is covered in spray as waves crash in Largs, near North Ayrshire, Scotland

The towns of the Clyde coast in Scotland have been hit particularly hard by the severe weather. The main Skelmorlie to Largs road has been badly damaged and a number of businesses in Largs were flooded overnight on Saturday.

In Gourock, a boat ended up on the side of the road and there have been reports of power being out in Girvan all throughout Sunday.

In Dumbarton, on the north bank of the River Clyde, Muhammad Zubair Ashraf's mobile phone shop was flooded overnight.

He estimated between £5,000 and £10,000 of damage was caused and said he was "heartbroken" at the scale of the losses.

Travel has been affected across the country, with police in Scotland warning against unnecessary road journeys.

Ferry services have been impacted, some flights to and from Belfast, Glasgow, Aberdeen and Dublin airports have been cancelled, and train services across the UK have faced disruption.

Man and boy's deaths during water activities 'could have been avoided'

Kayden Walker and Ruaridh Stevenson drowned five years apart during outdoor water activities

The deaths of a boy and a man who drowned five years apart during outdoor water activities could have been avoided, a joint fatal accident inquiry (FAI) has found.

Kayden Walker, 12, died after he became trapped on the upstream side of a weir on the River Tay in Perthshire in July 2019 while on a supervised trip.

Ruaridh Stevenson, 39, drowned after he tried to help a client who got into difficulty in the waters flowing through Dollar Glen, Clackmannanshire, in April 2024.

In his determination, , external Sheriff Keith O'Mahony identified precautions which might realistically have prevented both deaths.

In relation to Kayden Walker's death, these included his group leaving the river and bypassing the weir, before re-entering the water downstream.

In Ruaridh Stevenson's case, precautions included the availability of an effective bank-based rescue system, such as a reach pole or throw line.

Kayden was airlifted to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee but died the following day

Kayden, from Bridgeton in Glasgow, was separated from his board for more than three minutes before an instructor could free him during the boogie boarding session near Stanley.

Outdoor Pursuits Scotland Ltd, who ran the activity, were fined £10,000 in 2024 after admitting a breach of health and safety legislation at Perth Sheriff Court.

The FAI noted that Kayden had previously taken part in several organised water-based activities, noting that while he had "limited swimming ability", he had previously been observed as "confident in the water".

During the excursion, the group encountered Stanley Weir, a low barrier built across a river to raise the upstream water level, which had previously been identified as hazardous.

After escorting two other children, instructor Callum Gracie took up position approximately 15ft (4.5m) downstream.

He watched two adults navigate the feature before Kayden's board resurfaced without him.

Gracie paddled back upstream and found Kayden trapped underwater, describing his legs as being "hair pinned" around branches.

After failing to release him, Gracie entered the water, placed a sling beneath Kayden's legs and used a sawing motion to free him.

Kayden was carried downstream by the rapids, where Outdoor Pursuits Ltd director Philip Robinson caught him and began CPR.

Kayden was airlifted to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, but died the following day.

Fatal Accident Inquiry to investigate water sport deaths

Company fined over boy's death after boogie board accident

Man, 39, dies and two rescued from water at Dollar Glen

The sheriff identified two precautions which could have prevented Kayden's death.

He said the group could have left the river upstream of Stanley Weir and then re-entered downstream.

The inquiry also considered the Adventure Activities Licensing Authority (AALA) scheme, which covers canoes, kayaks or similar hand-paddled craft, and rafts, but not riverboarding.

The sheriff recommended a review of whether commercial riverboarding for under 18s should fall within the adventure activities licensing remit.

A floral tribute was left to Ruaridh Stevenson at Dollar Glen following his death

Ruaridh Stevenson was a director of another outdoor pursuits company which offered "canyoning" experiences.

The FAI heard that two sisters had taken part in a canyoning experience as part of a birthday gift.

One of Dollar Glen's best-known features is a plunge pool known as the Witches Cauldron or Devil's Cauldron.

The inquiry heard that heavy rainfall can create powerful waterfalls and turbulent pools, and that there had been several days of heavy rain in the Dollar area.

When the group reached the cauldron, Stevenson descended first before instructing one of the women to descend.

After entering the pool she became submerged and did not immediately reappear.

Stevenson saw she was in difficulty and entered the pool to help, but the pair became caught in the powerful current.

They repeatedly disappeared beneath the water and briefly resurfaced.

The woman escaped but Stevenson remained in difficulty and a rope thrown to help was carried away by the current.

Stevenson resurfaced unconscious about 45 seconds later.

Two walkers helped remove him from the pool and began CPR.

Emergency services arrived and resuscitation efforts continued for more than an hour, but Stevenson died at the scene.

More stories from Scotland

Sheriff O'Mahony said the activity should not have proceeded through the cauldron because of the depth and force of the water.

He said the appropriate course would have been to postpone the excursion, relocate it or omit the cauldron.

The sheriff added that a reaching aid, such as a pole or branch, might have helped the woman without Stevenson entering the water.

Sheriff O'Mahony said he was satisfied that this might have avoided Stevenson's death.

Man Utd stick with Carrick - inside a turbulent 48 hours at Old Trafford

An emotional Michael Carrick was cheered as he walked around the pitch after Sunday's defeat at Old Trafford

When Michael Carrick disappeared down the tunnel after Manchester United's loss to Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the support from fans for a legendary player turned to hostility and anger at the current squad.

The atmosphere afterwards was said to be emotional.

Carrick was the last to leave the stadium and, as usual, patiently posed for selfies and signed shirts for the fans who remained on what had been a foul day weather-wise, and an awful one on the pitch.

Asked in his post-match news conference if he expected to be in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea, Carrick said: "I'm not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I'm carrying on as normal."

Few felt that was sustainable. Even Carrick's coaching team wondered whether they would survive.

And yet, that is what has happened.

United have decided Carrick and his players will have the chance to turn the present situation around. No timescale has been put on this, but Carrick will be in charge at Chelsea, with his team 16th in the table.

They have a crucial Champions League match against Roma three days later, then a Premier League encounter with in-form Aston Villa before a two-week international break.

No-one from Manchester United is saying so, but that would be the most obvious time to decide if a change of coach is required.

On Monday morning, when it was widely anticipated an announcement terminating Carrick's tenure would be made, a senior figure at United said calmness and a clear head would be needed to navigate the turbulence around Old Trafford.

Carrick had been treading water since the crushing 4-1 defeat at Como on 21 October - one of the worst European nights in club history.

Respected United fan and United We Stand fanzine editor Andy Mitten, who interviewed chief executive Omar Berrada on behalf of the club last June, described the performance as "an affront to the name of Manchester United".

In addition to the catastrophic nature of the performance, captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick's tactics and the inability of his coaches to spot what was going wrong.

Fernandes' comments came a week after defender Lisandro Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad and - turning attention to Jason Wilcox - "more from our technical director".

It painted a picture of a squad out of control, posing an immediate dilemma for the United hierarchy.

Feeling it would look reactionary and impulsive to remove Carrick based on the negativity of one game, United stuck with the 45-year-old for the Bournemouth match - only for that to turn sour thanks to a performance that, arguably, was worse than the one in Italy.

Fernandes played no part and was dropped to the bench. Afterwards, the Portugal star liked an Instagram post which included the caption: "Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care".

Late on Sunday night, BBC Sport was led to believe a final decision to sack Carrick had not been made, and the judgement would stretch into Monday.

There was no decision then, either. The United players who started against Bournemouth were given the day off but bizarrely, Fernandes and Carrick were both at Carrington. Fernandes was having pre-planned treatment while Carrick watched a closed doors Under-21s game.

Also at the training ground were Berrada and Wilcox, discussing what the immediate future should look like. Sources say it is inconceivable minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family would not have been part of those discussions.

It was early evening before it became clear there would be no update on Carrick's future. His arrival at Carrington at 07:30 GMT on Tuesday was a sign he would take training as normal and, along with Fernandes and several other players, Carrick signed autographs and posed for photographs with a group of fans invited to the training ground that day.

Four hours later, United sources confirmed he would be in charge at Stamford Bridge.

Players were jeered by the crowd as they left the pitch after the loss to Bournemouth

The current predicament at the club is seen as not being entirely Carrick's fault.

Senior figures at the club feel United's players - a squad they think are capable of qualifying for the Champions League - are underperforming badly and should shoulder some of the blame.

There does seem to be a general desire to help Carrick out. One player told BBC Sport: "The feeling is that we all want to put it right. Players, staff, everyone."

It is not known if the "we" includes Fernandes, and BBC Sport has not been made aware of what, if any, conversations have taken place between the captain and his boss.

Obviously, it is easier to get rid of one manager and his backroom team than an entire squad of players - and if results do not turn around, Carrick will pay the price.

One former senior United official told BBC Sport: "Ordinarily, Michael would have gone. The last two performances were unacceptable and team discipline is broken. Not doing it is fascinating and risky."

Cynics may argue the main reason Carrick is still in a job is because of the inability to secure a replacement before the Chelsea game. Additionally, some of the coaches current Under-18s boss Darren Fletcher called on to help him during his spell as interim manager in January are now part of the senior set-up.

As highlighted by BBC Sport on Monday, Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann were among the options explored by United as they weighed up whether to make a change. Any decision to appoint Howe would trigger a multi-million pound compensation payment from his former club Newcastle. Some observers think compensation payments may be a factor in United's reluctance to make a change, given the sums that have previously gone on hiring and firing coaches.

BBC Sport has also been told former Chelsea boss Antonio Conte is willing to have a conversation about the job, although there has been no direct contact.

That trio are all out of work - as is Kieran McKenna, who worked with Carrick as part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at United and then left for Ipswich.

Aston Villa's Unai Emery also has strong backing at United, but the club are realistic about their chances of tempting the Spaniard from Villa Park.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (left) and director of football Jason Wilcox watched the Bournemouth match from the stands

Wilcox's future has also come under intense scrutiny.

One source close to United feels it is inevitable the former Blackburn and Leeds player will eventually lose his job if a third managerial change in as many seasons is made.

There is sympathy with Wilcox, who did not set the summer transfer budget. Others say Ratcliffe has provided significant funds for transfers since he took charge of football affairs in early 2024, as well as injecting £300m of his own money into the club.

While disgruntled fans may point to the recruitment of teams such as Brentford and Brighton as proof good players can be signed without paying astronomical fees, options for bigger clubs such as United were said to be scarce during the summer window.

Nevertheless, it has never been explained why it was decided to focus on bolstering the midfield last summer, rather than address clear personnel issues at left-back and central striker. Injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko have made that issue even more acute.

Another senior figure in the game told BBC Sport both Wilcox and Berrada may be vulnerable, suggesting Ratcliffe could be considering a wider overhaul of senior staff.

For now, though, minds are focused on Stamford Bridge, with Carrick due to speak to the media on Thursday.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

Nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola

As fears grow that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could spread further, Kenya, which announced its first Ebola case three weeks ago and has since had eight more cases, is hoping for the opposite.

Nine cases and two deaths have so far been confirmed.

With the first 20 of the people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient being released, the government has described it as a "milestone worth celebrating".

The government expects the outbreak to be declared over in less than two months, if efforts to contain the spread holds. But that is assuming there are no more cases, including from the 98 people still in quarantine and due to be freed next week.

Despite the initial release of the people in quarantine, Kenya's Health Director-General Patrick Amoth has reiterated that the focus was "firmly on the finish line".

The outbreak can only be declared over after 42 days from the time the last confirmed patient twice tests negative for Ebola, he said on Monday.

"We cannot afford to drop our vigilance until we reach that point," he said

In the days after the first case was announced, concerns had been rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government sought to assure citizens.

The US warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia remain on alert.

Concerns remain among Kenyans that the disease could still spread more widely.

Nearly 5,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.

With more than 10,000 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.

The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified . He died days after his arrival in Kenya.

As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading remains a big concern.

The doctors' union in Kenya expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.

Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.

In the latest update on Monday, Amoth says that "each milestone brings us closer to the end of this outbreak, and together we will get there".

When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.

Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.

Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.

Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.

It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.

The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.

Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.

Kenya has increased screening at border points

Following confirmation of the first Ebola case on 6 October, the health ministry conducted "robust contact tracing of anyone who may have been exposed", the World Health Organization (WHO) says. By 22 October, all contacts had been traced, both in Kenya and internationally, and placed in quarantine, it adds.

The government says that the confirmed cases so far are connected and there is no evidence that the virus has spread to the community.

Earlier, the International Rescue Committee noted that with all of those infected having links to the first victim, it showed Kenya's early response was working.

The government has been working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the WHO to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.

A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.

Amoth earlier said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".

The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

Despite that, Kenya's health ministry said nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.

The ministry urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.

The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."

In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.

Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).

With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.

Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment should be provided to hospitals so that they were fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.

He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.

The International Rescue Committee also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.

Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.

Despite confirming nine cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.

The US on 19 October issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.

No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.

Kenyan authorities have ruled out travel restrictions

Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.

But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.

The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.

A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.

The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.

Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.

One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.

Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".

The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak

In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.

Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health". It later said that 60 people who had

The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.

Uganda later said 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient had all been discharged.

Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.

On 20 October, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.

The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national is a wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday.

The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.

She has since been evacuated from Nigeria to Switzerland.
