Barcelona fined £503 over approach for Alvarez

Julien Alvarez scored his first La Liga goal of the season last weekend

Barcelona have been fined 602 euros (£503) following a complaint by Atletico Madrid over contact the club made with striker Julian Alvarez.

Atletico accused La Liga rivals Barcelona of approaching Argentina international Alvarez without first notifying them in writing.

The 26-year-old remained at Atletico and has a contract which runs until June 2030.

The fine was issued by the Spanish football association. Atletico also complained to Fifa, but football's governing body declared it had no jurisdiction over the case.

Alvarez has frequently been booed by his own supporters this season but received a standing ovation from some after he scored the winning goal against Deportivo La Coruna on Saturday.

Following that victory, which took Diego Simeone's side within two points of leaders Barcelona, Alvarez took the opportunity to apologise to Atletico's fans.

Referring to an interview he gave during the summer in which he said he wanted to "fulfil his dream" of playing for Barcelona, Alvarez said: "It was a mistake. I understand why the fans are angry.

"If I were a fan, I'd be angry too. Especially given how they've supported me since I arrived."

Alvarez joined Atletico Madrid from Manchester City on a six-year deal in a move worth up to £81.5m in August 2024.

After scoring 36 goals in 103 appearances for City, he has found the net 51 times in 115 games for Atletico.

Police criticised for delay in 999 mountain call response after two young climbers die

Jayden Long, 19, and Eddie Hill, 20, died walking on a mountain ridge in Eryri

More people could die on remote mountains unless police do a better job in responding to dropped 999 calls, a coroner has warned.

The bodies of friends Eddie Hill, 20, and Jayden Long, 19 , both from Dereham, Norfolk, were found on a mountain ridge in Eryri, also known as Snowdonia , on 19 February, a day after a call from Long to North Wales Police was disconnected.

Officers did try unsuccessfully to call him back, but then made "limited" efforts to find out who owned the phone and took more than three hours to alert mountain rescue, assistant coroner Sarah Riley said.

North Wales Police said it had taken steps to strengthen its policies and procedures.

Hill and Long died in extreme winter conditions on Crib y Ddysgl, a ridge that peaks at 1,065m (3,494ft), less than a mile north of Yr Wyddfa's summit and linking it to the notoriously narrow ridge of Crib Goch.

A Prevention of Future Deaths , external report said police received a discontinued call from Long's mobile phone at 16:27 GMT on 18 February.

A playback captured him saying "hello" and "can you hear me?" before the call was lost.

Eddie and Jayden died on Crib y Ddysgl - less than a mile north of Yr Wyddfa's summit

The mountain rescue team told an inquest into their deaths that it did not have enough information about the location or nature of Long's 999 call to act immediately.

After further inquiries, including making contact with family members, mountain rescue teams and a coastguard helicopter searched the last known position of the two men but found no trace.

A decision was made to continue the search at first light.

A search and rescue dog team joined the mountain rescue teams for the search on the following morning, when the walkers' bodies were found.

Several rescue teams were involved in the search for the men despite "challenging" wintry conditions

The coroner identified several areas of concern following the inquest, including a lack of guidance or training for staff dealing with calls from remote mountainous locations and inadequate systems for sharing lessons learned from the incident.

"Unless action is taken to address the above concerns then there is a significant risk of future deaths," Riley said.

North Wales Police said it amended its communications centre policy in September 2026 to include specific guidance on handling silent or disconnected 999 calls from remote or mountainous locations.

Call handlers are now expected to consider alerting mountain rescue teams where a caller's location can be confirmed and, learning from the incident has been shared with communications staff.

The force said it hoped the response would "provide reassurance that the concerns identified have been addressed and that lessons arising from this tragic incident have been recognised and acted upon".

Australian sunscreen brands face stricter rules after safety scandal

A sunscreen safety scandal sparked massive backlash in Australia, which has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world

Australian sunscreen manufacturers will be subject to stricter rules in the wake of a safety scandal that saw popular brands pulled off shelves.

The reforms, announced by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) on Tuesday, include stronger testing and quality requirements for specific ingredients.

This comes after a bombshell report last year by consumer advocacy group Choice which found that some popular sunscreens did not provide the level of protection their manufacturers claimed.

The new proposed regulations are "about making SPF claims more reliable" and giving the agency "faster access to evidence when concerns arise", Robyn Langham, the TGA's chief medical adviser, tells the BBC.

"Australians expect the SPF on the label to be backed by robust evidence," she said in a statement over email.

"These proposed reforms put that expectation at the centre of sunscreen regulation, with stronger testing requirements for the finished product consumers buy and repeat testing throughout its time on the market."

Under the new regulations proposed by the TGA, cosmetic sunscreen brands will also be limited in the skin protection factor (SPF) claims they can make.

This is to ensure "clear distinction for consumers" between sunscreens that are mainly made for UV protection and cosmetic products where UV protection is a secondary function.

Suppliers would also be required to provide their SPF testing data to the TGA when they list a sunscreen, and keep periodically testing the product throughout its shelf life.

Under current regulations, it's not mandatory for sunscreen manufacturers to provide testing data to the TGA unless requested.

The TGA said the reforms would be "implemented in stages, with further consultation where required".

The Choice report, published in June 2025, found that 16 of 20 tested sunscreens - including several premium, expensive brands - failed to live up to their advertised SPF rating.

The sunscreen scandal shocking Australia - the world's skin cancer hotspot

Australia sunscreen scandal grows as more products pulled off shelves

One product, Ultra Violette's Lean Screen Skinscreen, which was voluntarily recalled last year, was marketed as having an SPF of 50+ but was found to offer only SPF 4.

The scandal sparked massive backlash in Australia, which has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world.

More than a dozen products were pulled from shelves or had their sales suspended as a result of the scandal.

The TGA proposed sweeping reforms to the sunscreen industry earlier this year , which included plans to make sunscreen labelling simpler and more oversight at testing labs.

Its statement on Tuesday said that changes to labelling would be made after further review and consultation.

Choice welcomed the reforms, saying in a statement on Tuesday that it was "pleased to see" the stricter rules proposed by the TGA.

However, the group pointed out that the TGA has not proposed to "routinely monitor and evaluate test results".

Choice also argued that that sunscreen test results should not be provided only to the TGA - as proposed by the regulator - but rather made publicly available and routinely monitored, "in the interest of transparency and public safety".

'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on

'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on

"I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career...I would absolutely do it again."

Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.

It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.

It proved both inspirational and divisive.

In his first interview with BBC Sport, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.

The former quarterback says he decided to protest despite suspecting it could risk his career.

"History shows us…that is a reality for athletes", he says.

"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."

Having initially sat to raise awareness of the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.

At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."

His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.

Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.

Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.

The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.

Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.

Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.

Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.

Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.

That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present. Hopes of a comeback never materialised.

The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".

Colin Kaepernick speaks to BBC's Dan Roan

Available now

Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick gives his first interview with BBC Sport, 10 years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status

Kaepernick first took the knee in protest in September 2016

Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.

England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.

"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.

"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.

"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.

"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."

Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.

But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice , external , he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.

It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.

Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".

Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.

"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.

"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.

"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."

Kaepernick is all too familiar with how polarising it can be to take a political stand in sport.

Opponents of taking the knee have claimed it is a political and divisive statement, and that rather than demonstrating backing for the Black Lives Matter movement , it has shown support for the organisation of the same name.

In 2018, critics encouraged people to destroy Nike goods after the sportswear giant used Kaepernick as the face of an advertising campaign featuring the caption 'Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.'

So what does he say to those who argue that sport and politics should be kept apart?

"They ring hollow and feel very hypocritical, because politics is inherently part of sports," he says.

"We see within [American] football, we see taxpayers funding NFL stadiums. We see our NFL owners going out and supporting political candidates... so to try to position this as if sports aren't political, in many ways feels just laughable to me, and disconnected.

"Now, where the question comes in for people is: 'We don't want the athletes to be political. Everything around them can be political, but the athletes themselves, we don't want them to have a voice in the politics, because that interrupts our entertainment and our ability to disconnect.' For me, that's where society has a challenge with it."

Having encountered significant opposition from high-profile athletes during his first term, Trump seems to have encountered less challenge from the world of sport during his second, notably becoming the first sitting US president to attend the Super Bowl.

He has also appeared at golf's Ryder Cup, and the finals of football's Club World Cup and World Cup, though he was also booed when attending the NBA Finals in New York in June.

"It ties into the conversation of 'are sports political?' when he is going out and actively trying to use them to gain favour and popularity", says Kaepernick, adding that Fifa's controversial decision to award the US President its inaugural 'Peace Prize' last year was "regrettable".

"The part that I think is great to see is when he's showing up to these events and getting booed by the crowd, which speaks to the political environment that he's created, that the majority of the country does not agree with…when it comes to sports, people need to continue to respond accordingly."

Despite backlash, Kaepernick repeated taking the knee before 11 regular-season NFL contests

Now 38, Kaepernick has published a memoir titled The Perilous Fight, detailing his childhood in California having been adopted by a white family, encountering racism, and his education and evolution. "People saw the moment. But they didn't see the years that made it possible", he says. "The questions about who I was; the injustices I could no longer ignore; the voices of those who came before me that I carried into that stadium...When I took a knee, it wasn't a sudden act. It was the result of years of becoming."

So how did he find the process of reliving that journey?

"Are there moments that are challenging going back to? Yes. But I hope that insight helps other people navigate situations...that helps them move forward or helps them to go accomplish things."

Kaepernick also supports community organisations via his Know Your Rights education campaign, is a philanthropist, and has written a number of children's books.

Even now, he maintains the fitness regime he had during his time at the 49ers, just in case an unlikely opportunity to resume his NFL career arises.

Kaepernick may not have thrown a ball in anger for almost a decade, but he is widely regarded as one of the most significant athletes in modern history.

The way he used his platform to promote change has been compared to legendary boxer Muhammad Ali's support of the anti-war movement, and US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos giving the Black Power Salute at the 1968 Olympics.

"To even be in the same conversation with the likes of [them], is extremely humbling," he says. "But more importantly, I just try to stay focused on the work.

"What can we do to help people? And how do we collectively move forward as a society? And, ultimately, how we build a society that works for everybody. That feels like a very simple principle that has been lost.

"I know in the US specifically, we have a lot of work to do there. I hope we begin taking the steps to get back to a place where we are actually addressing people's needs. And create a society that is equitable for everyone."

Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises

Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget.

"The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now… Britain has it harder now," Chancellor John Healey said last month.

And from Andy Burnham, days before he became prime minister: "This change... is the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years."

So what happens when the economic realities confront the political ambitions of this new government?

As Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), puts it , external : "We have a relatively new government with seemingly big ambitions but facing a long list of constraints.

"Some of those constraints… are self imposed, others are being worsened by global events, most noticeably war in the Middle East."

Let's be clear, plenty in Westminster in all parties will say that the amount of money around isn't everything – how well taxpayers' money is spent and where it is spent matters too.

And spending less and taxing less, plenty argue, should be a priority.

But in the bones of many in the Labour Party is an instinct that the government, the state, can and should be a vital agent in driving change and improvements in people's lives – a world-view grounded in a sense that governments should proudly step in, rather than one that believes they should get out of the way.

And how do you deliver a proudly proactive state, delivering for people in a noticeable way, when the tax burden is generationally high, the national debt is sky high, energy bills are rising and inflation is higher than expected?

In short: it is not easy.

Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase

Tax on banks, energy bill help and minimum wage rise - what could be in the Budget?

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

But ministers argue all of this doesn't mean the government is powerless.

Many are expecting support on the cost of living, and in particular energy bills, to be targeted at the most vulnerable. On the eve of the Budget, Healey said he wants to "start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good".

The banks are braced for a levy or surcharge that may pay for this.

There will be an announcement about further spending on defence, but not yet how spending 3% of national income on our security will be delivered by 2030 – that will come in next year's Spending Review.

And one of the prime minister's key ideas - handing power away from Westminster and closer to you, devolution - will be central too.

There will be, the chancellor told BBC Newscast, a "really radical devolution of powers and resources to local leaders that are often better placed to get beyond the departmental systems."

But some at Westminster fret extra money for mayors and others in local government are not yet accompanied by adequate checks and balances to ensure that money is well spent.

The chancellor will argue the economy is becoming more robust – and yes, there are some economic indicators that are more positive than forecast: growth is better than expected, as is productivity and unemployment is down.

But as the Resolution Foundation think tank points out , external : "John Healey's problem is that conflict in the Middle East has once again pushed up energy prices and interest rates.

"So, despite the signs that the UK economy is becoming more resilient, household and public finances are in for another shock."

Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax

Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain

In essence, we can expect a smaller Budget this time, compared to some in recent years, when it comes to the scale of tax and spending changes.

The chancellor has been talking up a desire to offer "breathing space" and "hope" - a tacit acknowledgement that there is a limit to what the government can do given the constraints it faces.

It has promised not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, a self imposed constraint, as the IFS put it. And there are the international ones beyond its control too.

The big question for many will be whether the Budget is – or can be - big enough to meet the moment? Opposition parties will argue it amounts to tinkering.

Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith argued the public finances are "on a cliff edge" and wants Healey to use the Budget to "take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road".

For the Liberal Democrats, Daisy Cooper warned a "steady as she goes" Budget is "not going to cut it", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said the chancellor "can't keep fiddling while the economy burns".

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns wanted a "bold" approach but fears it will be "business as usual".

The government will try to convince you it is one of many moments in the coming weeks and months that will attempt to deliver the scale of change the prime minister has promised.

article:
How 'anti-superstar' Kane defied doubters to become world's best

Kane won the Ballon d'Or on Monday night

Harry Kane has taken the scenic route to the Ballon d'Or - a road littered with doubts and diversions, but one that eventually led to the ultimate destination: being crowned as the world's best player.

The 33-year-old's glory at the London Palladium on Monday is fitting reward for an exemplary career that has seen records fall at his feet for England, Tottenham Hotspur and Bayern Munich.

Kane is England's top goalscorer with 91 goals. He has 125 England caps, joint-highest with Peter Shilton. He is Spurs' record scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances. He scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025–26 season.

This is the Kane of recent vintage, the world-class striker and complete footballer who beat Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe, as well as Spain's teenage Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal, to the sport's biggest personal honour.

Kane's humility has seen him described as an 'anti-superstar' and his achievement has been commended both inside and outside the football world.

One post on social media from Kane as he celebrated the greatest moment of his career said it all: "Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise."

And yet, Kane's journey was not always smooth.

It was one that started with loan moves around the lower divisions with Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City before he developed into a great for club and country.

The same Kane sat on the bench on loan at Leicester City – alongside future England team-mate Jamie Vardy – when the Foxes lost a dramatic Championship play-off at Watford in May 2013.

Kane went through hard schools and hard times away from his more familiar environment at Spurs, joining Orient on loan as a 17-year-old in January 2011, playing 18 games with nine starts and scoring five goals.

He joined Millwall in similar circumstances a year later, with some behind the scenes at Spurs fearing the traditionally hostile atmosphere at the New Den might intimidate the teenager, but he acquitted himself well, scoring nine goals in 24 starts.

Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend

Tributes pour in as Kane wins Ballon d'Or - reaction & your views

Kane scored against Blackburn Rovers in February 2013 during a loan spell at Leicester City

Former Spurs manager Tim Sherwood said: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there'.

"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him'."

Kane made his Spurs debut in August 2012 before a spell at Norwich City, where he failed to score in three starts and suffered a serious foot injury.

It was an unhappy time but Chris Hughton, the former Spurs defender who was manager at Carrow Road, said: "What I saw in him was a desire to do well. Did I see him having the mobility and flexibility he has in his game now? Probably not. He was a very good finisher. He would stay out after training for half an hour every day, left foot, right foot."

Next stop was Leicester City between February and May 2013, when he made five starts and scored two goals, a stint best remembered for that dramatic Championship play-off game when Troy Deeney scored for Watford to send them to Wembley seconds after Anthony Knockaert's penalty was saved by Manuel Almunia.

Kane was not even selected in Leicester's starting line-up, only being sent on after 61 minutes. And who was alongside him on the bench? Vardy, who later won the Premier league with the Foxes and played alongside Kane for England.

He later admitted this was a time of self-doubt, saying: "That was probably the time in my career where it was the hardest - I was 19 and I was thinking, 'If I can't play for Norwich or for Leicester, even in the Championship, then how I am going to get back and play for Tottenham?'"

Ranking England's Ballon d'Or winners - how does Kane compare?

Quiz: Kane and who else? Name every men's Ballon d'Or winner

This video can not be played

'Anything is possible' - Kane wins Ballon d'Or

It is testimony to Kane's strength of character, even as a youngster, that he not only returned to Spurs but left for Bayern Munich in August 2023 as one of their greatest ever players.

Even at Spurs, Kane's superb record always carried the qualification that he never won a trophy, a stick used to unfairly beat a player whose remarkable consistency and approach marked him down as the consummate professional.

Kane has put that right spectacularly at Bayern, winning the Bundesliga twice, the move propelling him to the level of global superstar, giving him the profile and platform to win the Ballon d'Or - the first English player to win the trophy since Michael Owen in 2001 and the fifth overall.

Former England midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport recently: "He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career."

There is still that one space on his roll of honour, namely success with England after losses in two Euros finals and two World Cup semi-final defeats, but who would bet against Kane being fit and motivated enough to have one last crack at Euro 2028 in the UK and Ireland.

Kane is England's top goalscorer with 91 goals from a record-equalling 125 appearances

Kane is now at the peak of his powers and fitness, not just a goalscoring machine but the complete player capable of dropping deep into midfield to play the sort of breathtaking defence splitting pass exemplified by Alphonso Davies' goal against Arsenal in the recent Champions League game.

One of Kane's illustrious predecessors in England's number nine shirt, Alan Shearer, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "It was so well deserved because he hasn't had things all his own way. He's had to go round it the hard way. He had to start off the hard way by someone telling him, 'You're not quite good enough, you're going to have to work a lot harder to get to where you want to'.

"He did that. He went out on loan and worked harder than anyone else. He's got to the very, very top and now he's the best player in the world and that's what dedication does for you. It's a message to everyone.

"Harry said it in his speech - that if you're told you're not good enough, then go and try again and work harder. He did that and look where he is now. He's been scoring goals at a phenomenal rate for so many years now and he deserved it."

Shearer added: "I think the best thing for me is how humble Harry is. Footballers are like movie stars nowadays. You see them walking down the red carpet and some of them are in sunglasses when it's pitch black and eight o'clock at night. Harry is just normal, as normal as they come."

Once the celebrations die down, it will be back to business for the humble superstar, with Bayern playing Magdeburg in the German DFB Pokal second round on Wednesday before the big home fixture against Borussia Dortmund on Saturday evening.

Kane's career has not been without its obstacles but he remains as focused as ever to conquer whatever is placed in front of him by Bayern Munich and England.

Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets?

Fleetwood Town reached the League Cup quarter-finals for the first time by beating Arsenal

Arsenal suffered a shock Carabao Cup exit at the home of Fleetwood Town, as the League Two side recorded one of the biggest upsets in the competition's history.

Mikel Arteta's Premier League champions lost 5-3 on penalties to a Fleetwood outfit ranked 84 places below them in the English football pyramid.

Following Fleetwood's victory, BBC Sport looks at some of the biggest shocks of all-time in the FA Cup and League Cup.

This isn't an exhaustive list, and you can leave your thoughts in the comments, rank the historic upsets and share your results.

Fleetwood Town celebrated the biggest victory in the club's history as they stunned Champions League finalists Arsenal to reach the EFL Cup quarter-finals at Highbury Stadium.

The League Two club stunned the visitors when Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood, who sat 19th in English football's fourth tier, a 21st-minute lead.

Viktor Gyokeres pulled Arsenal level after the break - but they could not kick on and were reduced to 10 men in the 86th minute when teenager Max Dowman kicked out following a challenge by Harrison Neal.

In the shootout, Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch saved Bruno Guimaraes' spot kick before Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty to spark scenes of ecstasy on the pitch and in the stands.

An upset as astonishing for its manner as it was for its proportions. Grimsby Town, a League Two side, beat top-flight Manchester United.

Not only did they win against Ruben Amorim's side, but they were 2-0 up after 30 minutes following goals from Charles Vernam and Tyrell Warren.

The visitors pulled one back through Bryan Mbeumo with 15 minutes to go and United looked like they might squeeze through when Harry Maguire went on to level in the 89th minute.

But an incredible shootout followed, with Clarke Oduor for Grimsby and Matheus Cunha for Manchester United missing the only penalties as each side's 11 took one.

The players then went again and, after Darragh Burns scored to make it 12-11, Mbeumo struck his second spot-kick against the crossbar.

Arne Slot made 10 changes to his Liverpool side after they had won an EFL Cup semi-final in their previous game and the Reds were made to pay.

Eight minutes after the interval, the Pilgrims were awarded a penalty after Harvey Elliott's handball and Ryan Hardie drilled home from the spot in emphatic fashion.

Hardie almost added a second shortly afterwards when his shot was turned on to the post by Liverpool keeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

The bottom club in the Championship held on, with Conor Hazard making crucial late saves, to beat a team who would go on to win the Premier League title.

Bradford ranked 49 places below their opponents as they travelled to Stamford Bridge to take on Chelsea, who at that point were top of the Premier League.

Gary Cahill and Ramires netted to put the hosts 2-0 up and give Chelsea firm control of the fourth-round tie.

Bradford had other ideas, though, as Jon Stead pulled one back before Filipe Morais side-footed in an equaliser.

Andy Halliday then blasted the Bantams ahead before Mark Yeats slotted a fourth to inflict a crushing defeat on Jose Mourinho's side.

Premier League giants Liverpool had ample strength at Boundary Park, with the likes of Luis Suarez, Raheem Sterling and Daniel Sturridge all starting.

League One hosts Oldham were in the midst of financial problems but produced a spirited display against the odds, with Matt Smith nodding in a Youssouf M'Changama cross to open the scoring.

Suarez levelled, but Smith soon took advantage of an error from Liverpool goalkeeper Brad Jones before Reece Wabara netted a back-post header to give the Latics a 3-1 lead.

Joe Allen volleyed home to pull one back and Liverpool brought on Steven Gerrard, but it was not enough to avoid defeat.

A fourth-tier side against Premier League opposition in the quarter-finals of the league cup - Arsenal were clear favourites.

Bradford had already caused an upset in the tournament, beating Wigan on penalties in the round before.

Up for a fight at home to Arsene Wenger's Gunners, Garry Thompson volleyed the Bantams ahead before Thomas Vermaelen headed home a Santi Cazorla cross with just two minutes of normal time remaining.

Just as Mbeumo missed the decisive kick for United against Grimsby after scoring in normal time, the same happened for Vermaelen here as Bradford prevailed 3-2 on spot-kicks.

Another surprise cup exit for Liverpool.

This one happened in the League Cup - at Anfield.

Milan Jovanovic fired in an opener for Liverpool, but Billy McKay equalised and Michael Jacobs tapped in to give the Cobblers a lead early in extra time.

David Ngog scored from a late header to set up the penalty drama, but Northampton were the victors from the spot, with Abdul Osman keeping his cool to slot in the decisive spot-kick.

Ruben Amorim at Grimsby was not the first Manchester United to suffer a shock in the League Cup - even Sir Alex Ferguson has faced the same.

The United boss didn't take the game lightly and made just four changes from the league game which they had played three days before, with the likes of David Beckham, Lee Sharpe and Ryan Giggs starting.

Paul Barnes, father of Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes, scored twice for Alan Little's visitors, including one from the penalty spot, before Tony Barras headed a third to inflict a crushing defeat at Old Trafford.

United put out another strong team at Bootham Crescent for the return leg two weeks later, with Eric Cantona in their squad, but despite getting two goals from Paul Scholes and another from Terry Cooke, the Minstermen went through 4-3 on aggregate thanks to a strike from Scott Jordan.

Arsenal were reigning First Division champions and second in the top flight.

Wrexham had finished 24th in the Fourth Division in the previous season.

The Gunners made the trip to Wales as firm favourites and were just 10 minutes from securing a spot in the fourth round after Alan Smith's first-half opener.

But Mickey Thomas sent a 25-yard free kick past David Seaman before Steve Watkin's strike earned victory for Wrexham just two minutes later.

Sutton United had a memorable cup run in 2016-17, beating three EFL teams - including Leeds United - before losing to Arsenal in the fifth round.

They have also produced one of the biggest shocks of all time.

The non-league side took on a Coventry team who were then in the First Division and had won the FA Cup in 1987.

The part-time side upset the odds at home, with Matthew Hanlan volleying home the winner just before the hour mark.

Top-flight Newcastle were beaten in the third round of the FA Cup by non-league opposition when they took on Hereford United in 1972.

Hereford took the tie to a replay after a 2-2 draw at St James' Park, but Newcastle looked destined to make it to the fourth round thanks to a late goal by Malcolm McDonald in the rematch.

However, the non-leaguers had other ideas and Ronnie Radford popped up to score the most famous 30-yard goal in FA Cup history to take the game into extra time.

Substitute Ricky George scored the winner - amid scenes of wild celebration at Edgar Street - as Hereford became the first non-league club to defeat a First Division side since 1949.

Unnamed celebrity accused of 'inappropriate sexual activities', court hears

A two-day trial is being held at the High Court in London

A celebrity has asked the High Court to prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations that he abused his status for many years to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".

The unnamed celebrity is seeking an injunction, and his legal team told the first day of a trial on Tuesday that any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself.

They told the court that his drastic reaction was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".

The man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them", the court heard.

The legal team for ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) told the court that the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be mitigated and there was no proper basis "to restrain the publication of public interest journalism".

A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".

The judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said there was "significant public interest" in the proceedings and that "this is a difficult and important case".

He added: "The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions."

Nicklin will not determine the truth or accuracy of the allegations, only whether they can be published.

He also urged the press and public not to speculate about the identity of the man, who is referred to in court as PPT.

"The existence of online speculation, however confidently expressed or widely repeated, does not authorise anyone to identify, or purport authoritatively to identify, PPT in connection with these proceedings," he said.

"Nor does repetition transform speculation into established fact."

Sara Mansoori KC, representing the man, told the court that any publication "would have a potentially fatal impact".

The barrister told the court: "The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life."

She said the man had made a suicide attempt after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his response to the allegations, and later absconded from hospital and attempted suicide for a second time.

She added in written submissions: "This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur.

"The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple - now more than 10 - doctors."

Mansoori also said the man "has no intention of returning to public life".

Gavin Millar KC, for ITN and GNM, said in written submissions that "numerous allegations" had been gathered during "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a "strong" public interest in publishing them.

He said reporters had spoken to more than 100 people, and that the resulting allegations "indicated a pattern of behaviour".

Millar later said many of the women "have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result".

He added that while the state may have a responsibility to protect life, applying that principle to this case would require the state to intervene in "lawful journalistic activities" to prevent "an autonomous act by the claimant himself".

Namibia take lead in ODI series against Ireland

Jan Frylinck top-scored for Namibia as they secured victory over Ireland

Third one-day international, Windhoek

Namibia 316-7 (50 overs): Frylinck 126, Erasmus 54, Kruger 42, Volschenck 36; McBrine 2-53, Campher 2-68

Ireland 253 all out (44.5 overs): Campher 106; Scholtz 2-31, Trumpelmann 2-37, Brassell 2-72

Ireland fell 2-1 behind in their five-match one-day international series against Namibia as they lost the third meeting between the sides by 63 runs in Windhoek on Tuesday.

Curtis Campher's century proved insufficient for the tourists, who were all out for 253 in the 45th over as they attempted to chase down their opponent's total of 316-7.

Ireland skipper Paul Stirling was unable to bat after injuring his finger in the field during the home side's innings.

Jan Frylinck shone for Namibia as he top-scored with 126 to lay the platform for the victory.

The sides will meet again on Friday and Sunday as Ireland continue their preparations for next year's World Cup qualifiers.

After winning the toss and opting to bat first, opener Louren Steenkamp's departure for 13 left Namibia 33-1.

When Malan Kruger (42) lost his wicket, the hosts sat 81-2 but a third-wicket partnership of 101 between Frylinck and captain Gerhard Erasmus (54) got their side back on track to achieve their impressive total.

Alex Volschenk chipped in with 36, while Campher and Andy McBrine were the pick of the Ireland bowlers with two wickets apiece.

In response, Ireland struggled at 56-4 before Campher's 106 off 86 balls put them in with a chance of securing what at one stage looked like an improbable victory.

Ultimately, their reply fell short however as wickets continued to fall regularly and they were all out with 31 balls of their innings still remaining.

article:
Prep time for Wallabies a challenge - Borthwick

Steve Borthwick won 57 caps for England as a player between 2001 and 2010

England coach Steve Borthwick says his players have tried to make most of limited preparation time for their Test against a comparatively battle-hardened Australia.

Borthwick has just finished working with his squad during a three-day training camp before they return to their club sides on Wednesday.

England face Australia in their opening match of this autumn's Nations Championship campaign at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Sunday, 8 November.

While England must balance their international preparations with the demands of the Premiership season, the Wallabies have much more time to focus on forthcoming matches.

Australia have played 10 Tests since July, including matches against South Africa and New Zealand.

"It's a case of doing more of less," Borthwick told BBC rugby union correspondent Chris Jones.

"Identifying the clear priorities and chasing them and not being side-tracked, not deviating from that.

"I think this is one of the challenges, particularly balancing the different stakeholders [the clubs and the national set-up]."

England's Feyi-Waboso set to return to action

Pepper to miss England games and Carreras' season over

England's preparations have also been affected by the Prem schedule, with players involved in Sunday's fixtures having less time for full squad training.

"We had a session today really that was affected obviously by the fact that we had a Sunday game in Prem Rugby," Borthwick explained.

"Fortunately, we don't have any Sunday games this coming week in Prem Rugby, which I'm pleased about.

"So that should allow players to be recovered in a proper run into the Test match."

Borthwick acknowledged the challenge of balancing club and international commitments, but said playing at the weekend could benefit England.

"They'll go back and play the rugby and in so many ways that will be a positive for us for next weekend," he said.

"The players are match fit at club level, playing regularly at club level, and as long as they don't get injured, then they're all available for selection next week, then that will be positive.

"I'd say on one side, I think it's a real strength of English rugby that the players have such great loyalty and passion for their clubs as we saw very evidently in this last round with the derbies that went on.

"They are team-mates and best of mates the next day for a couple of days [with England] and then they go back to being rivals again until they come back into camp next week."

Borthwick also identified the breakdown as an area where England need to adapt to the demands of international rugby.

He pointed to the recent European fixtures, in which English clubs collectively lost more of their own breakdown ball and won less opposition breakdown ball than teams from other competing nations.

"Part of my job is identify those bits of where I need to bridge from where the players are in Prem rugby to where they are in Test rugby," he said.

"The level of competition [at the breakdown] is at a different level in Test rugby."

article:
Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned

Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned.

Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year.

The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service.

But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

Labour MP Torcuil Crichton, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: "Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines."

He said that "when the power goes out people don't have the phone, they don't have the internet and often they don't have a mobile signal either".

Retail service providers have been giving back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers, which can keep landline phones operating for an hour or more.

But Crichton said this was "simply not adequate" and that mobile phone providers "simply don't have the means to maintain or keep their signal going during storms".

He urged the minister to get telecoms firms to "up their digital game" to protect places "on the edge where people are vulnerable, isolated from their neighbours, where the ambulance is an hour away and the storm is 70 miles an hour".

Similar concerns were raised by MPs from the West Country and the Lake District.

Markus Campbell-Savours, Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, said: "I ask the minister to imagine an elderly constituent living alone in an isolated Lake District valley where copper phone lines have been replaced by fibre.

"A storm takes out the power to their router in the night and by the time they wake, the modest battery back up has failed, as has the mobile mast, does the minister share my concerns that they would have no way to raise an alarm in an emergency and agree that we need a new technological solution to protect the elderly?"

'We won't be able to use our phones if we have a power cut'

Switchover must protect most vulnerable - MPs

Conservative MP Julian Lewis also raised concerns about the lack of a "back-up system" if digital phone services go down in the event of a cyber attack or other emergency.

He told Jarvis the copper-wire network "could have given us useful levels of resilience in an emergency".

Jarvis, who is spearheading the government's Be Ready campaign, which is advising people to stock up on supplies to be prepared for emergencies , said he would "look very closely" at the Tory MP's point.

He also assured West Country MPs that their concerns would be addressed at a government resilience summit, which was due to take place in Cornwall next month, and promised to raise concerns about telecoms firms with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.

"Our telephone networks are a vital part of our critical national infrastructure and our emergency response in weather-related crisis supports the functioning of essential services and keeping people connected when they need it most," he told MPs.

The government says the switch to digital phone services is needed because the traditional analogue network is becoming increasingly unreliable.

Digital signals will be sent over copper telephone wires where they have not yet been replaced by fibre connections.

The government's Be Ready campaign advises people , external who have not yet "migrated to a modern digital network" to contact their landline provider.

"If you are a vulnerable customer, for example if you are a telecare user, your communication provider must provide a free back‑up battery unit," it adds.

Murder accused tells court 'I'm terribly sorry' for zombie knife killing

Tristan Kerr killing: Connor Palfrey, Ricardo Elliot, and Elexi Manny all deny murder by joint enterprise

A drug dealer accused of murdering a 17-year-old has told a court: "I'm terribly sorry. I didn't mean to kill him."

Georgie Mears, 19, of Thornhill, Cardiff, is accused of attacking Tristan Kerr with a 13.5cm (5.3in) zombie knife in February.

Mears had gone to a property in Abertridwr, Caerphilly county, to deliver two £25 bags of ketamine to Kerr in February, Newport Crown Court heard.

There, he said, Kerr tried to attack him.

Mears, along with Connor Palfrey, 25, from Abertridwr, Ricardo Elliot, 27, of no fixed abode, and Elexi Manny, 25, from Senghenydd, Caerphilly, deny murder by joint enterprise.

Kerr died after being stabbed through the heart and lung.

The moment he collapsed and died was caught on the doorbell camera of a house further down Lower Francis Street.

"I honestly thought he was going to stab me," Mears said.

He said he was concerned when he went into the living room with the drugs and saw three other men there.

"There was a weird atmosphere, it was unsettling," he said. "I heard someone say, 'Chuck it here'.

"Tristan was moving towards me. The way he was walking, it was meaningful, not how you would approach someone if you were going to speak to them."

Kerr tried to punch him twice before pushing the defendant against a wall, Mears told the court.

A knife in Kerr's waistband became visible during the scuffle, the jury heard.

Mears said he knew Kerr had a history of knife use, and had seen a Snapchat video of him chasing Palfrey with a blade and a dog.

Connor Palfrey, Elexi Manny, Georgie Mears and Ricardo Elliot all deny the murder of Tristan Kerr

Mears said he took the knife out of fear.

He said: "I just stabbed him. If I didn't stab him he would have stabbed me. I feared for my safety.

"I knew he had a history of carrying knives and being a violent person. I genuinely thought he was about to attack me."

Mears, who the court heard had multiple driving offence convictions, demonstrated how he stabbed Kerr with a knife which he said was not his.

It did not seem, he said, to have any effect.

But as he drove away with his co-defendants he said he had an increasingly "sick feeling" about what had happened.

Mears told Chris Rees KC, defending him, that he just wanted to get out of the property and panicked when he saw the front room door handle was missing.

He told the court: "I was scared, I just wanted to get out of the room. There was no handle on the door.

"The only way was to go out through all these men."

The case continues.

article:
How much of Antonelli's success is down to his ability? - F1 Q&A

Kimi Antonelli's race engineer Peter 'Bono' Bonnington previously worked with Lewis Hamilton when he was at Mercedes

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is one step closer to becoming the new F1 world champion after winning the United States Grand Prix from pole position.

The 20-year-old Italian, who leads team-mate George Russell by 123 points in the standings, will secure the title in Mexico City on Sunday by finishing ninth or higher.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race in Austin.

Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'

This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - Julian

The dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.

In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.

Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.

He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.

But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.

The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.

As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.

On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.

Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year.

"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.

"We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."

Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.

However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.

The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.

So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.

This video can not be played

'He doesn't feel pressure!' - Antonelli making it look easy

With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - Liam

Lewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa.

"I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said.

"So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."

Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.

Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".

The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.

Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.

Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.

As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.

Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.

First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.

Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year .

But Bearman has higher ambitions than staying at Haas for the rest of his career.

If Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be at Ferrari for the next four years, Bearman would have every right to be asking the team what that means for him.

If he isn't going to get into the senior team, what can they do to further his career? Do they let him go, so he can pursue his ambitions elsewhere, or do they allow him to do that while still maintaining links?

These questions become even more pressing for Bearman now Brazilian Rafael Camara - also a Ferrari young driver - is joining Haas for 2027.

Bearman needs to beat the Brazilian if he is not to face an existential threat to his future as a potential driver for a top team.

Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'

Antonelli superb and Leclerc close to perfect - driver ratings

US GP Review: Antonelli is made to wait

What's been happening with Alex Albon this season? Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz seems to have the better of him, and the car doesn't look to be in a good place. - David

Of the two Williams drivers, in a team that is struggling, Carlos Sainz has had the better season.

But it's not as stark as it perhaps appears just looking on the surface.

Sainz leads Albon by two points in the championship, and while the qualifying comparison is skewed heavily towards Sainz on a head-to-head basis at 13-5, the time gap between them is 0.115 seconds.

As if Albon was not already having a rough season, to top it he incurred the wrath of Fernando Alonso in Austin after the two collided on the first lap, leaving both with damaged cars.

Alonso said: "The quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex."

Williams are in such a state this year that comparing the drivers should be treated with a degree of qualification.

The car has been slow, and the team have struggled with consistency between parts, as well as quality and degradation.

In other words, two parts that should perform the same have not always done so, and some of them wear out and lose performance quicker than others.

Of course that works across both drivers but it does make comparisons difficult.

Albon was asked about the comparison with Sainz in qualifying in Monza last month.

He pointed out that the crash he had in Canada when he hit a groundhog had been costly because there was a new engine in the car that weekend, which was written off. That meant he had to run an old engine longer than ideal.

And he alluded to Williams suffering from the same issues with varying engine performance that happened in the early days of the new engine rules at Mercedes and McLaren.

"There's a few things," Albon said. "In the beginning of the year, it was very battery-dominated.

"If you think even just the George and Kimi situation, that's the manufacturer side of it having issues. So you can imagine it's not just them two that have had problems.

"There's been a few qualifying sessions where the corners have been good, but you don't see it in the lap time. It's on the stopwatch.

"And then we're also going through our own issues as a team. And that's not just on my side. There's also a side where to say that both cars are performing in the same way would not be true. We've been fighting some inconsistencies in the cars that's been there since the beginning of the year.

"We're much better now at getting on top of them. If you look at the last four or five weekends, we're actually very close in terms of performance. But it's taken a while to get there."

Alex Albon, in 19th, is two points behind Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz

Do you foresee a world in which live F1 coverage ever returns to free-to-air telly in the UK or is it now stuck behind a paywall for eternity? I've now taken a different career path but becoming an engineer in F1 was my ultimate ambition when I was applying for university in the early 2010s, inspired by BBC's live coverage. - Ian

In the UK, the current situation is that Sky has exclusive rights to broadcast F1 behind a paywall, while Channel 4 has highlights on free-to-air television, with live coverage of the British Grand Prix.

Sky has the rights until the end of 2034, after it struck a new deal for a larger fee earlier this year.

That came in the wake of Apple buying the US rights starting from this season.

At the same time, the television market is in flux as streaming becomes increasingly prevalent as a means of consuming content.

In that context, as well as the wider sports broadcast situation, it's hard to imagine a situation where F1 could return fully to free-to-air television.

The wider picture is it is still on free-to-air in some countries - Brazil as an example.

But F1 would also argue free-to-air does not always mean more people getting sight of the sport, depending on how it's promoted in various ways, and viewing habits are not the same in all countries.

Social media output is also an important consideration. At the same time, F1 is a business that exists to make money.

Williams loses again - to opponent 28 years younger

Former world number one Venus Williams lost her 16th singles match in a row as she was beaten by an opponent 28 years younger at the Guangzhou Open.

The 46-year-old American, who has won seven Grand Slam singles titles, was beaten 6-2 6-2 by 18-year-old Lilli Tagger on Tuesday.

It is the biggest age gap between opponents in a WTA match this decade and among the largest in tour-level history.

Williams, ranked 599th in the world, has not won a match since July 2025 and relies on wildcards to play WTA tournaments.

This latest defeat continues the debate over whether she deserves them.

Some within the sport argue Williams is taking spots from younger players trying to develop their careers, but tournament organisers see the commercial value of inviting an all-time great.

The Guangzhou fans clearly appreciated the chance to see the American superstar. A sizeable and enthusiastic crowd encouraged Williams and gave a huge ovation as she walked off court.

Williams hasn't won for over a year - why does she get so many wildcards?

Williams sisters exit US Open but excite - what does future hold?

Williams won six of her Grand Slam singles titles - plus 30 WTA tournaments - before Austria's Tagger was born in February 2008.

Tagger's coach Francesca Schiavone - the Italian former world number four who won the 2010 French Open - is the same age as Williams, and lost all eight meetings with the American during her playing career.

"When I saw the draw I was super excited and a bit nervous - I respect her a lot," said Tagger, who is 53rd in the world.

"It is funny she used to play with my coach. I would love to play at this age - I want to congratulate her."

While the straight-set scoreline will embolden the critics, Williams did make Tagger - a rising talent who is predicted to have a bright future at the very top - work hard.

However, the teenager proved far too good. The 2025 French Open girls' champion was superb on serve - dropping just seven service points and not facing a break point - while handling Williams' pace and crushing groundstrokes off both wings.

Tagger broke her illustrious opponent's serve twice - for 1-0 and 5-2 leads - in two almost identical sets.

At times, Williams was able to use her powerful serve to get out of trouble - fighting off 12 of 16 break points - and the veteran's trademark competitive spirit never wavered.

But it was another example of how far behind the rest of the tour she now is.

Council rejects rollercoaster overlooking homes

Residents in Sandford Lane have complained about the rollercoaster

Plans to keep a rollercoaster overlooking homes in Nottinghamshire have been refused by a council.

The prototype has been erected at a former aerodrome near Sandford Lane, in Hucknall, prompting complaints from residents about noise, visual impact and a loss of privacy.

Ashfield District Council rejected a retrospective application by fairground operator Mellors Group , external to use Grade II listed hangars at the Watnall Road site as a rollercoaster testing and storage site on 20 October.

The firm said it would appeal against the decision and believed there had been a "misunderstanding of what we are seeking to achieve and hope to work towards an outcome that addresses the concerns raised".

The authority said the site would be "incongruous" and allow rollercoasters of "excessive scale" to have an "overbearing and oppressive" presence in the area.

Mellors Group wants to use the hangars as a rollercoaster testing and storage site

The buildings were first constructed in 1916 and used by the RAF and Rolls-Royce for the development of new and experimental aircraft technologies.

Mellors Group, the company behind Nottingham's Winter Wonderland and city beach attractions, submitted the change of use application on 25 August.

The application was submitted after Ashfield District Council said it had received reports from local residents that the buildings were being used for purposes which were "not in line with the approved planning use class for the land".

Application documents show the site was previously classed as being used for storage only, but was actually being used for both storage and manufacturing.

The application form states the change in use had started on 1 June 2025 without consent , external and involves the test assembly, dismantling and maintenance of amusement attractions within the existing site, including the use of the listed hangars and external operational areas.

The site began to change in June 2025

In the council's decision notice rejecting the change in use, the authority said rollercoasters would "detract the setting and appreciation" of the hangars at the aerodrome site.

Concerns were raised that workers repairing and inspecting rollercoasters at height could result in an "unacceptable perception and loss of privacy for neighbouring occupiers".

The notice also said the application had failed to demonstrate the planned rollercoaster testing depot could operate without negatively impacting its neighbours and the planned use had "potential to generate significant noise".

Concerns were raised about privacy for nearby homes

James Mellor, director of the Mellors Group, said there had been "delays" with sending off the rollercoaster to be painted before being put out for public use.

"It's been a very, very difficult year with multiple different issues, especially issues we've had at the Middle East," said Mellor.

Mellor said war in the region was causing shipping delays for materials and preventing work from taking place.

He added: "So it's just been there a lot longer than what was ever anticipated, even on our behalf. We want the coaster out as quick as possible."

Mellor added he wanted the change of use to be able to "work on other rides".

"Most rides are nowhere near the size of the coaster," he said. "A lot of things will actually be done below the fence line where people can't see.

"We don't want the coaster there any longer than they do because it doesn't make us any money while it's having work done on it in storage."

The news of her arrest came amid a major investigation into a number of vandalism attacks across Salford, Tameside, and Stockport.

Police are investigating about 50 incidents in which HMOs and family homes have been vandalised and cars targeted.

Jordan has struck what its military says were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation for an attack on a Christian funeral last week that killed nine people.

Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists", without giving further details.

Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified of Monday's attack.

It comes after nine people were killed and 34 injured in a shooting at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak on Friday.

In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan.

"The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, to ensure the safety of travellers and workers at the crossing," Syrian authorities said in a statement carried by state media.

It added that it had "opened direct channels of communication" with Jordanian officials and had launched "comprehensive investigations to establish the full circumstances of the targeting".

Nassib is the only passenger and commercial border crossing between Jordan and Syria.

Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law over the church attack.

The Public Security Directorate (PSD) said the unnamed "terrorists" were found hiding in an abandoned house in Karak before dawn.

Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told state-affiliated TV the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".
