Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88

Peter Jackson's 1994 film of the events starred Melanie Lynskey (left) as Pauline Parker and Kate Winslet as Juliet Hulme

To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray.

But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial.

As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker.

The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world.

The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way.

They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking.

This video can not be played

The teenage killers who started new lives in Scotland

By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good.

"It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to Christchurch, New Zealand, to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995.

"Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends."

Pauline Parker (middle) and Juliet Hulme (right) were tried together in Christchurch

His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder.

The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age.

In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand.

The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart.

Parker was just 16 when she was tried for her mother's murder

When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry.

She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film.

"It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing."

"It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you."

During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity.

"These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said.

"I hope she is never found."

But Parker was found - by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court.

She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school.

By 2004, now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney and was running another stable when her identity was discovered.

Her friend Louise Scott told the BBC that it was a "shock" to discover her past but people in Burray and South Ronaldsay just decided to accept her as the woman they had known before they found out.

Scott said Hilary was "mortified and saddened" that she had been tracked down because she thought she had found somewhere where she could live out her life in peace.

"She went and hid in her farm and wouldn't come out," Scott said.

"Quite a few of us went up to the farm and I had to talk to her through the letterbox to assure her that nothing had changed as far as we were concerned.

"After a wee bit of persuasion, she did eventually decide to stay.

"She just went back to being Hilary and we all just carried on.

"We all liked her and accepted her for the woman we knew she was."

Scott said Nathan lived an "incredibly frugal" lifestyle.

"She was religious and she devoted her whole life to helping other people," she said.

For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven.

While Nathan was a devout Catholic, Perry was a Mormon, who enjoyed the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released.

She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family."

Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion.

Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason.

Juliet Hulme became a successful crime author under the name Anne Perry

In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world.

"I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades."

We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is.

"Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted.

"Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position.

"The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had."

Anne Perry became a successful crime writer

Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 84.

Hilary Nathan's death last week brings their strange story to a close.

How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities.

"I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me.

"There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think."

Murderer-turned-novelist Anne Perry dies aged 84

More than third of deaths of ex-prisoners on probation drug related, says report

The report's author Dr Robert Jones says there is a lack of debate about finding a solution to the problem of drug-related deaths

More than a third of deaths of former prisoners on probation in Wales in a year were drug related, according to a new report.

This was higher than across England and Wales combined, where just over a fifth of total deaths were drug related.

The Wales Governance Centre at Cardiff University published the report and urged politicians to tackle "systematic failures" in the criminal justice system.

Report author Dr Robert Jones called on the UK and Welsh governments to find a solution to the "tragic" situation.

The Welsh government said it was working to reduce "harms caused by substance misuse", while the UK government said it was spending £3.4m to support prison leavers to overcome addiction.

According to the report, 37% of all deaths among prison leavers supervised by probation in Wales in 2024-25 were drug related.

The number of drug poisonings where the intent was "undetermined" in Wales accounted for 19 of the 52 who died.

Jones said this was "substantially higher" than the proportion across England and Wales as a whole, where deaths in this same category accounted for just over a fifth (21%) of the total - 131 out of 620.

Criminal justice in Wales is controlled by Westminster.

The Plaid Cymru Welsh government, and the previous Labour administration in Cardiff before it, argue it should be devolved.

Speaking to BBC Wales, Jones said the research looked at UK government data including Freedom of Information requests.

He said: "The added shock value to this is that these data point towards some systematic failures with incredibly tragic circumstances and consequences.

"Yet there isn't really a particular debate or discussion ongoing at the moment about these deaths, and indeed their causes, and how we might actually find a solution to them."

Jones said many areas of social policy, including "responsibility for tackling substance use, housing, education and local government" were devolved to the Welsh government.

"So what tends to happen is that criminal justice matters can often fall between the gaps between debates in the Senedd and debates in Westminster," he added.

Jones said the report raised "important questions about the current devolution settlement and whether the Welsh government has the powers and levers necessary to address the underlying causes of many of the challenges facing Wales".

He added: "Only by confronting the realities highlighted throughout this report can politicians and policymakers hope to overcome the many challenges facing communities across Wales."

The Welsh government has called for control of prisons and other parts of the criminal justice system to be devolved

David Bennett, from Wallich, Wales's largest homelessness charity, claimed most drug-related deaths "are preventable if we treat drug use as a health, not criminal justice, issue".

"Housing, health and justice need a joined-up approach," he said.

He said the charity supported "conversations to devolve justice and policing" and said without "co-ordinated" support prison leavers were "being set up to fail".

"The war on drugs hasn't worked," he added.

The report also says homelessness among former prisoners in Wales is continuing to rise.

The number of people leaving prison, supervised by Welsh probation services, who were recorded as rough sleeping on the day of their release rose by 24% in 2025-26.

In total, 695 prison leavers managed by Welsh probation services were rough sleeping on the day of their release.

Other findings include that more than a third (39%) of all custodial sentences given to women in Wales in 2025 were for offences related to thefts from shops.

Meanwhile, people from black ethnic groups in Wales remained the most overrepresented ethnic group in the prison population in 2025.

There were 58 black people from Wales in prison for every 10,000 of the population, compared with 15 white people per 10,000 of the population.

A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "Every drug-related death is a tragedy.

"We are working closely with health boards, local authorities, Public Health Wales and other key partners to reduce the harms caused by substance misuse, focusing on early intervention, prevention, treatment and recovery support."

They added that the findings "strengthen the case for the full devolution of justice to Wales".

"Bringing responsibility for justice into line" with devolved services "would enable a more effective and joined-up approach to improving outcomes, reducing reoffending and building safer communities across Wales", the spokesperson added.

That suggestion was dismissed by Reform Senedd member Adrian Mason.

"The idea that the answer to drug deaths is more devolution is demonstrably wrong, as proven by Scotland," he said.

"In Scotland, justice is devolved and run by nationalists, and they have the highest drug death rates in the whole of Europe .

"The people of Wales expect politicians to get on with the day job rather than pushing for more and more powers at every turn."

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We inherited prisons in crisis but we're acting on all fronts, including by reducing the number of women in custody through investment in community services and cutting the flow of drugs into prisons.

"In Wales we invest more than £3.4m into services which work across prisons, probation and courts to help support prison leavers overcome their addiction."

They added that prisoners at risk of becoming homeless can be offered temporary accommodation by the prison and probation service.

Chair of the Welsh Affairs Committee at Westminster, Ruth Jones, said: "It is devastating to hear that more than a third of all deaths among prison leavers in Wales were due to drug poisoning, and that the number of homeless prison leavers in Wales has increased.

"The data underscores the findings of our inquiry that reported earlier this year: the prison and probation system is struggling with increasingly complex demand, which has serious implications for rehabilitation outcomes."

She added: "Improving Wales-specific justice data is something my committee has consistently pressed the UK government on, and in light of several of Dr Jones' data requests to the Ministry of Justice not receiving a response, it is clear that there is still work to be done here."

Additional reporting by David Deans.

article:
Opposition leader María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump

This video can not be played

Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exile

Driving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, María Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.

Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.

She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration, which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.

Now, it appears, it is.

"María Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."

Gregory Noriega

"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out onto the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap.

"She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel. "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared."

Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.

Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty.

He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined.

The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro.

The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides.

When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.

The Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil.

The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.

Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.

President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".

But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcón.

"The return of María Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcón. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country."

"The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.

Alarcón provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.

Political analyst Beningno Alarcón

For instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.

Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.

In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.

Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution.

Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".

The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.

Young supporters of María Corina Machado

Having made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.

She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.

But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.

For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy.

Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.

The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer María Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing.

Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.

Additional reporting by Vanessa Silva in Caracas.

Parents who killed their baby have sentences increased

Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, were jailed in April

A couple who "fatally battered" their three-month-old son have had their "unduly lenient" sentences for murder increased.

Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, from Wirral, Merseyside, were sentenced in April to a minimum of 19 years and 15 years in April over the death of their son, 13-week-old Miguel.

The Court of Appeal has now increased Klevi Pirjani's sentence to 21 years and six months, while Nivalda Pirjani will have to serve 17 years and nine months.

Miguel was taken to Alder Hey children's hospital in November 2024. He had severe head injuries and died five days after being admitted.

Miguel was found to have suffered 41 separate bone fractures in at least four separate incidents.

The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves, referred their sentences to the Court of Appeal, with barristers for the government arguing that the original sentences did not "meet the justice of this terrible case".

Lord Justice Jeremy Baker, sitting with Mr Justice Goose and Mr Justice Hilliard, said the pair subjected their son to "routine" assaults which increased in severity, and culminated in his "particularly callous" murder.

He said: "We take the view that the resulting sentences significantly underestimated the aggravating factors, to the extent that not only do we consider that the minimum terms were unduly lenient, but that we should set them aside."

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, for the Attorney General, said in written submissions that Miguel's death was caused by an assault by his parents on 24 November 2024, which involved "a heavy blow, or series of blows, to the right side of his head".

Paramedics arrived two minutes after his parents called 999 following Miguel suffering a cardiac arrest at their home in Percy Road, Seacombe, Merseyside, but he never regained consciousness and was pronounced dead five days later.

Emlyn Jones said that while the boy was in hospital, a "wider picture of long-standing physical abuse emerged", including the discovery of multiple fractured ribs, fractured legs and a fractured sternum suffered across several incidents before the fatal attack.

He also said that while it could not be ascertained whether Klevi Pirjani or Nivalda Pirjani inflicted the fatal violence, "whichever it was, they did so with the encouragement of their partner".

Sentencing them in March, Mr Justice Andrew Baker said the pair were "in this together, encouraging each other" to attack their "defenceless" son.

He said that who "fatally battered" the infant "remains the guilty secret of a warped relationship, in which you came first for each other to an unnatural degree".

Rupert Bowers KC, for Nivalda Pirjani, acknowledged in court that "of course" her sentence was lenient, but that the sentencing judge "considered all of the factors".

He said: "There is nothing that would indicate that the sentences he passed are beyond the ambit of reasonableness, or an error of principle, so that this court should interfere with his exercise of discretion, having heard all the evidence."

Sarah Vine KC, for Klevi Pirjani, also said her client's sentence was "undoubtedly lenient, but not unduly, and leniency in itself is not a vice".

Klevi and Nivalda Pirjani, watching proceedings from HMP Wakefield in Yorkshire and HMP Styal in Cheshire respectively, showed no reaction as their sentences were increased.

article:
MPs and MSP detained by Israel and barred from entering West Bank

Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens, SNP MP Lara Bird and Labour MP Clive Lewis said they were detained by Israeli authorities for eight hours

Two MPs and an MSP have said they were detained by Israeli authorities for eight hours while trying to enter the West Bank.

SNP MP Lara Bird, Labour MP Clive Lewis and Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens said they were prevented from entering the territory on Monday before being questioned and eventually turned away.

Bird said they had intended to "stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land" after travelling as part of a Progressive International delegation.

A spokesperson for the Israeli embassy in the UK claimed the group "failed to cooperate with border officials" and provided "false information about the purpose of their visit".

The Israeli military announced on Monday that all West Bank land crossings would be closed as part of increased security measures during Tuesday's national elections .

Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, said the 23-strong group was "interrogated and ultimately prevented from crossing" the King Hussein Bridge between Jordan and the West Bank.

Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy

She said the group had their passports seized before they were taken one-by-one for individual interviews by Israeli border security.

Bird claimed these featured "a lot of shouting and screaming".

During her interview, Bird said she was accused of "hating Israel".

She said the delegation was made to wait for a further period before being told they were not allowed to cross and were put on a bus back to the Jordanian border.

She told BBC Scotland News: "It was an exercise in intimidation and fear.

"They said they had evidence that I hate Israel and that, I think, was one of the reasons they didn't want to let us in."

Lewis, who represents Norwich South, said the group had been "made to feel as though they had done something wrong" in a post on X.

He added: "We knew that by crossing into the occupied Palestinian territories, we risked being detained, interrogated and turned away by Israeli authorities. And that, alas, is exactly what happened.

"The simple truth is we had done nothing wrong. We went to show our support for the Palestinian people and highlight the terrible injustice and violence being perpetrated against them."

Nevens described the experience as "frightening" but added that the group was able to "leave safely".

She said: "What we experienced was only a small fraction of the terrifying reality Palestinians face when they try to cross the same border to reach their families or simply go about their lives."

About 2,000 Palestinian residents have been displaced in Hebron, a city in the southern West Bank, in recent days.

Footage shared online appeared to show one street being completely flattened by bulldozers .

That came as a reprisal for the killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinian gunmen.

Several other attacks on Palestinians during the annual olive harvest have also been reported in the run-up to the elections.

They are the first since the 7 October Hamas-led attack on Israel in 2023.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the Commons the UK government was "deeply concerned" about MPs and MSP being denied access to the West Bank.

He said the government had raised the issue with the Israeli authorities and had been in touch with the MPs to offer assistance.

"More broadly, it's very, very important that members of this House, as they go about their business – not just in the UK but internationally – have free access so that they can actually do their duties," he said.

A spokesperson for the SNP said the party was "proud to stand with the Palestinian people".

Funeral assault dad arrested after court no-show

Cole Robert Worthy, on the right, was one of seven killed in a head-on crash with a police car

The father of one of the victims of a fatal head-on crash, which also killed two police officers, has been arrested again after failing to turn up at court over an assault at his own son's funeral.

Gye Worthy, 40, was due to be sentenced for common assault against a celebrant at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough on 9 September.

At the time he was attending the funeral of his son Cole, 17, one of seven who died when the Volkswagen Passat he was in hit a marked police car on the A66 in South Bank on 22 August.

An arrest warrant was issued when Worthy failed to turn up at Teesside Crown Court on Tuesday where he was due to be sentenced for the assault and resisting arrest.

The court heard Worthy, of Ruskin Avenue, Middlesbrough, had not spoken to his solicitors or explained his absence to the court.

He was also due to be sentenced for stealing four bottles of wine worth £30 from a shop on 8 October.

Deputy District Judge Julia Baggs agreed to an application by the prosecution for a warrant to be issued, "not backed by bail", which meant he would be held in custody ahead of any future court date.

Prior to the A66 crash the Worthy family home had been rammed

Worthy previously admitted assaulting celebrant Paul Maull during the funeral service for his son, which was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.

PC Blades had been travelling along the A66 with his colleague PC Tom Clough when their car was struck head-on by the Passat travelling in the wrong direction.

The pair were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered a camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit which preceded the crash, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The others killed in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-old Theo Rae.

It later emerged the Worthy family home in Acklam had been rammed by a car shortly before the A66 crash.

Healey to promise £15m to tackle misogyny in Budget

Chancellor John Healey has pledged to give £15m to a fund established to tackle misogyny in schools, at work and in communities.

The government said the money will be provided over three years to schemes such as mentoring for young people, workplace training and communications campaigns designed to improve women and girls' safety.

Speaking on the eve of his first Budget, Healey said: "Every woman and girl deserves to feel safe, respected and able to pursue their ambitions - at school, at work and in their communities."

But Conservative shadow women and equalities minister Joy Morrissey said "not a single woman and girl is going to feel safer with this total waste of public money".

The "misogyny prevention fund" is expected to be confirmed in the Budget and is intended to support the work of a national taskforce established last month , external and chaired by Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson.

Healey said the money will support "practical action to tackle misogyny head-on" and he hopes it will attract additional funding from businesses and philanthropists to increase its reach.

Phillipson said daily incidents of misogyny, including sexist slurs and workplace discrimination, have "no place in modern Britain".

She said: "This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs."

Phillipson added that "everyone, from big business to members of the public, can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere".

When launching the taskforce chaired by Phillipson, the government said last month that it would aim to ensure government policy is "shaped by those most affected by misogyny".

It added its first meeting would focus on young people and later look at "workplaces, digital spaces and social cohesion".

Statistics published by the Office for National Statistics this month showed an estimated 12.8% of females aged 16 and over in England and Wales - around 3.2m - experienced at least one of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation or stalking in the year to March 2026.

The figure was an estimated 8.9% for males - around 2.1m.

For the Conservatives, Morrissey cited the estimates for women and girls as she criticised the announcement.

She said: "Labour simply aren't serious about tackling the crisis of violence against women and girls.

"This week it seems they will get the hard-pressed British taxpayer to fork out £15m to fund projects to tackle the 'manosphere'."

A tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.

The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".

The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.

The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.

The species nests independently and relies on the saltmarsh plant called sea aster for food

The sea aster mining bee has a particular taste in flowers and relies on the sea aster, a pink and yellow flower that blooms on coastal marshes, as summer moves into autumn.

The restoration project at Steart Marshes was completed in 2014, transforming former farmland into a coastal wetland by allowing seawater to flow back across the fields.

We're just tax-collectors, say pub landlords asking for help

The reserve supports a wide variety of coastal wildflowers, including plenty of sea aster, which is thought to have finally attracted the bees to the Steart peninsula.

"There were lots of them and several colonial nest areas in the dry sandy ground," said Phillips.

"At the time I thought they were only found in salt marsh areas around the Thames estuary."

Steart Marshes are an example of how restoring saltmarshes can boost wildlife

Of the 290 invertebrate species found in these habitats across the UK, 148 can only be found in saltmarshes.

Site manager Bay Alys Laver said: "People usually associate saltmarshes with huge flocks of wading birds, geese and ducks, but there is so much life here that goes unnoticed.

"Spotting such a rare species here is a testament to the brilliant work our staff do in maintaining the reserve in concert with local graziers.

"I was so happy to hear that we have been found by our first sea aster mining bees."

article:
'My home lost half its value due to Raac'

Yvette Hoskins is campaigning for affected private homeowners to receive financial support

A Dundee woman whose flat lost half of its value following the discovery of potentially dangerous concrete in the building has said private homeowners must receive financial help to repair affected properties.

A £21.6m repair scheme for Dundee council properties affected by Raac (reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete) has been approved by councillors.

However, 237 privately-owned properties in the affected buildings will have to contribute to the cost of the repair work.

Yvette Hoskins, who sold her flat in a Raac-affected building for £55,000 despite its £100,000 value, said the experience was "daunting and devastating".

The local authority said 783 properties within 171 cottages and 74 blocks of flats were affected.

Work on the scheme is expected to begin in January. It follows a £500,000 pilot project last year involving five unoccupied properties that were affected.

Craigie Drive is one of five areas affected by Raac in Dundee

Yvette, who lived at a flat in the Craigie area of the city with her husband and two children, managed to sell the property after an initial sale fell through.

The family had been in the process of selling their flat when the material was found in the block's roof.

The property was on the market for more than a year.

"Our future home fell through, because we were unable to purchase it," she said. "The whole experience was extremely daunting, devastating, emotional, tearful.

"We could not believe that we had to sell our property at such a low price, it was super difficult."

Yvette said the flat eventually sold for just over half of its value.

"The lowest price we were offered was £35,000 on a property valued at £100,000," she said.

Yvette, who chairs the Dundee Raac Campaign Group, is calling for private homeowners to receive financial help for their share of the repairs.

She said: "A lot of homeowners still believe they were mis-sold their properties.

"They bought their properties in good faith with no knowledge of Raac."

She said they had also never been informed of Raac being present in the properties.

"They are very angry that nothing is being made available to them at a local authority level or a government level," she said.

"They have no support, they face a lifetime of debt, their homes are their lifelines."

'RAAC in our roof has robbed us of our retirement'

What is RAAC concrete and why is it a safety risk?

Pilot project aims to make homes safe from faulty concrete

At Monday's meeting, when the repair scheme was approved, Yvette asked councillors to consider alternative options.

This included full Raac removal from homes or a buy-back scheme allowing private owners to sell their properties to the council.

Council officers said a buy-back scheme would not be viable.

Dundee City Council leader Mark Flynn put forward an amendment during the meeting.

This asked the chief executive to write to Angela Rayner, the UK government's secretary of state for housing, and the Scottish government's housing secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, to seek financial support and a dedicated funding mechanism for owner-occupiers affected by Raac.

He also asked for assurances that work carried out to remediate Raac would be accepted by both mortgage providers and insurers.

The move was unanimously backed by councillors.

More stories from Tayside and Central

More stories from Scotland

Raac, a cheaper alternative to standard concrete , was used mostly in flat roofing but also in floors and walls between the 1950s and 1990s.

However, it is less durable and susceptible to structural failure when exposed to moisture.

Dundee councillors were told the pilot repairs demonstrated that the preferred "fully supported" remediation approach was "technically viable" across a range of house types and could be delivered using conventional materials and construction methods.

The system uses plywood, timber joists and, where required, steel beams to provide support beneath the Raac so that it no longer performs a structural function.

article:
Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase

The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.

Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.

Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.

"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:

"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."

The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27.

That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.

Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to £13.20, the Times said.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.

"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."

The government has also announced a number of measures, including removing import taxes on some food and ending the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments.

It says removing tariffs from 100 food items could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June.

"We're not going to say it is everything," Reynolds told the BBC, but taken alongside the changes implemented in the summer on goods such as pasta, fruit juice and tuna, he said it would save around £500m a year.

Other measures the government announced on Tuesday included:

Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030

Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period

And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier

Speaking to the BBC's Newscast, Healey said: "None of this is going to change the world. But if it helps around the margins and its action the government can take, then I want try and fix it."

The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. The 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.

'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40.' What do you want from the Budget?

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes:

Baked beans

Garlic

Gherkins

Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles

Boiled sweets

Toffees, caramels and similar sweets

Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes

Throat pastilles and cough drops

Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed

Kerosene

Fertilisers

The government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targeted at households that rely on heating oil.

The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed.

A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas.

Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take."

But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs."

The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

article:
More high winds hit parts of UK as Storm Boelo clean-up continues

Around 22,000 properties are still without power as parts of Scotland and northern England were battered by Storm Boelo

Strong winds are expected to continue across Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland on Tuesday, after Storm Boelo brought flooding and power cuts to thousands over the weekend.

While conditions are set to improve for much of the UK after a wet and windy morning, clean-up efforts could be hampered elsewhere - including in Scotland, where a third of a month's rain fell during the storm.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said almost 8,000 people were still without power after more than 800,000 experienced cuts.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines , the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

A deep area of low pressure, while not severe enough to be a named storm, still brought strong winds with gusts of 65-80mph to parts of western England and Wales in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

Through the rest of Tuesday, the strongest winds will be across Scotland and the northern coast of Northern Ireland, where a Met Office yellow warning is due to be in place until 21:00 GMT.

Gusts will continue to reach 50-60mph, possibly up to 70mph in the most exposed parts of northwest and northern Scotland.

That is is likely to bring further travel disruption and more power cuts in places.

Elsewhere across the UK, Tuesday will be a blustery day, but the wind is not likely to cause any major impacts.

Strong winds and heavy rain will ease off later on Tuesday, with the rest of the week looking much calmer across the UK.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," he told the BBC.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

The Met Office has warned about the possibility of further power cuts and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

This video can not be played

Storm Boelo floods town centre of Largs, Scotland

Marcus Reed, operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Cumbria were without power until Tuesday evening.

"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.

"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."

Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, said the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".

Disruption to travel continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland were shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.

article:
Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

President Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.

Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.

However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.

For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.

He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.

The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.

The majority of states allow , external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.

Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.

What is the SAVE America Act and what would it do?

Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictions

However, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.

US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks , external .

Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.

The Brookings Institution policy research think tank , external looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.

The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.

We looked back in the database , external over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.

A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association , external looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.

For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.

Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".

It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.

The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.

Millions of people have already voted early in the US midterm elections

Critics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID.

"We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.

Can illegal immigrants really vote in the US election?

A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice , external suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.

However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws.

"When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.

A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice , external .

Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.

The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.

A 2026 analysis by Reuters , external of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction.

"The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

"There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."

Trump has also pushed for states to use a federal database - the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) database - to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens and remove them from voter rolls.

The tool has access to information about naturalised citizens and non-citizens who have contacted the federal government previously. It was launched in the 1980s to help government agencies verify individuals' eligibility for government benefits based on their immigration status.

Critics have questioned the reliability of using the data to remove people from voter rolls as they say it could be outdated and include people who have since become US citizens - but the US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using it this way.

US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship

Every US state allows some postal voting and 29% of voters cast a ballot that way in the 2024 presidential election

"Federal databases can be invaluable to states trying to update their voter rolls so long as their limitations are understood," says Olson. "So part of the Trump plan which requires the sharing of information is positive, even if the second part to require states to treat the database contents as reliable despite their continuing evident gaps and inaccuracies is bad."

The use of the programme by individual states is voluntary, and from those who have used it recently the number of non-citizens detected has been small.

In Georgia, after an audit of the state's voter rolls, 432 possible non-citizens were identified , external on its voter rolls over 30 years.

The Department of Homeland Security provided Nevada with a list of 185 names which it claimed identified non-citizens who had been improperly allowed to register to vote, but state officials found that they were all in fact citizens. , external

The White House has pointed to a case in New Jersey, where this summer a software glitch in the state's drivers licensing department registered about 6,600 non-citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. State officials have said fewer than 400 cast ballots and they have all now been removed from the system.

The US Justice Department requested that California doesn't count 20,000 postal ballots ahead of the midterms from people it claims are "likely non-citizen registrants" - but that request has been rejected by an appeals court.

Out of that 20,000, it has charged 28 people , external who the department says are non-citizens who had illegally registered to vote.

article:
Egypt court fines journalist Lina Attalah and orders news site's closure

Amnesty International called the verdict against Lina Attalah 'a crushing blow to press freedom' (file photo)

The editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr was detained for several hours after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure, her lawyers say.

Mada Masr said Lina Attalah was released once it paid the fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100) also handed down to her by the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court. It was the maximum possible penalty for the charge, which she had rejected.

Amnesty International said the verdict represented "a crushing blow to press freedom".

It comes only weeks after six journalists working for the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ).

President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has overseen what human rights groups say is an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since he led the military's overthrow of his predecessor, Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Morsi, in 2013.

Tens of thousands of people have been detained, mainly Brotherhood officials and supporters but also leading secular and liberal activists, media workers and academics.

Egyptian journalists from fact-checking website facing terrorism charges

AI 'SpongeBob' parody of problems in Egypt draws scrutiny of authorities

TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case

The CPJ said Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt and that it had long faced pressure from authorities over its journalism.

The site had repeatedly sought an operating licence from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) since a new media law was passed in 2018, but that its applications were either rejected or left unanswered, the media watchdog added.

Amnesty International said Lina Attalah had also faced "years of harassment and intimidation", including six criminal investigations over Mada Masr's reporting.

Last week, prosecutors summoned her for questioning over allegations of publishing "false news" and operating a website without a licence.

Mada Masr's lawyer said the investigation included a recent report that the website had published about a wave of protests in prisons across the country, as well as a letter from the SMRC regarding its legal status.

Attalah was released on bail and later referred to trial before the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court on the charge of operating a website without a licence.

During Tuesday's hearing, Judge Mohammed Mubarak ordered the courtroom to be cleared of everyone except Attalah, her eight-person defence team, and Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), an independent human rights group.

Bahgat told AFP news agency that security personnel then filed in before the judge announced that the court was denying several procedural requests made by the defence and appointing its own lawyer for Attalah.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," he said. "Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes.

"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer - who had not uttered a single word - and entered them into the official record," he added.

The judge then announced the fine for Attalah and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before she was detained, according to Bahgat.

On Tuesday evening, Mada Masr said it had paid the full fine to the court and that Attalah was released after several hours in custody.

"During the release procedures, Attalah learned of a one-year prison sentence issued against her in absentia in 2024, on charges of publishing false news and managing an unlicensed website," it added.

"Her lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November."

Amnesty International warned that the court's verdict marked "a dark day for independent journalism" in Egypt and demanded that it be overturned.

"This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices," said the group's senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed.

"Lina Attalah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job."

CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah said: "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting."

article:
West warns of famine risk in Sudan as civil war grinds on

War in Sudan has led to the worst humanitarian crisis with more than 33 million people in need of assistance according to the WHO

The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine.

In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production.

"There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted.

The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people.

The statement , external was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website.

It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger.

"I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said.

While the war in Sudan has led to what the World Health Organization has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, Roble said only 40% of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September.

"Their meals come from the community kitchen, which doesn't really even have very long-term support because of funding cuts," Roble added.

The joint statement warns that "the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000" without immediate action.

The crisis is being exacerbated by what the signatories describe as systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of Sudan.

"The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people," the statement says, urging them to lift all impediments to humanitarian assistance and allow full, safe, rapid and unimpeded access.

In June, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a measure of the severity and magnitude of food crises, estimated that 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.

The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

Manhunt under way for Tennessee killer who escaped prison through a fence

This video can not be played

Officials say this video shows escaped inmate stealing a truck

A manhunt is under way in Tennessee after a convicted murderer serving a life sentence escaped from prison.

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was found guilty of the 2022 killing of his co-worker and sentenced in 2025, prison records show.

He escaped on Sunday from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC).

It said security camera footage confirmed Morley had breached the prison's perimeter fence and escaped in his prison uniform.

Investigators have released security camera video they say shows him stealing a nearby farm's work car.

Morley was convicted of first-degree murder over the killing of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022

Morley has been added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's most wanted list, the TDOC said, and a reward of up to $2,500 (£1,900) is being offered for information leading to his arrest.

Prison staff confirmed he was "unaccounted for" on Sunday night and begun an emergency headcount and search within the prison, officials said on Monday.

"The Tennessee Highway Patrol has deployed aviation assets and state troopers to assist with the search," the TDOC said.

Prison records show his supervision level was listed as "low" and he was not eligible for release until December 2083.

On Tuesday afternoon, investigators said the stolen vehicle had been found in Illinois about 120 miles north of Tiptonville, but Morley was not there.

He was sentenced in June 2025 after being convicted of first-degree murder over the death of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a metal box under Morley's home, according to Carter County court records reviewed by the BBC.

Birchfield died "as a result of a gunshot wound to the back of the head", a pathology report cited in court said. Bullet casings matched a gun found in Morley's house.

The pair had developed a friendship while Birchfield was training Morley at the pallet manufacturing company they worked at, Birchfield's sister said in her victim impact statement to the court.

Besides murder, Morley was also convicted of vandalism, tampering with evidence, aggravated burglary, and evading arrest. His request for a new trial was denied in May.

This is not the first time Morley has led law enforcement officials on a manhunt. His 2022 arrest came after a police chase that crossed state lines into North Carolina.

Earlier this month, another prisoner Gregory Redden, 69, who is serving a 15-year sentence for aggravated robbery, escaped from custody but was recaptured shortly after.

Convicted murder Christa Pike survived a botched lethal injection in the state in September, leading to the resignation of TDOC Commissioner Frank Strada.

Chief executive Noel Mooney says the Football Association of Wales (FAW) retains the view that Fifa president Gianni Infantino should step down.

Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout

Macklemore has pledged to donate the proceeds from his tour to organisations supporting Palestinians

Macklemore has begun his Free Palestine tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran's controversial decision to drop the rapper from his tour last month.

The American star played to a crowd of up to 13,000 at the city's 3Arena, having promised "many incredible surprise guests" on the bill for the sold-out show.

The artist, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, announced the tour days after being dropped from Sheeran's Loop Tour after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.

He was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches, including referring to the death toll from Israel's military action in Gaza as a genocide - a claim that Israel rejects.

Sheeran later said that the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter , not by himself.

Among the acts who performed at Macklemore's Dublin show were singer-songwriter Hozier, rap trio Kneecap and folk band Beoga, who had also performed on Sheeran's tour.

Macklemore has said that proceeds from his Free Palestine tour will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.

He will perform in Paris on Thursday and in London on Friday.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 70,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

Tickets for the Dublin show sold out and dozens of concertgoers were queueing at the venue hours before its doors were opened.

Some were dressed in Palestinian jerseys, others had tied Palestinian and Irish flags to themselves, and many were wearing keffiyeh scarves, a symbol of Palestinian identity.

Vendors outside the arena sold Palestinian bucket hats and flags, as well as hats and flags with the Kneecap logo.

Nicola McCollough and her daughter Lily Rose Murphy say they are big fans of Macklemore

Nicola McCollough travelled with her daughter Lily Rose Murphy from Belfast for Lily Rose's first ever concert.

They both said they were happy Macklemore spoke out in support of Gaza.

"More people need to, if you have the platform, do it because not everybody has that kind of stage," said Nicola.

"I would speak about anything if I'm supportive of it," said Lily Rose.

Gillian Duffy and her son Joshua were among those in the queue for the gig

Gillian Duffy travelled from Cork with her son Joshua.

She said that if Macklemore had "put on 10 shows in Dublin, all 10 would have been filled".

"This is the hottest ticket because people want to be here, they really, really want to show their support," she said.

"You're going to hear [the chant] 'Free, free Palestine' all over Dublin tonight."

Jess O'Riordan, who also travelled from Cork, said it was "absolutely appalling" when Macklemore was "kicked off" Sheeran's tour.

"I wish we had more people out there that would use their platform the way he does," she added.

The controversy began when Macklemore, performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in New Jersey in early September, said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University in the US.

The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.

After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out.

He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.

Sheeran said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.

His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and fans to express frustration.

Sheeran then addressed the controversy during the start of a gig in Philadelphia.

He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".

He described the 7 October 2023 attacks as "horrific" and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

article:
Queen's University reverses ban on collarettes at Remembrance service

Jay Basra said the ban was a "deeply disappointing step backwards" for inclusion

Queen's University Belfast (QUB) has reversed a decision to ban the wearing of collarettes at its Remembrance Sunday service.

A document setting out arrangements for next month's wreath-laying ceremony, seen by BBC News NI, stated: "Please note that collarettes are not to be worn."

The move was criticised by the university's Young Unionists club, which said that banning collarettes - such as those worn by Orange Order members - "reinforces the perception among some unionist students that Queen's remains a cold house for their community".

In a statement, QUB said that "having listened to feedback" it had "agreed that they can continue to be worn".

The Remembrance service will be held at QUB's war memorial, which sits in front of the university's main Lanyon Building, on Sunday 8 November.

Several of the university's societies and clubs are expected to attend and lay wreaths at the memorial.

Orange Order members had worn their collarettes at previous Remembrance services at the university

Jay Basra, the chair of the Young Unionists club, described the original decision to ban collarettes as a "deeply disappointing step backwards" for inclusion and respect at the university.

Collarettes had been worn by some students representing the Orange Order at previous Remembrance events at the university.

QUB told BBC News NI that its original decision not to allow collarettes this year had been the result of an update to the "marching dress code" to reflect Royal British Legion guidance "at the request of some veterans and serving members of the armed forces".

But it added: "Having listened to further feedback from a wider range of stakeholders, the university recognises the importance of collarettes for some members of the procession and has therefore agreed that they can continue to be worn."

Poppy wreaths are laid at the university's war memorial during the Remembrance Sunday service

Basra welcomed the lifting of the ban, saying: "Nobody taking part in that act of remembrance should be told that part of their identity is not welcome.

"Remembrance should be an occasion that brings people together, irrespective of their background or tradition.

"Looking ahead, I would encourage the university to engage directly with those affected before making changes of this kind.

"That would avoid unnecessary upset and help build confidence among unionist students that Queen's is a welcoming home for their community too."

Democratic Unionist Party assembly member Phillip Brett said the reversal of the original decision was a sign that "common sense has prevailed".

"While I welcome the willingness of senior management to engage constructively with me and reverse this decision, serious questions remain about how it was taken in the first place," he said.

"Lessons must be learned to ensure that such an unnecessary situation does not arise again."
