article:
Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China

A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over Mbappé's comments on a "Chinese dictator"

Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.

Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.

The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement.

"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."

Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.

A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.

Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.

The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".

The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".

Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.

But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".

Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".

Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.

Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao

Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".

"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo.

As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.

The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".

Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."

According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.

China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Mbappé has a significant commercial presence in China

China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.

By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list.

"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.

Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.

His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.

His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.

So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.

Mbappé has said some of the memes "reveal a lack of political and human awareness"

It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.

Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.

In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.

France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.

In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".

"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.

"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."

Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

Apple to replace iPhone Duos affected by screen problem

One user said Apple had helped him to replace his faulty iPhone Duo

Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.

Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device , which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.

Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.

The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.

Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.

The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using AI.

Francisco Jeronimo, technology analyst at market research firm IDC, said that meant some caution was needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run.

But he added the early reports of issues also showed "that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables".

The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in similar flaws in folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.

Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.

Apple boss John Ternus showing off the new iPhone Duo

Android users already have a broad selection of foldable phones to choose from, technology that Apple spent years developing before the Duo's release.

It is Apple's most expensive iPhone ever, costing up to £3,199 for the most well-equipped models.

Jeronimo said because Apple had positioned the Duo as a "premium alternative" to established foldables, "how it handles this first-generation issue will shape buyer confidence in the category well beyond its own sales".

"Apple has a loyal customer base and a retail network that can swap devices on the spot, but with a further 28 markets launching on 30 October, it needs to clarify its warranty position quickly," he said.

The Duo marks Apple's first major iPhone redesign in almost two decades and was unveiled by new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.

When closed, the Duo looks like a wider version of an iPhone, then opens up to a device resembling a small tablet computer.

"Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together", Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters last month.

The Duo, he said, would "redefine the experience of using a foldable phone".

Lawrie, 15, eyes £501,000 live TV win over Littler

Lawrie was a world youth champion last year

At just 15 years old, Mitchell Lawrie has his sights on a £501,000 bullseye should he beat world darts champion Luke Littler in a potentially life-changing live appearance on national television.

The Renfrew teenager is one of 24 amateur players chosen to take part in Netflix's live special, Beat Luke Littler, which will be broadcast from the Manchester Central Convention Complex on Friday.

Each contestant has the chance to face Littler in a single leg of 501 but the first to beat the 19-year-old two-time world champion will land the big-money prize and bring the competition to an immediate end.

"If someone has already beaten Littler, that's the show done," Lawrie told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

'Beating Luke Littler will change my daughter's life'

Smith holds on to beat Schindler in Euros final

He added: "There's a bundle of good players in there and you're just hoping you get a chance before they get a chance. There's a few big names I want to go before."

Lawrie admits "there's going to be nerves there obviously" and "being live on Netflix at 15 years of age is just something else".

However, he points out: "Everybody there has a chance at the end of the day.

"He is obviously the best player in the world so it may be only one leg of darts but it is a very hard leg to win."

Nevertheless, Lawrie already has a victory over Littler under his belt.

"It was at the World Cup junior darts in Gibraltar in 2023, Scotland against England and we beat the team that Luke Littler was in," he recalls.

"We beat them 4-3 in a deciding leg and it's one of those memories that sticks with you forever.

"We also went on to win that tournament. It is the first time Scotland ever won the World Cup and it was my first year - it was something else.

"It was a surreal experience that I would love to have back."

Indeed, Lawrie was crowned WDF Open Youth World Champion last year before being described as "the future of darts" by Jimmy van Schie after the Dutchman beat the Scot when he became the first teenager to reach the WDF World Championship final in December.

Lawrie, whose inspiration is former world number one Gary Anderson, twice winner of the more prestigious PDC World Darts Championship, says he has been playing darts since his grandfather mounted a board on a chair when he was two years old.

"It just spiralled from there," he says. "But I never took it seriously until three and a half years ago.

"People still want to be a professional footballer, and it was the same for me, but I realised at a young age I wasn't good enough for it so I had to do something else and I just chose darts and I stuck to it and turned out quite good at it."

article:
Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say

The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or water

A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.

However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.

US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

This video can not be played

What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump

That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.

Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.

An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.

Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.

Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".

A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".

Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.

Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.

One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.

Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.

Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.

On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".

These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year

The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.

Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".

Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.

Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.

Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.

Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped

It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.

Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.

Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".

Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".

He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.

One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".

However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.

Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.

Russell Brand told police he never had non-consensual sex

Warning - this report contains graphic content

Russell Brand told police in interviews in response to allegations of rape and sexual assault that he had been "very promiscuous" in the past, but had never engaged in "non-consensual sexual activity", a court has heard.

Brand, 51, was interviewed four times between 2023 and 2025 by officers.

The TV and media personality is currently on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London on three counts of rape and other offences. He denies all the charges.

Jurors heard on Tuesday that he gave a prepared statement in each of the police interviews. In November 2023, he said: "I have repeatedly stated publicly and written extensively that I led a very promiscuous life, that I have spent years openly denouncing. I have never engaged in non-consensual activity."

Russell Brand's wife Laura accompanied him to court on Tuesday

Brand went on to say the allegations were made in "a defamatory and fictitious documentary", which he said contained "false and anonymised" interviews.

He added that "subsequently both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which has resulted in further encounters to be invented or reimagined".

In court on Tuesday, the jury was also asked formally to find Brand not guilty of a charge of indecent assault.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, said there was "insufficient evidence to support the charge of indecent assault".

This charge related to a woman who said Brand grabbed her arm and tried to drag her into a toilet in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

The jury was then given an amended indictment, which charges Brand with attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to this charge.

The prosecution will conclude on Wednesday morning before the defence is expected to start.

Brand denies three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

article:
Judgment reserved in appeal over Sean Brown murder inquiry

No-one has ever been charged or convicted in relation to Sean Brown's murder

The UK Supreme Court has reserved judgment in an attempt by the government to overturn a ruling which ordered a public inquiry into the murder of Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) official Sean Brown.

Brown, 61, was abducted in Bellaghy, County Londonderry, and shot by the Loyalist Volunteer Force (LVF) in 1997.

Intelligence material has since linked state agents to his murder .

The hearing in London lasted almost five hours, after which the court said it would deliver a judgement as soon as it could.

Five Supreme Court judges heard the case, which was brought by the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant.

The government has argued that Brown's murder should be examined by a Troubles Legacy Commission rather than by a court-ordered public inquiry.

It said its Northern Ireland Troubles Bill allows for a "reformed Legacy Commission with the ability to conduct Inquisitorial Proceedings, presided over by a judge, in cases such as this".

In May, the Supreme Court ruled in another case that the commission, which investigates deaths related to the Troubles, was capable of delivering an investigation which did not diminish victim's rights .

At Tuesday's hearing, Sir James Eadie KC, for the Northern Ireland secretary, said the decision of the Court of Appeal in Belfast to compel a public inquiry had been made on the same basis that the Supreme Court had found to be in error in May.

He said: "That should be the end of this appeal."

Sir James said there was nothing about the case which should have caused the courts to "overstep the normal constitutional boundaries and, for the first time in any court anywhere in the UK, order that the executive establish a public inquiry".

In written submissions, Des Fahy KC, for Brown's widow Bridie, said: "The murder of Sean Brown was initially attributed to the LVF.

"It is now clear that state agents were involved."

He added the "exceptional circumstances of the murder and the failed state investigations that followed" justified the Court of Appeal's ruling despite the recent decision of the Supreme Court.

He argued that an investigation by the Legacy Commission would lead to information being kept from the family and public "under the guise of national security".

Brown family members attended the hearing at the Supreme Court in London

Members of the Brown family attended Tuesday's hearing.

The case has been the subject of repeated legal battles since 2024.

Last year, the Court of Appeal in Belfast upheld a ruling ordering a public inquiry and found the government's refusal to establish one was unlawful.

The government has challenged that judgment on multiple grounds.

It accepts there has not been a proper investigation into the murder but it is at loggerheads with the Brown family over how the matter is remedied.

The government has argued the case can be dealt with by the Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery (ICRIR), once it undergoes reform and becomes the Legacy Commission.

Sean Brown's wife Bridie (centre) and their daughters Claire Loughran (left) and Siobhan Brown (right), pictured in 2025, have led a long campaign for justice

Brown's family want a public inquiry and are supported by the Irish government, Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP).

Claire Loughran, one of Brown's daughters, said it was "extremely frustrating" to be back in court on Tuesday.

"We thought whenever we had the judgment of five different High Court judges to say that a public inquiry was the only way to fully investigate and independently investigate my father's murder, we thought that was it... but unfortunately the secretary of state thought otherwise," she said.

"I was 19 whenever my father died so I feel like it's been my whole adult life that I've been trying to fight this and its been incredibly difficult.

"They have five of these public interest immunity certificates to say that there is sensitive information around his death and we just want to find out what's in that information."

Loughran said the Northern Ireland secretary has the ability "to right the wrongs of his predecessors".

Sean Brown's body was found beside a burned out car near Randalstown

Brown was locking the gates of Bellaghy Wolfe Tones GAA club when he was kidnapped.

He was driven ten 10 miles (16km) in the boot of his car to Randalstown, County Antrim, where he was found shot six times in the head.

No-one has ever been charged or convicted in relation to the murder.

A review of the murder investigation by the Police Ombudsman found it was "incomplete and inadequate".

Sinn Féin MP John Finucane said the treatment of Brown's widow Bridie and her family has been "nothing short of disgraceful".

"Rather than supporting the Brown family in their pursuit of truth and justice, the British government has fought them every step of the way," he added.

"Bridie and her family deserve truth, accountability and justice for Sean.

"Sinn Féin will continue to stand with Bridie and the Brown family and every other family seeking truth and justice for their loved ones."

article:
Dancer's family were told to say goodbye after stroke - now he hopes to perform again

Daniel Parsonage was preparing for a group dance at the Hawarden Summer Carnival when he felt "funny" and passed out

After a dancer suffered a sudden stroke, doctors told his family to say goodbye as there was nothing more they could do.

Daniel Parsonage, 29, underwent two emergency operations and spent four weeks in an induced coma in July last year. Severe bleeding on the brain meant his family feared the worst.

But he pulled through and while it was believed he would never walk or talk again, he has vowed to "keep fighting" to fully regain his speech and wants to be performing again before he turns 30.

Intensive speech and physiotherapy means he can now form sentences and walk short distances with a mobility aid.

Dan, from north Wales, began "feeling funny" and passed out while preparing for a dance in Hawarden, Flintshire, on 12 July 2025.

"I was taken to a family room on my own and [Dan] was taken through to A&E," said his mum Claire.

"All I remember is them saying 'you need to call the family in. There's nothing we can do... say your goodbyes'.

"It was horrible."

But Dan has defied the prognosis and, as he looks to the future, said: "I hope I feel normal again."

Dan, pictured with mum Claire, thought that his health and fitness was good

He had specialised in street dance since he was 11 and described his health over the years as "completely fine".

His fitness levels were good at the time of his sudden symptomless stroke, as he was playing weekly football matches and training for the Chester Marathon.

Two weeks before he collapsed, mum Claire even checked his blood pressure with a home device as she tested her own, and Dan's dad Wayne's.

He was "absolutely fine", she said, adding: "He had absolutely no symptoms."

When a friend called to say he had collapsed while preparing for the performance at the Hawarden Summer Carnival, they suspected it might just be from fainting.

When his parents arrived, Claire said they saw Dan on the floor with "sheets around him", he was limp on one side of his body and had been sick.

An ambulance arrived and rushed him to the Countess of Chester Hospital.

A stroke happens when blood stops flowing to part of your brain, according to the NHS , external .

It can affect things such as speech and movement, and take a long time to recover from.

It can be life-threatening if a patient does not get urgent medical help.

While strokes happen most often in people over 70, rates among younger adults (18 to 65) have risen in recent years , external , according to the Stroke Association.

The main symptoms of a stroke , external can emerge suddenly.

They may include:

face weakness - one side of your face may droop (fall) and it might be hard to smile

arm weakness - you may not be able to fully lift both arms and keep them there because of weakness or numbness in one arm

speech problems - you may slur your words or sound confused

In Dan's case, tests diagnosed a bleed on his brain caused by high blood pressure.

A consultant neurosurgeon made the call to send Dan to The Walton Centre in Liverpool, where thy could "give it a go" to try and save his life.

"If [consultant neurosurgeon] Prof [Andrew] Broadbelt hadn't stepped in, Dan wouldn't be here today," Claire said.

Dan's surgery to replace the missing section of his skull with an artificial plate was filmed for Channel 4 documentary Trauma: My Broken Brain

An emergency surgery on 14 July to stop the bleeding and another on 16 July where a large part of his skull was removed to allow his brain to swell more safely saved his life.

He then spent four weeks in an induced coma.

Doctors told the family there was a large section of Dan's brain that would not work again, so they should expect him to never walk or talk again.

Claire said: "As long as he woke up, we didn't care.

"That's all we wanted."

The mother-of-three said the four weeks waiting to see if Dan woke up were "tough" but she was "happy" when she saw his eyes flicker and then open for 10 minutes in mid-August 2025.

Dan, who worked as a supermarket team leader, said: "I remember waking up and thinking 'where am I?' and that I couldn't speak words."

The lack of speech continued for nine weeks until Dan's best friend visited him in hospital one day and Claire was shocked when he said "Hi Ben".

Dan has had speech therapy to improve his diction, as well as physiotherapy for eight months.

He has gone from not being able to lift himself up in bed to using a wheelchair and walking short distances with a mobility aid.

His speech has also gone from non-existent to speaking in sentences.

"I get up and shower, I put my clothes on, I do my [face] cream and I do my hair," Dan said, of his morning routine.

His confidence also grew when he no longer had to wear a helmet after he had surgery in February to replace the missing section of his skull with an artificial plate.

Claire has praised her son's "amazing" recovery after doctors said Dan would never walk or talk again following his stroke

Dan's goal is to be able to dance again before his 30th birthday in March.

"I hope I see a bigger and better version of myself than ever before," he said.

Claire said: "From us being told Dan was not going to make it, then he wouldn't be able to walk or talk, to where he is now, it's just amazing.

"We want to spread awareness that [strokes can] happen to younger people and even when you're told there's no hope there actually is.

"Daniel's showing that because he just keeps fighting all the way through.

"He keeps pushing himself and I'm very proud of him."

Dan is sharing his story as part of Channel 4's Trauma: My Broken Brain. , external

article:
Ghanaian twin brothers and US woman plead guilty to $9m romance scam

Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.

The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.

The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.

Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (£6.7m).

While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.

As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.

Jewellery was confiscated from the gang after they were arrested

The three accused go by several names:

Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement

Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster

Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman

In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.

Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.

In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (£5.9m).

He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.

The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

'I love to escape into a fantasyland of fairies': Fans rejoice as latest Sarah J Maas book hits shelves

Katie and Amy say they have been excited for the release of the newest ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony

Torrential rain and high winds may not be what many would consider fantastical.

But it didn't stop about 30 hardcore fans turning out for the latest release of author Sarah J Maas’ romantasy series, A Court of Splintered Harmony, in Carrickfergus, County Antrim.

The sixth book in Maas's multi-million book selling series, A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR), was released at midnight on Tuesday after a five-year wait.

On Monday evening, a midnight release event was held in The Secret Bookshelf, an independent bookshop just off the town's main street.

Friends Katie Mccabrey and Amy Savage were among those who went along to try and get one of the first copies when the embargo broke.

Like many others, Katie and Amy love reading books as a way to unwind from the stresses and pressures of every day life.

"I just love reading these kinds of fantasy books because the real world is a little bit terrible and I love to escape into a fantasyland of fairies and anything other worldly," Amy says.

"We're all here tonight because we all share just needing to escape from everyday life in common and this is a great way to do it," Katie adds.

Some of those who were at the release party took part in activities like friendship bracelet making and felting

Among the activities lined up at The Secret Bookshelf to distract excited fans from clock-watching are felting, friendship bracelet making and a dedicated fan-chat area for readers to discuss their theories.

Some attending opt for comfy clothing, sporting pyjamas and slippers as they waited for the midnight drop.

The wait has almost been too much for Katie.

"I couldn't sleep, I've been so excited - I've been hyped up for two weeks straight," she says.

"I'm actually halfway through another book that I couldn't pay attention to because I've been so busy thinking about the characters from ACOTAR," Amy jokes.

"So I'm going to have to go back and re-read the book that I'm 300 pages deep in because I've been so busy and so excited for this new launch."

For those whose social media algorithms do not revolve around "BookTok", the literary discussion side of TikTok, A Court of Thorns and Roses - or ACOTAR for short - is a fantasy romance series, which gets its name from the first book.

It's set in the fictional world of Prythian, and without spoiling the now six-book series, fans have flocked to the story in their droves to read about the protagonist's dealings with love and the fae.

Maas is also credited with fuelling interest in the romantasy genre, which has skyrocketed in popularity due to its discussion on social media.

There have been five books published so far:

A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015)

A Court of Mist and Fury (2016)

A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017)

A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018)

A Court of Silver Flames (2021)

Fans won't have to wait long for the follow-up, with the seventh book, A Court of Forgotten Melody, due to be released on 12 January 2027

Maas announced the series' latest installment, A Court of Splintered Harmony, back in March .

And fans won't have to wait long for the follow-up, with the seventh book, A Court of Forgotten Melody, due to be released on 12 January 2027.

David Jeroen and Sami Patrick are hard to miss amongst the stacked shelves in The Secret Bookshelf - they've donned their finest mythical attire for the evening, with crowns and elf ears included.

The pair's love of reading prompted them to start an Instagram account dedicated to books, and they're spending their two-year "bookiversary" in an apt place.

And Sami's excited to spend the night talking about one of her favourite genres with likeminded people.

"I've always been a fantasy reader and it's just escapism really," she says.

David and Sami were the event's quiz hosts as attendees counted down to midnight

David agrees.

"I think it's all about escaping reality and going into a different world and dimension where you get to live through another character and experience new things that you wouldn't be able to in real life," he adds.

"You can't ride a dragon in real life so you can read about it."

While the evening will conclude with the newest ACOTAR release, Sami says the five-year wait has led her to some of Maas's other series, which she prefers.

A Court of Splintered Harmony was released in UK bookshops at midnight on Tuesday

Monday's midnight release event is the brainchild of Jo Zebedee, who runs The Secret Bookshelf alongside her husband, Chris.

Harkening back to her time helping to run the midnight launches of the Harry Potter books, Jo decided to bring the same magic for fans of the much loved romantasy series.

"We are a big fantasy shop, I'm a fantasy, sci-fi writer so it's in my blood, so we very much celebrate the world's that sometime can be difficult to find a space in mainstream books," she explains.

"There's something around the excitement of books and just that whole vibe of here's something to really celebrate.. we just wanted to bring that all together to make a fun night."

Jo Zebedee runs The Secret Bookshelf in Carrickfergus alongside her husband, Chris

Jo enlisted the help of not only local crafters for the event, but local businesses who gifted attendees treats for the late night.

She thinks its the place of independent bookshops, like hers, to foster the excitement amongst young people for reading.

"I think events is when a bookshop comes to life," she says.

"It's about a love of books and tonight is just such a love of books."

article:
UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds says no "assumptions" have been made about what the future UK-EU relationship could look like

British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.

Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.

However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.

Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.

Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.

But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days

Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.

He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.

"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.

"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."

Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.

"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."

A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.

"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.

Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.

Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.

But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.

Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.

"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.

Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."

Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."

Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.

On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.

The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.

But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times , external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.

The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

article:
Deaths in detention cells in Nigeria were entirely preventable, inquiry finds

This video can not be played

The BBC's Madina Maishanu shows the conditions inside the cell where so many died

An inquiry into the deaths of 33 detainees in Nigeria's Minna state has found they died as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and failure by officers to respond to distress calls.

Forensic and medical evidence showed the "entirely preventable" deaths had resulted from acute respiratory failure linked to prolonged confinement, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration.

The evidence did not support initial claims of a disease outbreak.

The detainees were found dead on 17 September while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps on suspicion of illegal mining. The investigation found that the mining sites had been licensed.

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria

Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said those found responsible for the deaths would face the full force of the law.

He added that the detention hall had been cleaned before investigators arrived, raising concerns about possible attempts to compromise evidence.

Implicated officers will face suspension and the report would be forwarded to the attorney general of the federation for further legal action, Tunji-Ojo said.

Family members reclaimed the bodies of their relatives from Minna's General Hospital last month

The investigating committee found that the raid on the miners had been conducted without an approved operational order, proper planning or consultation with the Mining Marshals Unit.

It said that 50 detainees had been held in a cell measuring about 20 sq m, with no running water or functioning toilet, and inadequate food, drinking water and airflow.

Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods.

Officers reportedly ignored repeated calls for help, despite a medical worker having raised concerns about the conditions.

"Detainees repeatedly banged on cell doors and walls, shouted for assistance and pleaded for water," said the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure.

"These distress calls were heard by officers assigned to nearby duties... but were not acted upon."

Kure said the detention conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.

"The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities and the welfare of persons in custody," he added.

The investigating committee also recommended compensation of 30m naira (£16,683; $22,285) for each of the bereaved families and 10m naira for each survivor.

Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision again over Israel participation

Claude Kiambe was the last Netherlands entrant in 2025

The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to take part.

The Netherlands and four other countries boycotted this year's event, after Dutch network Avrotros pulled out.

Avrotros said it would also not take part next year, but NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, stepped in and pledged last month that the country would return in 2027 .

However, NPO's media director Jurre Bosman said on Tuesday that "Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division", and NPO "has decided to forgo participation in 2027".

NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.

"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.

"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.

"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."

NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".

Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.

"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."

Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all bocotted the 2026 contest over Israel's participation, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Eurovision organisers have announced a number of changes in an attempt to address the divisions, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition, and changes to the voting.

As well as the Netherlands, Ireland will also not take part in 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.

The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.

Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year with the dance track Bangaranga.

article:
Where are Celtic & O'Neill a year after Rodgers exit?

Martin O'Neill appears in good spirits despite the stormy weather

One year ago, Brendan Rodgers resigned as Celtic manager, with Martin O'Neill immediately taking the reigns in what the Scottish champions thought would be an interim period in charge.

Twelve months on, O'Neill is still there, albeit over two spells with 33 dismal days under Wilfried Nancy squeezed in between.

So where are Celtic at in terms of "moving forward", that cliched business term that has seeped into football parlance?

Shortly before his exit, Rodgers described the Celtic squad as "a Honda Civic rather than a Ferrari" as he bemoaned transfer spending, but how much longer will it be steered by his 74-year-old successor?

O'Neill on Johnston injury, Celtic milestone & No.1 battle

O'Neill had admitted he considered his position during the last international break, but he showed no signs of being ready to walk away when addressing the media before Wednesday's meeting with Dundee United.

Asked how he looked back on his latest year in charge, he replied: "Obviously with a lot of satisfaction and secretly probably delighted to get the call and happy with the results since. So it feels like a long year. Very long.

"The club has done more for me than I've done for the club in that sense. Seriously, it's rejuvenated me in many aspects."

Previous to his return, O'Neill had been "semi-enjoying my life watching the game from afar" and "talking nonsense most of the time" as a football pundit.

However, he was delighted with the opportunity to return to "a game that I absolutely love, will love forever".

One year of O'Neill - saviour or sticking plaster?

Scottish Football Podcast

27/10/26

Rodgers' second two-year spell as Celtic manager came to an end after a 3-1 defeat at Hearts that left his side eight points behind the Edinburgh side after nine games.

They had lost two of those nine, scoring 12 goals for the loss of eight.

Despite Hearts retaining their lead until the final day of the season, Rodgers' fellow Northern Irishman would turn it round in the end with a dramatic victory over their title rivals at Celtic Park to secure their 56th league title and fifth in a row.

This season, O'Neill's side have lost only one of their 10 league games, scoring 25 times for the concession of six, to lead Rangers in the title race.

On the surface, 16 wins in 17 league games since the closing stages of last season looks like progress.

As Celtic podcaster Tino Callaghan told the BBC's Scottish Football Podcast: "On the last day of the season - 16 May - everything did turn out fine and dandy.

"Currently, things are six out of 10 at Celtic. We're four points clear at the top of the league this week's midweek card can see us extend that lead, but things are far from correct in terms of the evolution of the club and the progress of the club."

O'Neill's win percentage of nearly 75% in his latest spell is similar to his club record level during his trophy-laden five years in charge to 2005.

However, the recent 7-1 thrashing of Hearts apart, performances this season have largely left the Celtic support underwhelmed, while it is results in Europe - and two defeats in a week by city rivals Rangers - that have caused most alarm.

When Rodgers left, Celtic had won eight games, drawn four and lost four overall at the start of last season.

This season, they have won 11 and lost six, but on their way to a Champions League exit and to the foot of the Europa League after three games, they have suffered heavy defeats against LASK, Ferencvaros and Benfica.

"O'Neill domestically is more than capable," Callaghan said. "But the Celtic squad is woefully inept when it comes to European football and you just need to have a glance at that for evidence when you look at the bench on those European nights."

That led former Celtic striker Chris Sutton to describe the side currently under his former manager as flat-track bullies only able to dominate in Scottish football.

"We're just falling way, way behind," Callaghan agreed. "But it wasn't that long ago where we were competing with Bayern Munich and beating Leipzig and pulling off some really decent results."

Striker Camilo Duran and midfielder Mika Baur have proved shrewd acquisitions

Last season was also marked by a damaging split between the board and sections of the support unhappy at the level of investment in the squad and the general running of the club.

The two sides united for last season's victorious climax to the season, but the splits have re-emerged.

"Ultimately it always comes down to recruitment, doesn't it?" Callaghan said. "I hear folks talking about entitled Celtic fans, but millions of pounds in the bank is no use unless you're spending it.

"It's about spending more effectively and it's spending certainly more efficiently and sooner within the window.

"The start of the window was exciting. Camilo Duran is a brilliant player. As good a signing as we've made in some time, Mika Baur the same.

"But the defensive midfield has been a serious issue. We haven't signed anyone there and you're now starting to feel sorry for Callum McGregor - he's been hung out to dry."

Daily Record football writer Michael Gannon agreed that O'Neill had been used as a human shield by the board.

"I feel for him a little bit because he's the only person at Celtic who fronts up and faces questions on a regular basis," he said.

"A lot of the questions, like where is the full-time chairman, where's the head of recruitment, where's the director of football, what's happened with the Green Brigade bans and fan problems, are not really for him to answer."

Callaghan appears to speak for many fans for whom O'Neill still feels like a stop-gap "holding position for all concerned".

"But, within that year, he's won a league and he's won a Scottish Cup as well, so not too bad," he said.

"I don't see him staying beyond this year. I think from his point of view, European football at Celtic became a thing again under O'Neill and I do think part of his decision-making in the summer to return will have been the prospect of a final chance at the Champions League, final crack at the big time.

"And he'll have been as devastated as anyone that we fell short against LASK. And I do think there's still a bit of a hangover amongst the players from that one."

After a poor start to the Europa League, will O'Neill now make finishing on a high domestically his priority?

"He will be conscious of his legacy whether he says so or otherwise and I think, whatever happens, he'll want to certainly move on this summer, if that is the case, with another league title under his belt," Gallacher added.

Michael: Rodgers appears somewhat vindicated. Since leaving, the board have proven their lack of direction and the resulting diminished quality largely confirmed what we all suspected. That the club is rudderless and outdated. Rodgers was the chewing gum holding the straw tower up.

Johnno: As time moves on, it appears that Celtic don't. The team has not improved since Rodgers engineered his exit. Had the board kept faith with O'Neill last year instead of appointing Nancy at the worst possible time, there would have been no final-day drama. However, last season appears to have drained whatever team spirit, confidence and cohesion was left. This season has been a mixture of underwhelming performances, dreadful tactics and utter chaos in defence.

Brian: The last year has proven the board are not fit for purpose and have absolutely no idea how to run a modern football club. The club is going backwards with the future looking increasingly dim.

Frank: Two out of the three major trophies cannot be bad and Europe can be an irritating sideshow to the quest for the championship. To only have lost one game in the league is very commendable.

Paul: Rodgers' departure was symptomatic of our current demise. The performance v Bayern in Feb '25 was an aberration and disguised a lot of the flaws that, even then, Rodgers was aware of. Can't blame him for leaving as the fish had been rotting for a while by then and we all know where that rot begins.

Nick: I feel we were very fortunate to win the league last year. Hearts and Rangers fell away badly at the end. I don't think O'Neill should have stayed in charge as he hasn't really achieved much since leaving in 2005. There is no style, no direction and little optimism from what I see with a very disgruntled fan base and a board that lacks vision.

Controversial Islamic cleric shot dead in northern Nigeria

Yahaya Masussuka was awarded a peace prize last year by Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency

A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina.

Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC.

The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said.

It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death.

It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels. If they answer correctly, their soul sleeps peacefully until the day of judgement - if not it will be tormented.

This understanding comes from what is known as the Hadith, a collection of texts believed to be the spoken words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.

This serves as a key source of Islamic knowledge to help interpret the Quran, the central religious text of Islam.

But Masussuka based his teachings mainly on what was in Islam's holy book, questioned some of the hadiths - and did not believe that the dead were reawakened and questioned.

He was once jailed for nine months because he teased some respected scholars over their belief in this hadith and other teachings.

Masussuka, who had two wives and seven children, began preaching at the age of 13 in Quranic schools.

He later attended Al-Azhar University in Egypt and later went to Oman for further studies.

At his home, he had a studio where he would record videos of his teachings for broadcast on social media for his followers.

The cleric was also outspoken about violent extremism, radicalisation and openly advocated for interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians, who make up nearly equal parts of Nigeria's population.

Thousands of Christians and Muslims have been killed in ethnic and religious violence here over the past 25 years.

For Masussuka's efforts, Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador Award last year.

Six other prominent Muslim preachers have been murdered over the last two decades in northern Nigeria - several targeted by Boko Haram for criticising the jihadist group that began its insurgency in 2009.

Founded in north-eastern Nigeria, it opposes Western culture, education, the secular government - and its political goal is the creation of an Islamic state.

Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar

US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden

The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.

It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.

Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.

During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.

"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.

Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.

Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.

Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high .

The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.

The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.

US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.

Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.

Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".

Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told" , external , arguing that "nobody is getting fired".

US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices

But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.

Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.

That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.

For Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar.

Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things.

"When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says.

"When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."

Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently

The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.

Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators.

"You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.

That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.

Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.

Trump has less room to do that.

Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.

"The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans.

"It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."

Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.

A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.

Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households

The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.

Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.

The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.

Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.

The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.

Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.

If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

article:
New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know

New Zealand holds a general election every three years.

New Zealanders will head to the polls on 7 November to elect a new government.

The rising cost of living, unemployment and healthcare are among the main concerns of voters, who will choose members of parliament.

There is no clear frontrunner, based on pre-election polls. The incumbent centre-right prime minister, Christopher Luxon, won the last election in 2023 with a promise to "build the economy".

Here is everything you need to know about New Zealand's 2026 general election.

New Zealand holds a general election every three years and uses a Mixed-Member Proportional system or MMP.

Each voter makes two choices - the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

The candidate in a constituency with the most votes wins and becomes an MP.

Political parties on the other hand must win at least 5% of the total party votes to secure a seat in parliament. The seats are also allocated proportionately - if a party wins 40% of the total party votes, it will get 40% of the seats alloted for parties.

The New Zealand parliament typically has 120 seats - 71 are allocated to constituencies and the remaining 49 are distributed to parties proportionately.

New Zealand elections rarely result in an outright majority and parties forge coalitions to form a government.

New Zealand adopted the MMP in 1996 to address concerns that small parties were being left out of the vote.

The current government is led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose centre-right National party came to power in 2023 . It governs in coalition with the ACT and New Zealand First parties.

His party emphasised economic management, restoring a budget surplus, and expanding KiwiSaver, New Zealand's retirement savings scheme.

The main opposition is the centre-left Labour party, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins.

Labour has focused on reducing living costs, improving healthcare and transport, and investing in housing, jobs and public services.

National's coalition partners also have their own priorities. ACT, led by David Seymour, has advocated stricter immigration policies, while New Zealand First, led by Winston Peters, has proposed changes to voting eligibility, with the party proposing that voting in New Zealand should be restricted to citizens only.

The Green Party, co-led by Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson, is another player. It has campaigned on issues including wealth taxes, renewable energy and public services.

Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, is also competing for parliamentary seats, with housing, healthcare, education and constitutional reform among its priorities.

Cost of living is a major concern for New Zealanders.

A September 2026 Ipsos survey found that 63% of respondents identified inflation and the cost of living as one of the country's most important issues. Healthcare and hospitals came second at 44%, followed by the economy at 34%.

Unemployment is also a growing concern, with 21% of respondents identifying it as a major issue in the same survey. It overtook housing to become New Zealand's fourth most important issue.

Polling places open from 09:00 local time on 7 November (20:00 GMT 6 November). Voting ends at 19:00. Advance voting started on 26 October while overseas voting began earlier on 21 October.

Preliminary results will be released progressively from 19:00 on election night through New Zealand's official election results website. These initial results will not be the official final count.

The Electoral Commission is scheduled to declare official results on 27 November, after the counting and verification process has been completed.

A clear result on election night could provide an early indication of which parties are best placed to form a government. However, a tight race could delay negotiations if no party wins an outright majority.

New Zealanders may therefore have to wait beyond election night to find out which parties will form the next government and who will lead the country for the next three years.
