Boy who stabbed girl at school was radicalised online, says father

Armed police officers were called to Thorpe St Andrew School after a teenage girl was stabbed by another pupil

Warning: The following report contains details that some may find distressing

The father of a teenager who tried to kill a fellow pupil in a school knife attack has described his devastation and belief that his son was "radicalised" by extreme material online.

The boy, now 16, was found guilty of attempted murder last week after a trial heard how he harboured a hatred of women, had a fascination with serial killers and had planned to target others in the attack at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC and calling for tighter controls, the boy's father said he did not want to "absolve" his son but suggested online material and "a culture of violence and horror" had influenced him.

The government said it was committed to ensuring all children were safe from radicalisation and threats online, pointing to its Prevent anti-terrorism scheme and the Online Safety Act , which compels social media platforms to remove and prevent the spread of illegal content.

The boy cannot be identified due to his age, and nor can witnesses and the victim in the case.

His father, who we are calling John, apologised to the 15-year-old girl injured in the attack on 11 March, saying: "We're so very sorry for what happened."

John spoke of his fears that young men were being radicalised towards violence and hatred.

"You can think... it can never happen to my family or my son couldn't be involved, but that's what we thought and that wasn't the case," he said.

John's son was convicted after a trial at King's Lynn Crown Court

A two-week trial at King's Lynn Crown Court heard how the boy dressed in black and wore a face mask to stab the girl with a kitchen knife.

John described his own "rising feeling of panic" on the day of the attack.

He said he and his wife had been "fearful for what he might have done and fearful for what would happen to him".

But John said he only learned the full details when they emerged during the trial.

"It was awful, really devastating," he said.

He acknowledged the attack would have had "major repercussions" for the victim, who spent a night in hospital but was not seriously injured.

"I hope the victim and her family can sort of get over it as soon as possible in terms of healing and move on," he said.

Roads around the school were cordoned off following the attack

Before the attack, John said, his family had been "normal".

His son was shy but had a group of friends and had been "kind and thoughtful" at home.

As a teenager, he began to spend more time on his own, but John saw nothing concerning.

However, police later found the boy had searched the internet for material on mass shootings and serial killers, including on the night before the attack - something John said he had "no idea" about.

"It was shocking and devastating that he would have been looking at that kind of stuff," he said.

While there were parental controls on his son's devices, these were mainly to limit screen time.

"There was nothing to indicate that anything sinister was going on," said John.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, you can visit the BBC Action Line for information and support

Asked if they should have known more about what was on their son's phone, he said: "I can see the argument.

"I doubt many parents will go through their kids' browsing history on a regular basis.

"Hindsight's a marvellous thing, isn't it?"

The kitchen knife used to stab the victim had a blade measuring 18cm (7in) and a handle measuring 12cm (5in) and was found in a wooded area

When police searched the family home after the attack, they found the boy had written notes planning a wider attack.

They talked about deaths and injuries, listing misanthropy, misogyny, suicide, bullying as motives.

John said reading the notes made him feel "physically sick".

"It's still perplexing to us that he would write those things and feel those things that he was feeling," he said.

"He just seems like a different person doing that; some different version of him that's emerged from whatever he's been watching or seeing online."

John said his son had told him he believed his interest in extreme violence began after he saw a clip on TikTok from TV drama Dexter, which tells the story of a vigilante serial killer.

"Once you watch one thing like that, the algorithm, of course, feeds you more of the same content," he said.

He said he believed some young men could be drawn towards increasingly extreme material online and called for tighter regulations on children's access to it.

"There's the radicalisation of young men in particular. They talk about it with regards to terrorism and political ideology, but [there's] a radicalisation towards violence and hatred," he said.

"There must be ways to block content or to monitor content. We see millions of pounds spent on other things. Is there enough being spent on this kind of thing?"

Ofcom, the official regulator for broadcasting and the internet, says it is the responsibility of tech firms to keep children safe online.

It says it is holding those companies to account, but has the following tips for parents , external :

Talk regularly to your children about what they do when they're online.

Make sure your children register with online services using their real age, to help prevent them from accessing content that is only suitable for people who are older.

Make sure they know how to report inappropriate or harmful content, how to block accounts that share it and encourage them not to share it themselves. If content is illegal, report it to the police.

Parental controls are a useful tool, helping you to monitor and limit the time your children spend online, and what they do when they're there.

John acknowledged parallels with his son's crime and the storyline of award-winning drama Adolescence starring Owen Cooper (left) and Stephen Graham

The attack by John's son had parallels with the storyline of hit Netflix drama Adolescence, which shows the aftermath of the fatal stabbing of a teenage girl by a fellow school pupil.

It highlighted the corrosive impact of social media and misogynist influencers on some teenage boys and prompted then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to pledge to tackle the issue .

John said while he had not personally watched the show, he was aware of discussion around it and could see why links to it might be made.

"Knowing what it was about did prompt a chat with our son about the manosphere and those sort of toxic influencers it references," he said.

Notes written by John's son expressed a hatred of women, and he had also researched Elliot Rodger , described to jurors as "an early influence on incel and manosphere culture".

But John said his son had never shown evidence of misogyny.

"He's always got on well with all the women he's known in his life... there's never been a problem."

Pictures shared with the BBC showed some children hiding underneath their desks after the school was put under lockdown

John said the family believed their son was dealing with mental health issues in the months before the attack.

He had wanted to self-harm and had attempted to take his own life, he said.

"We were worried about what he might do to himself."

John urged other parents not to be afraid to be "a bit intrusive" into their children's lives, adding: "Try and have a proper chat. It's difficult to find the time sometimes because you're wrapped up in your own things."

In a statement, a government spokesman said its thoughts were with the victim and all of those affected by the "terrible events" at Thorpe St Andrew School.

"We are committed to ensuring all children are safe from radicalisation and threats online," they said.

" Prevent plays a crucial role in this, moving more than 6,000 people away from violent ideologies since 2015.

"In addition, social media platforms must be able to remove illegal content and stop children accessing harmful material by law – or face penalties of up to £18m for failing to comply."

John acknowledged that his son was "looking at a long sentence" when he appears before the court again in December.

"We will support him as best we can, try and see that he gets the mental health support he needs and try and get back how he used to be," he said.

ACOTAR fans put real life on hold for latest release

Abigail Wright said the series was her "gateway back to reading"

As I arrive at Waterstones in York shortly before 08:00, there is already a queue forming outside the bookshop.

Fans of Sarah J Maas's bestselling A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series are waiting eagerly to get their hands on the latest instalment.

Among them is Olivia Bray, 28, who has spent more than a decade immersed in the American author's fantasy world.

For Bray, the appeal goes beyond magic, romance and fantastical kingdoms. It is the feminism running through Maas's books that has kept her coming back.

And with the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, Bray is prepared to put real life on hold, having booked an entire week off work to give herself time to recover from whatever awaits her between the covers.

"I'll be done [with reading] by tomorrow," she said. "I've just got the whole week off in case it's traumatising."

Set in the fictional world of Prythian, the series has amassed millions of fans across the world.

The series follows Feyre Archeron, a young huntress drawn into the dangerous world of the fae, where she navigates political intrigue, war and romance.

There have been five books so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021).

A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in the best-selling series, was released on Tuesday - five years after fans last heard from the characters.

A Court of Splintered Harmony was released on Tuesday morning

Another ACOTAR fan, 22-year-old Abigail Wright, hoped to finish the book on release day, which coincided with her day off, before returning to work.

She said the books were her "gateway back into reading" aged 19.

Like Bray, Wright believed the recurring theme of female empowerment was a key part of its appeal.

"I think it's so popular because, yes, the romantic side of it is very good, but the strong women you see in the books are just a way to make other young women feel really empowered," said Wright.

"It just gives them a sense of power and [makes them] see you can start from nothing, like Feyre does, and just make your way up… you don't need a man to do all these things for you, you have the power to do anything you want to do."

Doors opened at 09:00 GMT at Toppings and Company Booksellers, where copies of the book are available

Gabriella Booth, 29, was introduced to the series in 2013, but attributes ACOTAR's explosion in popularity to both the pandemic and "BookTok" - a TikTok community dedicated to sharing what people are reading and writing.

"The characters in general are so easy to read about. You can relate in different parts to a lot of them, I find," said Booth.

"For me, I love the fantasy world - that's something I've loved reading growing up. So, to have that combined with the romance side of everything... there's something that's just so exciting to read about."

Booth has previously taken time off work to read new releases and plans to do so when the seventh ACOTAR book is published in January.

However, on this occasion, she hopes to finish A Court of Splintered Harmony after work.

Alice Boyce, a bookseller at Topping and Company Booksellers on Museum Street in York, said ACOTAR fans had made their way straight up to the science-fiction area of the store as soon as doors opened at 09:00.

"People are really enthusiastic; we've had emails saying, 'can you put a copy aside for me?', and last night we had people asking to put it on pre-order."

An ACOTAR fan herself, 26-year-old Boyce said she felt she could truly disconnect when she read the books.

"You can dive into books and just escape a little bit," she added.

One reader looked particularly shocked at the Wolverhampton release event

Events were held across the UK, including in Wolverhampton and Northern Ireland , to mark the new book's release, with Waterstones on York's Coney Street hosting its first ever midnight release event.

Eighty ACOTAR fans, some of whom were dressed as their favourite characters, attended the event, while 100 members of the fandom flocked to a party in Wolverhampton.

Organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, told the BBC people were "ecstatic" when the book was finally released.

"The community was just lovely, it was so nice to see everybody come together and fan-girl over a book," Fellows said.

Fellows, who booked the day off work to read the book, said she was already through the first chapter.

"It sounds like it's going to be incredible", she said.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Tuesday, Abi Fraser, owner of the Throne and Heart bookshop in Market Harborough, Leicestershire, where a release party was also held, said: "We had about 45 people in the bookshop to celebrate the midnight release.

"We had quizzes, we had games, we had a countdown to midnight - there is a real community vibe to the fandom... it's fantastic."

Elizabeth Vaziri, commissioning editor at Voyager and Magpie at the publisher Harper Collins, told the programme fantasy had "always been a portal for escapism".

Combined with romance, Vaziri said the "romantasy" genre had "given people a safe place to navigate relationships or sexuality".

Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, (left) and Nouman Essghir, 24, attended court on Tuesday

Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford last month.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.

Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.

The pair appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.

Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The court heard vans bearing the logo "Fuel2You" were spotted close to the base.

In the early hours, the vans came across a Ministry of Defence Police cordon and re-routed to another location.

Police arrived and arrested five men. They later revealed that one had called 999 and reported what was going on.

During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, Essghir stood in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and confirmed his name and address.

His charge relates to an alleged "reconnaissance mission" on 22 August, around a month before the Fairford incident.

Abdulkarim is charged with helping with the plot.

He appeared in court in a wheelchair wearing a checked shirt, jeans and a baseball cap. He confirmed his name and address.

Both men are charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Essghir has been remanded in custody, while Abdulkarim has been granted bail with conditions including the surrender of his passport.

The case will be next heard at the Old Bailey on 20 November.

This video can not be played

Mohmed Abdulkarim seen leaving Westminster Magistrates' Court

Essghir was one of five men arrested near the base on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. All five were released on police bail the following day, but Essghir was re-arrested on 20 October.

A 25-year-old UK-Iranian national who was also re-arrested on that date on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service has now been released without charge. He remains on police bail after his initial arrest on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.

The re-arrests in October led to detectives interviewing Abdulkarim.

Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the release of the five men on police bail in September had raised significant questions and speculation about the investigation for members of the public.

He stressed that tactics used by counter-terror police can appear "illogical" at times but said that "there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them".

"In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I've announced today," he added.

This video can not be played

Watch: 'A range of incidents' believed to have been directed by Iran in recent months

US President Donald Trump at the time said he was "surprised" the men had been released, saying: "We would not have released them."

Taylor said counter-terror police had seen "a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state".

Iran has previously denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

The base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for it to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

After the incident in September the US pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base, without giving specific details.

Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up

UK prepper stores see massive sales following government campaign

Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.

The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.

The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.

Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.

The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.

"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.

Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.

In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."

An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."

Sales of torches and radio have risen sharply for some UK retailers

Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.

Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing – order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."

Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

Gambling addict swindled council out of £7k for rent and Amazon shopping

Karen Deakin from Haverfordwest admitted fraud by abuse of position

A gambling addict with previous convictions for fraud and theft swindled almost £7,000 from the local authority to pay for online shopping and rent.

Karen Deakin, 56, from Haverfordwest, was a purchase card officer for Pembrokeshire council, and was able to increase the limit on employee credit cards to spend £6,915.20.

In sentencing at Swansea Crown Court, Judge Geraint Walters KC said she had a "dreadful record of being dishonest" and should be "locked up".

But new sentencing guidelines meant Deakin received a 12-month suspended prison sentence and ordered to repay the money.

He also said he was "surprised" by the council's vetting procedure when employing Deakin.

Megan Williams KC, prosecuting, said Deakin used her own employee purchase card, as well as cards belonging to former employees, to buy personal items and pay her rent to the council.

Deakin's purchase card had a £1 credit limit because her role was to deal with purchasing queries.

But Deakin increased the limit to allow her to spend the council's money.

Between 22 March and 29 October 2024, she spent £6,915.20 of council funds.

Deakin made "full and frank admissions" to the council when confronted and was immediately suspended under investigation.

She pleaded guilty and told the court she had been experiencing financial difficulties because of an online gambling addiction.

Deakin has three previous convictions, dating from 1996 to 2012, for theft and fraud-related offences.

Emily Bennett KC, defending, said Deakin was "deeply ashamed" of her actions and apologised to the council.

She said Deakin had developed a gambling addiction and that "rather than seeking help she became embroiled within that addiction".

Sentencing Deakin to 12 months in prison, suspended for two years, Walters described her criminal record as "pretty unimpressive".

He said he was "surprised" by the council's vetting procedure when employing her.

The judge described Deakin as having a "dreadful record of being dishonest".

He said part of him believed she "should be locked up this time", but said he had to consider new sentencing guidelines which state when a sentence is 12 months or less the court should consider whether immediate imprisonment is "absolutely necessary".

Walters told Deakin that this was her "last warning".

Deakin was also ordered to repay the stolen money.

Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak

Henry Nowak was 18 when he was stabbed to death in Southampton in December 2025

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Chalk told Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that would include looking at whether any reports had been made but people or organisations had held back due to a "misplaced sense of cultural sensitivity".

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.

On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".

Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.

Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.

Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.

After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.

But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?

This video can not be played

Nasa reveals crew for Artemis III mission, which will not land on the Moon

Nasa has announced more details about its next Artemis mission, which is set to launch in the summer of 2027.

The Artemis III mission will not head to the Moon. Instead four astronauts will fly to low Earth orbit where they will dock with two prototype lunar landers, one made by Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin company and the other by Elon Musk's SpaceX.

This will pave the way for the Artemis IV mission, currently scheduled for 2028, which will see astronauts land on the lunar surface for the first time since 1972.

Artemis III has been described by Nasa as the most complicated mission it's ever attempted.

It involves four astronauts, three rocket launches, three different spacecraft and two dockings. It will last for 14 days, although it could be extended to 17 days if needed.

The first rocket to launch will be Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, blasting off from Florida. It will be carrying its prototype lander called Blue Moon. No astronauts will be on board and the lander will be placed into low Earth orbit.

Then Nasa's Space Launch System rocket will launch from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, carrying four Artemis III astronauts in the Orion capsule. This is the same type of rocket and spacecraft used for the Artemis II mission, which saw astronauts fly around the Moon and back to Earth.

Orion will also be placed into orbit around the Earth, and the crew will spend two days checking out their spacecraft.

Then on day three of its flight, Orion will dock with the Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The crew will open the hatch and enter the lander, where they will spend two days checking out its systems.

On flight day six, SpaceX's huge Starship rocket will blast off, also from Florida. The upper stage of its rocket, called "the Ship" is the prototype lander (although it has not yet been fitted out as a lander and lacks life support systems) and this will be placed in low Earth orbit.

Nasa's Orion spacecraft and its crew will undock from the Blue Moon lander and then dock with the SpaceX Ship. This will be a shorter demonstration lasting for two hours, and the Artemis III crew will not enter the SpaceX lander.

Once undocked, the Orion crew will spend the rest of their mission carrying out additional tests of their capsule and carrying out science experiments, before returning home.

The Artemis III crew will be aboard Orion for two weeks, slightly longer than the nine days spent there by the Artemis II team. Their return journey will test an upgraded heat shield during the capsule's fiery re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere.

The mission was originally conceived to be the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 in 1972, but Nasa changed its plans in February 2026.

The reason was simple: the SpaceX Starship lander contracted to carry astronauts to the surface is not ready, and the in-orbit refuelling it depends on has never been demonstrated.

Rather than slip the schedule further, Nasa repurposed the mission as a crewed docking rehearsal — so that when the landers do fly, the techniques to dock with them and the suits to enter them will already have been tested with people on board.

In terms of the in-orbit refuelling, a March 2026 report from the US Government Accountability Office found that Elon Musk's SpaceX had made "limited progress" maturing the technology. The first refuelling demonstration is, optimistically, scheduled for late 2026.

Nasa astronaut Randy Bresnik will serve as the mission's commander.

Luca Parmitano, of the Italian Space Agency, will be the pilot. He has spent more than 300 days in space.

Americans Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio will be the mission specialists.

Bob Heintz will serve as a backup crew member. A test pilot who has logged 170 days in space, he can step into any role.

Nasa hopes Artemis IV, targeted for 2028, will be the first crewed lunar landing of the modern era. Astronauts are expected to descend to the Moon's south polar region and remain on the surface for around a week.

The frozen water locked in permanently shadowed craters could one day be used for drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel during future missions.

But the biggest setback was on 28 May 2026, when Blue Origin's only launch pad at Cape Canaveral was seriously damaged after a rocket exploded during an engine test.

Rebuilding the New Glenn launch pad has taken months, but Nasa says it is working with Blue Origin and is confident the launchpad will be ready by December or January 2027, so it can meet the timeline to be ready for the Artemis III mission in summer 2027.

The overarching ambition behind Artemis is to establish a long-term human presence on the Moon. Nasa's Moon Base programme — unveiled in May 2026 by the agency's administrator, Jared Isaacman — sets out three phases:

Before 2029: robotic landers and hopping drones will survey the south polar region and deliver scientific instruments

From 2029 onwards: repeated crewed missions will expand the site

By the mid-2030s: Nasa envisages "semi-permanent" habitats with astronauts living on the Moon for extended stays

A working base would allow sustained scientific research, the testing of technology bound for future Mars missions, and the eventual extraction of lunar resources. It would also keep the United States ahead of China in a renewed space race.

Many in the field doubt that Nasa's timetable can be met.

Experts are concerned about the slow pace of the development of SpaceX's Starship lunar lander and the absence of any in-orbit refuelling tests.

But the biggest set back was on 28 May 2026, when Blue Origin's only launch pad at Cape Canaveral was seriously damaged after a rocket exploded during an engine test.

Rebuilding the New Glenn launch pad is expected to take many months. When SpaceX lost a pad in 2016 it took 15 months to rebuild it — and SpaceX had other pads to fall back on.

Blue Origin does not, which calls into question the company's ability to provide the Blue Moon Mk2 needed for one of the lunar landings.

"It would not surprise me at all if China gets [to the moon] first," the Open University's Dr Simeon Barber told the BBC. The limiting step, he said, was the lander — the most challenging piece of the mission's technical architecture, and the one least under Nasa's direct control.

Artemis II launched on 1 April 2026 from the Kennedy Space Centre.

Its crew of four - commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen - became the first humans to travel beyond low Earth orbit since 1972.

Over ten days, Orion flew around the far side of the Moon, passing within 4,000 miles of the lunar surface and reaching a maximum of 252,756 miles from Earth -further than any humans have ever travelled.

The mission tested Orion's life-support and communication systems and gave engineers their first detailed look at how the heat shield performs on a lunar return. The Artemis II flight was the essential proof that the hardware works with people on board.

The last human mission to the Moon was Apollo 17 in December 1972.

Astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt spent three days on the surface in the Taurus-Littrow valley.

No human has set foot on the Moon in the half-century since.

In total, 24 American astronauts have travelled to the Moon and 12 have walked on its surface - all as part of the US Apollo space programme. Five of the 24 are still alive.

America first went in the 1960s, primarily to beat the Soviet Union to assert its geopolitical and technological dominance.

Once that goal was achieved, political enthusiasm and public interest ebbed, as did funding for further exploration.

Chinese astronauts Zhu Yangzhu, Zhang Zhiyuan and Li Jiaying travelled to China's Tiangong space station on the country's Shenzhou-23 spacecraft in May 2026

Will a new strategy help protect Northern Ireland's nature?

A new strategy to restore and enhance protection for nature in Northern Ireland has been launched by the agriculture and environment minister.

About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".

And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status.

The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats.

Andrew Muir says nature must be put "back at the heart of everything we do"

Minister Andrew Muir said supporting nature was "not just a nice thing to do" but "a moral obligation to future generations".

But the minister acknowledged that money would be needed to address the challenges.

The strategy highlights the importance of nature as providing the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe.

Muir said nature must be put "back at the heart of everything we do because when nature thrives, people flourish".

"It is essential to a strong economy, healthier communities and a more resilient Northern Ireland," he said.

"With so much of our natural world lost, we must protect what remains, restore what has been damaged and create new habitats at scale."

Northern Ireland is one of the most "nature-depleted" parts of the world, according to one major report

Many places in Northern Ireland support rare or threatened plants, animals and habitats.

They can be legally designated to help ensure better management and protection of those species.

There are hundreds of such designated sites across Northern Ireland, covering about 10% of the land and 38% of coastal waters - classed as Areas of Special Scientific Interest; Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) which have international biodiversity importance; Ramsar Sites which cover wetlands of international importance; Special Protection Areas (SPAs); and Marine Conservation Zones (MCZs).

That should lead to work to protect the species and habitats they have been designated for.

But the Office for Environmental Protection found not enough sites are being designated and the condition of those that have been is worsening .

The number of sites that were in favourable condition dropped from 61.7% in 2008, to 51.5% in 2024.

It is now investigating how those sites are being managed , external by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, after it found implementation of the designation fell short.

Northern Ireland is one of the most nature-depleted areas in the world, according to the 2023 State of Nature Report.

It found 12% of species in Northern Ireland are under threat of extinction, and the number of flowering plants had declined by 14% since 1970.

The Nature Recovery Strategy identifies six external pressures affecting nature and biodiversity - invasive species; climate change; human impact through inappropriate development; land and sea-use change; increased intensive farming; pollution.

It says these must all be addressed effectively to allow nature to thrive.

Ulster Farmers' Union deputy president Glenn Cuddy said his organisation was "still a bit skeptical" about the strategy.

"There's always a concern that nature will be more thought of than the farming and farmers have been walking along with nature for a long time, even before some of these projects have started," he said.

"We have always been the guardians of the countryside and for nature too."

Heather McLachlan, the National Trust's Northern Ireland director, said: "What really needs to happen is that we need to see where are the priorities.

"How do we get this action going, who's going to do it and most importantly where's the money going to come from to get it done?"

Joanne Sherwood, the director of The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds Ireland said: "Species are really in decline so what it means for us is this charts out the strategy and the way forward.

"But of course a strategy isn't everything - we need now to act and take urgent action."

Dykes encountered elephants, gorillas and was chased by "killer" bees as he rowed more than 434 miles (700 km) along rivers in the Congo Basin, central Africa.

In his latest Project 6 challenge, Dykes will attempt six expeditions in very different locations.

He has previously walked 4,000-miles (6,437km) along the length of China's Yangtze River in 2019 and kayaked the length of the Coppename river in Suriname from source to sea in 37 days

On "going missing", Dykes said his "power bank just shut down".

"We were underneath the jungle canopy, because we were staying with a small community, and then it took me about 20 hours before I could get out the first message," he said.

China's families are now supporting more old people than kids

Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.

The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.

The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.

China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .

The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.

At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.

"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.

Birth rates in China have been falling for years now

China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.

The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.

But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.

Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.

Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.

The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.

Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.

It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

I'm one of a growing number of Gen Z birdwatchers - it helps my mental health

Glasgow-based Caitlin Andrew found a passion for birdwatching in her early 20s

"I would be such a grump," says Caitlin Andrew, recalling her teenage self on walks with her parents.

"They are both into birdwatching and they would stop and listen and look at things.

"We had some really nice walks and experiences, but I just didn't have an interest in them at the time. I do feel quite bad about it now."

Three years ago, during a difficult period in her life, Caitlin discovered birds offered an unexpected escape from her troubles.

She joined the growing number of young people flocking to birdwatching.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

More stories from Scotland

"I was 24 and living in Glasgow as a student," says Caitlin, who grew up in Midlothian.

"I had poor mental health and was feeling a bit low, and finding it quite difficult to connect to the world around me."

Around that time, Caitlin joined her family for a holiday on Islay.

The southern-most island of the Inner Hebrides is renowned for its wild birds, with more than 120 species to spot during the spring and autumn migrations , external .

"When we were there we did a lot of birdwatching," says Caitlin.

"And as you can imagine there are incredible things to see - choughs and white-tailed eagles."

Caitlin says, rather than feeling grumpy, she found a sense of peace and calm watching birds.

"Just taking time to look and listen and take in everything you are connected to the environment you are in."

Her parents were delighted when she asked for a pair of binoculars for her birthday.

Gannets are one of Caitlin's favourite birds

But making her first forays into birdwatching, Caitlin felt no-one else shared her passion for birds.

"I did feel a little bit embarrassed to say I was doing it," she says.

"It is a stereotype, isn't it? It's associated with older people with a sedate life and picking it up in retirement - all things which I don't think are negative at all.

"But among my peers I was certainly the only person doing it properly in any kind of capacity."

Caitlin enjoys how different birds give pointers to changes in the seasons

Caitlin, who is a Gaelic speaker, found she was far from alone as a young female birdwatcher when she made a BBC Alba documentary about her hobby .

She came across an Inverness chapter of the Feminist Bird Club - a group founded in New York in 2016 to help make the interest inclusive and safe.

Caitlin also met female professionals and volunteers involved in bird conservation.

She says: "In the birdwatching community, everyone is so friendly and happy to tell you they have something interesting in their scope or have seen something interesting."

Research carried out for the RSPB suggests there are more than four million birdwatchers in Britain, up from 2.7 million eight years ago.

The number of Gen Z enthusiasts - people aged 16 to 29 - rose from an estimated 61,000 in 2018 to 724,000 today, according to the study.

Crested tits are another of Caitlin's favourites to spot

Caitlin's favourite birds include crested tits, which in the UK are found in native pine forests in parts of the Highlands, Moray and Aberdeenshire , external .

"I love seeing crested tits in the Cairngorms. They are rare, so its a special thing to see them," she says.

Gannets are another favourite.

"I'm always happy to see a gannet. They are big and so powerful. They're like dinosaurs."

Caitlin enjoys how different birds signal changes in the year.

"When you start to hear a chiffchaff in maybe March or April you know spring is coming, and that is really exciting," she says.

"And then when coming into winter there are redwings and fieldfares.

"It feels like these creatures are giving you pointers that things are changing, and it's lovely to connect to that."

She adds: "Life can be so turbulent. Things go and down and you never know what's coming - the political nonsense and all the rest of it.

"And these little animals, they are just all about finding food, raising babies, fledging their young and then doing it all again - they're just trying to survive.

"It does make your problems feel very small."

India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions

This video can not be played

Watch: Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution

India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.

Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.

Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.

Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.

The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.

But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.

More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition ‌from Musk.

For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution , spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.

Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.

Jio's cheap tariffs democratised internet use in India a decade ago

This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.

Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".

But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.

"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.

"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."

Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.

The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.

"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".

For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.

While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.

India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.

Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.

All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.

"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.

The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.

At $3.2bn, the Jio Platforms IPO is India's biggest share sale

But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.

The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.

Dhirubhai Ambani , the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.

In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.

And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.

"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.

"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m in New York auction

This video can not be played

Meet Jodi: Rare dinosaur skeleton sells for $47.3m

The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (£35.5m).

Nicknamed Jodi, the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton was auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.

The Late Cretaceous carnivore was expected to fetch at least $9m when it went under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed Gus, for a record $50.1m in July.

The sale has reignited debate in the scientific community over whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately or displayed publicly.

Sotheby's described Jodi as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".

The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science". The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.

The identify of the buyer, who won after a thrilling 12 minutes of auction bidding between six interested parties, has not been disclosed.

It becomes the second-most valuable dinosaur fossil ever sold, behind Gus. The third-most valuable was a Stegosaurus named Apex, which was sold by Sotheby's in July 2024 for $44.6m.

Megan Jacobs, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".

"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jacobs said.

Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.

Jodi was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.

The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hell Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.

Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from Jodi in 2006.

The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.

The auction of Jodi comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.

Researchers told the BBC after the sale of Gus that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.

Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".

"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."

He said at the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.

Responding to Tuesday's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that Jodi could disappear from public view.

"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.

But Jacobs told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.

"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin

Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders

The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.

Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.

Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.

Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.

"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.

Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.

The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".

Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.

Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."

The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.

Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.

"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.

All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.

Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push

There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.

Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".

Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.

As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.

Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.

Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.

But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".

And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

Woman says 40-mile journey to hospital while having contractions was 'scary'

Natasha Daryaie said the 40-mile journey while in premature labour was "scary"

A woman who was rushed 40 miles (64km) to a maternity unit after going into premature labour says her experience shows why services must remain at her local hospital.

Because she required specialist care, midwives at Daisy Hill in Newry wanted to send Natasha Daryaie to Craigavon Area Hospital but were told there was no room.

The Southern Health Trust plans to temporarily transfer inpatient maternity services from Daisy Hill to Craigavon because it has been unable to recruit enough consultant obstetricians to safely staff both hospitals.

A spokesperson for the trust said that, following operational and workforce assessments, inpatient maternity care at Craigavon had been identified as the safest and most sustainable arrangement for maintaining services.

In 2025, 1,713 babies were born at Daisy Hill Hospital

The trust says it is continuing efforts to recruit consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill while preparing to temporarily consolidate births and inpatient maternity care at Craigavon from 23 November.

However, mothers in the Newry area say losing local inpatient maternity services would leave families facing longer journeys at a time when they may need urgent care.

"The journey was scary. I was having contractions every five minutes but a midwife from Daisy Hill travelled with me to the Ulster Hospital where I spent four nights, was stabilised and then sent home," Natasha said.

"What does it say if a woman can't give birth in her own city?"

The trust has five vacant obstetrician posts and said it cannot provide a safe maternity service at Daisy Hill without the required medical cover.

Its chief executive Steve Spoerry told Stormont's Health Committee that keeping women and babies safe was its highest priority.

He said the trust would not have enough consultants to staff both maternity units' daytime and out-of-hours rotas, adding that a transfer of services to Craigavon is "highly probable" from next month.

Natasha, whose son Odin was eventually born at Daisy Hill at full term, said her experience showed why having services close to home mattered particularly in rural areas which she believes should be treated differently.

"It's all well and good saying Craigavon is there but they didn't have room for me that night - that is the reality: Craigavon did not have room for one local mum from Newry," Natasha said.

"How are they going to accommodate 1,400 babies and mums in the future?"

Another mother, Seanan Martin, said removing a service was not the answer and that the safety of mothers, babies and staff should be the priority.

She said the workforce challenges should have been planned for years in advance.

The number of midwives employed in the acute maternity units at Daisy Hill and Craigavon has fallen since October 2019.

The trust says the way midwifery care is delivered has changed, with more midwives now working in the community.

The figures show the number of full-time midwives employed at the two hospitals.

The current vacancies equate to 0.61 full-time posts at Daisy Hill and 11.69 at Craigavon.

The trust says 16 newly appointed midwives are due to start between November 2026 and January 2027.

It employs 15 consultant obstetricians but says sickness, reduced working arrangements and maternity leave mean not all are available for the consultant on-call rota.

The trust says staffing levels remain below what is required to fully staff both maternity units.

In 2025, 2,768 babies were born in Craigavon Area Hospital

The number of babies born at Daisy Hill increased between 2019 and 2025, while births at Craigavon fell.

Dale Spence said more midwives are required to provide the care that women deserved

Dale Spence, the director of the Royal College of Midwives in Northern Ireland, said to provide the care that women deserve, more midwives were required and that those who are working are feeling overburdened.

Speaking publicly for the first time about the present condition of maternity services, she added that Northern Ireland should not be relying on the goodwill of midwives to keep some services afloat.

Midwives are doing the best they can to provide care for mothers and their babies, Spence said, but the system is under so much pressure that it feels like they are working with their hands tied behind their back.

The trust has been asked how Craigavon will manage approximately 1,400 additional births each year if inpatient maternity services move from Daisy Hill.

It says it is continuing to seek consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill while preparing continuity arrangements to consolidate births and inpatient maternity care at Craigavon temporarily.

The trust has also acknowledged that, following the withdrawal of emergency general surgery from Daisy Hill in 2024, maternity services introduced a risk-stratification standard operating procedure to support the safe delivery of care.

This means fewer women have been considered suitable for elective Caesarean sections at Daisy Hill, which has had a subsequent decline in overall birth numbers over the past two years.

Mark Annett, whose wife has just given birth, said "geography really matters" when it comes to health care

Other families are concerned about how Craigavon will cope with the additional births.

That includes Mark and Naomi Annett whose third child, a daughter, was born last Thursday.

Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America

"Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.

Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.

It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.

Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".

This video can not be played

Watch: How President Lula turned it around to beat Flávio Bolsonaro

If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.

When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt" .

Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back – and it paid off.

He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".

His approval ratings jumped.

He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic – a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.

Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.

The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.

Relations then improved.

The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".

Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader.

Fireworks heard after Lula's victory in São Paulo

So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?

Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".

Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round.

Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking.

Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.

The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.

Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit.

The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response.

If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.

Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels.

He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from Flávio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.

It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.

Then there is US tech.

Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro.

Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach.

Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.

Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.

The relationship has exposed political divisions.

In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused Flávio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.

Still, tensions can be overstated.

The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on.

Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

Wildlife appeal closes in on £30m target

The window for public donations to the Rothbury Estate appeal closes on Friday

Conservation groups aiming to raise £30m to buy a vast upland estate are within touching distance of their target following a £1.9m government pledge.

The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust are looking to acquire the 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate in its entirety as part of plans boost wildlife, restore bogs and promote nature-friendly farming.

Their fundraising efforts - now standing at £29m thanks to the latest donation - have attracted backing from the likes of Sir David Attenborough with the window for public donations running until the end of this week.

However, some members of the Northumberland farming community said they viewed the project as "a folly".

The wildlife groups previously purchased part of the estate, including the Simonside Hills, from the Duke of Northumberland's son, Lord Max Percy, in 2024.

If successful in buying the remainder, the organisations claim there is the potential to develop a "40-mile nature recovery corridor stretching from the North East coast to Kielder on the central Scottish border".

It could also see a reduction in the number of sheep from 1,500 to 500 with the number of cattle quadrupled to 200.

The government grant was announced on Monday at the UN Global Biodiversity Conference, COP17, taking place in Armenia.

Craig Bennett OBE, chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the funding would "take us another step closer to realising our vision for one of the largest nature recovery projects England has ever seen".

He added it was a "stamp of approval" for the project on the back of "millions generously donated by philanthropists, charitable funds and thousands of members of the public".

Earlier this year, though, tenant farmer Chris Armstrong, who oversees 1,000 acres (405 hectares) close to the site, warned local opinion was split .

He told the BBC: "I would put it very much akin to the Brexit vote. I would think it would be that finely split.

"I think the majority of the farming community see this as a folly."
