Scotland's recycling rates at five-year low. How is your area doing?

Waste experts have warned that landfill space in Scotland is rapidly running out

Scotland's recycling rate has fallen to its lowest level in five years, according to figures from the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).

The Scottish government's environmental regulator says households recycled 42.8% of waste in 2025 - down from 44.3% the previous year.

According to a roadmap set by the Scottish government in 2010, recycling rates should have hit 70% last year but are falling well short.

The share of waste processed at an incinerator remained broadly the same at 82% but the amount being diverted to landfill fell by 10%.

The Sepa figures show that recycling rates vary massively by local authority. South Ayrshire's residents recycled 55% of their waste, compared with 26% in Glasgow.

The islands have the lowest rates, with Orkney recording a figure of just 18.2%.

A total of 2.31 million tonnes of waste was created by households in 2025, which represents a fall of just 1,500 tonnes.

Recycling rates have remained similar - at about 45% - for more than a decade.

The biggest change has been seen in the way black bag waste is treated.

A rapid growth in the construction of energy-from-waste plants, which generate electricity by burning rubbish, has seen a shift away from landfill.

But this has not happened quickly enough to meet a landfill ban which was due to come in at the start of the year. It has now been effectively delayed to 2028.

This video can not be played

What's happening to our rubbish?

The figures do not reflect a disruption to Scotland's waste management by the long-term repairs being carried out to the incinerator at Polmadie in Glasgow.

The Glasgow Recycling and Renewable Energy Centre in Glasgow was shut down in April this year, with much of the waste being diverted to other incinerators or landfill.

The centre is operated, along with a facility at Dunbar, by Viridor.

Karen MacCormick from the company says waste incineration is a greener option than landfill because it can also generate electricity.

She added: "When it's in landfill you've got the landfill gasses, you've got methane, etc.

"This is a more sustainable way of dealing with the waste, coming through an energy recovery facility, and obviously we can create something at the end of it which is low carbon energy going straight to the grid."

A deposit return scheme for bottles and cans, which has seen recycling rates increase significantly in other countries, has been repeatedly delayed .

Experts have also suggested that the lack of consistency in what is collected by local authorities across the country makes it confusing for households.

While some councils take glass at the kerbside, for example, others are forced to drop them off at bottle banks.

Research from Zero Waste Scotland also suggests that more than half of the waste placed in black bins could be recycled.

Sepa's chief scientific officer, Dr Richard Allan, says the figures highlight an "ongoing challenge" with how waste is managed.

He added: "It's clear that where waste ends up is important, but we need to focus on preventing waste in the first place and recycling more of that material when it is produced."

Karen MacCormack says waste incineration is a greener option than landfill

Kim Pratt, senior circular economy campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said there had been a "shocking decline" in recycling rates.

She said this showed that Scotland had "lost its way", with households missing the 2025 target of 70% recycling "by a mile".

"Recycling levels have stalled in Scotland since the Scottish government encouraged a new generation of waste incinerators to be built, meaning that household waste which could have been recycled is being burned instead," she said.

"The Scottish government is expected to consult on new circular economy targets this year.

"If these are to be meaningful, it must learn the lessons from the past – setting targets is the easy part, meeting them requires real commitment and planning that puts people and nature first."

Waste sector crisis could see rubbish piling up on streets, experts warn

Truckloads of Scotland's rubbish will be sent to England, experts say

Sabotage, betrayal, secrecy... and recycling

Climate Action Secretary Gillian Martin said the amount of household waste generated in Scotland had dropped by 11% since 2011, and the amount sent to landfill had fallen by 10% in 2025.

"However, the decrease in household recycling rates in 2025 is clearly disappointing and underlines why the Scottish government is taking significant action," she said.

"The Circular Economy and Waste Route Map sets out how we are improving recycling and diverting recyclable material away from general household waste through the deposit return scheme, extended producer responsibility for packaging and a new household recycling code of practice."

Martin said the government had also invested more than £66m to increase recycling collections and the capacity to recycle "problematic materials" like plastic films.

New gas-fired power station at Peterhead is approved

The current Peterhead facility has been generating electricity for more than four decades

The Scottish government has given its consent for the construction of a controversial new gas-fired power station at Peterhead.

The scheme, by SSE and Equinor, will generate about 900 megawatts of electricity and includes provision for carbon capture.

Environmental group Friends of the Earth Scotland insist the decision locks Scotland into a dependence on fossil fuels.

But supporters say new carbon capture technology could slash emissions from the new site by more than 90%. SSE said its delivery was contingent on progress with the Scottish carbon capture cluster.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

The application for the power station was consented on the same day that Holyrood debated the issues of climate change and climate justice.

The current Peterhead facility has been generating electricity for more than four decades but it is now the last in Scotland to burn fossil fuels.

SSE has previously said it intends to replace this site with the new 'Peterhead 2' - though climate campaigners have raised concerns that both facilities will continue operating together.

North East Scotland Green MSP Maggie Chapman said the existing gas-powered station was "Scotland's largest source of climate pollution".

She added that "instead of tackling that and reducing its impact, the government has decided to expand it".

The decision was also condemned by campaign group Uplift.

A spokesperson said: "Our high dependency on expensive gas is what's driving our energy bills up and leading to millions of people facing impossible choices this winter.

"So, it is inconceivable why the Scottish government would want to lock ourselves into 30 more years of it."

A Scottish government spokesperson said the potential impacts on communities, nature and cultural heritage - including the cumulative effects of developments - were "important considerations" in the decision-making process.

They said the full grounds for the decision were set out in a letter and it "would not be appropriate to comment further".

Finlay McCutcheon, managing director of SSE Thermal, said: "This is an important milestone for a project which has the potential to provide the flexible, low-carbon electricity needed to support a renewables-led energy system while creating and sustaining good jobs in the north-east of Scotland."

John Underhill, Aberdeen University's Director for Energy Transition, said the Scottish government's decision demonstrated its acceptance that gas will be a "vital part of the country's energy and electricity mix for decades to come" while acknowledging its climate obligations.

He said: "The decision also provides a much-needed lifeline for the Acorn project (Scottish cluster) too since it gives the latter a new purpose to store emissions from the Peterhead power station after losing supplies of emissions from Grangemouth and Mossmorran when they closed."

article:
Kane's rise from childhood keeper to the best in the world

PE teacher Mark Leadon said Kane was a "real team player" and "wasn't one to keep the ball if a pass was on"

Harry Kane is on top of the world.

The Bayern Munich striker continued his remarkable career journey on Monday night by becoming the first Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or for 25 years.

He is already England's joint record appearance maker and his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in an international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut.

It hasn't been the smoothest of journeys. From being rejected by Arsenal to loan spells in the Football League, the 33-year-old has had to defy the doubters throughout.

BBC Sport takes a look at the origin story of the England captain.

England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender

Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend

When a six-year-old Harry Kane arrived for trials with Ridgeway Rovers in 1999, the youth side - who a generation earlier had produced David Beckham - thought they had found themselves a new goalkeeper.

Dave Bricknell, former Ridgeway Rovers coach: "We're doing a little shooting session, and I ask for a lad who can go in goal.

"This little boy puts his hand up and says: 'I'll go in goal.' We give him some gloves, and he performs heroics - makes some fantastic saves. He's tipping it round the post, tipping a couple over the bar.

"I'm thinking this is great, we've got a goalkeeper. And then this woman came up to me and said he's better on the pitch.

"We put him on pitch and he smacked goals in left, right and centre. So he ends up being our centre-forward."

Harry Kane with older brother Charlie and, right, with David Beckham and now wife Katie Goodland

Kane and his Ridgeway Rovers team-mates' goalscoring exploits were recorded in a notebook

Kane's prolific form for Ridgeway Rovers and his Waltham Forest district side caught the attention of professional scouts. Arsenal initially snapped up the youngster but decided not to keep him, while Watford also passed up the opportunity to sign Kane.

Trevor Bailey, Kane's manager at Waltham Forest: "Harry could have done nothing all game, but if that chance came up it was in the onion bag.

"He was always on the move up front. When he got a chance, guaranteed four out of five he was going to score or set someone up."

Alex Welsh, former academy coach at Arsenal: "I first met Harry in the academy and he was a very competent goalkeeper, but his real desire was to score goals.

"I am absolutely convinced that is the reason why he is such a clinical striker - he intuitively knows what the goalkeeper doesn't like. He shoots early when the goalkeeper's not set."

Bricknell: "I believe he was second top-scorer at Arsenal behind Benik Afobe, and then for some reason they decided at 11 years of age that they didn't want him any more."

Kane attended Larkswood Primary Academy before moving to Chingford Foundation School, where he was inevitably the star of the football team. But, as a dedicated student, Kane impressed his teachers across the board.

Mark Leadon, Kane's PE teacher: "Aged 11, Harry was technically very gifted, with a great first touch, and a very clever player. He always knew where to go, right from an early stage.

"He was also a very good cricketer - he opened the bowling from year seven to 10 and batted at four or five. But he loved football. He was never a prima donna, and he would always put a shift in.

"What came through more than anything else was his determination to succeed. That work ethic was clear."

Luke Robinson, Kane's childhood friend and team-mate: "The only thing on his mind was football.

"We used to have a laugh, a couple of games of Fifa, but he was always driven. He'd always keep himself to himself.

"He loved David Beckham, he came in with the Mohican, everyone was laughing but he loved it. He loved football, 24/7, he lived and breathed football."

This video can not be played

Kane's old coach: He always had 'thirst' for goalscoring

It was Tottenham Hotspur who offered Kane hope after his earlier disappointments, but the future England captain was by no means the pick of the bunch for his age group.

Kane's desire to learn and improve endeared him to the Tottenham academy staff and he signed scholarship terms with the club on his 16th birthday in July 2009.

Alex Inglethorpe, former Tottenham youth-team coach: "When I joined Spurs as under-18 coach, Harry was 13.

"I'd like to say he was the gold medallist in the group and we'd all spotted he was going to be the fantastic player, but I'd be lying. He probably wasn't even on the podium.

"If there was something that endeared him to you it was that he was very, very low maintenance. It became fairly evident when Harry became a scholar he was someone who could finish.

"He was wonderfully demanding to coach because he always wanted to stay out and do extra. That obsession to improve is undoubtedly his greatest strength.

"It was probably around 16 he started having an impact on the youth team. We trusted him to come off the bench and have an impact - anywhere from right wing, number 10, centre-forward, sometimes in midfield."

Kane (centre) scored five goals during an 18-game loan spell at Leyton Orient in 2011

Kane went to League One Leyton Orient - making his professional debut in January 2011 at Rochdale, coming on for veteran striker Scott McGleish. Kane would score five times in nine starts.

McGleish: "Harry was not like other Premier League players, where you feel they're going to come in 'Billy Big Time'. He wanted the experience of learning what I call men's football.

"From the word go he was ready to fight for his place. In training, he was willing to just knuckle down and work hard.

"You could see in training and subsequently the matches he had ability and a desire to go further, but you're still looking like a young 17-year-old: very slight, still needing to physically develop, not the quickest but technically excellent."

After a few first-team games for Spurs, he went on loan in January 2012 to Championship strugglers Millwall. Kane's nine goals helped save Kenny Jackett's side from relegation.

Former Millwall defender Alan Dunne: "I've seen a lot of players come to the Den and freeze, because within five minutes they're being called names they've never heard before and they can't cope with that pressure.

"But it didn't faze him - he was a focused lad, he was confident in his ability."

Former Tottenham manager Tim Sherwood: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall, and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there.'

"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him."

After making his Premier League debut for Tottenham in August 2012, Kane was sent on loan again. The 19-year-old only made three appearances in the top flight for Norwich because of injury, and then had a loan spell at Leicester where he and future England team-mate Jamie Vardy struggled for regular starts.

Kane (centre, pictured playing against Hearts in 2011) joined Tottenham as an 11-year-old and signed professional terms on his 16th birthday in 2009

After four loan spells in three seasons, Kane spent the entire 2013-14 campaign with Tottenham. But it was not until April, after Andre Villas-Boas had been sacked and replaced by Sherwood, that a 20-year-old Kane was handed his first Premier League start for Spurs, scoring his first top-flight goal in the process against Sunderland and also netting in the following two games against West Brom and Fulham.

Sherwood: "It didn't feel a gamble at all to give Harry that start. It was almost overdue to be honest.

"Roberto Soldado was in front of him in the team, and nobody wanted Roberto to do well more than me - but every single day in training Harry was outperforming him. He didn't let me down.

"Harry wanted to get to the top, and nothing was going to stop him achieving that because of the ability, desire and mentality he possesses.

"I was the biggest believer Harry Kane ever had, because I used to think he was a mix between Teddy Sheringham and Alan Shearer."

Kane became Spurs' all-time top scorer on 5 February 2023, passing Jimmy Greaves' old mark of 266

Kane never looked back after scoring 21 top-flight goals the following season - and earning his first England call-up in March 2015.

He ended up as the club's all-time top scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances - and three Premier League Golden Boots, but no trophies

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola, who tried to sign him, said in 2023: "What an exceptional player - the numbers and, more than the goals, the quality. Harry Kane remains one of the best strikers I have ever seen in my life."

Former Spurs team-mate Son Heung-min: "Leader, brother, legend.

"Since day one it has been a joy to play by your side. So many memories, amazing games and incredible goals together."

Then Tottenham boss Ange Postecoglou: "Harry was brilliant throughout. You want to work with the best players and he is a hell of a striker and I thought he could help me.

"He has left an indelible mark at this football club, will go down as one of the greats."

Harry Kane won the German double this season

The only thing missing from Kane's career CV was trophies - and in 2023 he joined German side Bayern Munich, where he has continued to impress.

He has scored 156 goals in 159 games for the club, won the Bundesliga Golden Boot three times and won two German titles and a German Cup. Now he has been named the best player in the world.

Former Bayern defender Lothaur Matthaus: "Kane has reinvented the centre-forward game, as Manuel Neuer did with goalkeepers.

"I don't see a better striker in the world right now. Not just because of his goals, but because of his versatility and the positions he plays.

"Kane also demonstrates qualities as a passer, dribbler, and tackler. He is simultaneously a goalscorer, playmaker, box-to-box player, and tackler."

Ex-England striker Alan Shearer, speaking this summer: " To me he looks fitter and stronger than before.

"He's come into this World Cup off the back of a brilliant campaign for Bayern Munich and looks very sharp and very confident - as you would do after scoring 61 goals in one season. Those numbers are just ridiculous."

BBC pundit Chris Sutton: "He has to be in that bracket when you talk about the world's best. Harry Kane has instincts that are simply uncoachable."

Some of these interviews were first published in 2016.

Can clubs stop team news leaking out through FPL picks?

Joao Pedro had been pictured in training before his shock absence from Chelsea's line-up last weekend

Chelsea head coach Xabi Alonso was caught off guard after Saturday's loss to Tottenham when asked whether he was aware that Joao Pedro's injury had been leaked through the popular Fantasy Premier League game.

His response was: "I am not into the fantasy team thing, so I didn't know that."

Accounts believed by FPL trackers to belong to Chelsea staff, a player and a relative of a player appeared to transfer out or bench Joao Pedro before the deadline.

One Fantasy Premier League manager, known online as FPL Karim, was among those who believed they had identified information by tracking selections made by a relative of Chelsea forward Morgan Rogers.

He said: "There were rumours that a player was missing from Chelsea 's attack. I went to check Rogers' team, but he'd sold Joao Pedro two or three gameweeks earlier when he was injured. He never bought him back.

"Then I checked his brother's FPL team and saw that he'd sold Joao Pedro that gameweek and brought in Nicolas Jackson. I thought it was a bit weird. Why would you sell him when he's one of the most-owned forwards in the game?

"That's when I felt maybe it was Joao Pedro who was missing out. I posted about it, it went viral, and that was basically it."

Confirmation of the injury emerged after the FPL deadline had passed, meaning 1.7 million managers had already selected Joao Pedro as captain, which doubles a player's points return.

The absence also came as a surprise to many following Chelsea 's 2-0 defeat by Tottenham , given Joao Pedro had been pictured in training during the week before the match.

Alonso later said the striker had missed the game because of "fluid on his thigh".

This video can not be played

'I didn't know that' - Alonso on Joao Pedro's injury leak

Alonso is one of a number of managers who have become increasingly guarded when discussing team news in media conferences.

Last month, he said: "I prefer not to give more information than needed."

On that occasion, his side went on to lose 3-0 at Brentford , having kept several injury concerns, including one involving Joao Pedro, under wraps.

Yet such is the popularity of Fantasy Premier League - a game played by more than 11 million people according to official figures - that many staff members, players and relatives of footballers also take part.

By identifying leagues or teams linked to players, staff or family members through the game, which provides an open database of participants, it can be possible to infer what is happening behind closed doors at various training grounds.

Previously, the highest-profile case involved Jack Grealish's absence from Aston Villa 's match against Leicester City in February 2021.

Leicester's manager at the time, Brendan Rodgers, admitted he had heard about the issue before the match, while Villa boss Dean Smith reportedly banned figures inside the club from playing FPL after the 2-1 defeat.

Later that year, Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola described the situation as "unethical and unprofessional".

There have been many further examples, claiming to suggest players from clubs like Arsenal , Liverpool , Leicester and Newcastle made revelatory changes to their teams.

Often that information is widely shared on social media, but it is also known that some top FPL players will withhold information for smaller circles to gain a competitive advantage in the game itself.

BBC Sport was able to find accounts that trackers claim are linked to staff, players and family members at clubs across the Premier League.

One of the experts in finding these club-linked accounts is FPL Focal, who told BBC Sport: "I am sure there are many more that have not been found. I have noticed some players have started using aliases. I've also had a couple of requests over the years to remove accounts, which I have always respected.

"The FPL leaderboard is completely public, so it is straightforward to look players up. Verifying that an account genuinely belongs to a player takes a bit more time."

Chelsea were subjected to three significant team news leaks during Liam Rosenior's short-lived tenure.

Two came before each leg of Chelsea 's record 8-2 aggregate Champions League defeat by Paris St-Germain, while the third occurred before the Englishman's final game in charge.

Remarkably, it later emerged that former defender Marc Cucurella's barber had revealed both Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro were unavailable because of injury.

Since then, Chelsea have reminded players to be careful about who they share information with before matches.

The club have also strengthened security measures at the training ground, including building new fencing around first-team pitches.

Chelsea appeared to have got on top of their leak problems earlier this season, but the Joao Pedro episode serves as a reminder that information can still emerge in unexpected ways.

Clubs can remind players and staff to be careful about what they share and with whom, while some may seek to discourage employees from selecting players from their own club in Fantasy Premier League. The nuclear option would be to ban the game entirely.

There is no league-wide rule against people involved in the sport playing the game and the Premier League defers any issues that emerge as a club matter.

Yet any measures are likely to have limitations.

While clubs can influence staff behaviour, monitoring the activity of players' friends and family members is considerably more difficult.

article:
Chair skills, quick brain - how O'Neill adapted to wheelchair rugby league

Finlay O'Neill made his England debut in 2025

"If you'd said to me when I was told I couldn't play rugby league again that it's going to be the best thing to ever happen to me, I'd have said 'you're lying'. But discovering wheelchair rugby league, which is even better, has been a blessing."

Rugby league has always been an important part of Finlay O'Neill's life. When he dislocated a knee while playing in a game at the age of 16, he put it down to the rigours of the sport.

The knee popped back into place but continued to cause issues, leaving the Halifax teenager struggling on the field and with increasing pain off it too.

After extensive medical tests, he was diagnosed with shallow kneecaps and hypermobility. His sporting hopes seemed to be over.

But after a lot of family encouragement, he transferred his skills to wheelchair rugby league with Halifax Panthers. Over the past three years, O'Neill has enjoyed a meteoric rise. Now he is part of the England squad who will be defending their Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup title in Australia.

"I think the first thing that really struck me was how similar the wheelchair game is in many ways to the running game," O'Neill, now 21, tells BBC Sport.

"From playing the running game, I had the rugby brain and skill - the ability to pass and see things happening, but I didn't have the physical skill of being able to move in a wheelchair, as I don't use one in my day-to-day life, and that was a big challenge.

"At the reserve or development level, if you've got good rugby knowledge, you can play the game, but you can't just rely on those skills in the Super League. You have to learn how to manipulate the chair and move it around the pitch.

"When you're playing a running sport, you just run and you don't really have to think about it, but in the wheelchair game, you've got to think at the same time about moving your chair to where you want to be, catching a ball, passing it and quickly moving on to the next play.

"At my first Super League training session, I was chasing the others, but playing against quick players means you have to get faster. It has taken a lot of hard work to go from having no chair experience to get up to the skill level of the top players."

Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup

30 October - 13 November

Wollongong, Australia

News and reports on the BBC Sport website

O'Neill has won back-to-back domestic trebles with Halifax Panthers

O'Neill earned his first England call-up in August 2025, playing in the Ashes series in Australia last October and November.

He was then selected alongside Halifax team-mates Jack Brown and Rob Hawkins in coach Tom Coyd's 10-player squad for the World Cup, to take place in Wollongong, south of Sydney.

England start their campaign against Wales on Friday (04:30 BST) before games against the USA and Ireland. Old rivals France, who England beat dramatically in the World Cup final four years ago, are in the other pool alongside Scotland, New Zealand and hosts Australia.

Brown and Hawkins were both part of the team who beat France in 2022 – a final O'Neill watched on television – and the trio helped a dominant Halifax claim a clean sweep of domestic honours for the second season in a row.

"Jack and Rob always say they're each other's biggest rivals and I say I'm the one trying to catch them," he says.

"From training together with Halifax and England, we have that connection and understanding on the pitch.

"One of my strengths is putting players through gaps and I am more of a playmaker than the one breaking through to score amazing tries.

"If I hold the ball a certain way, Jack knows I want him to run under me or go around me and it's the same with Rob.

"I don't necessarily need to talk to them on the pitch. It is just instinct."

O'Neill, who combines his sport with a job at a local supermarket, is one of five England World Cup debutants and is keen to justify the faith placed in him by Coyd and also his Halifax coach Wayne Boardman, who was part of the 2022 team.

"When I got the international call up last year, I said I would give it everything for the next two years to be in contention for the World Cup and I went for it and it has happened," he says.

"I think this is going to be the most competitive World Cup ever. With so many new players involved, it's a completely different sport to four years ago.

"We are very confident going to Australia. As a team we are not going out to defend the title, we are going to win it."

Wheelchair rugby league is played with an oval ball, and wheelchair rugby with a round ball

Wheelchair rugby league - the sport O'Neill plays - was developed in France as a way of bringing the sport to people with disabilities. It is fully inclusive, with disabled and non-disabled players able to play on the same team, and follows many of the same conventions as the running game.

Teams of five players have six tackles to score. Tackles on the ball carrier are made by pulling off an tag attached to each player's shirt. A try scores four points, with two points for penalties and conversions, which are taken by punching the ball off a tee over the posts.

The game is played with an oval ball and lasts for 80 minutes, with a maximum of two non-disabled and three disabled players allowed on the field at any one time.

Wheelchair rugby - which is part of the Paralympic Games programme, and is also known as murderball - is played by those with specific neurological and physical impairments including tetraplegia, cerebral palsy and amputations.

It is played by teams of four using a round ball like a volleyball, and a match consists of four eight-minute quarters.

Athletes are classified with a points system from 0.5 (highest level of impairment) up to 3.5. In international wheelchair rugby, the total number of points of all four athletes playing on court at any one time cannot exceed 8.0, unless there is a woman on the court, in which case the team are allowed an extra 0.5.

To score, an athlete must cross the opposing team's goalline in firm control of the ball. Two wheels must cross the goalline for a score to count. There are no conversions.

Unlike in the league version, no tackling is permitted in wheelchair rugby, but it is a full-contact sport, allowing collisions between players. Athletes must dribble or pass the ball every 10 seconds, with failure to do so resulting in the referee handing possession over to the opposing team.

Given their league positions, form and pedigree, there could surely only have been one winner.

Fleetwood played Arsenal on Tuesday with an 84-place gulf between the teams and most home fans arriving in hope rather than expectation. But remarkably, it was the hosts who booked their place in the Carabao Cup quarter-final thanks to their penalty shootout win over the Gunners.

For the side known as the Cod Army, who won six promotions in 12 years in an impressive journey from non-league, this result will surely be remembered longest of all. Against the reigning Premier League champions, the club from a small seaside town in Lancashire created history in claiming one of the biggest cup upsets ever.

Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave the hosts the lead after 21 minutes but, after the break, Viktor Gyokeres pulled the visitors level.

And from there, they might have been expected to take charge, but Fleetwood remained resolute, prospering from a wasteful performance from Arsenal that included Max Dowman being sent off for kicking out after a robust challenge from Harrison Neal.

Fleetwood, who sit 18th in League Two having won just once in their past eight league games, dared to dream and took the game to penalties, with fans spilling on to the pitch after Conor Haughey's decisive spot-kick.

"The biggest night in the club's history in terms of opposition coming to town and we've managed to beat the champions," boss Matt Lawlor told Sky Sports in the aftermath of his side's stunning victory.

"I'm a big football fan and I watch National League all the way through to the Premier League, Championship. So for me it was a tough game to prepare for, but I'm just so glad that the lads have the feeling the way they are and took that performance in to make that town, the club, everyone proud."

Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90

Walter Koenig as Pavel Chekov on board the USS Enterprise during an episode of Star Trek from 1968

Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.

The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise, from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991.

In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5.

His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes , external on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."

Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world."

They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece".

Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T Kirk.

Shatner said , external he was "deeply saddened" to learn of Koenig's death, describing him as a man "who genuinely loved the Star Trek community".

He continued: "That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him."

Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk speaking into his communicator with James Doohan as Montgomery "Scotty" Scott and Walter Koenig as Pavel Chekov (right) in an episode of Star Trek from 1968

Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania.

He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman.

His big break came as the capable, loyal and sincere young Chekov, who often proudly claimed that everything originated in Russia, a running gag that amused the crew and audiences alike.

The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Beatles/Monkees-style mop-top haircut.

But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied.

The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal.

Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter. , external

He was arguably more integral to the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).

Koenig's seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a Next Generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in the modern series Star Trek: Picard in 2023.

He also wrote an episode of the original show's animated series spin-off, in 1973, titled The Infinite Vulcan.

Actor Walter Koenig speaking during The Original Series panel at the 18th annual Official Star Trek Convention in Las Vegas in 2019

A published author, Koenig's other on-screen credits included Columbo and Futurama.

Earlier this year, his performance in the short film Mr Fleischmann saw him collect the Platinum Award for best actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards, in recognition of his craft and career.

He married Judy Levitt, who appeared with him in three Star Trek movies and Michael Straczynski's futuristic space opera Babylon 5, in 1965. And they were together until her death in 2022.

The family suffered a personal tragedy in 2010, when their son Andrew, who played Richard "Boner" Stabone on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died by suicide aged 41.

Koenig is survived by their daughter, the actress and screenwriter Danielle Koenig, who worked on the animated series Star vs. the Forces of Evil.

Hospital to pilot Hugh's Law after death of boy, 6

Hugh Menai-Davis died of cancer and now his father, Ceri Menai-Davis, wants to see better support for parents

The parents of a boy who died of cancer and a new children's hospital will work together to shape how families of seriously ill children are supported by the NHS.

Ceri and Frances Menai-Davis, from Hertford, lost their son Hugh, 6, in 2021, and have since been campaigning for Hugh's Law, which would provide paid leave for carers and guarantee job security.

Their charity, It's Never You, is part of a pilot with the Cambridge Children's Hospital (CCH), due to open in 2031.

Ceri Menai-Davis told BBC Look East he hoped it would lead to measures to support families.

"So when the worst does happen, there's a blanket for them to be cushioned with," he said.

Hugh died in 2021

CCH will be the first specialist children's hospital in the East of England - the only region in the UK currently without one.

Ceri Menai-Davis said his son had been "the most beautiful, courageous little boy you could ever want as a parent".

When Hugh was diagnosed with the rare cancer rhabdomyosarcoma , external in October 2020, there was a clear plan for his treatment, but no equivalent plan to help his parents cope.

Ceri Menai-Davis said they had promised "that we would fight to change that".

"When Hugh passed away, my wife and I wanted to do something where we felt like we could give back in his memory, as a legacy for Hugh," he explained.

"We wanted to change the way that parents as a whole were treated when their child was diagnosed with a serious illness.

"The system is set up at the moment where it's not preventive or proactive, it's more reactive... we need to look at what actually happens should that child die."

Hugh's parents met with Yvette Cooper during their campaign

The parents were able to get a government report commissioned in August bearing Hugh's name.

Hugh's Report is a review of the mental health , external impact of life-threatening child illness on families.

The government's consultation into new rights for parents and carers of seriously ill children specifically mentions Hugh's Law , external as a possible approach, although it does not make a detailed proposal.

CCH aims to bring physical and mental health care together with research.

A spokesperson said that by including the recommendations of Hugh's Report in its clinical models before it opens, it hoped to lead the way in making the wellbeing of parents, carers and siblings an integral part of children's hospital care.

Dr Rob Heushckel said the new Cambridge Children's Hospital was committed to embedding the recommendations of Hugh's Report into its care model

Dr Rob Heushckel, clinical director for CCH, said it was aligned "with exactly what Hugh's Report is seeking to deliver".

"The types of children we look after now very often need more time in hospital and that has an impact on the family, siblings and their education.

"They require a different level of support than previously when you were perhaps in and out of hospital quickly without the treatments that are now available."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has previously said there needed to be more support for families of seriously ill children.

"I want to pay tribute to Hugh's family, who have been campaigning for us to launch this report," she said.

"This is the starting point to hear from parents and families who face the most difficult circumstances of all, so we can hear directly from them what more support they need."

article:
NHS Tayside apology to patients after scientist's data breach

Dr Glen Gardener accessed the records of nearly 400 patients while working at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee

NHS Tayside has apologised to almost 400 patients whose records were accessed by a Ninewells Hospital scientist who was subsequently fired for gross misconduct.

Dr Glen Gardner was dismissed in June last year after accessing patient records 497 times while assigned to non-clinical duties.

The breach came to light after Gardner, who claimed he had a legitimate reason for accessing the records, had his claim for unfair dismissal refused , external .

The health board said it was contacting patients directly to offer "a sincere apology".

It said the incident was reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), which found that there was "no evidence that the personal data left NHS Tayside's systems".

The employment tribunal, which was first reported in The Herald , external , took place in Dundee over three days in August.

The tribunal was told that the records were accessed by the scientist in 2023 and 2024.

More stories from Tayside and Central

More stories from Scotland

Gardner had been employed as a clinical scientist for more than 15 years.

He was transferred to a non-clinical project in 2023 after allegations of "erroneous" advice he had given to a patient concerning her breastfeeding while undergoing treatment were investigated.

In May 2024, a colleague noticed that Gardner was using the patient records system, known as CRIS, and was in the record she was accessing.

She queried with a senior colleague why Gardner was accessing records as she had previously been told he was assigned to alternative duties.

A subsequent review established that Gardner had accessed almost 400 patient records on CRIS, some on multiple occasions.

The breach was reported to the ICO, which suggested that the police and the 386 impacted patients were informed.

During an investigatory meeting, Gardner admitted accessing the records, but disputed that his role had been changed.

He claimed "no discussions were held that my role was changed, just my location" and said he had not been instructed "in writing" not to use CRIS.

Gardner said he had explanations for accessing the records, including performing an audit of breastfeeding patients.

He added that he had not "recorded the audit as yet" and would do this on his return to the department "when my clinical systems had been reinstated".

The tribunal said Gardner did not provide a satisfactory explanation why he had accessed the data or provided evidence of its use for legitimate reasons.

Employment Judge Paul Rae concluded that the NHS Tayside board had acted reasonably in treating Gardner's misconduct as "a sufficient reason for dismissal".

A spokesperson for NHS Tayside said "Following a comprehensive investigation under NHS Scotland workforce policy, it was identified that personal information was viewed inappropriately by a single member of staff.

"This staff member was dismissed in June 2025."

The spokesperson said the employment tribunal had backed the dismissal.

They added: "NHS Tayside reported the incident to the Information Commissioner's Office who found that there was no evidence that the personal data left NHS Tayside's systems.

"Patients who have been affected are being contacted directly to explain what happened to their information in detail and to offer a sincere apology."

Bid to allow unaccompanied 12 to 15-year-olds into pubs

Cold Town House in Grassmarket is one of the venues seeking licensing permission

A hospitality company is seeking licensing permission to allow children as young as 12 to enter some Edinburgh pubs and restaurants without an adult.

Signature Pubs Limited has asked the council to approve plans that would let teenagers enter the premises alone or in groups of up to six to buy a meal, snack or soft drink.

If granted, they would be served at McClarens on the Corner in Morningside, Cold Town House in Grassmarket and The Fountain on Dundee Street.

Owners claimed there was a strong demand for family-friendly restaurants after school, but some councillors have raised concerns and intend to do a site visit.

More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East

More stories from Scotland

Caroline Loudon, a licensing solicitor representing the company, said at the licensing board meeting on Monday: "These are family friendly venues with well-trained staff.

"It offers an accessible space for children to start going out without parents or guardians but with the checks and balances you'd want for your own family."

Under the proposal, youths aged 12 to 15 would be permitted to enter the venues unaccompanied to purchase food and soft drinks until 20:00.

They would be required to provide proof of age with a valid Young Scot Card or passport and would be limited to face-to-face table service.

The company is also seeking a licence to serve children under 12 when with an adult.

Under 12s would be permitted until 23:00 unless attending a private function, in which curfew would be 01:00.

Loudon told the committee her own daughter was a similar age and struggled to find local venues she could go to by herself.

She said coffee shops often closed at 18:00 and teenagers tend to migrate to hotspots such as Lothian Road and St James Quarter.

Councillors questioned the proposal at the meeting and asked what staff would do if teenagers started acting in "feral way".

A representative from Signature Pubs said they would be treated the same way as any other person and be asked to leave.

Groups of children entering the restaurants would be capped at six with a total of 21 allowed.

Concerns were also raised about the idea the venues were more "alcohol-led" than fast-food restaurants.

Loudon said the three venues vary where alcohol is concerned and disputed the term "pub" in some cases as these are deemed to be more akin to a restaurant which serves alcohol.

A representative added: "The restriction is for the children to come in for the purposes of a meal or a hot chocolate after school."

A decision was paused until the next board meeting to allow councillors to inspect the premises.

article:
How the Budget affects you

Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.

The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by around £300 or more in January.

Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.

If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.

It will be paid directly into your bank account.

You can find your council tax band by looking on your annual bill, or by looking on the government's website , external - although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.

Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.

This is designed to help with soaring energy bills. Tariffs linked to regulator Ofgem's price cap, are forecast to soar by hundreds of pounds a year, to an annual bill of £2,000 or more in January.

The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.

Gas standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, during 2027 "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.

These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy.

The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will gain an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most - but not until after the projected big rise in bills in January.

Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.

The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.

The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.

It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52p per litre.

Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.

The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.

The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).

Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.

It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.

But that plan has now been ditched.

Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.

Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April.

However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.

For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.

But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.

The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.

It means:

the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now

the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.

The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.

Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.

Separately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Some announcements affecting your finances have previously been made by the government.

They include:

Tariffs removed from 100 food items such as baked beans and garlic, which it calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June

Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030

Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period

Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

The prime minister's plan to reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares in England from January to be in effect throughout 2027. Some cities already have caps, and funding is being given to the devolved nations

Phil Parkinson is hoping Wrexham can buck the unusual trend of Championship sides struggling in seasons after they have narrowly missed out on the play-offs.

Over the previous 15 second-tier campaigns, only one side have achieved a top-half finish - when Middlesbrough came fourth in 2022-23 - in the year after finishing seventh in the Championship.

article:
Train attacker asked man 'do you want to die?', jury hears

Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder 10 people on the train last year

Train passengers fled "in sheer terror" from a knife attacker who asked one victim "do you want to die?", a trial has heard.

Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025. He is also accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough the day before and then a boy at a London railway station.

Opening the prosecution case at Cambridge Crown Court, Christopher Paxton KC said that of those on the train "some stood tall, to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage".

Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder.

Williams is accused of attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett, and Samir Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon.

He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.

The jury heard he then travelled to London, where he stabbed a young boy on a Docklands Light Railway train in the early hours of 1 November.

Paxton said: "Across the Halloween weekend last year, to the many people he encountered the defendant Anthony Williams posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife.

"He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear."

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks.

Paxton said Williams had "brought terror" to the train passengers in Cambridgeshire "which resulted in them fleeing and some fighting for their lives".

"In the face of that threat and the defendant's sheer brutality some stood tall to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage, defending themselves and putting themselves in harm's way to protect strangers," he said.

He added that some had locked themselves in toilets, and some some showed "extraordinary bravery" in trying to fend Williams off by grabbing frying pans or toasters to protect themselves.

Huntingdon railway station was closed for a couple of days while evidence was gathered

Jurors were told they would see footage from the train involving one of the victims, 73-year-old Presland, who the court heard was attacked after he fell to the ground.

Paxton said jurors would be able to see a "hand come up from the floor of the train — that was Mr Presland. You will see above him, all in black, the defendant wielding the knife".

He said Presland had been "defenceless and powerless" and "was no threat to Mr Williams".

One of the victims, jurors heard, "tried to grab the knife blade itself", while another was stabbed in the head and stomach.

Paxton said one of the passengers, Crean, decided "he had to try to stop it" and "launched himself towards and at Mr Williams".

Paxton said Williams asked Crean "do you want to die?".

"We say [that was] clear evidence of the defendant's intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many," the prosecuting counsel said.

Paxton said "the attack was stopped only by the quick thinking of the train driver", with the London-bound LNER service making an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon — the next station south from Peterborough.

The jury, consisting of three women and nine men, were told by the judge Mr Justice Calver that Williams was appearing via videolink from Rampton Hospital in Nottinghamshire, rather than sitting in the dock.

He said it would "best ensure his effective participation in the trial", and would avoid a four-hour round trip to court.

The trial continues.

What do people in NI want to see in the Budget?

Stormont ministers are finding out how much extra money they will have to spend as a result of the Westminster Budget.

More money could help lead to a deal on the Stormont budget which is still not agreed, seven months into the financial year.

Chancellor John Healey, who is currently delivering the budget, is unlikely to deliver everything the Northern Ireland parties say they need.

The government has offered an additional £525m this year but the parties say they need about £1.5bn to produce a workable financial plan.

On Wednesday Stormont's Finance Minister John O'Dowd said there was a duty on the government to "fairly fund this place".

The Sinn Féin MLA said he wanted to see a "fair and sustainable settlement, the money currently on the table is not sufficient for us to be able to move forward, pay our public sector workers and sustain public services and grow our economy.

"I await the chancellor's announcements and I hope he does now meet the needs of this society."

Last week, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said it "wouldn't be realistic" to think the gap would be entirely closed by the chancellor but that it could be made "more manageable".

Government sources have played down the prospect of the Budget providing a transformational amount of money.

BBC News NI spoke to a number of people about what they would like to see.

Christina Taylor said another rise in the minimum wage would mean higher prices for customers

Christina Taylor, who owns Shed Bistro in south Belfast and employs about 30 staff, said that another rise in the minimum wage would mean higher prices for customers.

"The raise last year meant that every guest would need to spend £4.50 more to cover that," she said.

"That's so much money and people can't afford that.

"Raising the minimum wage isn't the answer to the cost of living because it goes in a circle and no one is better off.

"Everyone is still struggling and it's not sustainable for anyone."

Taylor added that there "needs to be support for households or else eating out will be a thing of the past".

She said she had noticed that people were not eating out as often, with the exception of special occasions.

"The cost of living affects us so much, more than Covid - eating out for people is now a luxury and it shouldn't be."

She echoed calls from business groups like Hospitality Ulster, which want to see a reduction in VAT.

"We really need to see a VAT reduction," she said.

"Comparing ourselves to the South (Republic of Ireland) at 9% and Europe at 10% and we're sitting at 20%, it's not sustainable.

"Something needs to happen to change that."

Derek Moore from Greysteel would like to see help with heating costs and for carers in Northern Ireland

Derek Moore cares for his parents Margaret and Douglas in Greysteel, County Londonderry.

He would like to see help with heating costs and for carers in Northern Ireland.

Social security is devolved, so any changes announced in the Westminster Budget would not automatically apply in Northern Ireland, as legislation would have to pass through the Stormont assembly.

Moore said he could not get his parents "out and about" as much as he would like to "because the cost of living has made it much harder".

"You also have to look at shopping and what things you can save money on," he added.

"You also don't turn the heating on as much as you would like, you have to go down the coal route and make sure it's cosy and warm for them.

"You have to make sure that one room is really warm, and close doors."

His mother is registered blind and his father had a stroke and a heart attack earlier this year.

He works full-time and his parents have carers who visit four times a day.

"It puts a lot of pressure on you that affects things like your social life, being able to go out and enjoy meals," he said.

The Harrisons say that the rising cost of groceries mean many families were tightening their budgets

Ahead of the Budget, BBC News NI also gauged the views of the public at a family event in Slieve Gullion Forest Park, near Newry.

The Harrison family lives in Craigavon.

Leanne Harrison said the price of groceries was "crazy" and she had her "fingers were crossed" for VAT cuts.

Tim Hanna said families were "feeling the pinch" and tax breaks on hospitality and fuel duty would be helpful.

"I know the hospitality sector is particularly hard hit, the price of a pint seems to keep going up and up, seems to deter people," he added.

Rozlyn Sheridan wants the chancellor to announce support for the arts sector

Rozlyn Sheridan, of the Sheridan Stage School in Newry, was hoping for a boost to the arts sector.

"In my own business in the arts, we are paddling our own boats and trying to survive in an industry that sometimes isn't valued within our society, within our government" she said.

"The arts brings so much to a community and gives so much value to people's mental health."

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

'Shortchanged' or 'fighting chance': Views differ as NI secretary meets parties on budget

Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay

Stormont gets a population-based share of additional spending allocated to public services in England.

The chancellor traditionally announces the headline amount during the Budget speech.

Later in the day, Stormont's Department of Finance will make its own calculations of when that money can be spent and what it can be spent on.

Stormont is already due to receive a small amount of money for spending this year, as a result of measures announced shortly after Andy Burnham became prime minister.

For example, his decision to freeze bus fares in England is likely to be worth about £10m to £15m to Stormont this financial year.

However, most of what Healey allocates on Wednesday is likely to be for next year.

John Healey, is unlikely to deliver everything the Stormont parties say they need

Healey is expected to focus on "breathing space" measures to help households with the cost of living.

However he said "breathing space today must go hand-in-hand with building for the future".

He said the Budget would provide targeted support for businesses and self-employed people, and "start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good".

He added that it would include backing businesses and entrepreneurs, investing in the technologies that drive future growth, and building more homes.

On Tuesday, it emerged that a rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years.

The government also announced a number of measures, including removing import taxes on some food and ending the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments.

Any help Healey announces with energy bills is unlikely to apply directly in Northern Ireland as it has a separate energy market with different regulations from the rest of the UK.

Instead there would be money for Stormont to set up its own support schemes.

Households in Northern Ireland have received a £63 reduction in electricity bills this month.

It is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain.

Serrano to end career in Puerto Rico in January

Amanda Serrano has won multiple world titles in seven divisions from super-flyweight to light-welterweight

Seven-weight world champion Amanda Serrano will face Australia's Skye Falzon in Puerto Rico on 9 January in the final fight of her illustrious professional boxing career.

The 38-year-old will defend her WBA and WBO featherweight titles on home soil at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan.

Serrano, who boasts a fight history of 50 wins, four defeats and one draw, will be seeking to break the all-time women's knockout record in her farewell bout.

"Boxing has been my life, and I never could have imagined the journey it would take me and my family on," said Serrano, who turned professional in 2009.

"To close my career at home in Puerto Rico, in front of the people who have supported me from the beginning, means everything. I'm going to give the fans one final night to remember."

Serrano's farewell bout, labelled The Last Walk, will be contested over 12 three-minute rounds against 37-year-old Falzon, who has won 12 of her 14 professional fights, including seven by knockout.

In her previous outing, Serrano edged a majority decision victory over Argentina's Lucrecia Manzur to claim her 50th professional win.

The contest was the first world title fight to be broadcast live on TikTok, generating 3.4m views.

But Serrano was unable to secure the knockout she needed to surpass American boxing pioneer Christy Martin's record of 32, leaving her with one final opportunity to make history.

Amanda Serrano shared a historic rivalry with Ireland's Katie Taylor

Serrano is the only Puerto Rican boxer, male or female, to become an undisputed world champion.

Her profile reached new heights after she became the first fighter to sign with Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) in 2021.

Founded by YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian, MVP has invested heavily in women's boxing in recent years.

"Nakisa, Jake and MVP believed in me and in women's boxing, and together we've helped change what's possible for women in this sport," Serrano said.

"We've fought for respect, equal opportunities, fair pay, and the choice to compete under the same rules as men.

"There's still more work to do, and I'll continue fighting for the next generation long after I hang up my gloves."

Serrano's career will perhaps be best remembered for her historic rivalry with Ireland's Katie Taylor, who won all three of their encounters.

The pair became the first women to headline a boxing event at the iconic Madison Square Garden in 2022, before meeting again in a hugely watched rematch on Netflix in 2024.

Taylor completed a clean sweep of the trilogy in July 2025, headlining an all-women's card in New York, before retiring in September this year following victory over Flora Pili at Dublin's Croke Park.

Paul and Bidarian said Serrano had "changed the entire landscape of women's boxing".

"Amanda Serrano is the MOAT. The Most Of All Time. The most accomplished female boxer of all time, the most watched, the most paid, and one of the most influential athletes this sport has ever seen," they added.

article:
Why Hurts played with blood clot and what it means for NFL

Jalen Hurts has led the Philadelphia Eagles to two Super Bowls, winning the NFL's championship game in 2025

News that Jalen Hurts played a game hours after being diagnosed with a blood clot had already shocked the NFL world.

The Philadelphia Eagles then said their star quarterback will probably miss the rest of the season after multiple blood clots were found in his lungs - a life-threatening condition if not treated quickly.

It raised questions over the NFL's handling of the matter and its general approach to player health and safety, partly because the game in question was part of the league's international series.

Hurts' initial diagnosis was in London, before the Eagles played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on 11 October, and he flew back with the team that evening.

What do we know about what happened? Why was Hurts allowed to play and then fly home straight after? And what does it mean for him, the Eagles and the NFL?

Send us your questions

Sunday, 4 October: Another player stepped on Hurts' left calf during Philadelphia's defeat by the Los Angeles Rams, although he completed the game.

Thursday, 8 October: Hurts first reported an issue to the team. He trained in full all week and had treatment on Thursday and Friday.

Saturday, 10 October: The Eagles arrived in London in the morning and Hurts visited the Cleveland Clinic that evening. An ultrasound showed he had a superficial blood clot (vein thrombosis) in his calf but he was cleared to play on Sunday.

Sunday, 11 October: Hurts returned to the team hotel at about 3am before playing the full game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. A follow-up ultrasound was recommended within 72 hours and Hurts was cleared for the flight home.

Wednesday, 14 October: After receiving daily treatment, Hurts had another ultrasound, which showed the clot had moved, and he was ruled out of the next game.

Monday, 19 October: Joint statement by the Eagles and Hurts' agent said further tests showed he now has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli (multiple blood clots in both lungs).

His treatment will involve blood-thinning medicine and he should make a full recovery but is expected to miss the rest of the season.

Hurts threw for 220 yards and a touchdown, but had just two carries for two yards, as the Jaguars claimed a last-gasp 19-17 win in London

Some of the initial reports said that Hurts did not sleep for 36 hours before playing in London, but his agent later confirmed that he slept after returning to the hotel and also at the stadium.

Dr Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, was in London that weekend and arranged for Hurts to be evaluated at the Cleveland Clinic, an American-owned private hospital which is an official supplier of sports medicine services for the NFL's London games.

The NFL has protocols in place for concussions, emergency preparedness and extreme heat, for games in the US and overseas.

But, speaking at a news conference last Tuesday, Sills explained the league does not have a protocol for situations such as this.

Nevertheless, Sills said that those who dealt with Hurts were "incredibly conservative" and that he had "complete confidence" in how the Eagles handled the situation.

Later that day, the NFL Players Association (NFLPA) called for a full investigation, adding that the NFL "previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care [Hurts] received".

However, on Sunday the league and NFLPA released a joint statement saying they are "working together to review the matter".

'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on

The NFL's next international game is in Madrid on 8 November and the local medical co-ordinator is Real Madrid's chief medical officer, Dr Niko Mihic.

Dr Mihic told BBC Sport that blood clots among athletes are "not that common" and remembers in a previous role it took three visits for a baseball player to be diagnosed with a blood clot, because it is not something immediately associated with sports injuries.

Medical advice on whether to sleep and/or stay active is decided case by case. The same goes for whether it is safe to board a long-haul flight with a blood clot, as Hurts was allowed to do.

"It's not as simple as some people think," said Dr Mihic. "There's an amount of judgement that goes into this. It's like you're stuck between a rock and a hard place, but then you make your call."

As he and the NFL finalise their medical preparations for the Madrid game, Dr Mihic expects them to discuss scenarios such as that involving Hurts.

Asked what the NFL can learn from Hurts ultimately getting blood clots in his lungs, the league's Dr Sills replied: "I don't think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process.

"Sometimes in medicine we do all the right things and other things develop... but we have a committee that looks at all these cases."

What the NFL learned from Hamlin & Tagovailoa injuries

Whatever the outcome of the NFL's joint review with the NFLPA, the league will face greater scrutiny over how they handle players around games played overseas.

Players had a 16-hour flight for Australia's first NFL game in September, while the NFLPA's executive director JC Tretter expressed safety concerns over the quality of the field for the game in Brazil.

There are a record nine international games this year and, although the NFL ultimately wants 16 per season, Tretter added that "the goal has to be growing the game while maintaining the standards our players deserve".

Only Hurts knows how he feels about the way he was treated by his team and the NFL's doctors, but even before this issue there had been talk of the 2025 Super Bowl MVP leaving the Eagles.

Even if he does make a full recovery and returns to action, the 28-year-old will always have to bear blood clots in mind.

"The worst risk factor for recurrent embolisms is having had one previously," said Dr Mihic.

As for Philadelphia, they do not have an experienced quarterback in reserve and back-up Tanner McKee could not prevent them suffering a fifth straight defeat on Monday.

They were beaten 38-21 at home by the Dallas Cowboys to extend their longest losing streak under coach Nick Sirianni, so this could be a long season for the injury-hit Eagles.

Or with the trade deadline two weeks away, this could be the start of a rebuild for a team that reached two of the past four Super Bowls.

You may get the right to find out what your colleagues earn - here's why

Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said.

Bosses should be required to respond to questionaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has proposed , external .

In addition, employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from carrying on, it said.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about colleagues.

The EHRC urged lawmakers to make it compulsory for employers to provide information including colleagues' basic pay and hours worked, how employees' pay compares with each other, and information about bonuses, overtime, shift-premiums and performance-related pay, within a specific timeframe.

The rights watchdog argued that this would help cut pay discrimination, especially against women.

Women would also benefit from employers publishing salary details in job adverts, the EHRC has said previously , external .

The job interview question you don't have to answer

John Kirkpatrick, the EHRC chief executive, told the BBC that employers should not be able to ask about salary history when setting pay.

"When they do, what tends to happen is that can embed a history of disadvantage or discrimination in future salaries," he said.

While employers should be able to offer a competitive salary, this should not "create a pattern that discriminates," he said.

The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, has previously said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality.

Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said.

article:
Disbelief as rare Tasmanian Tiger head found under bed

The extinct tiger head was hidden under a bed for years before its owners discovered how rare it was

The "most important item" ever to be sold at an auction house is about to go under the hammer after being found under a bed, an auctioneer has said

A newly discovered head of a thylacine, also known as a Tasmanian Tiger, was dug out from the owner's storage after they saw a similar specimen make the news in August.

Nicknamed Trevor, the new specimen is "only the third known taxidermy Thylacine head in existence" and could sell for up to £50,000, according to Bristol auction house Auctioneum.

Auctioneer Andrew Stowe said: "Hands down, it's the most important item we've ever sold. When I unwrapped it, I couldn't believe it."

Neighbourhood may be without library for 12 months

Women face 'hidden curfew' for exercise as evenings darken

The thylacine head is due to go under the hammer in Bath on 26 November, with an estimate of £30,000 to £50,000.

The thylacine was a wolf-like carnivorous marsupial, about the size of a large dog, which once roamed the forests of Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania. Hunted to extinction, the last known Tasmanian tiger died in Hobart zoo in 1936.

The thylacine was declared extinct in the 1930s

In the summer, a Victorian taxidermy head, mistakenly thought to be a fox head, sold for tens of thousands after eagle-eyed bidders recognised it as the head of an extinct thylacine.

Stowe said the find made international news.

"We thought it was a once-in-a-lifetime moment. To have unearthed another is extraordinary," he said.

"Scientists, academics, and collectors dedicate their lives to finding these rare specimens - to have two pass through our hands in a matter of weeks is nothing short of phenomenal."

Auctioneer Andrew Stowe said it was "the most important item we've ever sold".

It is thought the specimen was shot by a farmer in Sheffield, Tasmania, at the beginning of the 1900s and brought to the UK in 1905.

"Uncovering two-thirds of all known thylacine heads is extraordinary,' said Stowe.

"We've sold some incredible pieces over the years, but this goes way beyond another rare item."

The specimen has officially been added to the International Thylacine Specimen Database (ITSD).

Dr Stephen Sleightholme, from the ITSD, said these remains "provide an essential record of a species lost to extinction".

"Thylacine remains are exceptionally rare and rank among the most valuable zoological specimens," he said.

"The [database] is helping to establish a clearer picture of what survives and supporting the ongoing study of this remarkable marsupial predator."
