article:
Terminally ill mum who can't talk, walk or dress herself refused Pip payment

Rachael Field from Rhondda Cynon Taf has cancer of the tongue and been given around three years or less to live

A terminally ill mum who has been given three years to live has been denied disability benefit despite being unable to eat, talk, dress or use the toilet independently.

Rachael Field, 56, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, who has tongue cancer, was first diagnosed six years ago.

She uses a feeding tube, has had her tongue and voice box removed, and had her windpipe reconstructed using chest tissue. Field also has mobility issues.

Earlier this year, she was denied Personal Independence Payment (Pip), to support people with disability-related extra costs.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it needed further evidence to complete the claim and was sorry for "any distress" to the family.

Field said she has had cancer four times in six years, and now cannot do anything for herself.

"I need help to wash, dress and use the bathroom. I can only walk a few steps with help. I cannot eat or drink, everything has to go through my feeding tube," she added.

Rachael met husband Eddie at work 20 years ago

The former factory worker was forced to stop working following her terminal diagnosis, and her family has been managing the financial strain.

Field applied for Pip in May, but it was denied as she was awarded zero points across all assessed categories.

Pip is a benefit people with long-term illnesses and disabilities can claim if they need help with extra costs associated with living, work and care. Eligibility is determined through an assessment.

Under the current system, claimants are scored on a zero to 12 scale by a health professional on everyday tasks such as washing, getting dressed and preparing food.

Rachael's daughter Kyra has set up a Go Fund Me page to try and help her enjoy what time she has left

Field's family said repeated rescheduling of the assessment process caused delays, and that despite lodging an appeal several months ago, they are still awaiting an outcome.

Field said the treatment she received from her medical test "has been outstanding" but has an issue with "the system Pip uses to assess people".

She said: "People need the help while they are alive."

Her daughter, Kyra Hawkins-Field, 20, said it is "ridiculous" that her mum has not been able to claim Pip and does not want her "stressing about money" while she only has "a couple of years left".

She criticised the benefits assessment process and said it was too reliant on a checklist, and did not reflect people's real-life struggles.

"They've basically turned around and said, 'we think you're fine'," she said.

Kyra said her mum likes the "little things in life" and "loves doing jigsaw puzzles"

Hawkins-Field said her dad Eddie has become the family's "superhero", working full-time and then visiting his wife in hospital every day.

The couple married 15 years ago after meeting when they both worked in a factory. They enjoy visiting towns across Wales, and still hope to visit Scotland and Ireland one day.

Hawkins-Field said her mum likes the "little things in life", but "loves doing jigsaw puzzles, big, really, really difficult, intricate jigsaw puzzles" and reading.

Hawkins-Field launched a GoFundMe appeal with the aim of raising £1,000 to help her mum enjoy what time she has left with her family, including some trips around the UK, while she still can.

A DWP spokesperson said: "We're sorry for any distress Ms Field and her family are feeling at this difficult time.

"We have been unable to complete the claim as we need further evidence from Ms Field. We have attempted to contact her in order to resolve the situation and will continue to do so."

Field's family said they were in discussion with the DWP.

Alexander brothers each sentenced to 30 years in prison in sex trafficking case

Real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon, listen as their lawyers argue for a lesser sentence on their behalf in New York

Three brothers - two of them wealthy real-estate moguls - were sentenced to 30 years each in prison for drugging and raping dozens of women over decades.

Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, were found guilty in March of using their wealth and social status to lure women to parties and luxury homes, where they sexually assaulted them.

"Your conduct was monstrous," said Judge Valerie Caproni before sentencing them. "Your crimes wreaked havoc on their lives."

On Tuesday morning, the court in New York heard from 12 victims, including one who did not testify during the trial.

One by one, they spoke of the psychological trauma they endured after the Alexander brothers raped them, and their desire for the shame they had felt to instead fall on the defendants.

Many asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence of life in prison for each brother.

Maya Miller told the court that after Tal Alexander raped her in 2014, she lost all sense of safety. "I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might've become if this never happened to me," she said.

Another victim, using the pseudoym Isa Brooks, said after being raped by Tal and Alon Alexander when she was 16, she lost the ability to trust herself.

"I had no idea the danger I was in till it was too late," she said.

Another woman said when she planned to come forward about being raped, Tal Alexander threatened her, saying he knew where her sister worked.

Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers deserved the maximum punishment for their crimes, saying facts "paint a truly devastating picture".

"For years, they honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury," she said, adding that they were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them."

During the women's speeches, the three Alexander brothers showed little emotion. They stared ahead or conferred with their lawyers, who said they advised their clients not to look at the victims so it couldn't be misconstrued.

Attorneys for the brothers pushed for sentences of 15 years, arguing that they had become devoted fathers whose families would suffer in their absence.

The three men all addressed the court, continuing to profess their innocence.

"We had a work-hard, play-hard mentality," Tal Alexander said, adding he saw how his behaviour "hurt people's feelings".

But their statements did not assuage Caproni, who chastised them for refusing to admit their crimes.

"How can someone who never acknowledged the wrongs they did be rehabilitated?" she asked.

At the end of the hearing, she sentenced them each to 30 years in prison for certain crimes. She also sentenced each to 20 years in prison for additional crimes, but said the men would serve the sentences concurrently.

Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa addresses the court and argues for a life sentence during the sentencing of real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon

During the five-week trial, 11 women - several said they were minors at the time of the assaults - testified that the brothers gave them gifts and flew them places including Aspen and the Bahamas where they fed them drugs before raping them.

Prosecutors said the brothers' pattern of abusive behaviour began in high school, though the trial involved crimes starting in 2008.

They said the three slipped drugs into women's drinks, and "physically restrained and held down their victims during the rapes and sexual assaults and ignored screams and explicit requests to stop".

Lawyers for the brothers argued the sex was consensual and that they were womanisers, but not abusers.

Two of the brothers, Tal and Oren, became wealthy selling luxury properties in New York and Miami.

They worked for American real estate giant Douglas Elliman, with clients including Lindsay Lohan, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West. In 2022, they founded their own New York-based firm called Official. Alon worked at the family's private security firm, Kent Security.

As they heard their sentences, the brothers stared straight ahead.

Reform donor tied to £16m of property in Guernsey

Billionaire Christopher Harborne has been linked to £16m of property and land across Guernsey

Reform UK's largest donor has been linked to more than £16m of property and land in Guernsey including the site of a former seafront restaurant that burnt down.

Records examined by the BBC show British-Thai businessman Christopher Harborne is linked to seven properties, several plots of land, private jets and an aircraft hangar development at Guernsey Airport.

The most recent transaction linked to Harborne is the £2.5m sale of the former Octopus restaurant site in St Peter Port, which was destroyed in a large fire in February 2024 .

The BBC asked Harborne's lawyers whether he was behind the purchase but did not receive a response.

In March 2024 Guernsey Police said they found no evidence of foul play and closed their investigation into the cause of the blaze at the restauraunt site.

The site was subsequently sold for £1 by its then owner deputy Yvonne Burford who passed the land to restaurant owners Delphine Pesrin-Auder and Mickael Pesrin.

Since the fire the site has remained one of the most visible empty plots on the island's seafront.

But a copy of the conveyance deeds submitted to the States of Guernsey and reviewed by the BBC shows it was sold in July 2026 for £2.555m to Marbel Leopard Ltd, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands (BVI).

The most recent transaction linked to Harborne is the site of the former Octopus restaurant which burnt down in 2024

The change of ownership letter lists Marbel Leopard at the same BVI address as other companies that have held properties previously bought by Harborne.

The correspondence contact listed by Marbel Leopard is Rumrada Suppadit, who works for Harborne's company Sherriff Global Private Limited.

She also sits on the board of Kamalaya, his wellness resort on the Thai island of Koh Samui, according to business database dataforthai.

Harborne's lawyers was asked by the BBC whether he was behind the purchase and about redevelopment plans but did not respond.

Harborne has previously made other donations to Reform, the Brexit Party and the Conservatives.

The billionaire also gave Nigel Farage a £5m gift in 2024 , which is subject to a parliamentary standards investigation.

The three neighbouring properties are in Hauteville where 19 Century writer Victor Hugo lived

The Guernsey properties identified by the BBC as linked to Harborne had a combined transaction value of more than £16m, which was calculated using purchase prices recorded in conveyance deeds and cadastre reports.

Away from the Guernsey seafront, the trail leads uphill to Hauteville, a road in St Peter Port, famous for the home of 19th Century French author Victor Hugo.

Conveyance deeds and planning applications submitted to the States of Guernsey connect Harborne and companies linked to him to three neighbouring properties.

Two of the properties were bought in his own name and he later transferred one to a BVI company for £1.

The third was bought through a company registered in the US state of Wyoming, where company ownership can be difficult to establish from public records.

Planning application documents for one of the properties list Sherriff Global Private Limited as the architect's client. The formal planning permission names the Wyoming company as applicant.

The application stands out for what is proposed inside the house, with drawings showing an office and an eight-person boardroom.

Below ground there is a wellness suite with a hyperbaric chamber, sauna and cold plunge.

A lift, step-free access and disabled access bathrooms is also proposed.

Sundance has also been linked to the purchase of land and the development of two new hangars at Guernsey Airport.

Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says

Officers were visible outside the embassy in Belgrade later on Wednesday

Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.

Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".

Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.

The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.

Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.

Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.

This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.

The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.

Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

Aberdeen City Council is to stop new food and drink vans setting up at the city's beachfront after concerns about the number of street traders operating in the area.

A total of 36 businesses have permission to set up there, ranging from burger and burrito bars to sweet treats.

The local authority agreed proposals , external that will see no new licences granted while beach masterplan works are ongoing and a temporary presumption against street trading will brought in.

Those objecting to the plans include a coffee cart whose owners say the move has halted their ambition to move into the area.

Samuel and Darius Turcu-Georgescu run the Highlander Cafe bus which has operated for nearly a decade

Concerns have been raised recently about a lack of space for food vans to operate, while some have described the look of the area as "unsightly".

Some of the businesses operate for just a day or two per week.

Lauren Patterson-Strath runs LA Coffee with her partner Amy on the city's York Street, around the corner from the Beach Esplanade.

She told BBC Scotland News she had begun the process to apply for a licence to move her cart to the beachfront, only to be told the rule change meant it would no longer be possible.

Lauren and Amy Patterson-Strath want to set up at the beachfront

"Footfall is just much better up there which is why we want to be in that area," she said.

"I can get why they don't want more and more [businesses] continuously going up there, there is a lot of negativity online about the lack of space for parking now at the beach.

"My frustration is I just feel it needs to be monitored better in a sense of if people are not trading then the trailers really should be getting moved."

She said it could ultimately lead to her business moving somewhere else with better footfall.

One of the longstanding businesses in the area is the Highlander Cafe bus which has operated since 2017.

It is run by Samuel Turcu-Georgescu and his son Darius who said it was important to get the mix of vans right.

"If there's too many it is difficult for everyone," Samuel said.

"So, they should sort out what is already here first and if there is a need for more, they can add it after.

Darius suggested freeing up spaces if a trader was not operating to let others use them.

"Traders should come when they plan to trade and leave at the end of the day so there is space for everyone else," he said.

Councillors voted through plans which will mean permission will not be granted to businesses to occupy the road in the area while ongoing beach improvement works take place.

Jo Malone donates £100k for cancer-detecting 'nose'

Florin the labrador was trained to detect prostate cancer by analysing the scent of urine samples

A charity says a £100,000 donation made by the perfume entrepreneur Jo Malone will accelerate work on a cancer-detecting electronic nose.

Medical Detection Dogs (MDD), based in Buckinghamshire, has been working with quantum physicist Dr Andreas Mershin for more than 10 years to develop the device, which is modelled on the scent-detection abilities of dogs.

The donation was made after Queen Camilla was shown how a prototype of the technology successfully detected prostate cancer from a urine sample.

The charity said the funding would allow it to install a SniffSpace, so its dogs can sniff more samples in a secure room and generate more "robust data" to further develop the electronic nose.

Chief executive Dr Claire Guest described the donation as "game-changing".

"This technology gives us an unprecedented opportunity to decode those scent signatures and move closer to developing a reliable electronic nose for cancer detection," she said.

Medical Detection Dogs took a prototype of the electronic nose to its patron, the Queen, for a demonstration earlier this year

A dog's nose is a highly sensitive chemical detector capable of identifying odours far beyond human and technological capacity.

MDD said that every disease has an odour and that these biochemical changes can be smelt by its canine companions, which have 300 million sensory receptors.

Humans have about five million receptors. If we can smell a teaspoon of sugar in a cup of tea, dogs can sniff out that sugar in a volume of water equivalent to two Olympic-sized swimming pools.

The electronic version of the dog's nose, created by Mershin at RealNose.ai, works on a similar basis, using protein odorant receptors to capture scent molecules from a urine sample to detect prostate cancer.

It then uses artificial intelligence (AI) to make recognisable patterns in the receptors' activation. MDD has been assisting in training this AI element.

Mershin said the charity's facilities and protocols were "cutting edge" and were "inspiring others around the planet".

Other e-noses are being used in food and beverage quality control , environmental monitoring and security and crime prevention.

Data collected on the SniffSpace from the dogs could be used by the e-nose to detect other diseases

The prototype electronic nose is currently "sniffing" 500 urine samples provided by patients from Milton Keynes Hospital.

MDD-trained dogs previously correctly identified which of them were cancerous.

The charity said once it had that dataset, researchers could compare its results with those of the dogs.

At the moment, the charity said its dogs sniffed samples, arranged in up to eight stands, for the odours associated with disease.

However, after each row has been sniffed, trainers have to manually record the data - and swap the samples around. SniffSpace will automatically rotate the samples, meaning more can be sniffed in a shorter space of time.

MDD said this would accelerate its ultimate aim of creating an electronic nose that can do what the dogs do, but at scale across the world.

Malone said: "My sense of smell has given me so much throughout my life. So I have always wanted to find a way of using that world of smell to give something back."

A team of dogs will now be prepared for their training on the equipment.

Mershin added: "RealNose.ai and MDD are focused on establishing a formal partnership aimed at creating in vitro diagnostic medical devices specifically for the NHS to look at as potential solutions to the prostate cancer screening and early diagnosis problems before also trying out the same olfactory approach for other cancers."

article:
A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science

A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science

A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.

His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.

Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.

Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous Navier–Stokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.

But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.

They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".

Basecamp founder, Dr Oliver Vince, says just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet

OpenAI said that nobody at the company, human or AI, saw the other teams' work before it was published. Initially it said that while unlikely, it could not "rule out" that anonymised data from use of its products may have helped improve its models. Days later, it said Buckmaster's Codex prompts from the two months before the announcement "could not have influenced the system in any way".

It's a complicated story; we still don't fully know what happened. But it highlights a growing issue about the use of AI in science. Usually, those words make us conjure up images of robots building terrible genetically-engineered viruses, or chemical weapons, to wipe out humanity. But there's a more subtle problem that hasn't attracted the same headline-grabbing attention: that AI could undermine faith in the scientific process, raising questions about the novelty and accuracy of research.

And there's another concern. It's well known that AI chatbots like Claude or Gemini can sometimes hallucinate things that simply aren't true. They will tell you about a film that never existed, or a quote that was never said. Now there is evidence that this is increasingly happening in science. Eventually, it's feared, it will become difficult to separate true scientific discovery from AI-generated fiction.

And all of this could threaten to erode - if not explode - the rock on which scientific research rests: trust.

One threat is to scientific journals, the guardians of scientific integrity, which are seen to be failing to deal with a tsunami of AI-generated distortions.

"Generative AI has basically disrupted the whole scientific process," says Dalmeet Singh Chawla, a science journalist who has spent a decade reporting on research misconduct.

He tells the BBC that publishers' integrity staff - the people who screen submissions for accuracy and reliability - will need to "drastically increase [in number and effort] if they're anywhere near the fight". He says: "Right now, it seems like they're not."

On the face of it, AI seems just the right tool to power scientific research. Scientists deal with huge amounts of information. Telescopes and particle accelerators, for example, collect billions of data points – too large for the brain to comprehend. AI can pick the scientific highlights from the surrounding humdrum.

The poster child of scientific AI is the UK-based firm Google DeepMind, which in 2020 solved one of biology's biggest problems: how proteins in living things fold into their precise shapes.

It may sound dull, but proteins are the tiny machines that make life work, and the shapes they fold into determine what they can do; from building cells and fighting infection to helping form the tissues and organs of the body.

Before AI, scientists had to conduct time-consuming experiments in the lab. Then, Google DeepMind developed an AI model called AlphaFold that accurately predicted 200 million protein folds in just one year.

The equivalent experimental work would have taken hundreds of millions of years in laboratories. The firm gave the results away for free to researchers. The head of DeepMind and the project's lead scientist were both awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.

It was big hugs all round.

Dr Pushmeet Kohli, who leads DeepMind's science work, told me that AlphaFold could be seen as a "watershed moment".

But elsewhere, the use of AI in science has come with accusations of hype. Some computer models are accused of exaggerating the significance of their findings, with the human researchers that oversee them then believing some of the claims without enough scepticism.

Basking in its success over AlphaFold, for example, DeepMind turned its attention to predicting the structure of new materials. The work could lead to the development of better batteries, cheaper solar cells and electronic components that are not dependent on rare earth elements. (In theory, no-one would need to argue about mining rights ever again, and Greenland would be safe from invasion.)

DeepMind chief executive Sir Demis Hassabis celebrated his company's use of AI to solve one of biology's biggest problems

A DeepMind model came up with what the firm claimed were more than two million new crystal structures, announced as "nearly 800 years worth of knowledge" released in one go. Of those, some 380,000 were considered promising enough to make in a laboratory.

But then came a warning sign from two chemists at the University of California. Anthony Cheetham and Ram Seshadri went through a random sample of the supposed new crystals. Writing in the journal Chemistry of Materials, they concluded that they had "yet to find any strikingly novel compounds", arguing that many were "trivial adaptations of known materials". Their verdict was not that the method was wrong, but that the results need more scrutiny and validation from human chemists.

DeepMind rejects the charge, saying it tested each compound for novelty. Dismissing a new structure for looking familiar misses the point, the company argues: swapping a single atom is how many of today's most useful materials arrived, from phone components to sunscreen.

In those cases, at least, the science was mostly real and the issue was just AI potentially exaggerating its importance.

Arguably of even greater concern is the growing risk that scientific journals will become polluted with so-called AI "slop" - where a computer, not a human scientist, is writing the research, leading to fake citations and phantom papers.

In 2024, computer scientist Prof Dmitry Kobak, of Ghent University, searched more than a million biomedical research papers for trigger words favoured by the LLMs that generate AI writing. His team found that by December last year, nearly 90% had AI fingerprints on them. AI detection technology is not perfect; some forms of the software have labelled the US Constitution, written in the 1780s, as "AI-generated". But still, Kobak said he was shocked by the scale of apparent AI use. There is a risk, he told Nature, that "whatever bias the LLM may have will just suddenly permeate the (scientific) literature".

Kobak is among many researchers who worries that AI is slowly killing scientific journals.

And it matters: research papers are the lifeblood of scientific advance. When a discovery is published, another team in another part of the world might obtain funding to build on the results.

Pulsars - an unusual type of neutron star, depicted above by an artist - were discovered in the 1960s partly due to a hunch of scientists

The process of peer review - in which research papers are checked by other scientists before they are published - is also being compromised.

A team led by Weixin Liang and James Zou at Stanford University analysed referee reports submitted to four major computer science conferences, and found up to 17% of the text had been substantially modified by a language model.

A critical part of a scientific paper's integrity involves lead scientists listing earlier research in order to show what they have done is genuinely new. These are called citations. A separate team at Cornell University found that researchers were using AI to compile citations, and that it was inventing bogus research, with around 147,000 pieces of phantom research cited last year.

If AI continues to distort the integrity of the academic process in this way, then researchers will be sent up blind alleys, public money will be wasted, and the fruits of valid research - such as new drugs or green technologies - will be slowed or not realised at all.

Some publishers of scientific journals, such as Elsevier, are taking steps to avert this growing crisis of confidence.

Elsevier's research integrity team has developed some 100 signals that flag a paper for closer human scrutiny. Nature's journals forbid AI-generated images and tell referees never to upload a manuscript into an AI system. The website arXiv, where scientists share their early-stage results, bans researchers for a year if they submit invented references.

Prof Sarah Main, an Elsevier vice-president, is among those at the firm trying to work out how to responsibly use AI in research. "What we're calling research-grade AI would focus on ensuring the researcher is in the driving seat," she says.

Scottish scientist Sir Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in the 1920s

As AI agents process the mass of data emerging from particle accelerators, the cosmos and the natural world, how do we know they are getting it right?

And there's another worrying question: how do we know that AI agents are not dismissing an important result as an anomaly? The discoveries of penicillin, radioactivity and weird stars called pulsars all came from odd results that could easily have been dismissed. Hunches by humans made them into some of the biggest scientific moments of the last century.

Can AI really replicate that sense of serendipity and human ingenuity?

Kohli of DeepMind does not think the answer is to turn our backs on AI. That would be "like saying you should be computing without using calculators", he told me. But he accepts there should be human guardrails: "The agents today are imperfect. Somebody has to take accountability."

His test is a simple one: "You have to understand what the agent has done, and you have to take responsibility. You can't just specify the problem and let the machine write the paper and submit it as true."

Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over

AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people. But will it hold?

Tech billionaires seem to be doom prepping. Should we all be worried?

Prof Andrea Pauli of the Vienna BioCenter in Austria has followed that test. She spent almost 10 years on a question no-one has yet been able to answer: how a sperm gets into an egg. Responsible use of AI helped her toward an answer. Her lab found a protein on the surface of zebrafish eggs which pointed to a lock-and-key mechanism for allowing the sperm in.

Hers is a case for hope, in a sea of AI scientific slop. It shows that AI can help.

This is also a story about humans. Soon after the formation of Basecamp - the lab I visited in a former London watch factory - its co-founder, Oliver Vince, was ill in hospital with leukaemia (from which he has recovered). It motivated him to develop an AI system that stood a better chance of curing cancers. It might not work, he says, but it's worth a shot.

"We have a technically feasible path to curing cancer," he says.

Not a promise from Vince, but a direction. The big question is whether AI carries the science there, or quietly erodes the bricks it is built on.

Cundy 'no spring chicken' but nears 20-year unbeaten run

This video can not be played

'I'm getting older and the competitors are getting younger'

Four laps, flat out, from a standing start. Legs and lungs screaming, lactic acid building.

The kilo, track cycling's one-kilometre time trial, has a punishing reputation.

And yet Jody Cundy has been putting himself through it for decades.

"At the end of it, your legs don't want to pedal. You're fighting everything," he tells BBC Sport. "But when you get it right, it's really cool."

Cundy is king of the kilo. At the Para-cycling Track World Championships, he has been unbeaten in the event since 2006.

If he wins again at this year's edition - which starts on Thursday in Apeldoorn, the Netherlands - it will mark his 20th straight year in the rainbow jersey.

Not bad for someone who has just turned 48 years old.

"It's a fairly dominant run," he said. "There have been some moments where I thought it wasn't going to happen and somehow I've pulled something out of the bag.

"But I am getting older and the competitors are getting younger. It's going to be very hard to keep that unbeaten run.

"As much as I would love to do it, the people I have to race this year...I'm in trouble."

Some of that "trouble" comes from within the Great Britain squad.

Archie Atkinson, 22, was eight years from being born when Cundy won his first Paralympic gold medal - as a swimmer - at Atlanta 1996. Atkinson was just two when Cundy first became world champion as a cyclist, after switching sports.

"One of my first races was against him," said Atkinson. "That felt pretty special.

"This guy was Paralympic champion, world champion and held a world record at the time."

But Atkinson is catching up. Last year he beat Cundy at the National Track Championships, only to be beaten in turn by Cundy at the World Championships a few months later.

"I want to win," Atkinson said. "But if he wins, it's historic. There aren't many people who can win for 20 years."

In addition to his world titles, Cundy is a six-time cycling Paralympic champion - two of those victories coming in the kilo, which he won at the 2008 and 2016 Games.

Such is Cundy's standing in the squad that his team-mates call him "captain".

"It feels like I've earned a bit of respect from being here for so long," he said. "I try to be the person everyone looks up to.

"But I know at some point somebody's going to have to take my place and I'll be walking away from the sport."

Cundy won his first Para-cycling world title in 2006

When Cundy will walk away is anyone's guess.

He says he doesn't have a plan for his retirement, but he knows that qualifying for the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles will be difficult.

"If I'm still performing at the very top level and that means that they want to take me, because I can go win in LA, then I shall be there and I'm there to be counted," he said.

"I'm realistic in the fact I'll be 49 when it comes to LA and I'm no spring chicken any more.

"What we do afterwards I really don't know, whether it's in sport in some way, shape or form.

"It's 31 years I've been in elite sport. If I go away and take all of that knowledge away with me, I feel like I'm kind of cheating the system a bit.

"So there's part of me that wants to come back and help - whether it's in a coaching role or a managerial role, or even further up in governing body roles and trying to influence the UCI [cycling's world governing body] and the IPC [International Paralympic Committee] - to make cycling better than what it actually is."

The UCI, Cundy says, has "let the sport down" by the lack of Para-cycling track competitions it hosts outside of the World Championships and Paralympics.

At the upcoming Worlds, Cundy and Atkinson are among a 24-strong Great Britain squad - but it is the first time the team will have raced at a UCI track event since the last edition of the Worlds in Brazil last year.

"When it comes to track cycling we have one race a year, the World Championships, and then every four years we have a [Paralympic] Games. That's really not good enough," he said.

"When I first started we used to have competitions, we used to travel and go race in places. Now you go 12 months without seeing anybody.

"You see a start list and you don't know who half of the names are on it. You don't know whether they're going to be fast, slow, whether they're any good. There's not really any results or rankings to follow."

The UCI did not respond to a request for comment.

article:
'Tone deaf at best' - advice to stock up on essentials worries experts and low-income families

Samantha said she carefully budgets each month to be able to afford childcare for 12-year-old Oscar while she works

A single mum has said following government advice to stock up on emergency supplies would mean sacrificing her childcare budget for the school holidays.

Samantha Richards, who works full-time and relies on universal credit (UC) and her son's disability allowance to cover the bills, said the call to prepare reminded her of the "survival of the fittest".

Last week, Wes Streeting said people should have water , tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.

But one professor said the guidance "will appear at best tone deaf and at worst almost insulting" to households facing poverty.

The UK government said people did not need to buy everything at once.

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

But not everyone has the disposable income that allows these types of purchases, said Richards, 47.

"I think the advice is good, but we do want to know what [the government] plan to do in the event of us needing this.

"It just worries me."

Richards takes part in Changing Realities , external - a collaboration between more than 200 parents and carers on a low income from across the UK.

She has torches and blankets already and never lets food in the house completely run out.

But her autistic son's safe foods require a fridge and freezer, and she worries if an emergency did happen, he would not be able to eat the tinned food bought.

Instead, they would need to rely on other items in the cupboard.

"You may not feel very well after a few days but you can last more than three without eating," Samantha said.

But you cannot last very long without water, she believes, so that was what she would prioritise.

According to Prof Ruth Patrick, from the University of Glasgow, the UK government's guidance "will appear at best tone deaf and at worst almost insulting to the 14 million households currently facing poverty across the UK".

She is leading the Changing Realities project, and added: "There is a profound mis-match between this suggestion and the daily realities for parents and carers on a low income up and down the country who are struggling to get by, especially as costs continue to rise and the temperatures drop."

Ana said her childhood was spent watching her grandmother and mum stock their pantry for emergencies

"Preparedness shouldn't be just for people that really truly can afford to," said Ana, founder of UK Preppers Club on Facebook.

She said she was disappointed in the UK government announcement because it did not give people an idea of what to actually do in an emergency.

Ana said she would have welcomed advice being distributed about what to do if there is no running water - how do you flush your toilet for example?

The 42-year-old from Swansea said she was brought up to have "a rotating pantry" to give herself a safeguard for emergencies, including growing her own food and preserving it.

She said it was Covid which caused her to "up the ante" as she was heavily pregnant and ended up having an emergency C-section.

Unable to naturally feed her baby, she found she did not have enough formula and was quoted £300 online for it, with the supermarkets she tried out of stock.

That was when she started pushing for "preparedness", and said: "Look after your family, then, if something like this happens, you don't have to leave people, like myself at the time, vulnerable."

Ana said her Facebook group has increased by 300 members in just under three days

Ana said even just having a plan of who would pick up your child from school if the power went out, or where the family would meet if their property was inaccessible would be a good start.

"It doesn't have to be the Armageddon's happening, but just generally having a coherent plan of the family. What happens if?" she added.

"What happens if there's no power? What do you do? All those kind of little plans."

Ana said her advice would be for people to pick up an extra tin or pack of crackers every time they shop to slowly build up the supply.

Donna Lloyd said preparing for emergencies is not realistic for everyone but a tin here or there could help

Donna Lloyd, 60, a supply teacher in Denbighshire, has been preparing with her wife since a power cut in the Covid lockdown highlighted that they did not have any way to cook.

She said "in all honesty, no, it is not realistic" for everyone to be able to afford to buy emergency supplies.

Lloyd believes the UK government should use television programmes to explain how to prepare.

Alongside stockpiling, she also thinks people should learn first aid, how to gather, filter and purify water, and how to power items such as radios and fridges using solar power or power banks or a generator.

Yasmin Ibison said the UK government needed to provide more support for low-income households

Yasmin Ibison, a senior policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation , external (JRF) said preparing for emergencies was sensible.

There are 7.4 million low-income families in the UK who were unable to afford essential items in the last six months and 1.5 million households across the UK who have used a food bank in the past six months, according to JRF’s cost of living tracker published in July 2026 , external .

Ibison added: "When we have millions of people who already can't afford essentials like food, heating, basic toiletries, the question I ask is how are they going to afford to buy additional items in their cupboards if they're already struggling to meet these most basic and everyday needs?"

The UK government said: "This campaign is about providing the public with simple steps to ensure households are properly prepared, freeing up front line services to support those most in need in the case of emergencies like extreme weather or power outages.

"The advice is clear, you don't need to do it all at once. Build up your readiness gradually over time by taking it step by step, and picking up an extra item or two when you can."

article:
Liverpool gambled on Jacquet and it is paying off

No Liverpool outfield player has featured for more minutes than Jacquet this season

Jeremy Jacquet's choice of song for his Instagram post after Liverpool beat Brighton on Sunday and kept their fourth clean sheet of the season was telling.

"Trust in the process, trust in the plan" were some of the lyrics, accompanying a selection of images from the game.

That is very much what the 21-year-old has been doing - and more - since joining Liverpool in a deal worth £60m over the summer.

Things could have been very different had Liverpool pressed further with their pursuit of Leny Yoro in 2024. Yet in going down that route, they were alerted to another French centre-back in Jacquet, who was playing for Rennes.

Yoro chose to move to Manchester United from Lille and could well go on to be an elite centre-half but on Sunday afternoon, it was hard not to notice the difference between the pair.

Yoro, 20, made a calamitous error as United lost to Bournemouth while Jacquet put in another assured performance against Brighton . The ease with which he has adapted to playing for Liverpool has been impressive and even surprised senior figures at the club.

Liverpool great Alan Hansen, who was watching on at Anfield on Sunday, would surely have taken satisfaction from Jacquet's display.

Since arriving at Anfield, Jacquet has started every game in the Premier League and Champions League, playing more minutes (956) than any player at Liverpool bar Alisson (990) this season.

The transition is even more remarkable considering he spent most of the year recovering from injuries, having sustained a broken shoulder in February followed by a knee problem in the summer.

Jacquet did not play a minute of Liverpool 's summer tour to the United States and made his debut in a pre-season friendly against Como, when he scored at Anfield just a week before the Premier League started.

After the departure of Ibrahima Konate to Real Madrid, Liverpool had a space to fill at centre-back alongside Virgil van Dijk and given the injury struggles of Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni, Jacquet got the nod the following weekend at Newcastle .

A trip to St James' Park for a first Premier League experience is quite the task and, despite conceding early on, it was an encouraging display in which Jacquet played more accurate passes and successful final-third passes than any other player in the first half.

Losing to Manchester City and Erling Haaland was a timely reminder of the challenges ahead but, on the whole, he has excelled.

The way in which the Frenchman dealt with Brentford 's Igor Thiago a week later was a real standout, while social media compared his short sleeves and gloves look against Brighton to French great Marcel Desailly.

Jacquet has four clean sheets in the Premier League, ranks fourth in the top flight when it comes to interceptions (15), fourth in blocks (10) and has made more tackles (19) than any of his Liverpool team-mates.

With his stellar start to the campaign, a France call-up was inevitable under Zinedine Zidane and a debut followed for the boy from Bondy - the same area in the Paris suburbs that is home to Kylian Mbappe and William Saliba.

"Very good. Very, very good," said Zidane, when he was asked about Jacquet's performance against Italy earlier this month. "Brave. He wasn't afraid to come out a long way. Very good in the duels. He was, once again, very good. I said it four times."

On Wednesday, Liverpool will welcome Xabi Alonso back to Anfield when Chelsea visit in the Carabao Cup. Jacquet could easily have been wearing blue had Liverpool not accelerated their push for him in January,

Chelsea were keen and Jacquet was rated highly internally at Stamford Bridge but he chose the Reds.

At the time, the move raised eyebrows, particularly for a player who had only made 36 appearances in France's Ligue 1.

Liverpool missed out on Marc Guehi last summer and were having a poor season but Richard Hughes, the former sporting director, was prepared to wait until the summer, with Rennes unwilling to sanction a move in January.

On deadline day in January, journalist Julien Laurens, told BBC Sport: "It's a lot of money but Jacquet has everything to become one of the best centre-backs in the world in the next few years. He is arguably the best centre-back of his generation."

A few months into the new season, it seems Liverpool have settled on a gem.

Jacquet is part of a quartet at Anfield, alongside Bradley Barcola, Victor Munoz and Ronald Araujo, taking English lessons and like everything else, he is understood to be taking that in his stride.

He lives in Liverpool and spends a lot of his time with fellow youngsters including Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni, and those at the AXA Training Centre say he is mature and confident off the pitch, just like he is on the pitch.

Having two experienced figures in Van Dijk and Araujo either side of him on the field has certainly helped but in the space of a few months, Jacquet has made himself one of the first names on the teamsheet.

He went off early in the first few games as he worked built his fitness up but there are no such concerns any more.

"Our relationship is good. It's getting better every day that we work together. That's what I said from day one. It takes games especially but also training sessions and conversations off the pitch," said Van Dijk, 35, who is the only Liverpool defender to ever cost more than Jacquet.

"There's good moments and not, but it's how we react and help each other and you can see the partnership coming along.

"He's doing very well. Let's see where the ceiling will be. I don't think he's there yet so let's keep going."

More NI bee colonies survived winter last year

The latest honey bee husbandry survey had the highest number of responses in five years

Fewer bee colonies were lost last winter in Northern Ireland, new figures show.

The annual honey bee husbandry survey , external by the Agri-Food and Biosciences Institute (AFBI) found about one-in-four colonies were lost in 2025/26, compared to a third in 2024/25.

About half (51%) the losses were linked to problems with the queen bee. Others were lost because bees were dead or the hive was empty. Natural hazards including storms, flood and theft accounted for 10%.

AFBI entomologist Joanna Kirbas said the survey was "essential" for monitoring bee health and detecting long-term trends.

Bees are an important species for human survival.

They pollinate a third of our food groups and roughly 80% of wildflowers.

But globally, populations are under pressure from climate change, habitat destruction and human activity including farming.

The annual survey has been running for 18 years, creating a snapshot of beekeeping practices and challenges in Northern Ireland.

Kirbas said the latest survey had the highest number of responses in five years, showing how invested beekeepers are in providing up-to-date information on the honey bee population.

"This survey is essential and allows AFBI to monitor honey bee health in Northern Ireland, track colony losses over winter, and examine the best methods of disease prevention."

More than a hundred beekeepers took part in this year's survey

They had a total of 570 living colonies before the winter of 2025/26

Of those, 130 were lost over winter - 24%

That is significantly lower than the 33% loss average reported in the winter of 2024/25, but similar to the 24% loss rate in 2023/24

Around 14% of colonies were lost in 2022/23 and 11% in 2021/22

The highest number was in 2012/13, when 43% of colonies was lost

A colony is lost when either the entire hive of honey bees has died or left, sometimes leaving behind a queen bee and some nurse bees.

Dr Archie Murchie, the head of AFBI's Plant Health and Integrated Pest Management branch, said building a picture of long-term trends played an important role in monitoring an important pollinator.

"Honey bee losses are largely driven by weather, which influences the bees themselves, their food sources and their susceptibility to infections," he said.

Climate change and parasites can contribute to colony collapse disorder

"While we don't yet have enough data to analyse long-term trends, changing weather patterns could be contributing to colony losses," Dr Murchie continued.

"It is vital that we continue to track colony losses as well as threats to honey bees."

The survey also covers disease management and prevention measures taken by beekeepers to control the Varroa mite.

It is a parasite that attacks and feeds on honey bees and can lead to the collapse and death of a colony.

But Dr Murchie said other diseases also pose a threat.

"There is a possibility that the Tropilaelaps mite, which attacks honey bee broods, could soon spread to Europe.

"The mite was found in Georgia in 2024 and has just been found in Turkey.

"The mites breed rapidly and can quickly overwhelm a hive."

FBI raids California home tied to former Congressman Eric Swalwell - US media

Swalwell dropped out of California's governor's race earlier this yea

FBI officers raided a California home in connection with the investigation into former US Congressman Eric Swalwell, US media report.

Swalwell, 45, dropped out of California's governor's race earlier this year and gave up his seat in the House of Representatives after allegations of sexual misconduct while in office.

In August, the FBI stopped the former Democratic lawmaker at an airport, seized his electronic devices and raided his Washington DC home as part of the investigation into those allegations.

Swalwell has in the past denied any wrongdoing and his attorney has called them "fabricated".

"These accusations are false, fabricated, and deeply offensive - a calculated and transparent political hit job," his attorney Sara Azari said around the time they were first reported.

The BBC has contacted Swalwell's lawyer for comment.

In statements, the justice department and FBI said only that "early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment."

The enforcement action took place at a house in Beverly Hills, a source familiar with the inquiry confirmed to the BBC.

Public records indicate the address was associated with Stephen Cloobeck, a billionaire and former California gubernatorial candidate who had once backed Swalwell's campaign for governor.

Swalwell had stayed at the home previously, the Los Angeles Times reported.

"Mr Cloobeck was not home when the search warrant was executed and continues to have faith in the judicial process of this country," Cloobeck's attorneys David Chesnoff and Richard Schonfeld, and Elias Dabaie said in a statement.

In an April interview with the New York Post, Cloobeck said he had stopped supporting Swalwell after several women accused the former lawmaker of misconduct.

Swalwell has faced allegations that he raped one victim while she was too intoxicated to respond and that he sent women unsolicited nude photographs.

He is facing probes in New York City and Los Angeles regarding the allegations. Swalwell has denied wrongdoing and he has never been criminally charged.

But he was abruptly forced to end his gubernatorial bid after the allegations surfaced.

The House ethics committee also began investigating, but stopped once Swalwell left Congress.

Additionally, the White House in August declassified documents from a separate, unrelated FBI investigation into his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Many of those details regarding his 2015 relationship with Christine Fang were already known, and he never faced any charges.

What we know about the crash so far

Watch: Aerial footage shows train crash scene

Two trains have collided in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.

Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.

So far at least 60 people are confirmed to have died in the incident.

Here is what we know about the crash so far.

The two trains collided just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.

The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country collided with another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.

Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.

Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.

All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.

Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.

A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.

The cause has not been confirmed, though reports in Spain suggest a high-speed train hit another train which had stopped on the tracks.

Aerial footage shows the extent of the damage and the emergency response

More than 500 people were believed to be on board both trains.

Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.

A former government minister was also among those reported missing.

The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, Fátima Báñez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.

The Castilla La Mancha regional government said 64 people are now confirmed to have died.

Speaking separately to Spanish media, he warned the death toll could increase further.

Eighty people are being treated for injuries, according to authorities, with 50 of the casualties said to be in a serious condition , and 15 more in a critical condition.

A huge emergency response is underway

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo".

"I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha," Sánchez said on X, adding that emergency services were working on the ground "to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations".

"My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."

Sánchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.

Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.

A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.

A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.

Spanish news agency have reported that hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".

It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.

This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.

In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain , its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

Losing my legs ended my football dream - now skiing gives me freedom

Adam Golebiewski has been able to train in snow

A promising footballer who lost both legs after a car crash has a new passion in life - after finding "freedom" in skiing.

Adam Golebiewski was only 17 when the crash happened in 2024 in Macduff, Aberdeenshire. He needed a double amputation below the knee.

The former goalkeeper celebrated his 18th birthday during his rehabilitation in hospital, and was fitted for prosthetics.

Since then he has become a father, and - now aged 20 - is showing a flair for para cross-country skiing. Adam's coach thinks the Paralympic Winter Games could be a target.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Adam faced three months of rehabilitation at Woodend Hospital in Aberdeen following the crash which was caused by a drink driver.

He was able to walk again on crutches, and was "thankful and grateful" to be home with his family that Christmas.

Adam's dreams of becoming a professional goalkeeper were shattered, but in the face of adversity he found a new joy.

He now trains at the Nordic ski centre in Huntly, next to the field where he used to play football with junior side Deveronside.

There, he uses a special sit-ski with a board and wheels. The board is replaced with skis when he trains on snow - something he had the chance to do in America earlier this year.

With no previous experience of the sport, he has just qualified to enter international competitions as a para biathlete - which combines cross-country skiing and shooting.

This video can not be played

'I don't think of my injuries when I am on the board'

His sights are now set on para biathlon World Cup events in Finland and Sweden over the next six months.

"I don't actually think of my injuries when I'm on the board - I just forget that I have them," he told BBC Scotland News.

"I just feel so free and I just forget about everything else."

Of his training travels, he explained: "In Colorado, I didn't really know anybody and I was quite nervous to go and try it out, but once I was on the snow I was completely fine - even though I fell about 40 times.

"Then Italy, that was another good experience where I I tried biathlon, which is skiing and shooting.

"The last trip I was recently on was Oberhof in Germany which was again just an improvement from the first time being away on snow, and I learned a lot more again."

He said his mind was "completely focused" on what he is doing.

Adam needed a double amputation as a teenager two years ago

Adam's coach, Simon Bate of Snowsport Scotland, said he had made impressive progress.

Dowman sees red as Arsenal dumped out, but did Arteta go too far?

Arsenal's 16-year-old winger Max Dowman was sent off for the first time in his senior club career

Max Dowman has been getting used to making headlines for moments of magic, but the 16-year-old was in the spotlight for the wrong reasons when he was sent off as Arsenal suffered a shock loss to Fleetwood Town.

Dowman scored twice as Arsenal beat Ipswich in the previous round of the Carabao Cup and manager Mikel Arteta rewarded him with another start in the Gunners' last-16 tie.

And this one was perhaps more of an opportunity than it looked. Arsenal are light on wing options with Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke injured, so it was a chance to stake a claim.

But Dowman's red card in the 85th minute marred his night.

And after being held by Fleetwood during normal time where the Gunners went behind despite having 26 shots and 78% possession, the Premier League champions lost on penalties after a 1-1 draw in normal time.

Arteta gave his star youngster a scathing look as Dowman left the pitch and angrily said something to the winger as he went down the tunnel, revealing after the game that it was "something that we discussed already before the match".

The young winger reacted to a heavy challenge by Harrison Neal and, although he did not fully kick out, he made a movement towards Neal with his leg that gave referee Michael Salisbury a decision to make.

It goes down as Dowman's second red card this month after he was also sent off while representing England Under-19s in the last international break.

"You have to remember he is 16 years of age - he's a kid," former Arsenal midfielder Paul Merson said on Sky Sports.

"He wasn't having the greatest of nights so he's going to get frustrated. He gets the chance every now and then to play for Arsenal .

"He probably feels he should be playing more. He gets the chance tonight, isn't doing too great. It's an old-fashioned tackle.

"If that's Viktor Gyokeres, he [Arteta] isn't doing that. That's what I don't like. If it's an experienced international, I don't think he does that. He's a human being.

"He's not the last person to get sent off for Arsenal and he's not the first."

This was just Dowman's second start of the season - and the Arsenal players had been briefed about their task.

"When we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to respect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate. It was very clear," Arteta said following the game.

Dowman is one of the best young players in Europe and tough treatment from defenders is something Arteta has previously said he will have to get used to.

"For me, I'd put my arm round him. It's still 1-1 and you are in the game," Merson said on Sky Sports, looking at Arteta's reaction.

"We all say things in life when you think 'I shouldn't have said that'. For me that's a classic moment where if he [Arteta] could have that back, he'd do it different."

Former Everton midfielder Leon Osman also believes that it was a lack of experience that played into Dowman's red.

"It was on the far side of the pitch, but from what we saw [Dowman] can't have any complaints." Osman said on BBC 5 Live.

"Yes, there were a lot of challenges flying in thick and fast from both teams, and then there was that moment when a huge challenge came in on him, but as I mentioned earlier they happen so often.

"And you have to know as a good player, people are going to try to kick you at times, and that's what happened.

"It was a poor reaction from him and you hope he learns and he learns quickly."

Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets?

The surprising loss to Fleetwood, a team 84 places below Arsenal in the football pyramid, was made even worse by the fact that the Gunners' under-21 team had beaten AFC Wimbledon, a side in a division higher than the hosts, on the same night in the EFL Trophy.

The first incident of the match came with under two minutes on the clock when the game was stopped for more than eight minutes when a drone was flown above the pitch.

Perhaps Arsenal should have taken that as a warning this was to be an unusual night.

Arteta named an experimental side and gave a debut to 18-year-old forward Ceadach O'Neill, started 17-year-old Marli Salmon at centre back, 16-year-old Dowman on the wing while goalkeeper Illan Meslier was making his first start for the club too.

But the Gunners boss surrounded that inexperience with seasoned internationals such as Jurrien Timber, Piero Hincapie, World Cup winner Martin Zubimendi, Champions League winner Kai Havertz and Gyokeres.

All of those players played a huge part in the Gunners winning the Premier League title last season.

However, even after introducing captain Martin Odegaard and £75m signing Bruno Guimaraes from the bench, Arsenal produced a poor performance.

"First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through the next round. The manner that they have done it, and for us a very sad day," Arteta said of the result.

"There is nothing to criticise the players for their attitude, their application. The determination - you could see that was there from the start.

"Even with 10 men, we conceded a really poor goal to start with that gave them some momentum."

Arsenal have not won the League Cup for 33 years.

In 2012, they lost to League Two side Bradford City on penalties and they were also beaten by Championship side Sheffield Wednesday in 2015.

With Dowman now suspended, Saka out for around six weeks, Tzolis working to return and Arteta revealing after the match that Madueke was unavailable with an injury, their options in wide areas for the match with Liverpool on Sunday are looking highly limited.

Mum quits job as lawyer to voice Netflix cartoon

Emily McGonagle needed a career that better suited family life

A mum says she left her late-night legal career behind for voiceover work from home where she can care for her children.

Emily McGonagle started her working life as a lawyer in the capital, often finishing at 03:00, but started to question whether she could sustain it long term.

After having children, she decided to seek something "more flexible" than her daily commute from Colchester to Canary Wharf, and pivoted to voiceover work in 2019.

The 42-year-old voices eight characters for the children's television series Spike, which premiered on Netflix on 12 October and is its number one children's show on the site in the UK.

The cartoon began as a preschool animation on YouTube called Fire Spike!, which was about the adventures of a dragon and his friends.

It was created by a Lithuanian company called Bored Panda, founded in 2009.

When McGonagle joined the team, it had "less than 1,000 subscribers and minimal views".

It now has 1.25m subscribers and was the seventh most-watched Netflix show globally in its first week.

"It's insane," she said.

Is home-working under threat from the perks of office life?

McGonagle's curiosity was stirred while her toddlers were watching television.

She said: "I just kind of always wondered about it, and then I was also watching a lot of kids' TV, like Paw Patrol and Peppa Pig, on repeat.

"I'd be like, 'Oh, that'll be such a cool job. I'd love to do that,' but how on earth do you get into it?'.

"I kind of just wrote it off because I don't have an acting background."

The cartoon follows the adventures of a dragon and his friends

She told BBC Essex how she filled her home studio with professional audio equipment, and after several months of auditioning, got her first gig with Google.

She did commercials, signed up to some acting groups in Colchester and did a six-week acting course in London.

Three years ago she saw the advert for Spike.

"If you'd have asked me, when I was watching Peppa Pig all those years ago with my kids, that I'd be hearing my own voice on radio and Netflix, it would be beyond my wildest expectations."

Ahead of its Netflix debut, Bored Panda group's head of animation, Jonas Dovydaitis, said on social media he could not "get over how cool" that children around the world could now watch the show on the platform.

My decorations are up two months before Christmas

Christmas is the best time of year in the eyes of mother-of-two, Becky Evans

With Halloween just days away, it is no surprise to see people's houses covered in fake cobwebs and guarded by ghoulish creatures.

But Becky Evans, from Suffolk, is bucking the scary and spooky trend in favour of celebrating an altogether different holiday two months early.

"I am Christmas crazy. I love what it's about - the build-up, how it makes you feel, and I actually start [around] 100 days before Christmas, so the decks are up," said the 48-year-old from Felixstowe.

"It is in full swing, with shopping, decorations, lights and films – it's never too early."

One of three trees Evans is putting up inside her home this Christmas sits in the living room

Evans, who joked she lived with her "poor husband" and two children, started the trend of putting up her Christmas decorations early about eight years ago.

She set up a social media page with her love of all things festive, and her daily "countdown to Christmas" posts have gained her more than 100,000 followers.

"Last year I started on 4 October, so this year I'm actually a little bit late as I started on Friday," said Evans.

"I just love Christmas and I go very extra, but if you can't go extra at Christmas, when can you go extra? My house, my rules."

The 48-year-old's husband does not quite share her passion for Christmas decorations, she said

Over the years, Evans, whose five grandchildren "love" her Christmas cheer, said she had spent "a lot of money's worth" on decorations.

She has so many, in fact, she has had to convert her summer house into Christmas storage space.

Evans also used to go as big on the outside of her home as she did on the inside, but decided to "scale it back" over the years for her neighbours' sake.

Evans strives to match the wrapping paper of her presents with the colour theme of the room she keeps them in

Her home is decorated with everything from cedar garlands to miniature festive houses, animals and ornaments, to twinkling lights and glittering baubles.

This year her home will have three full-sized Christmas trees and each room decorated in a different theme, with the colours matching the wrapping paper.

"Christmas just gives you a fuzzy feeling that you can't explain, it's just magical," Evans added.
