article:
India and China were easing tensions - then a border official spoke out

India and China have a fragile thaw in relations since the 2020 clashes

For much of the past year, India-China relations appeared to be on a cautious path to recovery.

The two countries have seen ups and downs in their ties over decades - especially over the disputed Himalayan frontier.

But events of the past few days suggest that the thaw which has followed their most recent clashes in 2020 may be more fragile than it seems.

The latest concerns began when India's border police chief said Chinese troops had returned to disputed areas along the Himalayan frontier in large numbers earlier this year, pitching tents several kilometres inside territory claimed by India.

The remarks by Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, director general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), have triggered a political controversy in Delhi.

To begin with, such comments by serving officials are rare. Sensitive border issues are usually addressed by the federal government through its defence or foreign ministries.

At a recent gathering of officers in Rajasthan state, Kapur said face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops had taken place at several locations in the north-eastern state of Arunachal Pradesh and were continuing.

The confrontations began in July, he said, but both sides initially withdrew.

A few days later, Chinese troops returned in larger numbers and pitched tents "around six-to-seven kilometres inside India's perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC)", he added.

The LAC is an ill-defined line separating the areas controlled by the neighbours and India and China have sparred for decades over this disputed 3,440km (2,100-mile) border.

China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. But Delhi has always rejected the claim, saying the state was an integral part of India.

The dispute is one of the most persistent challenges inherited by independent India from the British colonial rule in 1947. It led to a brief border war in 1962, in which India suffered a humiliating defeat.

More than six decades later, much of the frontier remains undemarcated, with the two countries maintaining overlapping territorial claims.

The region's rugged terrain adds to the challenge: shifting river courses, lakes and snow-covered peaks make it difficult to establish a clear boundary.

As a result, troops from the two sides can find themselves face-to-face along the frontier, sometimes triggering violent clashes and diplomatic tensions.

India and China share an ill-defined border demarcated by mountains, rivers and lakes

The last major escalation came in June 2020 , when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in Ladakh. At least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers were killed.

It was the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975. Indian opposition parties accused the government of losing territory to China - a claim Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has repeatedly rejected.

The clashes triggered a sharp deterioration in relations, disrupting diplomatic engagement and affecting trade and travel. After several rounds of negotiations, the neighbours agreed in 2024 to take steps towards easing border tensions.

They have since moved to restore direct flights and ease visa restrictions imposed after the clashes.

Chinese President Xi Jinping also visited India in September for the Brics summit, his first visit to the country in seven years.

These developments raised hopes of a broader normalisation of ties. But the latest reported stand-offs have renewed questions about how much progress has actually been made on the ground.

After Kapur's comments, the main opposition Congress party once again accused Modi of making concessions to Beijing.

"The prime minister and his entire apparatus remain silent on this grave issue," senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh wrote on X , external .

The Indian government has not explicitly denied Kapur's account that Chinese troops had pitched tents several kilometres inside what India considers to be its side of the LAC.

Foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said last week that "the situation in the border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns".

He said both countries were using military and diplomatic channels to address outstanding issues, but gave no further details.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said that China had "consistently and strictly adhered to relevant agreements" reached with India and it conducted "normal patrol and management activities in the border areas to safeguard territorial sovereignty".

The Galwan clashes were the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975

Experts say Kapur's remarks offer a rare glimpse into what they describe as China's increasingly assertive military posture along the disputed frontier.

"This pattern of Chinese probing at various points of the Arunachal Pradesh border has been happening for some time," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary who led several rounds of border talks with China in the mid-2000s, told the BBC.

He said such actions were "not enough to result in an immediate war, but enough to sort of create new facts on the ground".

Indian opposition parties have long accused China of extending its presence in both Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, leading to tensions.

Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in China's People's Liberation Army who is now associated with Tsinghua University in Beijing, said both countries had learnt lessons from the 2020 Galwan clashes.

"The two sides should be more careful to avoid this kind of thing from happening in the future," he said, adding that Chinese media had not reported on the latest stand-offs in Arunachal Pradesh.

India and China's tensions also come against the backdrop of a complicated economic relationship.

Despite their differences, the countries remain major trading partners, with bilateral trade , external reaching $151bn last year. But the balance is heavily tilted in Beijing's favour, with Chinese exports to India accounting for about $131bn.

India continues to rely on Chinese imports for machinery, rare earth magnets, electric vehicle batteries and pharmaceutical products.

This dependence means tensions with Beijing can have consequences well beyond the border, particularly for Indian industries and infrastructure projects.

Last week, China also announced restrictions on exports of tunnel-boring machines used in metro rail and highway construction, saying they were intended to protect national security and national interests. Although these curbs were not India specific, they would have a bearing on India's infrastructure push.

"Chinese policy towards India is designed to complicate India's rise, including India's ability to master certain things in advanced technology and manufacturing," Christopher Clary, a professor at the University at Albany in New York, told the BBC.

A similar problem emerged last year when China restricted export of rare earth magnets - widely used in electric vehicles, smartphones, wind turbines and medical scanners.

The move temporarily caused supply problems for Indian industries, highlighting how Beijing's control over key materials can affect global supply chains.

India is now trying to build domestic capacity to produce rare earth magnets, but developing the industry will take time and investment.

Arunachal Pradesh has long been the focus of tension between India and China

For people living along the disputed frontier, the consequences of tensions with China are more immediate.

"Villagers living in some border areas tell us that they cannot access grazing lands because of Chinese intrusion and encroachment. It's not something new, it's been happening for a long time," says Tongam Rina, a senior journalist with the Arunachal Times.

This has created a "sense of insecurity among the people here," she adds.

Villagers usually do not return to those "prohibited" areas for hunting and yak rearing, and they are not sure when they would be allowed again.

The border dispute also has wider strategic implications for Delhi, with a growing realisation that President Donald Trump's focus on expanding economic engagement with China could limit Washington's willingness to back India in any future confrontation with Beijing.

China may have little interest in a full-scale conflict with India but, analysts say, it could see advantages in allowing the dispute to continue.

As China's economic and military power grows, it may calculate that a prolonged stalemate will strengthen its position in any future negotiations.

For India, the latest stand-offs are a reminder that improved diplomatic ties do not necessarily translate into lasting stability along the border.

article:
Women's alcohol deaths are increasing - my daughter died after fighting for decades

Paula Gibson with her daughter Clare, who was supported by local services throughout her addiction

The number of women who died last year in Scotland from alcohol-related illnesses was up by 3% on the year before, official figures show. , external

Overall, the total number of people who died from alcohol-related conditions fell slightly, to the lowest rate since the pandemic. There were 1,152 alcohol-specific deaths registered in Scotland, a decrease of 3% compared with 2024.

The Scottish government said the drop amounted to progress and that it would invest £160m this year on alcohol and drugs programmes.

But one mother from Aberdeen whose daughter died alone after decades fighting alcoholism described her illness as "relentless" and said sometimes all the resources available are still not enough to beat it.

Clare was supported throughout her life through local services

Paula Gibson's daughter Clare died in November 2023, aged 45, after spending the last 20 years of her life in and out of addiction services. She had periods of sobriety, but ultimately died at home alone.

The 74-year-old said her daughter started struggling with alcohol in her early 20s but over the next decade her behaviour escalated, even with help and interventions.

This led to Clare's parents taking custody of her youngest son, Craig, who was eight at the time.

"It probably took about 10 years of feeling like something wasn't quite right, while trying to support her through interventions, but it wasn't enough.

"Her behaviour was extreme and the impact it had on all of us was really difficult.

"We were living on a knife edge, not knowing what the next phone call would be or what would happen to her next.

"Her wellbeing became compromised. She was not making any rational decisions or the right choices for her or her children," she said.

With both of Clare's sons living with their grandparents, the family tried to maintain their relationship, but it became difficult when the addiction took over, Paula said.

"As a family we were firmly focused on trying to maintain the relationship with Clare and the boys.

"We tried to always keep contact between them, because family ties are so important. "

Clare grew up in Aberdeen

Things escalated months before Clare's death when she went into rehab while her younger son and parents went on a holiday to Greece.

She didn't make it through rehab and during a hospital stay was told that if she did not change her lifestyle she would die.

Paula said the boys had been looking forward to seeing their mother after rehab in a safe setting and breaking the news was one of the hardest moments of her life.

She said: "It was utterly destroying.

"Clare had been sober leading up to this and phoned me in floods of tears expressing huge regret about the pain she had inflicted on our family.

"We were both weeping on the phone and I told her to go back into rehab for support and she would get through this.

"I told her I loved her and I forgave her, and we would see her when we got back from Greece."

When the family got back, they received a phone call from a painter who was doing work in the house, who had found Clare.

She was not in rehab and had collapsed and passed out at the bottom of a set of stairs.

"We drove back from Glasgow to Aberdeen and I had to tell them mum had failed rehab and they couldn't see her because she had relapsed.

"This was the hardest thing ever because this time we really thought she was on the road to recovery.

"Within two months she was dead," Paula said.

On the night she died, Clare had reached out to emergency services overnight but it was a social worker who found her in the morning.

She died of fatty liver disease, or alcohol-related liver disease (ARLD), where the liver is damaged by drinking too much alcohol over a long period.

Paula spent over 20 years supporting her daughter and said they had all the resources you could need - but sometimes that is not enough.

She said, despite everything, Clare left a financial legacy so her children would be looked after.

"We spent so many decades living on edge and waiting for that phone call, so that when we found out Clare had died there was a sense of relief - she was finally at peace.

"Alcoholism is a crippling disease and a nasty cycle of horror for those in it and everyone around them.

"No one wants to be an alcoholic. The whole family suffers.

"She was just like Jekyll and Hyde with a drink, that's the reality and it is hell."

Clare volunteered at charities near her home

Despite her struggle Clare spent a lot of time volunteering for her local church and Home Start - a local family support charity offering volunteer-led services to families with young children in Aberdeen.

Her mum said: "Clare was such a kind, loving and caring person.

"She was empathetic and had so much love to give. She sent all of that love to everyone else because she couldn't love herself."

Throughout the addiction she was supported by Alcohol and Drugs Action (ADA) , external - a local charity who develop and deliver services to those affected by alcohol and/or drug use and the Aberdeenshire Council substance misuse team

Paula was still being supported by the charity years after her daughter's death and said they were an "exceptional service".

She said: "Both services were incredibly supportive until her last day. She had one-to-one counselling for years with the charity and they brokered the funding for her six-month stay in rehab.

"They were just astonishing. They never judged Clare and never stopped trying."

Scottish Health Action on Alcohol Problems welcomed the fall in alcohol deaths but raised concern over rising deaths among women.

The charity's chairman, Dr Alastair MacGilchrist, said: "It is deeply concerning that while deaths among men have fallen, deaths among women have risen.

"This comes after years in which the alcohol industry has made a targeted effort to encourage more women to drink, from products and packaging designed to appeal to women to marketing that links alcohol with wellbeing, celebration and empowerment."

MacGilchrist also said that alcohol deaths rose sharply during the pandemic and had been slow to come down.

"Despite this year's fall, deaths remain higher than they were before Covid, and people living in Scotland's most deprived areas are now 4.8 times more likely to die from alcohol than those in the least deprived.

"That is not a situation we can accept as the new normal. It is a reason to act," he added.

Residents baffled as Olympic gold postbox blocked

This new parcel box has left residents bemused as it hides the market town's gold postbox

A new Royal Mail parcel box has been placed in front of a celebratory Olympics gold postbox, leaving residents frustrated with where it has been put.

The postbox in Alcester, Warwickshire, was painted to mark Nick Skelton's gold medal at the 2012 London Olympics, and residents told the BBC they want it restored to prominence urgently.

Royal Mail said the new box would increase choice for customers, but councillor Tom Ballinger called for it to move to a "more suitable" location, highlighting the postbox's significance to the area.

"It symbolises something very special for the town: that we have someone who lives in the area that was part of those games," he said.

Ballinger said he was working with the MP for Stratford-on-Avon, Manuela Perteghella, to request action from Royal Mail.

In a letter to the postal service, Perteghella formally requested the red box be moved, saying that "Alcester residents and councillors are deeply concerned by the situation, and I urge Royal Mail to address it promptly."

Laurie-Mo Gullachsen (right) says she watched the Olympic Torch pass through Alcester in 2012

Perteghella recognised in the letter that Royal Mail has permitted development rights, a legal exemption that allows it to install postboxes without prior approval, but said neither she nor the Stratford-on-Avon District Council had been consulted.

Nick Skelton, who lives in the town, won team jumping gold at the London Games before winning the individual jumping title at Rio 2016.

Residents said the gold postbox was a source of local pride, and they could not understand why the new parcel box was placed so close to it.

"The postbox has got a lot of meaning for the local people, and it's a real shame that it has been covered up," said Laurie-Mo Gullachsen.

"I think a bit more thought should have been put into this, and if they could listen to the community's wishes for it to be moved, I think they should," she added.

Her view was echoed by social media posts describing it as "yet more clutter blocking the pavement" and saying "it could have been put somewhere more discreet".

"It's a bit of an eyesore for such a lovely part of Alcester, having that for Nick Skelton being a gold medallist. It's a shame it's distracting from such a lovely part of the high street," Matthew Stanley told the BBC.

MP for Stratford-on-Avon, Manuela Perteghella, and Councillor Tom Ballinger have sent a letter to Royal Mail outlining the community's concerns over the new parcel box

A spokesperson for Royal Mail said: "We're giving our customers even more convenient ways to access our services.

"Traditional postboxes, such as the Olympic gold postbox on Alcester High Street, can be used for letters and smaller items, while our new parcel postboxes make it easy to send and return larger parcels.

"We're pleased to see positive feedback in areas where parcel postboxes have already been introduced and hope local residents find this one just as useful."

King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins

King addresses 'suffering and injustices' in Bahamas past

King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.

His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.

King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.

The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."

The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.

"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.

During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".

He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".

The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change.

He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.

Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.

A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region".

For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".

Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.

The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.

The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.

He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.

The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

article:
M25 at 40: Keeping UK's busiest motorway moving

Margaret Thatcher said Britons ought to be congratulating the "magnificent achievement" of the M25

Sometimes referred to as "The Road to Hell" or "Europe's largest car park", the M25 remains an essential part of Britain's transport network.

Since it officially opened on 29 October 1986, many workers over the years have contributed to the establishment and maintenance of the UK's busiest motorway.

Chris Nutton, traffic officer for National Highways, said: "We have days when it runs very smoothly and we have days when all hell can break loose."

His colleague Esther Martin added that aside from dealing with daily incidents like vehicle breakdowns, they have encountered some unexpected ones like bolting horses.

Nutton recalled a driver discarding a lit cigarette from a car window and unwittingly setting ablaze the lorry load of hay bales behind them.

He added there were instances of drivers falling asleep while stuck in traffic jams and an extraordinary array of items strewn across the tarmac.

National Highway officers Chris Nutton and Esther Martin reflect on their experience working on the London Orbital

"During the festive period we have previously come across presents that have fallen out of car roof boxes and spread across the carriageway," Martin added.

"Sometimes we have been able to reunite them with owners, but sometimes they've ended up under lorry wheels."

Martin said on other occasions, items including wheelbarrows, bicycles, canoes and even a longbow were found.

Former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher cut the ribbon to mark the completion of the M25 on 29 October 1986, hailing it as a "magnificent achievement".

The 117-mile motorway, which runs through Kent, Surrey, Greater London, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire and Essex, quickly attracted huge numbers of motorists.

This has led to chronic congestion despite decades of efforts to keep traffic moving, including widening lanes, upgrading junctions and introducing "smart motorways".

Tony Ferris, who worked on the M25 in 1980, said he remained pleased with what the team achieved

Retired civil engineer Tony Ferris was one of the original team helping to create the M25.

He said he was proud of what they had achieved.

"It was a momentous piece of work over many years. I started working on it in 1980."

When asked if he believed the motorway deserved the criticism it sometimes received, he replied "I don't think so".

"When it runs smoothly and nicely it's great. It's almost a victim of its own success - everybody wants to use it," he said.

Simon Wilkinson said the M25 is a vital part of Britain's transport links

Since 2009, a consortium called Connect Plus has been managing the M25 after winning a 30-year £6.2bn contract.

Simon Wilkinson, commercial manager, said: "It's understandable it gets a bad rap sometimes.

"However it is because so many people want to use the M25 and we'd miss if it wasn't there."

Family of couple held in Iran meet with Ed Miliband

The family of Lindsay and Craig Foreman have held their first meeting with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband since he took the post in July

The family of a couple who have been detained in Iran for nearly two years say a change of approach is needed after meeting Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for the first time.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman, from East Sussex, have been held since January 2025 after being sentenced to 10 years in prison on espionage charges, which they deny.

Now the couple's family say they feel they are edging closer to freeing them after a first meeting with Miliband since he became foreign secretary in July, but they want the government to consider legal proceedings.

A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said the couple's health and welfare was "a top priority".

Lindsay's son, Joe Bennett, from Folkestone, said the family had came out of the meeting with Miliband feeling they had "edged closer to our goal - bringing Mum and Craig home".

He told BBC Radio Kent: "For him to hear it from us first hand what it would mean to us as a family, I really do think he took it on board."

"Nothing has changed today, so there is a little bit of disappointment, but we feel that what we asked really did resound with Ed.

"We are doing a good job, but at the core of it the two people who need to come home are still where they are."

The want the government to consider proceedings at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

Lindsay and Craig Foreman were detained in Iran after entering the country on a motorcycling holiday at the beginning of January 2025.

The couple began hunger strikes earlier this year, after claiming that prison authorities had began to prevent them from speaking to their families. The hunger strikes lasted 93 and 84 days respectively.

Their detention has coincided with widespread tension in the country and the US's war with Iran.

Ed Miliband took on the role of foreign secretary in July

Tuesday's meeting was also attended by Folkestone MP Tony Vaughan and Gravesham MP Dr Lauren Sullivan, as well as members of the family's legal team and Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty.

In September, Miliband reiterated the British government's request for the immediate release of the couple when meeting with Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

A spokesperson said: "Since their arrest last year, Britain's ambassador to Tehran, along with diplomats and officials in London, have been working to provide consular assistance. This includes the ambassador visiting them in prison.

"The Foreign Secretary set out how unjustified and appalling we consider Lindsay and Craig's incarceration to be, and the action that the UK Government is taking to try to secure their release."

Missing deaf cat hitches a ride 170 miles from home

Quinn was rescued after being found near some bins at an A1 service station

A deaf cat that went missing six weeks ago has been found at a service station about 170 miles (274km) away from home after apparently hitching a ride.

Quinn, aged eight, disappeared from St Helens in Merseyside, despite rarely venturing outside her owner's garden.

It is thought she managed to get into a van or lorry and ended up at services on the A1 in Peterborough, where she was found on Thursday, yowling and scavenging near some bins.

The white cat was more than happy to have some warmth and attention before her owner was able to make the eight-hour round trip to reunite the beloved cat with her family.

Quinn has been totally deaf since birth, and her owners have had her since she was a kitten.

She had been kept indoors but recently discovered she could "tailgate" another of the family's cats through the microchip-operated cat flap, so was occasionally stranded outside.

This video can not be played

Missing deaf cat hitches a ride 170 miles from home

"She developed a very loud yowl to alert us she wanted to come back in," said one of her owners.

"The neighbours would sometimes complain about the noise."

He thinks she managed to get out of the garden while a wall was being rebuilt and somehow found her way into a van or truck - "unless she's got a train pass or something we don't know about".

One of Quinn's owners made the eight-hour round trip on Sunday to collect the beloved family pet

Quinn's loud meowing alerted staff at the services to her presence.

Cat Attwell, who volunteers for the Facebook group Peterborough's Lost Pets , external and works at the services, managed to locate Quinn.

"I was calling her, but of course I didn't know she was deaf," she said.

"She was very nervous, but eventually she came to me and let me pick her up. She was so loving."

Quinn was later scanned and taken to be looked after by Jules Murray, one of the lost pets group's administrators.

Murray, who also volunteers at Woodgreen Pets Charity, said Quinn's rescue was "another story to show the importance of chipping your pets".

She said Quinn was the third cat she has been called out to at the A1 services.

"I think she got into the van, or even in the engine compartment, as she was quite grubby," Murray added.

"She's very vocal and very needy, but very much loved."

Speaking about microchips, Fiona Cooke, associate director of policy and impact at Woodgreen, said: "Even cats who rarely venture outdoors can go missing, but this tiny piece of technology can make an enormous difference in reuniting a lost pet with the people who love them."

She also stressed the importance of keeping details up to date.

Quinn's owner added: "I'm touched by the generosity and kindness shown by everyone who helped rescue her, and we are so happy to see our little Quinny again."

Multiple sclerosis patient living in 'horrific pain' due to UK-wide drugs shortage

Jill Kenning experiences constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker"

A woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) has said she is living with "horrific pain" after being unable to get a drug she uses to manage her condition.

Jill Kenning has used Nabilone for 17 of the 18 years since she was diagnosed with MS and said the drug had been vital for managing her pain and helping her live a normal life.

She said she had spent most of her time in bed since running out of the drug last Tuesday.

Northern Ireland's devolved health department said there was disruption to supplies of the drug across the UK, meaning Nabilone was out of stock with wholesalers and not expected to be available again until December.

Pharmaceutical manufacturing company Brown & Burk UK Ltd, which supplies the drug to the UK, said they are doing "all that [they] can at this point in time" amid "technical issues".

According to a tracker published by the industry reference guide MIMS, the average number of drugs in short supply in the UK has trended upward this year , external .

The number of drugs in short supply reached 157 this week, up from a low of 107 in January.

Pharmacists warn of medicine shortages in NI

Kenning, from Coleraine in County Londonderry, was diagnosed with MS in 2008 after experiencing problems with her sight.

She subsequently developed numbness down the left side of her body and was treated by a neurologist.

After a severe relapse, which resulted in a four-week hospital stay, she was prescribed Nabilone which she said made a massive difference to her quality of life.

"It helps me basically that I can get out of bed in the morning," she said.

But she said that without the drug she experienced constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker".

Earlier this year, pharmacists warned of medicine shortages in Northern Ireland

After contacting her health trust for her regular repeat prescription, she said she was told there were no supplies of Nabilone available.

She was told to contact her neurologist and has since been prescribed other medication.

Kenning said the alternatives had not been effective and that her health had declined to the point where she had to stay in hospital for several nights.

"I don't want to be here any more because the pain is so bad," she said.

"I don't know how to describe it.

"I have been living on painkillers... I can't sleep, I'm sick, I'm not eating."

Kenning said more should have been done to prepare patients for the disruption.

"How do I live my life? How do I cope with the pain?" she said.

"I'm not only fighting for me, I'm fighting for all the other patients that are on this drug."

Multiple sclerosis is a disease that affects nerves in the brain and spinal cord.

The nerves in these areas are surrounded by a protein called myelin, which helps signals from the brain get to the rest of the body.

The myelin becomes damaged in people with MS because the immune system mistakes it for something that shouldn't be there and attacks it.

This means signals from the brain struggle to get through properly.

Northern Ireland's Department of Health (DoH) said both licensed doses of Nabilone were out of stock from wholesalers across the UK.

It said the shortage began affecting 1mg capsules in July, with the 0.25mg strength becoming unavailable more recently.

The DoH said it was working with the UK's Department of Health and Social Care and health trusts to manage the disruption, and that guidance had been issued to healthcare professionals on alternative treatments, including unlicensed imports of Nabilone where available.

A spokesperson said the DoH recognised "that medicine supply disruptions can be concerning for patients and the healthcare professionals who care for them".

"If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to their specialist healthcare teams for advice about their treatment options," the spokesperson said.

Brown & Burk UK Ltd said it "puts patients' care first" and it is "hoping" to get Nabilone stocks into the UK by the end of November, ensuring it reaches users by mid-December.

The manufacturing of the drug's active ingredient "is extremely challenging", he added, and requires "special, dedicated, experienced people" and equipment, Managing Director Preetham Hiremat told BBC News NI.

Hiremat also highlighted that the global need of this active ingredient "is only in [the] few grams a year", which "becomes all the more challenging".

"We have had technical issues and have had to manufacture the active ingredient material all over again and hence we are in this situation."

Chapman thanks trainer and donors after 'freak' injury

This video can not be played

Boxer Raven Chapman speaking to BBC South Today

Boxer Raven Chapman believes the fast actions of trainer Stuart Scott may have saved her life when she suffered a bleed on the brain over the summer.

The 32-year-old was airlifted to hospital and placed in a medically induced coma following a sparring session in Denmark on 24 July.

Chapman had collapsed after training and was taken to hospital after Scott called for an ambulance, to be later diagnosed with a brain haematoma and cerebral oedema.

"I remember the final spar where it happened, It was the third spar of the week and I felt fine going in there," she told BBC South Today.

"It was just a sort of freak injury that I never thought it would happen to me, we (herself and Scott) have done hundreds of sparring rounds together and my fights.

"He knows the kind of things that I say and I wasn't acting myself from what he said, that's when he called an ambulance before anything even happened.

"I sat down and then it all sort of happened after that, luckily with where I was at the time, I think in under an hour from when the ambulance was called I was then into surgery."

After reaching hospital, the procedure Chapman underwent successfully stemmed the bleeding in her brain and helped to stabilise the swelling.

A fundraiser was then launched online for people to contribute towards getting her back to the UK and her long-term recovery.

A total of £97,792 was donated after the page was shared widely among the boxing community on social media.

Chapman's promoters Queensberry, Matchroom Boxing's Eddie Hearn and Most Valuable Promotions' Nakisa Bidarian were among the leading donors.

"All the support that I got was just amazing," Chapman added.

"That's why, with all the fundraising money, I'm going to use that to make sure I'm getting everything so that I get better as that's why people donated.

"It brings a tear to your eye when you see it and how much people are there for you in the community, it's a special world, the boxing world."

Raven Chapman was promoted by Frank Warren's Queensberry Promotions

Norwich-born Chapman trains at Warriors Gym in High Wycombe and as a professional won 10 of her 12 fights with just two defeats.

At one stage of her career she was based in Bournemouth, training alongside former WBO cruiserweight champion Chris Billam-Smith, who was one of many professional boxers to share a video message of support for her.

Chapman lost to Skye Nicolson in a bid to win the WBC featherweight belt in October 2024 , the only women's world title fight ever to be held in Saudi Arabia.

She admitted that not being able to now achieve what she had hoped in the sport will to be difficult to come to terms with.

"I probably would never get a licence again after this," Chapman said.

"Even if they said I could, I probably wouldn't want to risk putting my loved ones through that pain of it again.

"I'm gutted that I'm not going to achieve the dreams I did have, which I knew I would be able to achieve, but it is what it is.

"Maybe one day I'll help other boxers achieve those dreams, I've still got a bit of time before I decide exactly what it is I can do and see where I want to be."

Having initially been wheelchair-bound in the early stages of her recovery, Chapman finally managed to lace up a pair of gloves again this week.

Although her days of competing in the ring may be over, she can still enjoy some aspects of the sport as she continues into the next stage of her life.

"I loved it, I think I smiled my whole way through it," she added.

"As much as I may never spar again or fight again, I can still do the craft and hit the pads and hit the bags and enjoy it."

article:
'I earned my spot' - Lewis can be England hero after controversial selection

Mikey Lewis has scored four tries in nine appearances for England

Nobody understood how divisive England's selection of Mikey Lewis was for the Rugby League World Cup than the man himself.

The 25-year-old was picked by coach Brian McDermott as one of three half-back options alongside Harry Smith and captain George Williams, despite a Super League season pockmarked by inconsistency and disciplinary issues.

Lewis' selection ahead of 2025 Man Of Steel Jake Connor added fuel to the fire; the fact the Hull KR man was then left out of the squad for England's opening defeat to Tonga only added to the feeling of Lewis being more trouble than he was worth.

But Lewis, speaking to media on Wednesday from the England team hotel in Wollongong, said that despite his up-and-down season he never doubted that he had earned his place.

"The way my year went wouldn't be the best. I don't need anyone else to tell me," he said. "I just had to put myself in the shop window. I have earned my spot."

And after all the talk, Lewis has the chance to be the man who helps save England's floundering World Cup hopes.

The 30-12 loss to Tonga has England firmly on the back foot, but they gave themselves a chance last weekend with a crushing 82-0 win over France.

Lewis, named among the interchanges, came on for the final 20 minutes and scored two tries to boost England's points difference – and thus their chances of reaching the semi-finals.

To qualify, England must beat Papua New Guinea on Friday, hope Tonga defeat Samoa on Sunday, and make up a 68-point deficit on the Samoans.

So, piling up the tries is the name of the game for England in what might be their final match in Australia this year – and Lewis, again off the bench, will aim to be the man to provide that flourish.

"I will always represent my country to the best of my ability," Lewis said of his two-try cameo in Perth. "I was told to run with the ball, and I wanted to play with a smile on my face.

"We just have to go out and do what we have planned. It will be a tough game, but we have the strike and desire.

"We have a fighting chance, we believe in that. So, we just have to put the hard work in. It is a unique position, so just enjoy that."

Lewis took selfies with fans in Perth following England's Group B-C win over France

Not even Lewis' biggest detractors will deny he had the speed, skill and power to deliver what England need. His temperament is the question.

In 2026, Lewis scored 17 tries and provided 14 assists in 20 Super League matches. However, he also received four yellow cards – the most of any player in the division.

He started the season on the wrong foot with a deliberate trip of an opponent in Hull KR's shock loss to newly-promoted York Knights. Lewis avoided suspension, but the tone was set.

Then in July came the moment he fell from favour for many England supporters. Lewis was served with a four-game ban for a late tackle and a headbutt in a defeat against Warrington Wolves.

Lewis was sin-binned for the tackle during the match, but he then headbutted a Warrington player in an incident that was initially missed by match officials.

It was expected these aberrations would cost Lewis a World Cup place, but McDermott kept faith – now is the time to reward that.

Lewis has been contrite about his disciplinary problems, admitting his teammates were the ones to suffer, and he is seeking external help to deal with his on-field temperament.

Part of his contrition comes from the undoubtable passion and pride Lewis has about representing his country.

That was clear after his debut in October 2023 against Tonga at St Helens. Lewis was named man of the match after a game-winning display, scoring a try and providing an assist in a 22-18 triumph. His emotional post-match interview showed how much playing and delivering for England meant to him.

That will be on display in Wollongong on Friday, whatever the result means for England's progression or role Lewis has in it.

"Last week the hard work was done, my job was to go and cause havoc - that was my instruction, and I did that," he said

"I might get different instructions this week, but I'll do it, because I am proud to play for my country - 20 minutes is 20 minutes for England, I don't really care it's only 20 minutes."

Celebrity Traitors star and comedian Joe Lycett has paid colourful tribute to the Welsh grandmother who went viral on TikTok after getting caught in shop shutters and being hoisted into the air.

Joe Lycett was a contestant in The Celebrity Traitors, but banished after being too keen to be a traitor

Anne's interviews with BBC Wales and footage from the famous CCTV ended up being viewed at least 58 million times on the BBC News Instagram account alone.

Lilly, 28, who was very close to her grandmother, said: "I thought she's back from the dead, she's risen again and now my nan is in a museum.

"It's lovely, I would have it on my wall any day."

In the past 12 months, Lycett, 38, from Birmingham, has been producing works the museum has described as celebrating "nostalgia, grief and loss", from a sculpture of an extinct large woolly mammoth to an abstract painting of TV personality Cilla Black, who died in 2015.

Lilly and Anne were very close

The artwork, including Anne's moment, are painted in a child-like style and in bold and bright colours.

Lilly said her grandmother's legacy has lived on. She said: "Every time that it's mentioned people laugh about it. And then it just brings a smile to my face because I think 'oh nan, if you were here today'.

"It's absolutely hilarious, so it definitely helps with the grieving process."

BBC reporter Matt Murray with Anne Hughes after she found reluctant fame

The viral moment was previously immortalised by graffiti artist Tee2Sugars on the shutter she was caught on.

Lilly, who is a midwife and lives in Caerphilly, added: "Honestly if she was alive today she would say that the world has gone mad. I find Joe really funny and the fact that he's now painted my nan is a bit mind-blowing."

She also revealed her grandmother had told a "little fib" in her BBC interview about holding onto her trolley, and said she was in fact holding onto it because "she didn't want anyone stealing her fags".

Anne's family say her legacy lives on through the viral moment

Lilly says she still uses the story as an "ice breaker" in her work.

"I'll be looking after a woman and I will tell her about my nan and all of sudden I'm in the room with her whole family watching the video and they'll be absolutely peeing themselves. It's brilliant," she said.

Blindfolded wife 'felt stranger's hand' during sex with husband, court told

(From left to right) Norman Macksoni, Richard Wilkins, Connor Sanderson-Doyle and Mohammed Hassan are all on trial at Winchester Crown Court

A woman said she ran into and locked herself in a bathroom after realising her then-husband had allowed someone else in the bedroom while she was blindfolded and having sex, a jury has heard.

In a police interview played at Winchester Crown Court, Joanne Young said she was restrained when she felt a hand on her wrist which she believed did not belong to her now ex-husband Philip Young.

Joanne - who has waived her right to anonymity - said Young, who has admitted drugging and raping her, later apologised and told her he had invited someone to watch the couple have sex after browsing online forums.

Four men who Young is alleged to have recruited to abuse his wife at their home are now on trial.

Warning: This story contains distressing details

On the second day of the four men's trial earlier, two police interviews with Joanne were played to the court.

During the first interview, dated 29 July 2024, Joanne said the incident had happened after a night out with friends when they had a few drinks in February 2023.

She told police she could not "remember all of it", but said Young had come upstairs at some point after she had gone to bed to sleep.

She said she later "woke up with a blindfold and restraints on".

Joanne told the officer in the interview she loosened the restraint on her right hand as she was waking up, and then the restraint on her left hand.

At that point, she said, she felt a hand grip her wrist and as she tried to take her blindfold off Young, who she believed was at the end of the bed, said "get down" to someone.

Joanne Young has waived her right to anonymity

Joanne said she then saw someone ducking at the end of the bed and she ran to the bathroom and locked the door.

"I tried to undo the restraint and do the wrist on the left. There was a hand on my left wrist to stop me from doing those things," she told police.

"The bed is a really big bed. So to have someone on the end of the bed and the left was not possible… I knew immediately."

"I had that moment of 'that doesn't make sense'. I took the restraint and blindfold off. There were two people in the room," she added.

Joanne said her vision had been blurry as she did not have glasses on or contact lenses in, but she had seen a car outside which she did not recognise after leaving the bathroom.

The jury heard the couple later discussed the incident, with Joanne telling police it was the first time she had ever seen her then-husband cry.

She said: "His apology after, he was so upset, and he knew what he'd done and how hurt I was."

She described how she asked Young if he had ever invited anyone else to watch them have sex before, which he denied.

"It was so intrusive. I was so upset. He knows I would have never said yes to that," she told police.

Joanne told the officer in the interview: "I didn't know if I should stay in the relationship or get myself out of the situation.

"I put my head in the sand and carried on," she said.

Joanne said she took the incident as a "one off" and tried to "move on".

Asked by an officer if there was a discussion between Young and Joanne about having someone else in the relationship, she said: "There was a joke years ago, a bit of banter, where he said in the kitchen something like 'would you ever want to sleep with someone else?'.

"I said no, and he said 'as long as I can watch you'. We laughed it off but it was a no."

"It was never a part of our relationship. There'd never been a discussion. He never asked me what I wanted, it wasn't a conversation," she added.

On the day Young was arrested, Joanne said he admitted to her he had shared images of her online without her consent.

Joanne said it felt like a "kick in the stomach" and she was left in "shock and utter confusion".

She said: "What images? When? I'm assuming I was asleep? When did these get taken? It was such a split moment."

"How he could do that to me. How he could do something that's so intimate that's not allowed. How can he do it? How can you do that and think that was okay?," she added.

Philip Young admitted a string of sexual offences against his now ex-wife

Four men are jointly charged with Young, 50, with the following offences:

Connor Sanderson-Doyle, of Swindon, denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching during an incident in 2016.

Norman Macksoni, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, has denied one count of rape in 2017.

Richard Wilkins, of Toothill, Swindon, Wiltshire, has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration in 2016.

Mohammed Hassan, of Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching in 2023.

Young, a former Conservative Swindon councillor, has admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing an obscene article.

He also published more than 500 intimate images and videos of his ex-wife and recorded her doing private acts for his own sexual gratification without her consent between 2010 and 2024.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.

Young and Hamilton will be sentenced at the end of the trial, which is expected to last up to four weeks.

article:
Two cities, 480 miles apart, come together in a shipping container

The interactive installation marks 60 years of friendship between Birmingham and Frankfurt

It is not every day that a walk through Birmingham city centre leads to a conversation with someone hundreds of miles away in Germany.

But that is exactly what is happening inside a brightly decorated shipping container that has appeared outside the Hippodrome.

Step through the door and, for a few minutes at least, Frankfurt feels a lot closer than 480 miles away.

The installation is part of Sister Cities Dialogue, a project marking 60 years of friendship between Birmingham and Frankfurt. Through a life-sized digital portal, people in the two cities can sit down together, chat and share a glimpse of their daily lives.

It does not take long for strangers to start talking.

"Hello Birmingham!" says Julie Cazenave from Frankfurt, who has worked on the project.

She said the portal was created to celebrate the relationship between the two cities and encourage people to make new connections.

Manuella dropped into the portal during her daily walk through Frankfurt

Shortly after our conversation ends, shop owner Manuella appears on the German side of the portal during her daily walk through Frankfurt.

We explain that we are sitting in Birmingham.

"This is cool," she says with a smile.

"I was just walking around like I do every day. I have lived here for more than 50 years and I love this city."

For a few minutes, it feels less like a video call and more like two groups of people sitting in the same room.

Soon, Manuella is saying goodbye and heading off to dinner with colleagues.

"See you in Birmingham. Bye bye!"

Not long afterwards, Michael and Max take a seat.

"It's a very nice idea, to communicate with people in other parts of Europe. Birmingham, of course!" they say, waving virtually from across the continent.

Those spontaneous encounters are exactly what organisers hoped for.

Jen Wilbur, from non-profit arts and heritage organisation Bertz Associates, has been helping deliver the Birmingham side of the project.

"It's been magical being in the container and being part of those conversations, seeing people open up," she said.

"We've had a lot of comments from people on the Frankfurt side saying, 'aren't Brummies so friendly?', because we're really keen to come in and have conversations. It's been really fantastic."

Jen Wilbur said it had been "magical" watching strangers strike up conversations

Inside, the experience has been carefully designed to feel as natural as possible.

The container is dark, with lighting focused on a wall-sized screen showing the other city. Six chairs face the portal, while a microphone suspended from the ceiling means everyone can be heard.

An identical set-up has been created in Frankfurt.

"What makes this special is that it really feels like you are in the room with somebody," Wilbur said.

"It's a full-body live experience. It takes up a whole wall of the container, so it really feels like you are in one room together."

The project links Frankfurt not only with Birmingham but also with its twin cities Krakow in Poland and Lviv in Ukraine.

For Birmingham residents, however, Frankfurt may already feel familiar.

The German city has been twinned with Birmingham since 1966 and is well known to many through the Frankfurt Christmas Market, which returns to the city next month.

Councillor Deborah Harries, Birmingham City Council's cabinet member for culture, said the project would help bring people in both cities closer together through "conversation, engagement and understanding".

The free attraction is open on weekdays until 4 November.

article:
Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs

The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in Cambodia

A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.

The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.

The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.

Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.

The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.

Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.

The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.

"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."

"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."

Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.

"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.

"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."

Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.

Cruise passenger Holly Hennessey and her cat, Captain, have now found themselves in Cambodia

During their time onboard the Villa Vie Odyssey, passengers had access to several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.

Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month.

Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.

In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package.

Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".

For Canen and Bodin the experience was "worth it", despite the fact it was shorter than expected.

"We loved our two years on Odyssey—the adventures, the places we visited and the friends we made along the way."

Many of the passengers have already made plans to "settle together off the ship, so those friendships and that sense of community are continuing on land", they said.

The couple plans to spend a few days in Sihanoukville, before travelling to different parts of South East Asia while they "figure out our next chapter".

But others, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Odyssey will set sail again soon.

"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said.

"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."

Plan to create the Highlands' first area of linguistic significance

Skye, along with the neighbouring island of Raasay, could be designated an ALS

Highland Council is to hold a consultation on plans to make Skye and Raasay its first area of linguistic significance (ALS) for Gaelic.

The local authority has proposed using powers in the new Scottish Languages Act to introduce the designation.

Places where 20% of residents have Gaelic skills qualify as an ALS, but areas with strong cultural or historical links to the language can also meet the criteria.

Highland Council is to recruit a community engagement officer to help take forward the proposals for Skye and Raasay.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

There are 18,552 people in the Highland Council area with Gaelic skills, according to the latest census data , external .

The local authority's Gaelic committee heard earlier this year that Skye and Raasay would qualify as an ALS .

Councillors were told the status would confirm Highland Council's "clear commitment" to Gaelic.

Officials said evidence from Irish Gaeltacht areas suggested the designation could bring economic and educational benefits.

Gaelic and Scots were recognised as official languages as part of a range of new measures that came into force on St Andrew's Day last November.

The Scottish Languages Act, which MSPs voted through in June last year, also empowers parents to ask for a Gaelic school to be established in their area and aims to ensure that more qualifications are available in Gaelic.

It includes powers for ministers to commission research into the use of Gaelic and Scots and establish teaching standards for the languages.

Scotland's then Deputy First Minister Kate Forbes - a Gaelic speaker - called it a "historic milestone".

article:
Woman hit by falling tree trunk 'lucky to be alive'

Nina Lunn said her injury showed how dangerous weather could be

A mum has said she is "lucky to be alive" after being hit on the head by part of a tree trunk that broke away during a storm.

Nina Lunn was walking through Allestree Park in Derby at about 11:00 BST on Sunday morning when Storm Boelo brought gusts of over 50mph to the East Midlands.

The injury caused bleeding and concussion requiring hospital treatment for the 42-year-old.

"The hospital staff said 'wow, you're lucky to be here'. The paramedics were actually quite worried, especially because my blood pressure was very high," she told the BBC.

"It just shows how dangerous the weather can be."

Lunn says she is "lucky to be here" after a large section of tree snapped off and hit her on the head

Lunn said she had been a keen walker from a young age and valued getting outdoors multiple times a day as a way of managing her attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

On the weekend of her birthday, Lunn was keen to brave the storm for a quick stroll before celebrating with her family in Yorkshire.

"I stuck to the footpaths because of the storm, thinking that I'd be OK. I wasn't in the woods or anything," she said.

The mother of one was chatting to a friend via her headphones when she heard the tree snap but did not have time to react.

"My teeth shattered together. Then I could just feel the blood dripping down my face. I panicked," she said, having been knocked to the ground by the impact," she said.

"My AirPods had been knocked out of my ears. I managed to grab my phone and tell my friend 'how fast can you get to Allestree Park? I need you'."

She used her fleece sleeve to stop the bleeding and was approached by a woman with a pushchair.

"Had it been 30 seconds previous, it could have got the baby, and to be honest, I am lucky to be here," said Lunn.

"The paramedics were actually quite worried, especially because my blood pressure was very high. The swelling on my face, the left side of my head is quite bad."

Lunn said she felt her teeth "shatter together" and blood drip down her face from the impact

Lunn rushed to the A&E department of the Royal Derby Hospital where she had her head glued and returned on Monday with further concussion, swelling, blurred vision and high blood pressure.

The teaching assistant attempted another walk on Tuesday but felt "really, really nervous" so intends to spend the remainder of the half-term holiday resting.

"I've been ill every single half-term for the last year and was really excited to have a good one, but it's just not been meant to be," she said.

A Royal Derby Hospital spokesperson said: "We're very happy to hear that Nina is doing well after what must have been a really frightening experience."

Meanwhile, the Met Office has advised people stay to indoors as much as possible during stormy weather.

"Being outside in high winds makes you more vulnerable to injury. If you do go out, try not to walk or shelter close to buildings and trees," it said.

article:
Anger in Kenya over extradition hearing delay for ex-British soldier accused of murdering woman

Agnes Wanjiru was discovered in a septic tank near a British army camp in Kenya in 2012 aged 21

The family of a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by a former British soldier 14 years ago has expressed outrage after being told an extradition hearing for the accused had been postponed until May 2027.

Relatives of Agnes Wanjiru, whose body was found in a septic tank near a British army training camp in Kenya in 2012, described the delay as "completely unacceptable" and have accused the authorities of failing to keep them informed.

Robert James Purkiss was arrested in the UK last November and is fighting extradition to Kenya to face trial for the murder of the 21-year-old mother.

He denies the allegation. His hearing was due to be held in London next month.

Murdered Kenyan's friends want UK soldier to face justice

Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family had learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.

"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.

"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."

The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.

It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.

The family said a UK court was expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.

Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.

Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.

A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.

In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.

Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest his extradition to Kenya.

He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link , where he was further remanded in custody.

Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.

The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

article:
Four investigations Democrats could launch if they win control of Congress

Democrats have signalled a willingness to launch probes into both Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth's handling of the Iran war

Democrats in the US Congress are already planning how they would use their power if they win a majority in the House or Senate in next week's midterm elections.

Success is by no means guaranteed, even if midterms can sometimes be brutal for the incumbent party that holds the White House.

Control of the chamber, however, would give the party power to issue subpoenas - summons to testify or produce documents - as well as additional funding to launch investigations early next year.

Democrats are weighing whether to investigate senior figures in the Trump administration - and possibly the president himself. Staffers have begun assembling a list of possible investigations and witnesses, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Here are a few potential Democratic targets if the party emerges victorious on 3 November.

Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations.

"We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC.

Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities - particularly cryptocurrency firms - as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Other topics could include the $400m (£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family.

"What's shocking to me is not only that this administration, cabinet officials and even the president and his family have been corrupt and self-dealing, but they've been so brazen and open about it," Subramanyam said.

The White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.

"President Trump is focused on retaining Republican majorities in Congress and doubling down on the progress he has made to lower costs for families," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said.

"Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump's commonsense agenda," she added.

A White House official said the administration is "always prepared" to respond to oversight requests regardless of who is in Congress.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to look into Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran that began in February - including the number of civilian casualties, munitions shortfalls, spending and claims of poorly prepared troops and facilities.

Other topics, according to a source familiar with the discussions, could include boat strikes in the Caribbean that the administration says are aimed at stopping the flow of drugs into the US.

In April, a group of House Democrats filed rare articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They cited the war in Iran and accused him of "high crimes and misdemeanours".

Impeachment requires only a simple majority in the House, but conviction - and removal from office - would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. No cabinet official has ever been removed this way.

Watch: "I don't know why we're doing it" - Americans on US strikes on Iran

Some experts believe that the negative publicity that would come from congressional hearings could ultimately lead to Hegseth being fired or resigning from the position.

"[If] it looks bad for the White House, and it's a drag on their media attention, President Trump might be likely to cut loose those officials, because he doesn't want that bad press," said David Miller, a political science professor and expert on the presidency at American University in Washington DC. "In a sense that could be a win for the Democrats."

Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told the BBC that the decision to launch the war should come under scrutiny.

"The bigger issue is this: this war was never authorised by the United States Congress, and I don't care who the secretary of defence is," he said.

"The constitution says that Congress declares war," he said, and lawmakers should "haul these folks in" to answer questions.

In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record, calling him a "transformative leader" who has "slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters".

"By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," she said, using the administration's preferred name for the defence department.

The aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One is also likely to be the target of Democratic investigations

Senior Democrats - including Robert Garcia, the California Democrat tapped to lead the House Oversight Committee should the party take back the chamber - have identified immigration enforcement as a key priority for potential congressional investigations.

These could examine allegations of misconduct by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents during immigration raids across the country.

But these investigations may prove difficult and politically tricky.

In 2024, Trump campaigned on a promise of mass deportations of undocumented migrants - a message that resonated with many of his supporters.

But recent polls suggest many Americans, including those who backed Trump in that election, are uncomfortable with some of the tactics used by ICE in American cities so far this year.

It means Democrats will have to walk a fine line between opposing ICE tactics and appearing to dismiss broader immigration concerns, Painter told the BBC.

Democrats are split on the possibility of attempting to impeach Trump for a third time.

Some, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have expressed support for an impeachment, citing what they view as an unauthorised war with Iran and other alleged impeachable offences.

Others have called for a more cautious approach, arguing that any impeachment is unlikely to end in the Senate voting to remove Trump - who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing - from office.

It is also unclear whether the party could agree on a reason to launch impeachment proceedings.

"I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office in October, adding that he sees the impeachment efforts in his first term and the later criminal cases brought against him as "very illegal things".

James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told the Washington Sun news outlet in June that Democrats were "one-trick ponies" who were "going to go after Trump".

There is no guarantee for Democrats that any potential investigation would end with a meaningful outcome.

But Subramanyam said their efforts would send a message.

Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years

The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nation

Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.

Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.

He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.

The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.

Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.

Gas from the field will be for domestic and industrial power generation and also for vehicles

"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.

Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.

In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.

Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.

Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.

The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.
