Bonfire Night policing in Scotland will be 'largest operation since Trump visit'

Police Scotland are preparing for a large-scale operation on Bonfire Night

Scotland's biggest police operation since the visit of President Donald Trump last year is to take place on Bonfire Night, in the face of a "unique" combination of safety concerns.

As many as 1,700 officers could be deployed on and around 5 November to deal with fireworks-related disorder, a European football match involving Celtic and potential protests in Glasgow.

Additional public order vehicles and drivers are being brought in from 18 English and Welsh police forces under mutual aid arrangements.

Police Scotland says the plan, titled Operation Amberlight, is intended to ensure the safety of the public and emergency services.

The force has already vowed that anyone caught up in disorder around Halloween and Bonfire Night will face "very real consequences ".

This will be enforced through Fireworks Control Zones (FCZs), which ban the use of pyrotechnics in certain areas of Edinburgh and Glasgow from 30 October.

In recent years, emergency crews have been pelted with petrol bombs and missiles - though police said there were fewer instances of this last year.

This video can not be played

Police tackle Bonfire Night disorder in 2025

The deployment will beef up Operation Moonbeam, the annual police response to fireworks-linked criminality which is now in its ninth year.

Moonbeam involves local police divisions receiving additional specialist support in case trouble breaks out on their patch.

This year's Bonfire Night will see police coping with two further challenges - both in Scotland's biggest city.

Celtic will take on Turkish side Beskitas in a Uefa Europa League match at Celtic Park.

Officers say they are also aware of images circulating online, suggesting "planned protest activity" will take place in Glasgow the same night.

The force is planning what it calls "one overarching policing operation" to ensure a co-ordinated approach.

Operation Amberlight's gold commander, Ch Supt David Robertson, said: "Bonfire Night remains one of the busiest nights on the calendar for Police Scotland.

"We are committed to supporting local policing divisions with dedicated nationally co-ordinated specialist capabilities.

"Operation Amberlight builds on what is already in place to further enhance our capability and capacity to respond to the unique challenges we may face on 5 November.

"Whilst we have seen improvements in recent years, we are not complacent, and with these additional challenges, our enhanced model will see the largest deployment of police forces since the visit of President Trump."

The worst Bonfire Night disorder in recent years took place in 2023, when more than 60 officers were injured across the country.

Youths targeted officers with petrol bombs and fireworks in the Niddrie area of Edinburgh.

Similar incidents were reported in other parts of the city, while fire crews were targeted in Dundee, Glasgow, Blantyre in South Lanarkshire, and Blackburn in West Lothian.

Further instances of anti-social behaviour around Halloween in 2024 saw another officer injured and bus services withdrawn from Niddrie despite police seizing a cache of fireworks and petrol during pre-emptive raids.

This year, Fireworks Control Zones (FCZs) banning the use of pyrotechnics in certain areas are scheduled to come into force in Edinburgh and Glasgow from 30 October.

Under the restrictions, it is a criminal offence to set off a firework within the FCZ boundary or throw one into a zone.

The FCZs run from 30 October to 8 November in Edinburgh and until 9 November in Glasgow.

The police response to President Trump's visits in July 2025 - Operation Roll 2 - cost £21m and involved 7,340 officers.

Government minister calls for review of 'unacceptable' BBC Scotland channel closure

The BBC announced the Scotland channel will move online next year

Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan has urged Ofcom to review "wholly unacceptable" plans to close the linear BBC Scotland channel.

The BBC last week announced the dedicated Scotland channel - as well as BBC Three and Radio 4 Extra - would move online as part of measures to make £500m of savings by 2028.

McAllan said moving the channel online would "reverse progress in improving the visibility and representation of Scotland within the UK's broadcasting landscape".

She called on Ofcom, the UK's independent press regulator, to scrutinise the decision and its implications.

McAllan wrote: "The Scottish Government considers the proposed closure of the linear BBC Scotland channel to be wholly unacceptable, and we oppose such a move in the strongest possible terms."

BBC Scotland TV channel to close amid cuts to services

In the letter, to the watchdog's chief executive Melanie Dawes and director for Scotland Glenn Preston, McAllan said she understood that broadcasters must adapt to evolve with audience habits.

But she added public service broadcasters had a "unique responsibility to ensure their services remain accessible and relevant".

McAllan continued: "Closure of the linear channel would also be impossible to reconcile with a supposed ambition to move power and decision-making away from London and towards audiences across the UK who are paying for the service.

"Many viewers continue to rely on linear television services, and any move away from those services risks disproportionately affecting audiences who are less likely to access content through online platforms."

The culture secretary added that plans to close the nightly News at Seven programme would be a "totally unacceptable reduction in nationally relevant journalism".

The closure of the programme is expected to see about 10 posts cut in addition to the 60 BBC Scotland announced earlier this year.

McAllan also called out a "disparity in indigenous language broadcasting" and highlighted the "total absence" of Commonwealth Games coverage on BBC One Scotland.

Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan has urged Ofcom to review the decision

The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland.

Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay.

The current plans won't see any changes to BBC Scotland's main news programme Reporting Scotland, which is shown on BBC One or the broadcasters radio or online services.

After the announcement, Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine said more cuts could be on the way.

The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years.

In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts.

In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus.

Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced.

The broadcaster, which has about 21,500 full time employees, gets most of its income from the licence fee, but the number of TV licences sold has been declining in recent years.

As a public service broadcaster, the BBC's mission is "to act in the public interest, serving all audiences through the provision of impartial, high-quality and distinctive output and services which inform, educate and entertain".

Legal bid to overturn Drumcree march ban fails

Orangemen have made numerous attempts to begin their march from Drumcree church but have been blocked by police each time

An attempt to overturn the Northern Ireland secretary's decision to ban the Drumcree parade has failed.

The High Court in Belfast has ruled that Sir Chris Bryant's decision made on 9 October was lawful.

The judicial review was brought by a Portadown Orangeman against Sir Chris and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher.

The secretary of state's intervention to stop the parade came after he received security advice from Boutcher.

A lawyer for the Orangeman told the court that an appeal of the judgment is "likely".

The Drumcree dispute led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.

Mr Justice Scoffield said: "The secretary of state's decision was lawful and within the margin of discretion properly afforded him, although it is highly regrettable that it was required in the circumstances which arose."

He said those who opposed the march should "take no particular joy in the outcome of this case".

The judge added that "the position which has now been reached has been brought about at very significant cost to the people of Northern Ireland - financially, through the diversion of police resources, and in terms of community relations".

"Depressingly, the threat of serious and widespread disorder has loomed large," he said.

He went on: "Significant concerns have now been expressed about respect for the rule of law in this jurisdiction.

"That includes among some elected representatives, by reason of their participation in the unnotified protest."

Dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on Garvaghy Road, court hears

Orange Order add police chief to court challenge of Drumcree parade ban

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

Loyalist activist Jamie Bryson spoke to reporters outside court alongside members of the Portadown District Lodge

In a statement posted on social media, , external Portadown Orange District said its legal right had been "thwarted" by unlawful activity.

"We note the damning commentary of the Judge in respect of the lawbreakers, and ask, in particular that these concluding remarks are given careful consideration by our political leaders."

The district confirmed it would lodge an appeal in respect of the PSNI and secretary of state, adding: "Our district will now proceed toward ensuring the legal right established is vindicated, and we will exercise it.

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister maintained his position that "the legality of the right of Portadown District is not removed.

"Though, I note the severe criticisms of the protesters, this outcome carries the risk of more of the same."

Speaking outside the courts Sinn Féin MLA Deirdre Hargey said that she believes defending the residents "was the right thing to do" and that they "make no apology for that".

Hargey said that the recent events in Portadown have "set the work back" of community relations and said no one in "the community in Portadown or more widely, wants to go back to the days of 28 years ago".

Breandán Mac Cionnaith and Darragh Mackin speaking outside the High Court following the ruling

Speaking after the rulling, Breandán Mac Cionnaith said: "The position we took in relation to this Orange march was fully justified. All we sought was the right that was promised under the Good Friday Agreement, the right to live free from sectarian harassment."

"That right has been vindicated and upheld today - there is no getting away from it."

Solicitor Darragh Mackin said "no amount of spin will change the legal reality" of the ruling.

He praised the residents for conducting themselves "impeccably" throughout the legal proceedings.

"We now look forward to drawing a line on this horrendous chapter and moving forward," he said.

Speaking outside court, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson said the case had been "difficult" but there were "some very important comments" from the judge.

"What has been established in court today can be summarised very simply. The Portadown District established a legal right to walk the Garvaghy Road," he said.

"The Chief Constable's ultimate position was he could not protect 35 Orangemen against the risk of disorder. That is a very, very serious finding indeed."

Before the parade was banned, the chief constable had written to Sir Chris stating: "The PSNI's current assessment is that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession have been exhausted.

"Any remaining options would require a substantial public order intervention and this is not assessed to be proportionate, and which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion affect across Northern Ireland."

Last week, the court heard PSNI intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on the police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

John O'Dowd said he had been "attending a police interview in regard to his attendance" at the protests on the Garvaghy Road

The Garvaghy Road residents' case is that the Northern Ireland secretary's decision was lawful.

Senior Sinn Féin politicians have attended police interviews over their roles in the protest. They have defended their attendance and said they "stood with the residents on the Garvaghy Road".

On Wednesday morning, the Finance Minister, Sinn Féin MLA John O'Dowd said he had been "attending a police interview in regard to his attendance" at the protests on the Garvaghy Road.

The latest flare-up of the Drumcree dispute has featured a number of legal challenges, involving the Parades Commission, Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents.

The dispute first came to prominence in the mid-1990s and almost derailed the Northern Ireland peace process at the time.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

An almost two-week-long stand-off began between protesters on the Garvaghy Road and members of the Orange Order and their supporters.

If a drama-filled weekend amid a wild storm wasn't enough, the Scottish Premiership quickly returns with a stacked midweek card packed with intrigue.

Derek McInnes seems to have accepted he is in for a fiery welcome when the former Hearts boss takes his Rangers side to Tynecastle, while Jim Goodwin's buoyant Dundee United head to Celtic Park hoping to bring an end to a long-standing curse.

And will Marink Reedijk finally get his Hibernian tenure up and running when his struggling side travel to Paisley?

A visit from one of Glasgow's big two under the lights at Tynecastle is always something to anticipate. Then you throw in the added spice of this one.

Just four points behind Rangers, Hearts have a fresh opportunity to show last season wasn't a one-off after collapsing in spectacular fashion at Celtic Park 10 days ago.

The Ibrox side's trip to Gorgie on Wednesday also marks the return of McInnes, who came within minutes of leading the Jambos to a historic title triumph in May.

Then came the summer. McInnes was prised away by the Ibrox hierarchy after striker Lawrence Shankland had already made the move to Govan, with midfielder Cammy Devlin following thereafter.

Injured pair Shankland and Devlin will miss the trip back to Tynecastle, but McInnes, who admitted feeling "guilt" about his exit, can probably expect a frosty reception, despite the wonders he worked during his year at the club.

"Well, the hope would be you get on to the pitch and clap the fans and there's an acknowledgement both ways," McInnes said. "But that's not going to happen. I totally understand it, though."

Dundee United are emerging as one of the stories of the season as Goodwin's side continue to thrive following a radical change in style from their manager.

As a coach, and certainly as a player, expansive, continental-inspired football was never really something associated with Goodwin, a Scottish football veteran who has been part of the furniture for more than 16 years.

But the former Aberdeen and St Mirren boss has said he has taken inspiration from Jens Berthel Askou's work at Motherwell last season to reshape himself, and his side are lighting up the league after overcoming a difficult start.

An exhilarating 3-2 victory over Aberdeen in chaotic weather at Tannadice extended United's unbeaten run to five matches, moving them up to fourth.

Now they face the Premiership's acid test: a trip to Celtic Park.

Goodwin has got the better of the champions in two of his past three encounters with them, but both of those victories came at Tannadice last season.

Staggeringly, Celtic are unbeaten in 51 home games against United in all competitions since a 1-0 league defeat in December 1992.

Goodwin will be wary of the way Martin O'Neill's men dismantled a bold Hearts side at Parkhead, but the reinvented Irishman is urging his United players to embrace a trip to the venue where his life in the Scottish game began.

Despite Sunday's narrow defeat by Celtic leaving Hibs rooted to the foot of the Premiership, manager Reedijk says the reaction from supporters after the game told him "we are in the right way".

Former midfielder Kevin Thomson also believes his old club will come good under the Dutchman, so will Paisley prove to be the place where Reedijk's reign ignites after three straight defeats?

The Leith club travel to face a St Mirren side who ended their own wretched run by defeating Dundee on Saturday, bringing a five-game losing streak to an end.

The fact Hibs have lost on only two of their past 14 Premiership visits to St Mirren is perhaps a good omen for Reedijk, although fans remain unconvinced that the team's current plight can be turned around.

Goodbye to Wawrinka - an everyman who gatecrashed the greats

This video can not be played

Fond farewell: Wawrinka retires after first round defeat to Lehecka in Basel

Whether through technique or toil, Stan Wawrinka has always been able to whip fans into a frenzy.

The ability to stir the emotions of a crowd never left him - even in what proved to be the final tour-level match of the 41-year-old Swiss star's glorious career.

Former world number three Wawrinka might have lost to Czech opponent Jiri Lehecka in front of passionate home support in Basel on Tuesday, but he did not wave farewell without showing the hallmarks of a stunning career that exceeded expectations.

The stylish one-handed backhand down the line. The finger pointing to the temple. The demand for more noise from the stands.

The roar of "Allez!" after winning a point he probably should not have won.

The temptation to snap his racquet over his knee after missing a shot he felt he should have made.

There were tears, too, of course.

Wawrinka, his family, and his team were dabbing their eyes once the reality of an honourable 7-5 7-6 (7-2) defeat dawned.

It meant a professional career spanning 23 years, 985 matches and three Grand Slam titles was over.

"All I wanted in my career was to give everything, have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100% in every match - out of respect for myself, the opponent, the tournament, the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP website. , external

"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and the only way you can leave the sport - without any regrets."

Stan Wawrinka was beaten but not outclassed by world number 21 Jiri Lehecka on a night of celebration in Basel

Wawrinka is loved by millions of fans because he is relatable - an everyman personality who reached the pinnacle of his sport by pushing himself to the limit.

So many talented players of his generation lamented the presence of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, believing the 'Big Three' to be a blockade preventing them from becoming a Grand Slam champion.

It did not stop Wawrinka. With explosive shot-making, relentless endurance and indomitable spirit, he barrelled past the trio of superstars on his way to winning his trio of majors.

Wawrinka had been a player whose career was ticking along steadily, rather than spectacularly, until he lifted one of the sport's biggest prizes at the age of 28.

Seeded eighth at the 2014 Australian Open, he saw off Djokovic in the quarter-finals before completing an unforeseen triumph against top seed Nadal.

"I never expected to win a Grand Slam because, for me, I was not good enough to beat those guys," Wawrinka admitted as he clutched the trophy in Melbourne.

In fact, he was more than good enough - proving it again and again.

At the 2015 French Open, Wawrinka brushed past Swiss compatriot Federer in the quarter-finals, then demolished Djokovic in the final with a display of unrelenting power - a performance which must be ranked among the greatest of his era.

His last major title arrived at the 2016 US Open, when he escaped from match point down against Britain's Dan Evans in the third round and went on to beat Djokovic for the title.

Wawrinka was the only man outside of Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Andy Murray to win multiple Grand Slam singles titles between 2006 and 2022

It is little wonder that 24-time major champion Djokovic - considered by many the greatest player of all-time - described Wawrinka as a "legend".

"Stan's had an incredible career. The competitor he is on court, talent, strength, power, precision - he had it all," said the 39-year-old Serb, who practised with Wawrinka in Basel.

Wawrinka was good enough to win majors, but he wasn't as consistently good as his illustrious rivals.

The 'Big Three' is often expanded to a 'Big Four' featuring Britain's three-time major champion Andy Murray, who soared to world number one, won two Olympic singles gold medals and lifted the ATP Finals trophy.

Wawrinka recognises he was "really far" from creating a 'Big Five' - and the evidence underlines that.

Spending 267 weeks in the top 10, winning one Masters 1,000 tournament and claiming 15 other tour-level titles is well below Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Murray, but it is also more than most players can dream of achieving.

The Grand Slam triumphs are what really set Wawrinka apart from most peers - which, coupled with his connectability and commendable attitude, is why 'Stan the Man' will be remembered for emerging as a great himself in a golden generation where others came up short.

"Of course there are tears. Of course tomorrow will feel like a hangover – not necessarily because of alcohol, more because of the sadness," said Wawrinka, who famously liked to celebrate after matches.

"But at some point you have to close the book."

The world number 151 showed a willingness in recent seasons to drop down to the ATP Challenger Tour - demonstrating his eternal love for the game which he knew owed him nothing

After turning professional in 2002, Wawrinka won 590 matches - including eight in his final season - and claimed 16 titles

Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the Budget

Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.

Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.

If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice .

Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.

The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.

"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."

She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee , external scheme extended.

The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.

She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."

Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.

He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.

He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."

The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.

"The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and the BBC understands it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."

Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.

Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.

"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."

Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.

He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently.

He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."

Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.

She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."

She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.

"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."

Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.

Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.

"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."

Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.

His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.

"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."

More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors.

"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."

Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.

"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."

Healey has said standing charges will be removed from gas bills , but Christine, who has a gas boiler, says it's not clear yet whether she will benefit, because those costs will be added on to the unit rate.

"I'm not sure I'll be better off," she says.

She thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.

She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit , external , a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.

She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".

Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".

article:
Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority

Arab parties could end up holding the balance of power

With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted, with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.

His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.

A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls – with turnout reaching more than 77%.

In Israel's fragmented political system, the signs are that Netanyahu's main rival, the former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to command a parliamentary majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority. According to partial results, they have equalled or gained on their previous record number of seats.

On the campaign trail, most Jewish opposition parties pledged not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values.

However, Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if others were prepared to join forces with them. In this election, Arab Israelis – who often identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel and represent one-fifth of the population – appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers.

Netanyahu, on the other hand, would need to convince one of the smaller opposition parties to join his coalition, if he is to secure a majority at this point.

Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner with Eisenkot's bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu

Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global

Many saw this as a make-or-break election to defeat Israel's most right-wing-ever government, accusing it of stoking racism and hatred.

A huge caveat in all of the current analysis is that the high number of as-yet-uncounted absentee ballots – mostly representing the votes of Israeli soldiers – mean that we are not expecting to have a clear idea of the final results for another day or two.

Overnight, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot addressed their supporters, pledging to form the next government.

"The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state. That is what has become clear. A decisive majority," the PM told his celebrating supporters – although he stopped short of declaring victory.

"We must form a strong, national, right-wing government. That is what must be done," he added.

"The public has chosen change," Eisenkot told his Yashar party after exit polls came out – most of which were initially more favourable to the opposition. "The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust. The Israeli public voted against Benjamin Netanyahu continuing as prime minister."

"I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israeli's citizens. And quickly – because that is what this moment demands, and because the country needs to be brought back together."

There are deep divisions in Israeli society which have been underscored by this and previous elections. They have served not just as referenda on Netanyahu's leadership – as he faces a corruption trial on charges he denies – but also as votes on what kind of country Israel should be.

The PM and his current coalition partners have taken the country on a hardline religious, nationalist trajectory over the past four years. There were mass protests over their plan for a judicial overhaul prior to the unprecedented Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 which triggered a series of wars – in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

Many Israelis want to see their country more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values.

Remarkably, the past four turbulent years do not appear to have significantly changed voting patterns.

"We see in the polls, that the relative weight of the two main sides: pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu is about the same," Professor Tamar Hermann, a pollster at the Israeli Democracy Institute told me, just prior to the election. "People expected that after October 7th, Netanyahu will be down the drain or even toppled but it didn't happen."

Already, overnight, the main Israeli parties will have begun their intense political wrangling to try to form a new coalition government.

"Each side will try to pull over defectors, or will try to see if they can make a minority government and will try all these different political kinds of wizardry," is how veteran Israeli journalist and author, Yaakov Katz described the process to me. "But it might not work, and it could take weeks or months to see if someone is actually capable of forming a government."

The leaders of the bigger parties typically try to win over smaller ones with promises of cabinet positions, budgets or specific policies.

Short of pursuing a unity government, this might be the only option for Netanyahu - but the opposition parties fought this election on a platform of "anyone but Netanyahu".

It is key now to see if those in the main opposition "change bloc" are ready to break a taboo by seeking a political deal with the Arab parties.

On the campaign trail, one of the bloc's leaders, right-wing politician Avigdor Lieberman, went as far as to say that he would not sit in a minority government that relied on their support. It was a sign of the increased mistrust and hostility towards Arab citizens since the 7 October assault.

When I recently met Mansour Abbas, head of Ra'am – the smaller of the two Arab lists – he told me that having been part of the diverse coalition that temporarily unseated Netanyahu between 2021 and 2022, he wanted to join the next government. He believed that potential partners would be more open to an alliance after the election.

"These are familiar and well-known party-political considerations. All politicians in Israel say one thing before elections and speak a different language after elections," he said. "We have experienced this before, and it does not concern us."

Meanwhile, Netanyahu and his allies have already begun an intense campaign of delegitimising the Arab parties – casting their fellow citizens as a threat from within.

So what are the next steps?

After the final results are presented to Israel's largely ceremonial president, Isaac Herzog, next week, he will consult all the leaders of elected parties and ask the candidate who appears most likely to form a coalition to do so.

If that candidate is unable to pull together a majority within a maximum of six weeks, then others could be allowed to try.

If, after all the haggling, no-one is able to form a governing coalition, a new election will be held in the following months, and the entire process will be repeated.

In the meantime, Netanyahu's government stays on in a caretaker role but without the authority to enact major policy changes.

Gas is cut over unpaid bills despite payments made

Lucy Baxter said she had struggled to cope without heating and hot water, particularly with a one-year-old at home

Residents at a block of flats in north-west London have been left without heating or hot water due to historic unpaid bills of £600,000, despite monthly payments being made over several years.

About 126 homes have been affected since 23 October. In a letter to residents, the developer and buildings management said about £300,000 is owed to the gas provider and £300,000 to the electricity provider.

The building's management company, Rendall & Rittner, said: "We fully recognise the seriousness of the situation and the impact it is having on residents, particularly families and those who may be vulnerable."

The freeholder did not respond to a request for comment from BBC London.

Rendell & Ritter added: "Our immediate priority is to support residents and to work with the freeholder and energy supplier to have the gas supply reinstated as quickly as possible."

Rendall & Rittner took over management of the building in Dollis Hill in May this year.

Lucy Baxter, who moved in four years ago when the building was new, said: "I have a one-year-old, so it's very difficult.

"I haven't been able to give her a bath and our flat is on a lower ground floor, so it's much colder and we're really struggling.

"There are other disabled residents here, disabled children, elderly residents and lots of families. I'm very concerned."

She said tenants had received a warning letter from a debt collection agency about three weeks earlier but had since been "left in the dark" about the situation.

But management claimed residents had been kept informed since the outage began and that it intended to hold a residents' meeting in the near future.

Baxter said owners and renters pay for their own hot water and heating usage through metered supplies managed by a company called mySycous.

"We don't actually know where that money goes afterwards.

"So we don't know what's been paid, but obviously there's a mismanagement of funds on their behalf.

"This is not just recent, it's been going on for years. It's accumulated. So I just don't understand how they've let it get this far."

Rendall & Rittner said it did not know the "full extent of the historic energy debt" when management of the development was transferred to it.

Baxter added: "I also think we need an explanation to how this happened - where our payments are going, why the funds are being so mismanaged.

"We don't want it to happen again, so we want to be assured that it's not going to happen again."

Shower facilities have been installed at the front of the building for residents

Rendall & Rittner said discussions with the freeholder and energy supplier were "continuing urgently", but it could not currently confirm when heating and hot water would be restored.

The company and the freeholder said they were providing residents with temporary heating and alternative access to shower facilities, "with further arrangements also being explored".

"We are particularly conscious that some residents may be more significantly affected by the loss of heating and hot water," they said, encouraging tenants with specific support requirements to get in touch.

Another tenant, Kaniz Gatt, said she was concerned about who would ultimately cover the cost of the temporary measures.

She said: "Portable showers outside is not going to solve the solution. We are very concerned. Who is going to pay for those showers?

"All I just can't believe that this is happening to us in the UK as well and that this was allowed in the first place. It's not the residents' fault."

Kaniz Gatt said residents were worried about who would ultimately bear the cost of the temporary facilities

The buildings management said any historic costs that are "properly recoverable" through service or heat charges would need to be reviewed and apportioned before individual charges could be confirmed.

Gatt added: "I'm very, very anxious because, it's my right, and I worked so hard to buy this apartment and it's out of my control."

A Rendall & Rittner spokesperson said that the "historic financial position is also being reviewed" including "the previous budgeting and recovery of energy costs, heat tariff and metering arrangements, and sums outstanding in relation to the development".

"As that work remains ongoing, it would not be appropriate for us to speculate about responsibility for the historic shortfall or to suggest at this stage what individual residents may ultimately be asked to pay," they added.

Trial date set for seven accused of vandalism at Trump Turnberry

The group are alleged to have daubed buildings with paint at the resort

Seven people are to stand trial in 2028 accused of vandalising US President Donald Trump's Turnberry golf resort.

Kieran Robson, 35, Uzma Bashir, 56, Ricky Southall, 34, Autumn Ward, 23, Rebecca Sian Davies, 29, John Moxley, 58, and Dylan Chiaramello, 25, are suspected of causing "malicious mischief" during a protest on 8 March last year.

Prosecutors claim the allegation will be proved in terms of section 31 of the Counter-Terrorism Act 2008 and said the charge is aggravated by having a "terrorist connection".

Defence lawyers pled not guilty on their behalf, other than Southall's advocate who said she only became involved in the case this week.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

More stories from Scotland

A trial date has been set for 14 February 2028 in Glasgow, and it is expected to last 15 days.

The group are accused of damaging property at the five-star Ayrshire resort, digging up turf at its golf courses and spraying weed-killer Glyphosate on fairways and greens.

Political slogans were allegedly painted or scored on the grass as well as on a building, walls and pillars.

The indictment states damage to a sprinkler system caused flooding and that a light was also broken.

Robson, Bashir and Davies face a separate charge of then attempting to defeat the ends of justice.

It is claimed they drove to Turnberry in vehicles with fake number plates.

After the alleged crime, the trio are said to have escaped in the same cars to "conceal and disguise" their movements, in a bid to prevent being arrested for the vandalism.

Robson is stated to be on bail at the time from Edinburgh Sheriff Court on 9 January last year.

A hearing at the High Court in Glasgow was told that a "significant draft joint minute" of agreed evidence was under consideration.

Lord Arthurson fixed the trial with a further hearing due to take place before then in March 2027.

Robson, of Galashiels in the Scottish Borders, Bashir, of Leeds, Southall, of Wakefield, both Yorkshire, Ward, of Liverpool and Davies, Moxley and Chiaramello, all of London, remain on bail meantime.

Rollercoaster looming over homes divides opinion

Plans to keep the rollercoaster had been refused by Ashfield District Council

Some residents living in the shadow of a prototype rollercoaster that overlooks their properties have said they are pleased it may have to be taken down - but others say they will miss it.

The test ride was erected at a former aerodrome near Sandford Lane, in Hucknall, Nottinghamshire, in September 2025 but has prompted complaints about noise, visual impact and a loss of privacy.

Ashfield District Council rejected a retrospective application by fairground operator Mellors Group to use Watnall Road as a rollercoaster testing and storage site on 20 October.

In response, the firm said it would appeal against the decision and that there had been a "misunderstanding" over the purpose of the site.

Nanaka Kurama was pleased to hear the rollercoaster could be removed

Nanaka Kurama, who lives nearby, said the structure had caused significant disturbance to her and her family.

"This thing is very noisy and when they're using it, it affects everybody, especially me and my family because I have a child with special needs. He would be screaming about it," she said.

"So I was happy to hear that it could be removed. They should take it away."

Kurama described the noise as loud metal banging that could be heard from inside her home.

"Sometimes when you're sitting down, you'll hear it banging. It's not comfortable," she said.

"It's like metal banging together all the time, and it affects you even when you're inside your home. You'll still be hearing it.

"Residents have tried to complain, but we don't even know where to go to make a complaint."

Another resident, Bridget Akintayo, said: "Considering how close residents are to the coaster, it's not ideal for it to be there.

"There are children around and that rollercoaster could attract trouble to the area. I'm happy to hear that it could be coming down."

The prototype rollercoaster has been in place since September 2025

But some of those living nearby have said they were happy to have the rollercoaster next to their street.

Kirsty Welsh said she had grown used to having the structure on her doorstep.

"I think it's amazing. We'll certainly miss it. It's been exciting watching it grow from day one," she said.

"Other residents don't like looking at it in front of their homes, but for us, it's not a problem.

"I really don't know what it will look like without it because we're used to it now. It'll be a shock, but it is what it is.

"It's been there so long that it's become part of the furniture. You don't know any different. It's attracted a lot of people, but not horrible people, just kids who are interested.

"It's been exciting for me and my kids. We're not moaners."

James Mellor, director of the Mellors Group, said there had been delays in sending the rollercoaster away to be painted before it could be put into public use.

Mellor said the war in the Middle East had caused shipping delays for materials, preventing work from taking place.

"It's been there a lot longer than was ever anticipated, even on our behalf. We want the coaster out as quickly as possible," he said.

Mellor added he wanted the change of use application to allow the company to "work on other rides".

"Most rides are nowhere near the size of the coaster," he said. "A lot of the work will be done below the fence line where people can't see it.

"We don't want the coaster there any longer than they do because it doesn't make us any money while it's having work done on it in storage."

article:
Neil Young sues Trump campaign again for playing Rockin' in the Free World at rally

Rock veteran Neil Young has filed a $10m lawsuit against a fundraising committee that supports US President Donald Trump, citing "unauthorised" use of his 1989 song Rockin' in the Free World.

The Canadian-American star alleges that the Trump 47 Committee infringed on his copyright when it played the song before Trump took the stage at a 12 October rally in Ohio. Playing the song amounts to an "unauthorised public performance", the lawsuit says.

The singer-songwriter sued the Trump re-election campaign in 2020 over its use of the same song and Devil's Sidewalk. Young said the parties settled the matter shortly thereafter.

The White House referred to the Republican National Committee, who the BBC has contacted for comment.

Through his company Silver Fiddle Music, Young alleges that the song was played without a licence or Young's permission at a political event in Youngstown, Ohio on 12 October.

In the US, music used at campaign rallies often requires a public performance licence for it to be played for an audience, even if a campaign has already purchased a legal copy of the recording.

According to US Congress, because sound recordings do not have a general public-performance right, permission is only needed from the musical-work copyright holders, which can be obtained directly from the copyright holders themselves or through performing rights organisations.

The five-page federal lawsuit says that Trump "was personally aware that a licence would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required licence". It also says the song has been played "numerous times at other rallies".

The Grammy Award winner, 80, who has strongly opposed Trump's politics, characterises the song as "a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten".

Young says that the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for".

In 2020, Young sued Trump's re-election campaign for copyright infringement over the same song, as well as Devil's Sidewalk.

The new lawsuit claims that the campaign, at the time, "asserted no defence and immediately settled shortly after it was served", promising to never use the song without permission again.

Young posted about the lawsuit on his website on Tuesday, thanking Trump for coming to so many of his shows in the 1980s and 1990s, but stopped short of allowing him to play his music.

"I am sorry it came to this, but money and transactions are something you understand," he wrote.

Young, The Rolling Stones, Rihanna, Adele, REM and the estate of Prince have previously criticised the president for using their music at campaign events.

article:
'Domestic violence changes who you are, but there is hope'

This video can not be played

Grace has now registered her group as a charity to help reach out to as many people as possible

Lianne and Rebecca are in fits of giggles as they compare their paintings to the one they are copying, created by the artist leading their sip and paint event.

From the outside they look like any normal group of friends. But as little as six months ago, some of these women were in situations they felt they might never escape.

Everyone at this event shares a lived experience of domestic violence.

"I didn't know it was possible to feel as low as I felt in my darkest times and there's so many people that are feeling like that all the time," said organiser and fellow survivor Grace.

Her experiences led her to set up Held by Grace, a social networking group designed to help victims combat loneliness and isolation.

Having been helped in the past by Coventry Haven Women's Aid, Grace said she was grateful for the crisis support she was given but soon realised there was something missing as survivors like her looked to rebuild their lives.

"You've had that period of support when you're in a group and you've gone from being incredibly isolated to then being supported," she said.

"After that support drops off I don't want people to be isolated again, when they've already been through a situation that is incredibly isolating."

Despite only starting in May the group has already organised events like Pilates, therapy sessions and a yoga class, and Grace has recently registered it as a charity.

Bec (right) has attended some Held by Grace events after having to leave her home

For Bec, who had to leave her home after experiencing domestic abuse, the events are a much-needed opportunity to find a sense of normality.

"A lot of women, they have to come away from an area that they were more familiar with," she said.

"So just having somewhere to go with a community around them, and to start feeling normal again and just to do normal things and to bring life back into their everyday is really important, especially for me.

"I'm a single mum as well so I'm juggling that at the same time, so it's really important just to be able to go out somewhere and be around other people."

All the Held By Grace events are free to attend thanks to fundraising and the support of local businesses.

Their most recent sip and paint event was sponsored by a cafe in Earlsdon, Coventry - the walls of which are adorned with messages of positivity.

They were a deliberate addition to the Gym Junky cafe by owner Ed Durnion, who only left prison in 2025 having served a sentence for a drugs offence.

After turning his life around, he said, he is now focusing on giving back to the community as much as possible. As part of that effort, he allowed Grace to use his premises at no cost.

Durnion said he wanted to help Grace build positivity through her group

"I don't think enough people support things like this - I'm all up for second chances and I think Grace needed help, so I stepped in and helped her," he said.

"When you come in here there are lots of messages of positivity on our walls, so when you leave, you feel better than when you came in and I know Grace is trying to do the same with her events."

Up to fifteen women at a time have been attending the events, but Grace hopes they will reach more people who need support.

"I don't think you can ever be back to the version of yourself that you were before because the nature of domestic violence is that it changes who you are as a person, it changes your core," she said.

"So if coming away from an event we put on, [they leave] feeling more positive, feeling like there is hope, feeling like there are other people that understand you and there is a community of people where you don't need to explain why you feel this way or why you're a mess or why you didn't sleep at all last night because they get it, that's massively important."

article:
Plaid demands more cash, but how could the Budget affect Wales?

Wales' Finance Minister Elin Jones has called for a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly".

Plaid Cymru ministers say they want extra cash for railways and public services in Wales ahead of the UK government's Budget on Wednesday.

Wales' Finance Minister Elin Jones called for Chancellor John Healey to set out a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly".

The Budget announces Westminster's tax and spending plans for the year ahead - and more cash given to English public services could result in extra spending in Wales where they are devolved.

A UK government spokesperson said the chancellor would focus on giving households and businesses "a bit of breathing space where we can".

Healey announces £100 energy payment for 20 million households as he delivers Budget

Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase

Meanwhile, shoppers in one of Wales' busiest markets told BBC Wales that, once again, the cost of living was their biggest concern before the spending announcement.

Any extra spending for things in England that are controlled in Wales by the Welsh government - such as healthcare, schools and roads - could trigger additional cash for the country.

Jones had asked the chancellor to bring forward £1bn of the £14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.

Backbench Labour MP Alex Barros-Curtis told Radio Wales Breakfast that he was "sure" there would be announcements about Welsh rail funding in the budget.

"Andy Burnham has committed to it, it's what we've been campaigning on and we are going to deliver it," he said.

Jones also asked for extra money to help the Welsh government set its budget for 2027-28, which currently faces a real-term cut in day-to-day spending.

She previously claimed Wednesday's settlement could be the worst for the Welsh government since the Covid-19 pandemic .

Jones had asked the chancellor to bring forward £1bn of the £14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales

Jones said Wales had been short-changed "for years".

"This UK Budget is the moment of truth, and we need the chancellor to act, not just acknowledge the problem," she said.

"Wales pulls its weight in the UK economy. We contribute. Now we need the UK government to match that ambition with action and deliver a budget that finally treats us fairly."

There have also been calls from Labour MP Nia Griffith to give the Welsh government greater flexibility to borrow to fund investment projects.

A senior Welsh Labour source said they had been "pressing really hard for fiscal flexibility", along the lines of Griffith's request.

Ahead of Wednesday's announcement, shoppers and traders at Swansea Market said the cost of living was their biggest concern.

"Will we be able to see through the winter without having to borrow money," said shopper Louise. "It's quite a worry."

Like others at the market, Louise admitted feeling "anxious" about the winter, despite having saved some money with her supplier.

Help with energy costs was the top of many people's lists of things they wanted help with in the Budget.

Prices rose at the beginning of the month and typical bills are forecast to increase by 16% in January because of the conflict in the Middle East .

Louise says she is worried about the winter because "everything is getting more expensive"

Dad-of-two Richard said his wage did not keep up with rising energy bills, leaving his family "penny pinching towards the end of the month".

"Things that we used to have as a bit of luxury are out of the question, days out with family cost a fortune," he said.

Rural homes that use heating oil have also seen a dramatic increase in costs. The chancellor had already announced he will remove import taxes to bring the price down a little.

Healey has talked about giving people "breathing space" from cost-of-living pressures, and revealed a package of small measures he is calling "everyday fixes" ahead of the Budget.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham also wants to cut standing charges from gas bills.

If further support is offered in the Budget, it would be likely limited and targeted to the poorest households.

Richard, from Swansea, says "a lot of things that used to be affordable are now out of reach"

The cost of filling up cars soared this year as the conflict in the Middle East pushed up the price of oil.

Petrol prices hit a four - year high in September , and diesel has also shot up.

The cost of transporting fruit and veg is one issue putting pressure on Gareth Evans, who is the fourth generation of his family to run the Get Fresh stall at Swansea Market.

"It's a struggle at the moment," he said.

"We get costs passed on to us from our suppliers.

"We've also got vans ourselves and we supply caterers and diesel is very expensive."

Emma, who runs a pet store, said her rising costs meant she has had to increase prices for customers, as "it goes down the line".

She believes many working people are "struggling to live now".

The chancellor is expected to freeze the planned increase in fuel duty in January.

The rate was reduced by 5p by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and that measure has already been extended twice.

Gareth took over the running of the family fruit and veg stall from his dad Chris who had worked there for 50 years

One of Elin Jones' requests is for the UK government's help for a flagship scheme to help address child poverty.

The Welsh government is planning a trial scheme paying 15,000 children in families on universal credit £10 a week.

The Cynnal scheme , external is modelled on the Scottish government's child payment which helped to reduce child poverty in Scotland.

Welsh ministers have asked the UK government to exempt the payments from tax and benefits calculations, so recipients do not see a cut to their income.

BBC Wales has been told discussions about the child payment are still ongoing, which suggests there will be no announcement on Wednesday.

Burnham had previously said he was "open" to considering this, and it has already been granted to facilitate the scheme in Scotland.

The chancellor will also announce how much the state pension will increase by next year.

It looks likely to top £13,000 a year with the full, flat rate expected to increase by £488 a year in April due to the triple lock guarantee .

One thing that has already been announced is that pensioners who rely entirely on the state pension will be shielded from paying income tax, which usually kicks in at £12,570.

The specific details will be announced in the Budget.

On working age welfare, Healey has been rolling the pitch to prepare Labour MPs for potential cuts to the benefits bill, with a carefully scripted speech at this year's party conference.

There are reports that young people not in education, work or training may see big changes to their support, but that could be unveiled after the Budget when former Health Secretary Alan Milburn publishes his recommendations for reform .

Meanwhile, former miners have said they are hopeful a decades-long pensions battle could come to an end when the government unveils its Budget later.

Mine workers say they lost out after the Conservative administration took over the miners' pension scheme when British Coal was privatised in 1994, when the government was allowed to keep half of any investment surplus.

But asked about reports of a row over whether the government intended to renege on Labour's promise to resolve the dispute, Labour's Alex Barros-Curtis said he was "waiting to see what the budget says".

He added: "The government has made clear to me, to many other Welsh Labour MPs... that they are keen to work together with the scheme to deliver those better pensions for its members."

"Let's wait and see if that is just speculation or if there is something more to it."

Reform UK Senedd member Cai Parry Jones said his party "would stop using Welsh people as cash cows", and would build an M4 relief road, scrap family farm tax, and "reward working people" by raising tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

Welsh Conservative Senedd leader Darren Millar called for the UK government to make money available for major road projects, including an M4 relief road, and more defence spending in Wales, calling for a "pro-union Budget deal".

David Chadwick, Welsh Liberal Democrat MP, said his party wanted a Budget that gave Welsh families "some much-needed breathing space", calling for a 10p cut in fuel duty, a guarantee to bring down energy bills, and a temporary VAT cut for hospitality.

The Budget comes ahead of the first substantive meeting between the prime minister and the first minister at the National Economic Council later this week, where devolution is expected to be discussed.

A UK government spokesperson said: "The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That's why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, extended the 5p fuel duty cut and frozen rail fares."

Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner in pivotal general election

This video can not be played

'No clear winner' in Israel election - what happens now?

Exit polls suggest there is no clear winner of Israel's pivotal general election, with neither veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor former military chief Gadi Eisenkot on track to secure a majority.

Two Israeli broadcasters projected that Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his "Change Bloc" would win 51 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, as would Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies. A third broadcaster's poll gave Netanyahu a lead of three seats.

Much will depend on the role played by the two Arab parties, which were projected to win a record 18 or 19 seats.

Voter turnout on Tuesday was the highest in decades.

It stood at 77.7% when polls closed at 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT), which was the highest at that hour since 1999, the Central Elections Committee said.

Official results will start to be published overnight, but an estimated 600,000 absentee ballots cast mostly by military personnel - around 10% of the total number of votes - will not be fully counted until Thursday.

Benjamin Netanyahu (left) and Gadi Eisenkot both claimed victory in response to the exit polls

Once the final results are confirmed, and following consultations with all the political factions, Israel's president will invite the party leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a governing coalition - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

At the headquarters of Eisenkot's Yashar party in Tel Aviv, his supporters cheered and chanted "Bibi, go home!" after the initial exit polls published by public broadcaster Kan, Channel 12 and Channel 13 projected that his bloc would emerge as the biggest in the Knesset, with between 52 and 53 seats, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's governing coalition.

Eisenkot said they had "made history" and promised to "ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israel's citizens".

His ally in the Beyachad party, former prime minister Yair Lapid, said Netanyahu's bloc had suffered a "crushing defeat".

However, there was no sign of surrender at the Jerusalem headquarters of Netanyahu's Likud party, which was projected to be the largest party in parliament.

Supporters there told the BBC that they were nervous. "It's not over until it's over, but I'm sweating," Itzik said.

Netanyahu's ally, Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, said celebrations on the left were "premature", while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told supporters of his far-right Jewish Power party to pray that the final results would lead to a "full-on right-wing government".

In the early hours of Wednesday, the broadcasters updated their exit polls. Kan and Channel 13's projections showed the blocs tied on 51 seats, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu's bloc 52 seats and Eisenkot's 49.

Later, Netanyahu appeared at Likud's headquarters and declared in a speech that his right-wing bloc had a "great majority". He also called for the formation of "a strong, right-wing national government".

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - were projected to win several extra seats in parliament following a reportedly strong turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

They are emerging as the kingmakers in the election, but only one party has openly backed working with them in government.

"I hope that the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats," United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas said.

After the 2021 elections, Abbas's party was part of a governing coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, which lasted a year before collapsing.

The chairman of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, warned that the grouping "cannot be ignored under any political scenario".

Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, how to share the growing burden of military service, judicial reforms, and Israel's international standing.

Outside a polling station in an opposition stronghold in northern Tel Aviv, campaigners young and old were out in force, using every last moment to win that extra vote.

Zivit Abramson, 88, told the BBC that she had voted for Eisenkot because Netanyahu was "ruining this country". "He's all about himself, only about himself," she added.

Elsewhere, Claire Tugendhaft said she had voted for Netanyahu "because I think he's the best man in the country to lead the country towards the outside world".

The prime minister and his government allies urged their supporters to head to the polls with warnings about a surge in turnout among left-wing and Arab voters.

"If you don't vote, we'll wake up tomorrow with a left-wing government, Arab parties, extreme Islam, and we'll lose the country," Netanyahu was filmed saying.

Likud and several other right-wing parties asked for voting hours to be extended beyond 22:00 local time - a move many of their opponents saw as a sign of growing desperation.

The Central Elections Committee ultimately rejected their request, saying that "the current circumstances do not justify an extension" and that the high turnout "reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process".

Gloucester lock Freddie Thomas says the disappointment of being overlooked by Wales has given him a point to prove.

Thomas says he will go into the game with "extra energy" after being left out of Steve Tandy's Wales squad for the Nations Championship, which includes his Kingsholm team-mates Max Llewellyn, Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan.

Thomas told BBC Radio Gloucestershire: "It was really disappointing when I got the call. I get on well with (Tandy) so he was pretty clear with me, he called me up and let me know what kind of things I need to work on, which was good.

"It does obviously give me a bit of extra motivation because that's where I want to be - that's what I'm playing for.

"It's given me some extra energy and maybe an extra lift that maybe I needed."

Thomas - who has won nine caps since switching his allegiance from England in 2024 - said he is aiming for more consistency but also revealed he may be hamstrung by his versatility, mixing playing time between lock and the back row.

He said: "It's something I find quite hard, trying to break through into that consistency in performance, I have still not locked it down yet.

"I have still got more to give every week. I am starting to build on those foundations and trying to get better every week and hopefully get back into that Welsh squad.

"I think it has helped me playing both second row and back row (though) having spoken with some of the Welsh coaches it may potentially be hindering me, making me a question mark. For me it's out of my control, I am just trying to play the best I can."

6 Music Festival 2027 heads to Newcastle

BBC Radio 6 Music Festival will return to Newcastle in 2027

BBC Radio 6 Music has announced the 2027 edition of its annual festival will take place in Newcastle.

After four years in Greater Manchester, the festival will take place across Newcastle's independent and grassroots venues in March with five days of performances and DJ sets.

Tyneside last hosted the festival in 2015 but principal advisor for events and culture at Newcastle City Council, Jim Mawdsley, said since then "Newcastle has become a true music city".

Head of BBC Radio 6 Music Samantha Moy said: "The city and the region have such a rich musical legacy and a thriving creative community, which will make for another wonderful setting."

Newcastle has enjoyed recent success with national music events, having just hosted the Mercury Prize for the second year in a row.

The city also hosted the MOBO Awards in 2025.

The 6 Music Festival has been running since 2014 and initially was a roving event, moving around the country each year before settling in Manchester in 2023.

Newcastle hosted the Mercury Prize for the second time last week, where Raye took home the top prize

6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne said: "Having grown up in the North East, I know just how much music means to people here and the important role it plays in local culture and communities.

"It's fantastic to see the festival return to the North East, and I can't wait to join listeners, artists and presenters for what promises to be a brilliant celebration of live music."

In 2026, the festival saw performances from the likes of Bloc Party, Courtney Barnett and Jacob Alon.

Mawdsley said: "Since it was last here, Newcastle has become a true music city with many of our artists being recognised not least by awards like the Mercury Prize, which has shortlisted Sam Fender, Jade and Knats in the last two years, but there is a real collaborative spirit in the city.

"We believe that our moment is now.

"Music is a vital element of our cultural lifeblood, and we can't wait to welcome 6 Music listeners to learn more about how vibrant the city has become."

6 Music Festival 2027 will take place 15-19 March and the full lineup and venues will be announced next year.

From rivals to team-mates - Ball links up with Pope

James Ball (left) won two silvers with Matt Rotherham for Wales while Aaron Pope (right) piloted Neil Fachie to two golds for Scotland

Henry VIII famously had six wives during his time on the throne.

While Para-cyclist James Ball has had a more harmonious time with his pilots than the former king had with his spouses, he too is on to his sixth partner, Aaron Pope.

Ball will be hoping for a better relationship with this Pope than Henry VIII had with the papacy!

Three months ago, Ball and Pope were rivals at the Commonwealth Games, where the latter piloted Neil Fachie to two golds in Glasgow.

Ball and Matt Rotherham, meanwhile, settled for silver in the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial and the men's sprint .

Now they are team-mates rather than opponents, Pope will aim to help Ball retain the world titles he won with Steffan Lloyd in 2025.

"It's not me, I promise," jokes Ball as he announces his latest new partnership.

"I'm now with Aaron, so that's been a lot of learning and that's quite important because it's like a proper reset.

"It's like when I had Steff Lloyd for Paris [Paralympics 2024]. It was a whole new exciting time to be on the bike together. We're looking forward to seeing what we can do now."

Ball's first taste of world championship glory came with two golds in Los Angeles in 2017 alongside Rotherham, with whom he won the 1km time trial and sprint events.

And the Californian city is again on the horizon as it hosts the Paralympics in 2028.

For the moment, the focus is the Para-cycling Track World Championships in Apeldoorn, Netherlands, which start on Thursday.

"This world championships would be a good place to see where we're at and where the rest of the world is," Ball said.

"We've got the big one next year in Paris to sort of solidify our place for LA [Paralympics 2028]."

Aaron Pope (right) is the sixth different pilot for James Ball (left) who races as an athlete with a visual impairment

While the partnership is in its relative infancy, Ball says there have been some nerves as they ready themselves for action.

"I think he [Pope] was quite nervous at the start as well and obviously he wanted to prove that he was good enough sort of thing," Ball said.

"But if you're on the programme, you're good enough. Training's been good and it's completely different with every pilot, the way they approach training and how we gel together.

"It doesn't take me very long to realise if it's working or not so it's really good to see. I feel like I'm teaching him some things even though he's way better than me power-wise, but it's nice to show some of my experience to him."

Ball, 35, has embraced the positivity that can come with change.

"Paris [Paralympics 2024] was the crowning moment of what I've achieved and I was like, how can this get any better?" he said.

"Changing pilots all the time keeps it fresh though, especially for me.

"If we had the same tandem partnership, I feel like you'd find it hard to always progress those goals. I feel like every [new] pilot is like fresh air and a reset."

A new cycle brings fresh competition for Ball and Pope.

While the duo develop their chemistry on the bike, Ball says he has not put too much pressure on results in the Netherlands.

"If there's any mistakes and stuff, then brush them off," he said.

"We know a lot of learning is going to be done at this world championships because we've got a lot of the big, heavy-hitting bikes coming as well, some we've never even seen before."

Ball, however, says competition is good for the growth of the sport.

"We've looked and there's so many more tandems on the start list now, which is great," he added.

"There's two Australian bikes now, two German bikes, the French as well.

"We've got a lot who we've raced before, but obviously that was two years ago. We don't know what everyone's form is like but this year will be the year that everyone's going to put a time down, just to show what they can do, and then build on that over the next two years."

Steffan Lloyd (left) and James Ball (right) won Paralympic gold in the men's sprint and the 1km time trial in Paris

Ball has medalled at all nine of his previous world championships, with a haul of four bronzes, six silvers and eight golds.

He also has five silvers and a gold at three Commonwealth Games, a Paralympic silver medal in 2021 and two golds in Paris in 2024.

But the hunger remains for the Ponthir native, who feels there's plenty more to achieve in the sport.

"Another Commonwealth gold would be nice, that would be good," he said. "I think defending my Paris Paralympics title too. Unfortunately they've taken out the kilo (1km time trial), so to win the sprint then in LA, that will be a big moment for me.

"We don't know what the situation is like in Brisbane [for the 2032 Paralympics]. We're hoping, fingers crossed, they bring back more sprinter events specifically."

And with his long-term rival Fachie finally calling time on his career at 42 years old this summer, it stands to reason Ball could keep going.

"To have this much time being an elite athlete, it's incredible," he said.

"I still feel great. I think I'll know myself [if it is time to retire] before my performance [shows it]. But yeah, I have absolutely no thought of stopping any time soon."
